entries.text: Acute Aortic Dissection Initial Medical Management

entries.title: Acute Aortic Dissection
entries.nodeLabel: Suspected or confirmed acute aortic dissection
entries.text: Suspected or confirmed acute aortic dissection — CT angiography; Stanford type A or B — CT angiography is the standard first-line test: it is fast, widely available, and characterises the dissection flap, its extent, and any branch-vessel involvement in a single study. The Stanford classification that follows — type A involves the ascending aorta; type B begins distal to the left subclavian artery — is the single determinant of all downstream management. Type A is a surgical emergency, since the ascending aorta may rupture into the pericardium or compromise the coronary ostia; type B is managed medically unless it becomes complicated. — Classification by anatomy, rather than by symptom severity, keeps this first decision objective and rapid. This matters because medical therapy (Step 1) begins in parallel with the surgical referral, not after it. — computed tomography angiography — A contrast-enhanced CT scan that outlines the inside of the vessel lumen — fast enough and detailed enough to be the first-line test for suspected dissection.

entries.title: Acute Aortic Dissection
entries.text: Immediate measures — Monitored bed · bilateral BP · IV opioid analgesia · urgent consult — Bilateral blood pressure measurement is not a formality: a dissection flap can occlude or narrow a subclavian origin, producing a falsely low reading in that arm. Treatment decisions should use the higher, more accurate reading. An arterial line is specified “when feasible” because the vasoactive infusions that follow require minute-to-minute titration, which a cuff cannot support. “Anti-impulse therapy” is this protocol's term for the combined heart-rate-and-blood-pressure strategy used from Step 1 onward: the therapeutic target is not blood pressure alone, but the rate of pressure rise in the vessel wall with each heartbeat (dP/dt). — IV opioid analgesia is listed here, before any drug titration, because uncontrolled pain is itself a sympathetic stimulus: it raises heart rate and blood pressure independently of the dissection and can be mistaken for drug-refractory hypertension later in the algorithm (see Step 2). Early analgesia is therefore part of anti-impulse therapy, not a separate comfort measure. Urgent cardiothoracic or vascular surgical consultation is sought for every suspected dissection, type A or B, since a type B dissection can become complicated at any time. — Morphine — 1–10 mg IV, titrated to effect — Ongoing/breakthrough pain — morphine PCA — 1 mg bolus, 5-min lockout — Renal impairment — substitute fentanyl — 10 µg bolus, 5-min lockout — Morphine is renally cleared, and its active metabolites accumulate in renal impairment; substitute fentanyl rather than simply reducing the morphine dose. — Regular paracetamol alongside the opioid is standard adjunct analgesia here, unless contraindicated; it supplements, but does not replace, adequate opioid dosing in the acute phase. — patient-controlled analgesia — A pump letting the patient self-deliver small, pre-set IV analgesic boluses within a safety lockout interval — used once initial titration has established a safe, effective dose, so ongoing pain does not require re-paging for every top-up. — rate of pressure rise — How fast pressure rises inside the vessel with each heartbeat. Driven by heart rate and contractility together — lowering either one lowers dP/dt, which is the actual therapeutic target of “anti-impulse” therapy, not blood pressure alone.

entries.title: Acute Aortic Dissection
entries.text: Contraindication to beta-blockade? — This question is assessed before the first drug is given, because the logic of Step 1 — blocking the heart first — assumes the circulation can tolerate a reduction in heart rate and contractility. In a subset of patients it cannot; the adjacent box lists the findings that define that subset. — Performing this check first, rather than discovering intolerance after dosing, allows Step 1 to default to “beta-blocker before vasodilator” without a qualification attached to every box. — β-adrenergic receptor blocker — A drug that competitively blocks β-adrenergic receptors. The β1 subtype — concentrated in the SA/AV nodes and ventricular myocardium — mediates the effect this protocol actually wants: negative chronotropy (slower SA-node firing) and negative inotropy (reduced contractile force), which together lower dP/dt directly. β2 blockade (airway and vascular smooth muscle) is the unwanted side effect that β1-selectivity is designed to minimise, not eliminate. Esmolol, metoprolol, and labetalol (a combined α1/β-blocker) are the agents used in this protocol; non-selective or slow-onset agents are not first-line for acute titration here. — How forcefully the heart muscle contracts for a given fill volume — together with heart rate, one of the two drivers of dP/dt.

entries.title: Acute Aortic Dissection
entries.text: What counts as a contraindication — SBP <90, shock, tamponade, severe acute AR, HR <60, high-grade AV block, bronchospasm — Each item describes a state in which tachycardia is already performing compensatory work. In tamponade and severe acute aortic regurgitation, a faster heart rate partly sustains forward cardiac output against rising pericardial pressure or a sudden regurgitant volume. In shock or SBP <90 mmHg, no physiological reserve remains to absorb further negative inotropy. HR <60 bpm or high-grade AV block leave little margin to slow conduction further without provoking symptomatic bradycardia or complete heart block. Bronchospasm is included because even a beta-1-selective agent retains some beta-2 cross-reactivity, particularly at higher doses. — These are physiological warning signs, not an exhaustive list of drug interactions. The common principle is that blunting the sympathetic response in these states would remove a compensatory mechanism the circulation is actively relying on. — cardiac tamponade — Pericardial pressure rising to meet or exceed diastolic chamber pressures, impairing ventricular filling — in dissection, typically from blood tracking retrograde into the pericardial sac. Produces equalisation of diastolic pressures across chambers and, classically, pulsus paradoxus. It becomes rapidly fatal once compensatory tachycardia can no longer sustain cardiac output against the rising pressure — which is exactly why it is a beta-blockade contraindication above. — atrioventricular block — Conduction delay or failure at or below the AV node. First-degree and Mobitz I block carry some safety margin; Mobitz II, 2:1, and third-degree block ("high-grade") are the ones that matter here — they leave no AV-nodal reserve to absorb a drug that slows conduction further, risking symptomatic bradycardia or complete heart block. — Sudden narrowing of the airway's smooth muscle. A risk with any beta-blocker, since even a “beta-1-selective” agent keeps some beta-2 cross-reactivity, more so at higher doses. — Preferentially blocks β1 receptors (concentrated in the heart) over β2 receptors (airway and blood-vessel smooth muscle) — the selectivity is relative, not absolute.

entries.title: Acute Aortic Dissection
entries.text: If contraindicated: withhold & resuscitate — Immediate surgery/TEVAR as indicated; low-dose esmolol only if rate control is essential — The priority is reversed here. Rather than rate control, the immediate goal is resuscitation and definitive source control — surgery or TEVAR — with pharmacologic rate control reduced to a rescue measure rather than a routine step. — If rate control genuinely cannot wait, esmolol is specified rather than metoprolol or labetalol because its effect resolves within approximately half an hour of stopping the infusion (elimination half-life ≈9 minutes; metabolised by blood esterases rather than the kidney or liver). In a patient already identified as intolerant of beta-blockade, this reversibility is the rationale: if hypotension or decompensation follows the first low dose, the drug is largely cleared from the circulation before the next clinical decision is required. — The pharmacologic state of adequate β1 antagonism — judged clinically here by the heart-rate target being met, not by a fixed dose. Establishing this first is what keeps a vasodilator added later (Step 2) from provoking reflex tachycardia. — Thoracic EndoVascular Aortic Repair — A stent-graft placed inside the aorta through a catheter (usually from the femoral artery) to seal off a dissection or aneurysm from the inside, without open chest surgery. — red-cell (blood) esterases — Enzymes that break a drug down chemically within the bloodstream itself, rather than relying on the kidney or liver. This is why esmolol's action does not lengthen in kidney or liver disease.

entries.title: Acute Aortic Dissection
entries.nodeLabel: STEP 1 — IV beta-1-selective blocker before any vasodilator
entries.text: STEP 1 — IV beta-1-selective blocker before any vasodilator — This is the central sequencing rule of the algorithm: a beta-blocker is started first, and a vasodilator is never the first drug given for a dissection. — A vasodilator given to an unblocked heart lowers afterload, which the baroreflex counters with a rise in heart rate and contractility. The resulting increase in dP/dt — the rate of pressure rise in the vessel with each beat — together with the shortened diastolic interval, adds dynamic load to an already-weakened aortic wall: precisely the stress the protocol aims to reduce. Establishing beta-blockade first blunts this reflex, so any vasodilator added later (Step 2) lowers pressure without a compensatory tachycardia offsetting the benefit. — Pheochromocytoma or cocaine-intoxication-associated hypertension: giving a pure beta-blocker first leaves peripheral α1-vasoconstriction unopposed and can paradoxically worsen hypertension. If either is suspected, alpha-blockade first — or a combined agent, below — takes priority over the default sequence. — Labetalol, a combined α1/β-blocker, is an accepted single-agent alternative to esmolol or metoprolol, and is often preferred when combined alpha/beta effect is required, or in pregnancy. Dosing: 10 mg IV slow bolus every 2 minutes, to a maximum 200 mg course, with an infusion started alongside the boluses at 15 mg/hr and titrated across approximately 10–60 mg/hr. — Decompensated heart failure or cardiogenic shock is treated as a relative contraindication even when the SBP <90 mmHg threshold above is not met; the withhold pathway and hemodynamic support take priority over rate control in this situation. — β-adrenergic receptor blocker — A drug that competitively blocks β-adrenergic receptors. The β1 subtype — concentrated in the SA/AV nodes and ventricular myocardium — mediates the effect this protocol actually wants: negative chronotropy (slower SA-node firing) and negative inotropy (reduced contractile force), which together lower dP/dt directly. β2 blockade (airway and vascular smooth muscle) is the unwanted side effect that β1-selectivity is designed to minimise, not eliminate. Esmolol, metoprolol, and labetalol (a combined α1/β-blocker) are the agents used in this protocol; non-selective or slow-onset agents are not first-line for acute titration here. — The pharmacologic state of adequate β1 antagonism — judged clinically here by the heart-rate target being met, not by a fixed dose. Establishing this first is what keeps a vasodilator added later (Step 2) from provoking reflex tachycardia. — A catecholamine-secreting adrenal (or extra-adrenal) tumour. If present or suspected as a precipitant of the hypertensive crisis, giving a pure beta-blocker first leaves peripheral α1-vasoconstriction unopposed, which can paradoxically worsen hypertension — alpha-blockade must precede or accompany beta-blockade in that specific scenario. — rate of pressure rise — How fast pressure rises inside the vessel with each heartbeat. Driven by heart rate and contractility together — lowering either one lowers dP/dt, which is the actual therapeutic target of “anti-impulse” therapy, not blood pressure alone. — How forcefully the heart muscle contracts for a given fill volume — together with heart rate, one of the two drivers of dP/dt. — The pressure the left ventricle must pump against to eject blood. A vasodilator lowers it directly; an unblocked heart's reflex response can offset that benefit by raising heart rate instead. — The body's fast, automatic reflex that adjusts heart rate and vessel tone to counteract a change in blood pressure — it is this reflex, not the drug itself, that raises heart rate when a vasodilator drops afterload suddenly.

entries.title: Acute Aortic Dissection
entries.text: Esmolol pathway — Hemodynamic course uncertain — This pathway is for patients whose clinical trajectory may still change. In that setting, an agent whose effect can be stopped within half an hour is preferable to one with a longer or less predictable offset. “Type A awaiting surgery” requires a rate-control drug that will not still be active at anaesthesia induction. “Possible tamponade or AR” follows the same logic as the contraindication criteria above: if either proves more significant than initially assessed, the drug must be reversible, not simply low-dose. “Reactive airways” avoids committing a bronchospasm-prone patient to hours of exposure to a longer-acting beta-1-selective agent. “Renal/hepatic disease” is relevant because esmolol is hydrolysed by red-cell esterases rather than cleared by the kidney or liver, so organ dysfunction does not prolong its action the way it can with metoprolol. — Published dosing ranges for esmolol vary by indication and source. General hypertensive-emergency protocols commonly cap the infusion near 200–300 µg/kg/min, while some point-of-care references give a narrower range specific to aortic dissection. The values above fall within the broader range reported for hypertensive emergency and reflect this protocol's own titration ceiling; the half-life (≈9 minutes) and offset within approximately half an hour are well supported in the literature. — Loading dose — 500 µg/kg IV — Starting infusion — 50 µg/kg/min — Titration — stepwise upward, max 300 µg/kg/min — Hypotension risk — more frequent above ~150 µg/kg/min — Offset after stopping — ≈18–30 min — Hypotension and bradycardia are dose-related and the most common reasons to hold or down-titrate the infusion; monitor most closely during the loading dose and the first steps of titration. — The concentrated formulation is hyperosmolar and can irritate a peripheral vein on prolonged infusion; a dedicated or central line is preferable beyond the first hour. — Because clearance depends on blood esterases rather than the kidney or liver, esmolol is often preferred specifically in renal or hepatic impairment, where metoprolol's effect is harder to predict. — cardiac tamponade — Pericardial pressure rising to meet or exceed diastolic chamber pressures, impairing ventricular filling — in dissection, typically from blood tracking retrograde into the pericardial sac. Produces equalisation of diastolic pressures across chambers and, classically, pulsus paradoxus. It becomes rapidly fatal once compensatory tachycardia can no longer sustain cardiac output against the rising pressure — which is exactly why it is a beta-blockade contraindication above. — aortic regurgitation — Retrograde flow through an incompetent aortic valve — here, from the dissection flap disrupting leaflet coaptation or prolapsing a leaflet. Acute AR is hemodynamically distinct from chronic AR: the non-dilated, non-compliant left ventricle cannot accommodate the sudden regurgitant volume, so left ventricular end-diastolic pressure rises sharply. Tachycardia is a compensatory mechanism maintaining forward output here, which is why blunting it with a beta-blocker is dangerous. — Sudden narrowing of the airway's smooth muscle. A risk with any beta-blocker, since even a “beta-1-selective” agent keeps some beta-2 cross-reactivity, more so at higher doses. — Preferentially blocks β1 receptors (concentrated in the heart) over β2 receptors (airway and blood-vessel smooth muscle) — the selectivity is relative, not absolute. — red-cell (blood) esterases — Enzymes that break a drug down chemically within the bloodstream itself, rather than relying on the kidney or liver. This is why esmolol's action does not lengthen in kidney or liver disease.

entries.title: Acute Aortic Dissection
entries.text: Metoprolol pathway — Hemodynamically stable — e.g. uncomplicated type B — This pathway is for the more predictable trajectory: a stable patient who does not require a drug that can be switched off within minutes, and who is already being transitioned toward the oral beta-blocker they will be discharged on (final box). Dosing in small IV boluses, reassessed before each dose, is simpler to administer than a titrated infusion and bridges directly into that oral regimen. — The 2.5–5 mg stepwise bolus pattern and the ~15 mg ceiling are consistent with how IV metoprolol is dosed for rate control more broadly. The specific claim that most of the benefit is seen by a cumulative dose of 10 mg is this protocol's own clinical teaching point; it could not be independently sourced in the literature search behind this page, and is flagged for the author team to supply a citation or confirm as empirical practice before wider distribution. — Dose — 2.5–5 mg IV — Interval — every 5 min, reassess before each dose — Usual maximum — 15 mg — Most benefit seen by — cumulative ≤10 mg — flagged below — Hepatic metabolism via CYP2D6: clearance slows in significant hepatic impairment, and a genetically slow-metabolizer phenotype can prolong the effect unpredictably — favour esmolol instead if the course may need to stay reversible. — Can blunt the tachycardic warning sign of hypoglycaemia in patients on insulin or sulfonylureas; relevant if diabetes is also being managed acutely. — Relatively contraindicated in decompensated heart failure and significant reactive airway disease; β1-selectivity lowers but does not remove bronchospasm risk (see contraindication criteria above). — β-adrenergic receptor blocker — A drug that competitively blocks β-adrenergic receptors. The β1 subtype — concentrated in the SA/AV nodes and ventricular myocardium — mediates the effect this protocol actually wants: negative chronotropy (slower SA-node firing) and negative inotropy (reduced contractile force), which together lower dP/dt directly. β2 blockade (airway and vascular smooth muscle) is the unwanted side effect that β1-selectivity is designed to minimise, not eliminate. Esmolol, metoprolol, and labetalol (a combined α1/β-blocker) are the agents used in this protocol; non-selective or slow-onset agents are not first-line for acute titration here. — cytochrome P450 2D6 — The hepatic enzyme chiefly responsible for metabolising metoprolol. Reduced hepatic function — or a genetically slow-metabolizer phenotype — can prolong and intensify its effect unpredictably, which is the pharmacologic reason to favour esmolol when the course needs to stay reversible. — Sudden narrowing of the airway's smooth muscle. A risk with any beta-blocker, since even a “beta-1-selective” agent keeps some beta-2 cross-reactivity, more so at higher doses.

entries.title: Acute Aortic Dissection
entries.text: TARGETS — HR 60–80 bpm (≤60 if tolerated) · SBP <120 mmHg (100–120) — These are the numeric endpoints both pathways above are titrated toward, not independent goals. Heart rate is addressed first, as it is both the safer parameter to adjust and the one that directly lowers dP/dt. Blood pressure is then addressed, either by the same beta-blocker if sufficient, or by adding a vasodilator (Step 2) if not. — “Reached within minutes to 1 hour” sets a genuine time constraint: every interval of uncontrolled wall stress is a further opportunity for the dissection to propagate, rupture, or compromise a branch vessel. These targets are therefore an active endpoint for this hour of care, not a background goal. — β-adrenergic receptor blocker — A drug that competitively blocks β-adrenergic receptors. The β1 subtype — concentrated in the SA/AV nodes and ventricular myocardium — mediates the effect this protocol actually wants: negative chronotropy (slower SA-node firing) and negative inotropy (reduced contractile force), which together lower dP/dt directly. β2 blockade (airway and vascular smooth muscle) is the unwanted side effect that β1-selectivity is designed to minimise, not eliminate. Esmolol, metoprolol, and labetalol (a combined α1/β-blocker) are the agents used in this protocol; non-selective or slow-onset agents are not first-line for acute titration here. — rate of pressure rise — How fast pressure rises inside the vessel with each heartbeat. Driven by heart rate and contractility together — lowering either one lowers dP/dt, which is the actual therapeutic target of “anti-impulse” therapy, not blood pressure alone. — A side artery — renal, mesenteric, iliac, and so on — that originates from the aorta and can be cut off if the dissection flap crosses its origin.

entries.title: Acute Aortic Dissection
entries.text: SBP ≥120 mmHg despite HR control? — This determines whether beta-blockade alone has achieved blood pressure control. Most patients who reach the heart-rate target also reach the pressure target on the same drug; this decision identifies the minority who require an additional agent. — This question is asked only after heart-rate control is established, not in parallel. That sequencing is what keeps Step 2 safe: a vasodilator is added only onto a heart in which beta-blockade is already established. — The pharmacologic state of adequate β1 antagonism — judged clinically here by the heart-rate target being met, not by a fixed dose. Establishing this first is what keeps a vasodilator added later (Step 2) from provoking reflex tachycardia.

entries.title: Acute Aortic Dissection
entries.nodeLabel: STEP 2 — optimise analgesia, then add a short-acting vasodilator
entries.text: STEP 2 — optimise analgesia, then add a short-acting vasodilator — Clevidipine or nicardipine — nitroprusside alternative — “Optimise analgesia (± sedation)” precedes the vasodilator for the same reason opioids appear in the first box: unaddressed pain or agitation can present as blood pressure that will not respond to treatment, and escalating a vasodilator in that setting treats the wrong problem. Once pain is adequately controlled, clevidipine or nicardipine is added on top of the beta-blockade already established in Step 1 — never in place of it. — Both agents are short-acting, arterial-selective, and readily titrated within minutes, which suits a target that may shift as heart-rate control and analgesia are adjusted alongside it. They are specified here as alternatives to sodium nitroprusside, whose recognised drawbacks — cyanide/thiocyanate accumulation with prolonged infusion or renal impairment, and the requirement for light-protected delivery — make it a less practical first choice when a comparably fast, titratable alternative is available. — Nicardipine — start — 5 mg/hr IV — Nicardipine — titration — +2.5 mg/hr every 10 min — Nicardipine — ceiling (this protocol) — 15 mg/hr — Nicardipine — maintenance — 2–4 mg/hr once at target — Clevidipine — start — 1–2 mg/hr IV, doubled every 90 sec initially — Clevidipine — typical effective dose — 4–6 mg/hr — Clevidipine — maximum — 32 mg/hr (limited experience above 16 mg/hr) — Clevidipine is delivered in a lipid emulsion (20% soybean oil / egg-yolk phospholipid, as with propofol) — avoid in confirmed egg or soy allergy, defective lipid metabolism, or severe hypertriglyceridemia, and count its fat load toward daily intake if the infusion runs long. — Nicardipine given peripherally carries a genuine phlebitis risk; change the infusion site approximately every 12 hours, or use central access for infusions beyond a few hours. It is hepatically metabolised, so titrate cautiously in significant hepatic impairment. — If sodium nitroprusside is genuinely the only agent on hand, co-infuse thiosulfate and limit the dose/duration in renal impairment rather than using it unmodified — see the cyanide-accumulation point above. — The pharmacologic state of adequate β1 antagonism — judged clinically here by the heart-rate target being met, not by a fixed dose. Establishing this first is what keeps a vasodilator added later (Step 2) from provoking reflex tachycardia. — Inflammation of a vein, here typically from a concentrated or irritant infusion running peripherally for too long — the reason to rotate the site or step up to central access for a prolonged vasoactive infusion. — A fat-based IV vehicle (soybean oil and egg-yolk phospholipid — the same base as propofol) used to keep certain poorly water-soluble drugs suspended for infusion. The reason for the egg/soy-allergy and triglyceride cautions on clevidipine above. — sodium thiosulfate — A sulfur donor that accelerates the body's own conversion of cyanide — released as nitroprusside is metabolised — into thiocyanate, which is renally excreted. Co-infused specifically to blunt nitroprusside's cyanide-accumulation risk.

entries.title: Acute Aortic Dissection
entries.text: Continuous monitoring — Hypotension · bradycardia · urine output · mental status · malperfusion — Each item monitors for a different failure mode of treatment itself. Hypotension and bradycardia indicate overshoot from the drugs just titrated. Urine output and mental status serve as perfusion proxies for the kidneys and brain, respectively, because a dissection flap can progressively compromise a branch ostium at any time, independent of how well blood pressure is controlled. Malperfusion is therefore monitored as an ongoing risk, not assessed once at triage. — “SBP <90 mmHg or hypoperfusion → reduce/stop infusion” relies on the same reversibility logic as the esmolol pathway: because its effect wanes within approximately 30 minutes of stopping, overshoot can usually be corrected quickly, without requiring an antidote. — Elderly patients or chronic hypertension: the autoregulatory curve is shifted rightward, so a blanket SBP <120 target can underperfuse an already-adapted brain or kidney (a risk for AKI) — individualise the target rather than enforce the number. — Pregnancy: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated throughout pregnancy; labetalol is the standard agent for combined rate and pressure control. Beta-blocker/antihypertensive therapy is continued through pregnancy and postpartum, and delivery timing and mode are planned at a center with cardiothoracic surgical support — dissection risk does not end at delivery. — β-adrenergic receptor blocker — A drug that competitively blocks β-adrenergic receptors. The β1 subtype — concentrated in the SA/AV nodes and ventricular myocardium — mediates the effect this protocol actually wants: negative chronotropy (slower SA-node firing) and negative inotropy (reduced contractile force), which together lower dP/dt directly. β2 blockade (airway and vascular smooth muscle) is the unwanted side effect that β1-selectivity is designed to minimise, not eliminate. Esmolol, metoprolol, and labetalol (a combined α1/β-blocker) are the agents used in this protocol; non-selective or slow-onset agents are not first-line for acute titration here. — Inadequate blood flow to an organ or limb because the dissection flap has narrowed or blocked the vessel supplying it. Can appear or worsen at any point, not only at diagnosis. — The mouth of a branch vessel where it opens off the aorta — the point a dissection flap most often compromises flow to that organ. — acute kidney injury — A sudden drop in kidney function. Here, a reason to individualise rather than enforce the SBP <120 target by default, since the kidney may already be under-perfused. — autoregulation — The range over which an organ (brain, kidney) keeps its own blood flow roughly constant despite swings in systemic pressure. Chronic hypertension shifts this range upward, so a “normal” pressure can under-perfuse it.

entries.title: Acute Aortic Dissection
entries.text: Definitive care and transition — Type A → surgery · complicated type B → TEVAR · uncomplicated type B → medical therapy — This returns to the classification made in the first box. Type A is managed surgically, because the ascending aorta's proximity to the pericardium and coronary ostia makes medical management alone an unacceptable rupture or tamponade risk. Complicated type B — malperfusion, rupture, or pain/hypertension refractory to the steps above — is managed with TEVAR. Uncomplicated type B continues on medical therapy with imaging surveillance: a randomised comparison of early stent-grafting against medical therapy in stable type B dissection found this to be a reasonable default strategy, with stent-grafting reserved for patients who develop complications. — The long-term plan deliberately mirrors the acute one: transition to an oral beta-blocker (the same drug class started acutely in Step 1), then add an ACE inhibitor/ARB or calcium-channel blocker if blood pressure targets are not yet met. The specific caution against calcium-channel blockers in heritable aortopathy is not a generic precaution: a combined mouse-model and patient-registry study found that calcium-channel blockers accelerated aneurysm growth and rupture in Marfan syndrome, at a blood-pressure-lowering dose comparable to losartan, which did not cause the same harm — indicating a drug-specific signalling effect rather than a blood-pressure effect. — β-adrenergic receptor blocker — A drug that competitively blocks β-adrenergic receptors. The β1 subtype — concentrated in the SA/AV nodes and ventricular myocardium — mediates the effect this protocol actually wants: negative chronotropy (slower SA-node firing) and negative inotropy (reduced contractile force), which together lower dP/dt directly. β2 blockade (airway and vascular smooth muscle) is the unwanted side effect that β1-selectivity is designed to minimise, not eliminate. Esmolol, metoprolol, and labetalol (a combined α1/β-blocker) are the agents used in this protocol; non-selective or slow-onset agents are not first-line for acute titration here. — Thoracic EndoVascular Aortic Repair — A stent-graft placed inside the aorta through a catheter (usually from the femoral artery) to seal off a dissection or aneurysm from the inside, without open chest surgery. — cardiac tamponade — Pericardial pressure rising to meet or exceed diastolic chamber pressures, impairing ventricular filling — in dissection, typically from blood tracking retrograde into the pericardial sac. Produces equalisation of diastolic pressures across chambers and, classically, pulsus paradoxus. It becomes rapidly fatal once compensatory tachycardia can no longer sustain cardiac output against the rising pressure — which is exactly why it is a beta-blockade contraindication above. — Inadequate blood flow to an organ or limb because the dissection flap has narrowed or blocked the vessel supplying it. Can appear or worsen at any point, not only at diagnosis.

entries.title: Butyrophenone Selection
entries.text: Butyrophenone Selection Acute Agitation & Hyperactive Delirium

entries.title: Butyrophenone Selection
entries.nodeLabel: Agitated or delirious patient: assess ABC, glucose, vital signs; attempt verbal de-escalation; identify medical, toxic or psychiatric cause
entries.text: Agitated or delirious patient: assess ABC, glucose, vital signs; attempt verbal de-escalation; identify medical, toxic or psychiatric cause — The algorithm opens on a differential, not a drug. Agitation and hyperactive delirium are presentations, not diagnoses: hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, sepsis, alcohol or sedative withdrawal, intoxication, a seizure's postictal phase, and primary psychiatric illness can all produce an identical bedside picture of a combative, uncooperative patient. ABC and a point-of-care glucose are checked first because several of these mimics are rapidly reversible with treatment that has nothing to do with sedation, and giving a butyrophenone to a hypoglycaemic or hypoxic patient treats the symptom while leaving the actual emergency untreated. — Listing verbal de-escalation as an explicit, attempted step — not an assumed formality — keeps the algorithm honest about what parenteral sedation actually is: chemical restraint, reserved for when a less invasive approach has already failed, not a default first response to an uncooperative patient. — airway, breathing, circulation — The primary-survey check done before anything else: is the airway patent, is the patient breathing adequately, is the circulation intact. Several agitation mimics (hypoxia, shock) surface here before a drug is ever considered. — A chemical class of antipsychotic drugs — droperidol and haloperidol both belong to it — that act principally by blocking dopamine D2 receptors. The same class shares a mechanism relevant to the safety box on this page: blockade of the cardiac hERG potassium channel, which prolongs the QT interval. — The agitated, restless subtype of delirium — as opposed to hypoactive delirium, which presents as lethargy and withdrawal and is easily missed. Hyperactive delirium is the only subtype this algorithm's right-hand branch addresses with sedating medication.

entries.title: Butyrophenone Selection
entries.nodeLabel: Danger to self/others persists despite de-escalation → parenteral sedation required
entries.text: Danger to self/others persists despite de-escalation → parenteral sedation required — This is the single threshold statement the whole protocol pivots on. Below it, the correct management is everything this page does not show — environmental modification, treating the underlying precipitant, further verbal de-escalation. Only once danger genuinely persists despite that attempt does the algorithm below apply. — Framing parenteral sedation as a safety threshold, rather than a convenience or comfort threshold, is what keeps the choice of agent on the next screen tied to least-invasive, most-reversible practice rather than a single reflexive default drug for every uncooperative patient.

entries.title: Butyrophenone Selection
entries.text: Indication? — This is the one branch point in the whole protocol, and it separates two situations that look alike at the bedside — an uncooperative, potentially dangerous patient — but differ sharply in underlying physiology and risk. The left branch is acute, usually reversible agitation in a patient who was ambulatory moments earlier. The right branch is hyperactive delirium layered onto existing critical illness, in a patient who is typically older, more comorbid, and far less tolerant of oversedation. The split mirrors exactly how the evidence itself is organised: this page's algorithm is reproduced, unchanged, as Figure 1 of a 2026 systematic review that synthesised eighty records — including seventeen randomised trials — on haloperidol versus droperidol, and that review treats agitation and delirium as two separate evidence bases rather than one, for the same reason. — That difference in baseline vulnerability is why the two branches default to different intensities of treatment: a standard weight-independent IM regimen on the left, against a routine-use avoidance and lowest-effective-dose, as-required approach on the right. — The agitated, restless subtype of delirium — as opposed to hypoactive delirium, which presents as lethargy and withdrawal and is easily missed. Hyperactive delirium is the only subtype this algorithm's right-hand branch addresses with sedating medication.

entries.title: Butyrophenone Selection
entries.text: Droperidol available? — Psychotic / undifferentiated agitation — ED, prehospital, psychiatric unit — Droperidol and haloperidol are both butyrophenones with a similar dopamine-D2-blocking mechanism, but droperidol is more lipophilic and carries additional alpha-1 adrenergic antagonism that contributes to its sedating and antiemetic effect. Their pharmacokinetics diverge sharply: droperidol reaches peak sedative effect within 10–20 minutes by the IM route against 20–30 minutes for haloperidol, and its elimination half-life (~2 hours) is a fraction of haloperidol's (12–36 hours), so it accumulates far less with repeated dosing. The question asked in this box is availability, not comparative efficacy — droperidol became intermittently hard to obtain in many health systems after the FDA's 2001 boxed warning for QT prolongation, a warning based largely on spontaneous adverse-event reports at doses far exceeding those used for agitation, and it predates most of the real-world safety data gathered since. — The single adequately powered head-to-head trial randomised 228 patients in a psychiatric intensive care unit to 10 mg IM droperidol or 10 mg IM haloperidol: median time to sedation was identical in both arms (20 minutes), but haloperidol-treated patients needed additional sedation more often (13% vs 5%) and were the only group to develop dystonia (3 of 110 vs 0 of 118). A prehospital paramedic comparison of 218 patients and a prospective ED cohort comparing the two drugs' usual combination regimens point the same direction, which is why this algorithm treats droperidol as the preferred default and haloperidol as the fallback when stock does not allow it, not the reverse. The 2024 ACEP clinical policy on severe agitation lists droperidol monotherapy among its first-line options rather than preferring haloperidol, and the American Academy of Emergency Medicine's 2015 position statement separately endorses droperidol up to 10 mg IM as at least as safe and effective as the alternatives. — A large retrospective cohort found QT prolongation uncommon and torsades de pointes rare with ED droperidol dosing (1 case in 16,546 patients, 0.006%), and the one case had compounding risk factors (alcohol use disorder, hypomagnesaemia, active vomiting); a separate prospective cohort of 1,009 patients given droperidol for acute behavioural disturbance found an abnormal QT-nomogram reading in only 1.3%, with no torsades de pointes and no attributable deaths — the boxed warning's absolute risk at typical agitation doses appears considerably lower than its wording implies, though the cardiac cautions in the final safety box still apply to both drugs. — The Cochrane review of droperidol for psychosis-induced aggression (4 trials, 578 participants) found it effective and associated with fewer repeat injections than haloperidol, but rated the underlying trial evidence as low quality — a limitation this algorithm's preference for droperidol inherits, pending the adequately powered head-to-head emergency-department trial that review, and the 2026 systematic review behind this page, both still call for. — A second mechanism droperidol has beyond dopamine blockade. It contributes to droperidol's sedating and antiemetic effect, and is also responsible for its characteristic non-cardiac side effect — mild, usually self-limiting hypotension — which haloperidol, lacking this action, does not share to the same degree. — A polymorphic ventricular tachycardia specifically associated with a prolonged QT interval, named for the twisting appearance of the QRS axis on the rhythm strip. The arrhythmia both butyrophenones carry a boxed warning for, though real-world incidence at typical agitation doses is low. — Sustained, involuntary muscle contraction — of the neck, jaw, or eyes, for instance — another extrapyramidal reaction to dopamine blockade. Treated with an anticholinergic or antihistaminic agent (promethazine serves this purpose above), not with more antipsychotic.

entries.title: Butyrophenone Selection
entries.text: Droperidol 5–10 mg IM — 5 mg if ≥65 y or frail; repeat after 15–20 min if needed. Add midazolam 5 mg when speed is paramount — The lower dose in older or frail patients reflects reduced lean body mass and slower clearance, and the same higher sensitivity to QT prolongation and post-sedation falls that runs through every age-based adjustment on this page. The 15–20 minute repeat interval exists because IM onset is not instantaneous; judging response before the first dose has had time to act risks re-dosing unnecessarily and drifting the cumulative dose toward the >10 mg ECG-monitoring threshold in the final safety box faster than the clinical picture justifies. Where droperidol has remained in continuous use — Australian and New Zealand acute behavioural disturbance protocols, in particular — 10 mg IM, repeated once if necessary, is the standard adult dose, and a dedicated prospective study in patients aged 65 and over specifically supports 5 mg as the appropriate starting dose in that group, with a low rate of adverse events. — Midazolam is added specifically for speed, not depth: randomised trials of IV droperidol or olanzapine added to midazolam found faster time to sedation and less need for further sedation than midazolam alone, which is the same logic applied here in reverse — a benzodiazepine's onset can outpace droperidol's, so it is reached for when time-to-safety is the limiting factor, as a co-agent rather than a substitute for the antipsychotic. — Droperidol — 5–10 mg IM — Age ≥65 y or frail — 5 mg IM — Repeat interval — after 15–20 min if needed — If speed is paramount — add midazolam 5 mg

entries.title: Butyrophenone Selection
entries.text: Haloperidol 5 mg IM — 0.5–2 mg if older — WITH promethazine 25–50 mg IM or a benzodiazepine; avoid monotherapy — The "avoid monotherapy" instruction is not a generic caution — it is the direct, specific conclusion of the trial cited below. A pragmatic randomized trial of over 300 patients found haloperidol alone both slower to achieve tranquillity by 20 minutes (55% vs 72% with promethazine added) and solely responsible for the dystonia seen in the study (~6% of the haloperidol-alone arm, zero in the combination arm). Promethazine therefore does double duty: sedative synergy, and anticholinergic/antihistaminic cover against the extrapyramidal reaction haloperidol alone produces. The same weakness shows up outside that one trial: in a prospective comparison of four IM agents used in over 700 ED patients, haloperidol 5 mg was the slowest to work, achieving adequate sedation at 15 minutes in only 28% of patients against 71% for midazolam — the lowest result of the four drugs tested, and the one most often needing rescue sedation. — Haloperidol given without promethazine or a benzodiazepine was explicitly judged by that trial's authors as "not an acceptable way of managing acute aggression" — an unusually direct trial conclusion, which is why it is written into this algorithm as a hard WITH, not a suggestion. — Haloperidol — 5 mg IM — If older — 0.5–2 mg IM — Co-administer — promethazine 25–50 mg IM, or a benzodiazepine — Promethazine carries its own anticholinergic load — sedation, dry mouth, urinary retention, and delirium risk in the elderly — so a benzodiazepine is the better co-agent in a frailer or more confused patient where that burden matters more than the dystonia-prevention benefit. — A Cochrane review of 41 haloperidol trials found that adding promethazine improved both speed of sedation and tolerability, while adding a benzodiazepine instead "conferred no advantage" in that pooled analysis. That does not make the benzodiazepine option wrong — it still avoids promethazine's anticholinergic burden, as above — only a genuine tradeoff rather than a like-for-like substitute, and worth knowing when choosing between the two co-agents this box allows. — Sustained, involuntary muscle contraction — of the neck, jaw, or eyes, for instance — another extrapyramidal reaction to dopamine blockade. Treated with an anticholinergic or antihistaminic agent (promethazine serves this purpose above), not with more antipsychotic.

entries.title: Butyrophenone Selection
entries.text: Reassess every 10–15 min — RASS/SAT, SpO₂, BP. Not settled at 20 min → second dose; then consider olanzapine or ketamine (profound agitation) rather than escalating haloperidol — The 10–15 minute cadence is matched to typical IM onset for both agents, avoiding the two failure modes of reassessing at the wrong tempo: stacking a second dose before the first has had time to work, or leaving a genuinely under-treated patient and bystanders at risk for too long. The 20-minute checkpoint lines up with the primary-outcome timepoint used in the haloperidol/promethazine trial above, and with how a rescue-ketamine protocol in the literature below judges a droperidol-first regimen to have failed. — Escalating further doses of the same antipsychotic has a ceiling: each additional dose adds cumulative QT and extrapyramidal burden without reliably improving response once two doses have failed. Olanzapine (a different receptor-binding profile) or ketamine (a dissociative agent acting through NMDA-receptor antagonism, not dopamine blockade) are offered as a genuinely different pharmacologic approach rather than simply more of the same drug — in line with a randomized trial finding IM droperidol achieved adequate sedation at 15 minutes in 64% of patients, against 25–35% for ziprasidone and 29% for lorazepam, which is the kind of ceiling-breaking difference a change of mechanism, not a bigger dose of the same drug, tends to produce. — Rescue ketamine (literature dose, not this protocol's own) — 4–6 mg/kg IM — In an observational cohort of patients not sedated after a droperidol-first protocol, rescue IM ketamine achieved sedation at a median of 20 minutes, with a 6% adverse-event rate (vomiting, one transient desaturation to 90% responsive to oxygen) and no hypotension — reassuring, but drawn from a single non-comparative study, not a head-to-head trial against escalating haloperidol. — Ketamine's own risk profile — laryngospasm, hypersalivation, emergence phenomena, and a transient rise in heart rate and blood pressure — means it still needs the same monitoring discipline as the antipsychotics it is being offered as an alternative to, not less. A separate prehospital comparison found ketamine faster than haloperidol for severe agitation but at the cost of substantially higher rates of endotracheal intubation, a tradeoff worth weighing explicitly before reaching for it rather than olanzapine.

entries.title: Butyrophenone Selection
entries.text: Optimise non-pharmacological care — Treat precipitants, avoid scheduled antipsychotics — delirium (ICU / ward / palliative) — This reflects the clearest finding in the delirium literature: MIND-USA, a multicentre, placebo-controlled trial of 566 critically ill patients with delirium and respiratory failure or shock, randomised participants to scheduled haloperidol (up to 20 mg daily), ziprasidone, or placebo, and found no difference in days alive without delirium or coma, mortality, or duration of mechanical ventilation. "Treat precipitants" is the alternative this evidence points toward — delirium is a syndrome with an underlying driver (pain, the sedative already in use, sleep disruption, infection, a metabolic derangement), and a scheduled antipsychotic treats none of those. — Avoiding scheduled dosing here is therefore not caution for its own sake; it is the direct clinical translation of a null trial result, carried into practice as a guideline recommendation.

entries.title: Butyrophenone Selection
entries.text: Dangerous hyperactive symptoms only — Haloperidol 0.5–2.5 mg IV/IM (older) or 2.5–5 mg (younger), as-required, lowest effective dose, shortest duration. Droperidol 2.5–5 mg IV/IM is a rapid-onset alternative for a single episode (untested by RCT) — These doses are deliberately much lower than the agitation-branch doses on the left (5–10 mg), because this population is older, more comorbid, and often already carrying other QT-prolonging exposures from unrelated ICU or ward therapy — the goal here is symptom control for safety, not full sedation. "As-required" rather than scheduled is this box's direct operationalisation of the no-routine-use finding in the box above it. Droperidol's faster onset and much shorter half-life (see the first decision box) are exactly the properties that make it pharmacologically attractive for a single dangerous episode rather than ongoing control. — The parenthetical "untested by RCT" is an honest evidence caveat, not a hedge: no randomised trial has evaluated droperidol for delirium specifically — a gap this page's own independent literature search identified, and which the 2026 systematic review behind this algorithm reaches the identical conclusion about, strengthening rather than merely repeating the point. — Haloperidol — older — 0.5–2.5 mg IV/IM — Haloperidol — younger — 2.5–5 mg IV/IM — Droperidol alternative — 2.5–5 mg IV/IM, single episode

entries.title: Butyrophenone Selection
entries.text: Reassess daily — CAM-ICU/ICDSC; stop when hyperactive symptoms resolve; do not continue in expectation of shorter delirium or survival benefit — The once-daily cadence (rather than the 10–15 minute checks on the agitation branch) reflects a different treatment goal: this is symptom-triggered dosing for immediate safety, re-assessed on the same cycle as the structured delirium screen already built into ICU and ward rounds, not a dose being titrated to a numeric target. — "Do not continue in expectation of shorter delirium or survival benefit" is close to a direct restatement of the placebo-controlled trial result for delirium duration specifically — on that outcome, three large placebo-controlled trials and the meta-analyses pooling them agree there is no effect, and continuing an antipsychotic on the hope of shortening the episode is explicitly what this line warns against. — The survival half of that sentence is more actively contested than it might sound, and worth stating precisely rather than simplifying. MIND-USA (566 patients) found a non-significant trend toward higher 90-day mortality with haloperidol; AID-ICU (1,000 patients), a later and larger placebo-controlled trial, found lower mortality with haloperidol (36.3% vs 43.3%) in a secondary analysis its own investigators interpreted cautiously; and a 2025 Bayesian and frequentist meta-analysis restricted to double-blind placebo-controlled ICU trials estimated a probability above 90% that haloperidol reduces all-cause mortality specifically when used to treat established delirium, alongside a substantial probability of clinically important QTc prolongation and no benefit for prevention. None of this is confirmatory — the 2026 systematic review that reaches the same reading explicitly calls for a dedicated trial with mortality as its primary outcome before treating the question as settled — and none of it supports scheduled or prophylactic use. It is exactly why this box's instruction is to reassess and stop once hyperactive symptoms resolve, not to keep dosing on the strength of a secondary finding from a single trial. — corrected QT interval — The QT interval (time from the start of ventricular depolarisation to the end of repolarisation) adjusted for heart rate, since the raw QT shortens and lengthens with heart rate on its own. A prolonged QTc is the electrophysiological substrate for torsades de pointes.

entries.title: Butyrophenone Selection
entries.text: SAFETY FOR BOTH DRUGS — 12-lead ECG when feasible for IV use, cumulative dose >10 mg, cardiac disease, electrolyte disturbance or co-prescribed QT-prolonging drugs; correct K+ and Mg2+; continuous monitoring if QTc >500 ms or QT nomogram abnormal. Recognise and treat akathisia/dystonia (do not re-dose). Avoid in dementia-related behaviour unless danger persists (Beers 2023). — Both drugs share the pharmacology behind every caution in this box: as butyrophenones, they block the cardiac hERG potassium channel (IKr), prolonging ventricular repolarisation — measured at the bedside as the QT interval. Droperidol's additional alpha-1 adrenergic antagonism is responsible for its other main side effect, mild and usually self-limiting hypotension, rather than any further cardiac risk beyond the shared QT effect. A large retrospective cohort found the real-world torsades risk at typical ED dosing to be low (0.006%), which is why monitoring here scales with risk — IV route, cumulative dose, cardiac disease, electrolyte disturbance, other QT-prolonging drugs — rather than mandating maximal monitoring for every single low-dose IM injection. — Correcting potassium and magnesium matters because hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia lower the arrhythmia threshold, turning a borderline QT into a dangerous one. The QT nomogram is specified alongside a flat QTc cutoff because the usual correction formulas are rate-dependent and can mislead at the extremes of heart rate the nomogram is designed to catch instead. Akathisia (subjective motor restlessness, easily mistaken for worsening agitation and answered with a dangerous re-dose) and dystonia (sustained abnormal muscle contraction) are named separately because each needs to be recognised for what it is, not treated as a reason to give more antipsychotic — haloperidol produces both more often than droperidol across the comparative literature cited throughout this page. The dementia caution follows the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria directly: antipsychotics, haloperidol included, are flagged there for increased risk of stroke, cognitive decline, and mortality in people with dementia, which is why this algorithm's own exception — danger persisting — is written narrowly rather than left open-ended. — Pregnancy: evidence specific to droperidol and haloperidol in pregnancy is limited; use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration and involve obstetric/psychiatric specialist input where time allows, rather than defaulting to the standard adult dose. — Other QT-prolonging co-medication is common in exactly the patients most likely to need this algorithm — macrolide or fluoroquinolone antibiotics, methadone, and some antiemetics (e.g. ondansetron) among them — which is part of why the trigger for ECG monitoring here is "co-prescribed QT-prolonging drugs" generally, not a fixed drug list to check against. — For haloperidol specifically, a systematic review of 34 clinical trials and 34 case reports of IV use found that torsades de pointes was almost always associated with cumulative doses above 30 mg, co-prescribed QT-prolonging drugs, electrolyte disturbance, or structural heart disease, rather than occurring at ordinary single-dose use — part of why this box's own cumulative->10 mg threshold for ECG monitoring is set well below that higher-risk cutoff, as a margin of safety, not because 10 mg itself has been shown dangerous. — A second mechanism droperidol has beyond dopamine blockade. It contributes to droperidol's sedating and antiemetic effect, and is also responsible for its characteristic non-cardiac side effect — mild, usually self-limiting hypotension — which haloperidol, lacking this action, does not share to the same degree. — corrected QT interval — The QT interval (time from the start of ventricular depolarisation to the end of repolarisation) adjusted for heart rate, since the raw QT shortens and lengthens with heart rate on its own. A prolonged QTc is the electrophysiological substrate for torsades de pointes. — A polymorphic ventricular tachycardia specifically associated with a prolonged QT interval, named for the twisting appearance of the QRS axis on the rhythm strip. The arrhythmia both butyrophenones carry a boxed warning for, though real-world incidence at typical agitation doses is low. — A chart plotting heart rate against the raw (uncorrected) QT interval, used because standard rate-correction formulas such as Bazett's become less reliable at the extremes of heart rate. A reading that falls in the nomogram's at-risk zone is treated as abnormal here independently of the calculated QTc number. — A subjective, distressing sense of inner restlessness and an inability to stay still — an extrapyramidal side effect of dopamine-blocking drugs that is easily mistaken for the agitation being treated, which can trigger a dangerous cycle of re-dosing the very drug causing it. — Sustained, involuntary muscle contraction — of the neck, jaw, or eyes, for instance — another extrapyramidal reaction to dopamine blockade. Treated with an anticholinergic or antihistaminic agent (promethazine serves this purpose above), not with more antipsychotic. — American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria — A periodically updated, explicit list of medications considered potentially inappropriate in older adults, compiled by the American Geriatrics Society. The 2023 update flags antipsychotics, haloperidol included, for increased risk of stroke, cognitive decline, and mortality when used for dementia-related behaviour.

entries.title: Influenza Antiviral Selection
entries.text: Influenza Antiviral Selection Baloxavir Marboxil vs Oseltamivir

entries.title: Influenza Antiviral Selection
entries.nodeLabel: Adult or child with suspected or confirmed influenza (clinical syndrome ± rapid antigen/NAAT test)
entries.text: Adult or child with suspected or confirmed influenza (clinical syndrome ± rapid antigen/NAAT test) — The algorithm opens on clinical suspicion, not a confirmed result. Rapid antigen tests are specific but miss a meaningful share of true infections, and NAAT (nucleic acid amplification testing, e.g. PCR) results often return too late to guide a same-day treatment decision — which is why every downstream box is written around "suspected or confirmed" rather than "confirmed" influenza. — Starting from syndrome rather than a positive test keeps the first real decision point — how sick is this patient right now — ahead of any laboratory turnaround time, consistent with how the WHO guideline frames treatment timing below. — nucleic acid amplification test — A molecular test (e.g. PCR) that detects viral genetic material directly; more sensitive than rapid antigen testing but often with a slower turnaround.

entries.title: Influenza Antiviral Selection
entries.text: SEVERE ILLNESS? — Hospitalisation needed, hypoxaemia (SpO2 <94%), radiological pneumonia, sepsis, altered mentation or ICU need — This is the first branch point, and it separates two populations with very different stakes: a patient sick enough to need hospital-level care, versus everyone else. Each criterion listed is itself a marker of a complication influenza can cause directly (viral pneumonia, sepsis from bacterial co-infection, hypoxaemic respiratory failure) rather than a marker of influenza severity in the abstract. — Routing on organ-level severity rather than on test result or symptom duration is what lets the "treat even if >48 h" instruction on the next screen make sense: a patient who is hypoxaemic or septic is not treated on a symptom-duration clock the way an outpatient is.

entries.title: Influenza Antiviral Selection
entries.text: Start OSELTAMIVIR immediately; — do not wait for test results; treat even if >48 h from onset — Oseltamivir, not baloxavir, is the drug named here for severe illness. The WHO guideline's recommendation against routine oseltamivir use is scoped specifically to non-severe influenza; antiviral treatment of hospitalised, severe influenza is treated as a distinct clinical question the same guideline also addresses, and starting promptly rather than waiting on a test result or a 48-hour symptom-duration cutoff is standard practice once a patient meets severe-illness criteria. — A rapid antigen test's sensitivity is not high enough to safely rule out influenza in a patient who is already hypoxaemic or septic, and NAAT turnaround is frequently measured in hours to a day — treatment delayed until either result returns can mean a clinically meaningful delay in a patient who may deteriorate during that window. — nucleic acid amplification test — A molecular test (e.g. PCR) that detects viral genetic material directly; more sensitive than rapid antigen testing but often with a slower turnaround.

entries.title: Influenza Antiviral Selection
entries.text: HIGH RISK OF COMPLICATIONS? — Age ≥65 y or <5 y, pregnancy/post-partum, chronic cardiopulmonary, renal or metabolic disease, immunosuppression, obesity — For patients who are not severely ill, the next fork is risk status rather than drug choice directly, because the WHO guideline's two recommendations for non-severe influenza point in different directions depending on exactly this. Each listed risk factor is a recognised correlate of influenza-related complications and hospitalisation in the surveillance and trial literature this algorithm draws on. — Splitting on risk before splitting on drug choice mirrors how the evidence itself is organised: CAPSTONE-2 enrolled specifically high-risk outpatients, while CAPSTONE-1 enrolled an otherwise-healthy population, and the two trials' results are not interchangeable across that line.

entries.title: Influenza Antiviral Selection
entries.text: Oxygen and supportive care; — antibiotics only if bacterial co-infection suspected; continue oseltamivir ≥5 days — Antiviral treatment does not replace the supportive measures severe influenza itself can require — supplemental oxygen for hypoxaemia, fluid and haemodynamic support for sepsis. Antibiotics are reserved for suspected bacterial co-infection rather than given empirically to every severe case, consistent with general antimicrobial stewardship practice around viral respiratory illness. — The 5-day minimum course mirrors the standard oseltamivir treatment duration used across the trial literature (CAPSTONE-1, CAPSTONE-2) rather than a shorter, symptom-driven course, reflecting that a hospitalised patient's viral burden and complication risk justify completing a full course rather than stopping once symptoms begin to improve.

entries.title: Influenza Antiviral Selection
entries.text: Treat promptly, — ideally ≤48 h of onset (later if progressive) — For a high-risk but non-severe patient, timing still matters even though the WHO recommendation to treat this group is not conditioned on a hard 48-hour cutoff the way some older guidance was. Both CAPSTONE trials enrolled patients within 48 hours of symptom onset, and that window is where the strongest direct trial evidence for symptom-duration benefit comes from; "later if progressive" reflects that a worsening trajectory, not the clock alone, is what should prompt treatment outside that window. — Treating promptly in a high-risk patient is where the WHO guideline's conditional recommendation for baloxavir carries most of its weight — the evidence-to-decision judgement behind it rests partly on reducing progression to hospitalisation in exactly this population.

entries.title: Influenza Antiviral Selection
entries.text: Symptomatic care; — antiviral optional if ≤48 h from onset — This is the lowest-risk, non-severe branch, and it is also where the WHO guideline's strong recommendation against routine oseltamivir sits most squarely: for an otherwise healthy, non-severe patient, that guideline recommends against routine oseltamivir use on moderate-quality evidence, which is why antiviral treatment here is framed as optional rather than routine, and tied to the same early-treatment window where benefit is best established. — Framing treatment as optional rather than withheld outright leaves room for shared decision-making — faster symptom resolution is still a real, if modest, benefit an individual patient may reasonably want even outside a risk group the guideline singles out.

entries.title: Influenza Antiviral Selection
entries.text: Do NOT routinely add baloxavir — (FLAGSTONE: no clinical benefit of baloxavir + NAI) — FLAGSTONE directly tested this question in the population it matters most for — hospitalised patients with severe influenza already receiving a neuraminidase inhibitor — and found no benefit to adding baloxavir: median time to clinical improvement was 97.5 hours with baloxavir added versus 100.2 hours with standard of care alone, a difference that was not statistically significant. — This is the one box in the algorithm where a specific combination strategy was tested in a large randomised trial and came back negative, which is why it is stated as a direct instruction rather than left to clinical judgement the way most of the rest of this branch is.

entries.title: Influenza Antiviral Selection
entries.nodeLabel: BALOXAVIR single dose (WHO preference for high-risk non-severe)
entries.text: BALOXAVIR single dose (WHO preference for high-risk non-severe) — or OSELTAMIVIR for 5 days — The WHO guideline's wording for this group is a conditional recommendation in favour of baloxavir, based on low-quality evidence for reducing hospital admission, applying to patients aged 65 or older or with one or more major risk factors, started within 2 days of symptom onset. The guideline's overall certainty across outcomes for this recommendation is rated moderate — high for mortality and adverse events, moderate for symptom alleviation, low for hospital admission specifically. Oseltamivir for 5 days remains the alternative named in this box, reflecting that the WHO recommendation is conditional rather than strong, and that oseltamivir has the much larger safety experience in exactly the populations (older adults, people with chronic disease) this risk category covers. — A conditional, low-certainty recommendation is not the same as a mandate — the algorithm preserves oseltamivir as a listed alternative here rather than removing it, consistent with the guideline's own conditional framing.

entries.title: Influenza Antiviral Selection
entries.text: Either agent is clinically equivalent; — baloxavir favoured for influenza B, adherence or household protection — For a non-severe, standard-risk patient who wants treatment, CAPSTONE-1 found baloxavir's symptom-relief benefit over placebo similar in magnitude to oseltamivir's, with the two active drugs not meaningfully different from each other on the primary symptom-alleviation endpoint. CAPSTONE-2 separately found baloxavir's time-to-improvement advantage particularly pronounced in influenza B infection. Baloxavir's practical edge in this group is less about symptom relief and more about it being a single oral dose rather than a twice-daily 5-day course, which matters for adherence, and that BLOCKSTONE separately showed a single baloxavir dose reduced clinical influenza in household contacts by 86% relative to placebo when used as post-exposure prophylaxis. — Naming the single-dose regimen and household-protection data as reasons to favour baloxavir — rather than superior efficacy — keeps the "clinically equivalent" framing honest: the trial evidence does not show baloxavir outperforming oseltamivir on symptom relief in this population, only convenience and transmission-related advantages.

entries.title: Influenza Antiviral Selection
entries.nodeLabel: Exception: proven/suspected NAI resistance or immunocompromised host with persistent shedding
entries.text: Exception: proven/suspected NAI resistance or immunocompromised host with persistent shedding — → consider baloxavir ± oseltamivir with expert advice and virological monitoring — This exception sits on the severe-illness branch, where FLAGSTONE otherwise argues against routinely adding baloxavir to a neuraminidase inhibitor. Proven or suspected neuraminidase-inhibitor resistance removes the premise FLAGSTONE tested under (an NAI that is actually working), and immunocompromised patients with persistent viral shedding are a population in whom prolonged replication raises the chance of a resistant variant emerging under treatment, independent of baseline resistance. — Naming "expert advice and virological monitoring" rather than a fixed regimen reflects that this is a genuinely individualised scenario with comparatively little direct trial evidence — the combination strategy that failed in FLAGSTONE's general hospitalised population may still have a rationale once the underlying premise (a working NAI) no longer holds. — neuraminidase inhibitor — The drug class that includes oseltamivir and zanamivir, which block the viral neuraminidase enzyme needed for new virus particles to leave an infected cell.

entries.title: Influenza Antiviral Selection
entries.nodeLabel: Prefer OSELTAMIVIR in pregnancy/post-partum, infants, or when cation co-ingestion (dairy, antacids, supplements) cannot be avoided
entries.text: Prefer OSELTAMIVIR in pregnancy/post-partum, infants, or when cation co-ingestion (dairy, antacids, supplements) cannot be avoided — CDC guidance recommends oseltamivir as the preferred antiviral in pregnancy and for up to two weeks post-partum, and explicitly advises against baloxavir in both pregnancy and breastfeeding — not because of a demonstrated harm, but because of an absence of human safety and efficacy data in this population; the only data are animal studies, including one rabbit study at a maternally toxic dose that showed fetal skeletal variations and two pregnancy losses among nineteen pregnancies. Oseltamivir's recommendation instead rests on multiple observational studies in pregnancy showing no increase in adverse events. Separately, baloxavir's US approval begins at age 5 (based on the MINISTONE-2 paediatric data), so infants fall outside its studied and approved age range regardless of the pregnancy question. The cation-interaction caveat is a practical rather than a safety one: the FDA label specifically warns that dairy products, calcium-fortified beverages, and polyvalent-cation-containing antacids, laxatives, or supplements (calcium, iron, magnesium, zinc) can chelate baloxavir and reduce its plasma concentration, with no defined safe spacing interval given — only "avoid co-administration". — Grouping three different populations in one box works because the underlying reason is the same shape in each case: a real or practical gap in baloxavir's evidence or pharmacokinetics that oseltamivir's much larger experience doesn't share. — The FDA label's pregnancy section states plainly that there are no available human data on baloxavir use in pregnant women.

entries.title: Influenza Antiviral Selection
entries.nodeLabel: Return precautions: dyspnoea, chest pain, confusion or persistent fever
entries.text: Return precautions: dyspnoea, chest pain, confusion or persistent fever — → re-assess for pneumonia — This is the safety-net for the lowest-risk branch: a patient sent home on symptomatic care alone can still progress to viral or secondary bacterial pneumonia, and the listed symptoms are the standard red flags for that progression rather than an exhaustive list of every possible complication. — Explicit return precautions matter most exactly where the algorithm has just offered the lightest-touch management (symptomatic care, antiviral optional) — without a clear instruction for when to come back, the patients least closely followed are the ones a deteriorating course is easiest to miss in.

entries.title: Influenza Antiviral Selection
entries.nodeLabel: SAFETY NET: re-evaluate if symptoms rebound after baloxavir
entries.text: SAFETY NET: re-evaluate if symptoms rebound after baloxavir — (possible PA/I38X variant, especially children with A(H3N2)); post-exposure prophylaxis for high-risk contacts (baloxavir or oseltamivir); vaccinate — Baloxavir resistance arises from substitutions at polymerase acidic protein residue 38 (PA/I38X), and the available surveillance data show this is not evenly distributed: in one Japanese seasonal survey, pre-treatment PA I38 substitutions in A(H3N2) virus were found in 12.1% of specimens from patients aged 0–11, compared with under 2% in adults over 20. A separate 2022–2023 season study of paired A(H3N2) samples collected before and after baloxavir treatment found the substitution emerged in roughly 15% of post-treatment specimens, and every post-treatment case in that study was a child aged 7–14 — the one adult case in the whole dataset was a pre-treatment detection, not a treatment-emergent one. This is the clinical basis for singling out children with A(H3N2) as the group in whom a symptom rebound after baloxavir should specifically raise suspicion of a resistant variant. Post-exposure prophylaxis closes the loop back to the top of this algorithm: BLOCKSTONE showed a single baloxavir dose reduced clinical influenza among household contacts by 86% relative to placebo, with benefit seen across age groups including children under 12, both influenza A subtypes, and regardless of vaccination status. — Ending on vaccination rather than treatment is deliberate — every box above this one is about managing an infection that has already happened, and the single intervention with the largest effect on influenza-related severe illness at a population level remains preventing the infection in the first place. — polymerase acidic protein, isoleucine-38 substitution — A substitution at residue 38 of the influenza polymerase acidic (PA) protein — the site baloxavir binds — that reduces the drug's effectiveness when it emerges.

entries.title: Dexketoprofen vs Ibuprofen
entries.text: Dexketoprofen vs Ibuprofen Selecting an NSAID for Acute Pain

entries.title: Dexketoprofen vs Ibuprofen
entries.nodeLabel: Adult with acute pain (ED, perioperative, dental or primary care) in whom a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) is considered
entries.text: Adult with acute pain (ED, perioperative, dental or primary care) in whom a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) is considered — The algorithm opens wherever an NSAID is genuinely on the table as an option — not only in the emergency department, but equally in a perioperative setting, a dental surgery, or primary care. The evidence behind this page spans exactly that range of settings: dental extraction pain, acute low back pain, long-bone fractures, laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and ankle sprain. — Starting from the clinical context rather than from a single care setting keeps the algorithm usable across the full range of acute-pain presentations the underlying systematic review actually covers, rather than artificially narrowing it to one department.

entries.title: Dexketoprofen vs Ibuprofen
entries.text: Contraindication to NSAIDs? — This is the first and most consequential branch point: before any question of which NSAID or what dose, the algorithm checks whether an NSAID belongs in this patient's treatment at all. The criteria in the adjacent box are absolute contraindications, not relative cautions — a single one being present routes straight to a non-NSAID pathway. — Checking this before any dosing or route decision keeps the rest of the algorithm — which is entirely about choosing and dosing an NSAID — from ever being reached in a patient for whom that choice was never appropriate in the first place.

entries.title: Dexketoprofen vs Ibuprofen
entries.text:
CONTRAINDICATIONS — • NSAID hypersensitivity or N-ERD
• Active GI bleeding or peptic ulcer
• AKI, eGFR <30 or hypovolaemia
• Severe heart failure
• Third trimester of pregnancy
• Peri-CABG period — Each item here is a state where an NSAID's mechanism — COX inhibition — causes direct, predictable harm rather than a statistically elevated risk. NSAID hypersensitivity or N-ERD can precipitate acute bronchospasm within about two hours of exposure, pharmacologically rather than through a classic allergic mechanism, and cross-reacts with ibuprofen in 60–100% of affected patients. Active GI bleeding or peptic ulcer disease is a direct extension of the same COX-1 inhibition that causes NSAID-associated ulceration in the first place. AKI, an eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m², or hypovolaemia are states in which renal prostaglandins are doing compensatory work to maintain glomerular filtration — work an NSAID directly removes. Severe heart failure can be worsened by the sodium and fluid retention NSAIDs cause. Third-trimester pregnancy carries the FDA's strongest warning: from 30 weeks, NSAID use risks premature closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus. The peri-CABG period is excluded because of a specific, trial-demonstrated cardiovascular hazard with NSAIDs in that setting. — These are stated as absolute exclusions, not items to weigh against benefit, because in each case the mechanism of harm is the same mechanism the drug is being given for — there is no dose or short-course adjustment that avoids it. — NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease — A pharmacological (not allergic) reaction to NSAIDs causing acute bronchospasm, often with nasal symptoms, within about two hours of exposure — classically seen alongside chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps and asthma. Ibuprofen cross-reacts in an estimated 60–100% of affected patients. — acute kidney injury — A sudden drop in kidney function. NSAIDs remove a compensatory renal-prostaglandin mechanism, so AKI (or a low eGFR, or hypovolaemia) is a reason to avoid them rather than merely dose-reduce. — estimated glomerular filtration rate — A calculated estimate of kidney filtering capacity (mL/min/1.73 m²). Below 30 is an absolute NSAID contraindication here; 30–59 is treated as a high-risk feature requiring caution rather than avoidance. — coronary artery bypass grafting — Open-heart bypass surgery. NSAIDs carry a specific, trial-demonstrated cardiovascular hazard when used in the peri-operative period around CABG, independent of the drug's general cardiovascular risk.

entries.title: Dexketoprofen vs Ibuprofen
entries.text: AVOID NSAIDs — Paracetamol, local/regional anaesthesia; titrated opioid if pain remains severe — This is the non-NSAID pathway, not a doorway back into the algorithm — once a contraindication is identified, the rest of this page (which is entirely about choosing between two NSAIDs) no longer applies to this patient. Paracetamol and local or regional anaesthetic techniques are first-line; a titrated opioid is reserved for pain that remains severe despite those measures, rather than used as a routine substitute for the NSAID that was withheld. — Naming paracetamol and regional techniques before opioid analgesia keeps this branch consistent with ordinary multimodal-analgesia practice: an NSAID contraindication is a reason to avoid that one drug class, not a reason to escalate directly to an opioid.

entries.title: Dexketoprofen vs Ibuprofen
entries.text: High-risk features? — For a patient with no absolute contraindication, the next question is whether they carry a risk factor that should shape how an NSAID is used — not whether one should be used at all. This is a softer line than the first decision: none of the features in the adjacent box rules out an NSAID outright, but each raises the chance of a complication enough to change dose, duration, or co-prescription. — Separating "should an NSAID be used" from "how cautiously" keeps the first decision clean (a true yes/no on safety) while still giving the algorithm a place to route patients who need a more conservative course without excluding them from treatment altogether.

entries.title: Dexketoprofen vs Ibuprofen
entries.text:
HIGH-RISK FEATURES — • Age ≥65 years
• eGFR 30–59 mL/min/1.73 m²
• Cardiovascular disease
• Anticoagulant, antiplatelet, SSRI
• Previous GI bleeding
• Child or pregnancy <20 weeks — Each of these raises a specific, well-characterised risk rather than functioning as a generic "be careful" flag.
