Age 65 or older and an eGFR of 30–59 both sit on the same renal-reserve continuum as the AKI/eGFR <30 contraindication, just short of the absolute cut-off. Cardiovascular disease is relevant because NSAIDs raise blood pressure and can precipitate fluid retention. Anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents, and SSRIs each independently raise bleeding risk when combined with an NSAID — the SSRI combination specifically raises the odds of upper GI bleeding by about 75% compared with an NSAID alone. Previous GI bleeding is the single strongest predictor of a repeat event. Pregnancy under 20 weeks sits just inside the FDA's own cut-off (NSAID avoidance is recommended from 20 weeks), so it is flagged here as a feature to reassess as the pregnancy progresses, not yet a contraindication. — Listing anticoagulants, antiplatelets, and SSRIs together reflects that all three raise bleeding risk through different mechanisms (clotting factor inhibition, platelet function, and gastric mucosal effects respectively) that are additive with an NSAID's own COX-1 effect on the stomach lining — the shared downstream risk, not a shared drug class, is why they are grouped. — acute kidney injury — A sudden drop in kidney function. NSAIDs remove a compensatory renal-prostaglandin mechanism, so AKI (or a low eGFR, or hypovolaemia) is a reason to avoid them rather than merely dose-reduce. — estimated glomerular filtration rate — A calculated estimate of kidney filtering capacity (mL/min/1.73 m²). Below 30 is an absolute NSAID contraindication here; 30–59 is treated as a high-risk feature requiring caution rather than avoidance. — selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor — An antidepressant class that itself impairs platelet aggregation. Combined with an NSAID, this raises the odds of upper GI bleeding by roughly 75% compared with the NSAID alone.

entries.title: Dexketoprofen vs Ibuprofen
entries.text: Lowest effective dose, ≤3 days — Add PPI if GI risk; avoid IV ibuprofen 800 mg; check renal function. Child/pregnancy: prefer ibuprofen — This box modifies how the NSAID is used rather than which one is chosen — that choice still comes later, at the route-and-drug decision. Limiting the course to the lowest effective dose for three days or fewer reduces cumulative renal and GI exposure. A PPI is added when GI risk is present (prior ulcer, anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, or age-related risk), consistent with standard prescribing guidance. Avoiding IV ibuprofen 800 mg in this group reflects the review's own finding that the step up from 400 mg to 800 mg buys only a small, sub-MCID improvement in pain relief for a correspondingly larger drug exposure in patients already flagged as higher-risk. Renal function is checked because several of the high-risk features (age, reduced eGFR, cardiovascular disease) compound each other's effect on the kidney. Ibuprofen is preferred over dexketoprofen specifically in children and in pregnancy because it has the larger safety and dosing experience in both populations. — None of these adjustments removes the patient from NSAID therapy — they narrow the dose, duration, and monitoring around it, which is the entire point of separating this decision from the first, absolute contraindication check. — estimated glomerular filtration rate — A calculated estimate of kidney filtering capacity (mL/min/1.73 m²). Below 30 is an absolute NSAID contraindication here; 30–59 is treated as a high-risk feature requiring caution rather than avoidance. — proton pump inhibitor — An acid-suppressing drug added alongside an NSAID in patients with GI risk factors (prior ulcer, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use, age) to reduce the chance of NSAID-associated ulceration. — minimal clinically important difference — The smallest change in a pain score a patient would perceive as meaningful. This page anchors it to roughly 10 mm on a 100 mm visual analogue scale — a slightly conservative rounding of Kelly's empirically measured ≈12 mm minimum clinically significant difference.

entries.title: Dexketoprofen vs Ibuprofen
entries.text: Oral route feasible? — Having established that an NSAID is appropriate (with or without the precautions above), the next fork is practical rather than pharmacological: can this patient take an oral dose right now? A patient who is nil by mouth, vomiting, or awaiting a procedure cannot use the oral pathway regardless of which drug would otherwise be preferred. — Asking this before naming a specific drug and dose keeps the two route-specific boxes below genuinely parallel — oral and parenteral are presented as two complete, self-contained regimens rather than a single drug choice with a route attached as an afterthought.

entries.title: Dexketoprofen vs Ibuprofen
entries.text:
ORAL — Dexketoprofen 25 mg OR fast-acting ibuprofen 200–400 mg
Equivalent efficacy (d −0.24, below MCID) — At oral doses, the review's own pooled estimate — drawn from the dexketoprofen and ibuprofen 400 mg arms of a dental-pain trial — put the between-drug effect at Cohen's d ≈ −0.24, slightly favouring dexketoprofen numerically but well inside the band the review treats as not clinically meaningful (|d| < 0.40, roughly under 10 mm on a 100 mm VAS). "Fast-acting" ibuprofen refers to salt or solubilised formulations (e.g. ibuprofen lysine or sodium) with faster absorption than standard tablets, relevant because oral onset speed is one of the few genuine practical differences between the two drugs at this route. — Naming both drugs as options rather than recommending one keeps this box consistent with the review's overall conclusion: oral dexketoprofen 25 mg and oral ibuprofen are clinically equivalent choices, so the decision comes down to what is already stocked, tolerated, or preferred, not to a meaningful efficacy difference. — visual analogue scale — A 100 mm line patients mark to rate pain intensity, from "no pain" to "worst pain imaginable". The standard continuous pain-intensity measure the between-drug effect sizes on this page are anchored to.

entries.title: Dexketoprofen vs Ibuprofen
entries.text:
PARENTERAL — Dexketoprofen 50 mg IV OR ibuprofen 400 mg IV (800 mg adds ≈6 mm VAS, below MCID)
Migraine/renal colic: larger DKP trial base
Perioperative: stronger IBU opioid-sparing data — The IV comparison pools four trials (dexketoprofen 50 mg vs ibuprofen 400 mg across low back pain, long-bone fractures, laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and ankle sprain) with low heterogeneity (I² 0%), and the result still falls short of the MCID band even though its confidence interval sits slightly higher than the oral comparison's. The parenthetical — "800 mg adds ≈6 mm VAS, below MCID" — reflects that stepping ibuprofen up from 400 mg to 800 mg IV produced a measurable but sub-threshold improvement in at least one of the pooled trials (the fractures trial found a statistically significant difference favouring the 800 mg dose at 60 and 120 minutes), which is why it is framed as "not equipotent" with the 400 mg dose rather than as a simple dose-response the algorithm recommends using routinely. The two context-specific notes route a tie-breaker toward whichever drug has the stronger evidence base for that specific indication: a larger dexketoprofen trial base for migraine and renal colic (indications not directly covered by the five pooled RCTs behind this algorithm, but reflecting dexketoprofen's broader use in those settings), and stronger ibuprofen opioid-sparing data perioperatively, where a meta-analysis of IV ibuprofen found it reduced 24-hour postoperative opioid consumption by a mean of 6 mg morphine-equivalent compared with IV paracetamol. — Giving two narrow, indication-specific tie-breakers rather than a single default acknowledges that "equivalent on average" does not mean equivalent in every clinical context the pooled trials happen to cover — migraine, renal colic, and perioperative opioid-sparing are each areas where one drug's evidence base is simply deeper than the other's, independent of the pooled analgesia comparison. — minimal clinically important difference — The smallest change in a pain score a patient would perceive as meaningful. This page anchors it to roughly 10 mm on a 100 mm visual analogue scale — a slightly conservative rounding of Kelly's empirically measured ≈12 mm minimum clinically significant difference. — visual analogue scale — A 100 mm line patients mark to rate pain intensity, from "no pain" to "worst pain imaginable". The standard continuous pain-intensity measure the between-drug effect sizes on this page are anchored to.

entries.title: Dexketoprofen vs Ibuprofen
entries.nodeLabel: Reassess at 30–60 min — meaningful relief = VAS fall ≥10 mm or NRS fall ≥1.3, or residual VAS ≤33 mm
entries.text: Reassess at 30–60 min — meaningful relief = VAS fall ≥10 mm or NRS fall ≥1.3, or residual VAS ≤33 mm — Both route pathways converge here: whichever drug was chosen, the same reassessment window and the same definition of meaningful relief apply. The 30–60 minute window matches the onset profile of both drugs at both routes. The VAS fall ≥10 mm threshold is the review's own MCID anchor, drawn from Kelly's empirical finding that patients perceive roughly a 12 mm change on a 100 mm VAS as clinically significant; the NRS ≥1.3 and residual VAS ≤33 mm criteria are alternative, validated ways of capturing the same "meaningfully better" judgement when a different pain scale was used. — Defining "meaningful relief" numerically, rather than leaving it to unstructured clinical impression, is what makes the next decision reproducible — the algorithm needs a clear answer to "did this work" before it can say what happens next. — minimal clinically important difference — The smallest change in a pain score a patient would perceive as meaningful. This page anchors it to roughly 10 mm on a 100 mm visual analogue scale — a slightly conservative rounding of Kelly's empirically measured ≈12 mm minimum clinically significant difference. — visual analogue scale — A 100 mm line patients mark to rate pain intensity, from "no pain" to "worst pain imaginable". The standard continuous pain-intensity measure the between-drug effect sizes on this page are anchored to. — numerical rating scale — An 11-point (0–10) verbal or written pain-intensity scale, used interchangeably with the VAS in some of the trials behind this page. A fall of ≥1.3 points is treated as equivalent to a ≥10 mm VAS fall.

entries.title: Dexketoprofen vs Ibuprofen
entries.text: Meaningful relief? — This is the only point in the algorithm that loops back on the treatment decision already made — not by changing drug class, but by deciding whether to continue the same course or add to it. A clear, affirmative answer against the numeric criteria above, not a vague sense of improvement, is what this decision is meant to capture. — Placing this decision after a fixed reassessment window, rather than leaving reassessment open-ended, prevents both premature escalation (switching drugs before the first one has had time to work) and silent undertreatment (never formally revisiting a patient who is still in pain).

entries.title: Dexketoprofen vs Ibuprofen
entries.nodeLabel: Continue the same NSAID, short course; discharge advice and safety-netting
entries.text: Continue the same NSAID, short course; discharge advice and safety-netting — A patient who has met the meaningful-relief threshold continues on the drug and route already chosen — there is no reason, on this evidence, to switch to the other NSAID once one is working. "Short course" ties back to the three-day ceiling already named for high-risk patients, and is reasonable practice generally given that the trials behind this algorithm studied short-term, acute-pain use, not maintenance therapy. — Ending on discharge advice and safety-netting — rather than simply "continue" — keeps this box from reading as a one-time decision; the patient needs to know what a worsening course would look like after they leave clinical observation.

entries.title: Dexketoprofen vs Ibuprofen
entries.nodeLabel: Do NOT switch to another NSAID
entries.text: Do NOT switch to another NSAID — Add paracetamol; consider regional block or titrated opioid; re-evaluate — This is the direct consequence of the review's own central finding: since dexketoprofen and ibuprofen perform equivalently at the group level, a patient who did not respond to one has no strong pharmacological reason to respond to the other — the evidence behind this page gives no basis for an NSAID-to-NSAID switch. The instruction is therefore to add a different analgesic class (paracetamol, a regional block, or a titrated opioid) rather than trial the second NSAID, and to re-evaluate the patient rather than assume the pain is simply refractory to analgesia in general. — This box is stated as an explicit "do not" — the same way the absolute contraindications above are — because switching within a drug class that this review found clinically equivalent is a plausible but evidence-unsupported instinct, and naming it directly closes off a pathway the algorithm would otherwise leave ambiguous.

entries.title: Anticoagulant Reversal
entries.text: Anticoagulant Reversal In Gastrointestinal Haemorrhage

entries.title: Anticoagulant Reversal
entries.text:
STEP 1 — Immediate assessment (all patients) — • Interrupt the anticoagulant; haemodynamic assessment and resuscitation (IV access; crystalloid / blood products as indicated)
• Identify agent, dose and time of last intake; baseline tests (FBC, coagulation, renal function, crossmatch)
• Risk stratification: GBS / AIMS65 (upper GIB); Oakland score (lower GIB)
• GI consultation; prepare for endoscopy — This step applies to every patient with suspected anticoagulant-associated GI bleeding, before any branching on severity. Four things happen together rather than in sequence: the anticoagulant is interrupted; resuscitation begins with IV access and crystalloid or blood products as indicated; the specific agent, its dose and the time of the last intake are identified alongside baseline bloods (full blood count, coagulation, renal function, crossmatch); and bleeding risk is stratified with a validated score — the Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS) or AIMS65 for suspected upper GI bleeding (UGIB), the Oakland score for lower GI bleeding (LGIB) — while GI is consulted and endoscopy prepared for. — A risk score takes minutes and decides much of what follows: whether reversal is even likely to be needed, and how urgently endoscopy should happen. The GBS identifies patients who need hospital-based intervention versus those safe for early discharge; AIMS65 and the Oakland score add prognostic and discharge-safety information respectively. This matters because the 2022 ACG/CAG guideline frames pharmacological reversal as an adjunct for selected high-risk patients, not a routine step — so this initial stratification is the gate the rest of the algorithm passes through. — Glasgow-Blatchford Score — A risk score for upper GI bleeding, calculated from blood urea nitrogen, haemoglobin, systolic blood pressure, heart rate and several clinical features, used to identify patients safe for early discharge versus those needing hospital-based intervention. — albumin, INR, altered mental status, systolic blood pressure, age ≥65 — An upper GI bleeding risk score combining albumin <3.0 g/dL, INR >1.5, altered mental status, systolic blood pressure ≤90 mmHg and age ≥65 years, used mainly for prognosis — rebleeding and in-hospital mortality — rather than discharge triage. — Oakland score — A validated risk score for lower GI bleeding; a score of 8 or below identifies patients at low enough risk for safe discharge and outpatient investigation rather than admission.

entries.title: Anticoagulant Reversal
entries.text: Haemodynamically stable? — This is the algorithm's central branch point. "Unstable" here tracks the indications for pharmacological reversal described in the wider literature: active, haemodynamically significant bleeding — hypotension, tachycardia, syncope, or a haemoglobin drop of 2 g/dL or more — that has not responded to initial resuscitation, or a high-risk endoscopic lesion found before haemostasis is secured. — Contemporary guidance is explicit that reversal is not universally required: most patients with GI bleeding, including those on anticoagulants, do well with resuscitation, anticoagulant interruption and timely endoscopy alone, with pharmacological reversal reserved for a smaller group with haemodynamically significant or uncontrolled bleeding. Routing every patient through this single question before any drug is chosen keeps that distinction explicit rather than assumed.

entries.title: Anticoagulant Reversal
entries.text:
STEP 2 — Stable: conservative management — • Resuscitation + anticoagulant interruption
• Upper GIB: endoscopy within 24 h
• Lower GIB: non-urgent colonoscopy after bowel preparation
• No reversal unless INR >2.5 (VKA) — For a haemodynamically stable patient, management stays conservative: continued resuscitation and anticoagulant interruption, without a reversal agent, while endoscopy is arranged on a non-emergency timeline. Upper GI bleeding is scoped within 24 hours — earlier than that has not been shown to improve outcomes. Lower GI bleeding is more often self-limiting and is managed with non-urgent colonoscopy once bowel preparation is adequate. The one exception that still prompts reversal in an otherwise stable patient is a markedly supratherapeutic INR (>2.5) in someone on a vitamin K antagonist (VKA). — This pathway reflects the same evidence that routes most anticoagulated GI bleeding away from pharmacological reversal: in stable patients, reversal has not been shown to add benefit over resuscitation, interruption and timely endoscopy, and exposes the patient to reversal-agent risk (thrombosis, transfusion reactions) without a clear offsetting gain. The 24-hour and non-urgent timeframes for upper and lower GI bleeding respectively come from the same society guidelines that define routine endoscopic timing more broadly. — "Stable" is a point-in-time assessment — a patient who re-bleeds or deteriorates after this step should be re-routed through the unstable pathway rather than kept on the conservative one by default. — international normalised ratio — A standardised measure of the extrinsic/common coagulation pathway, used to monitor and dose VKA (warfarin) therapy and to track the response to its reversal.

entries.title: Anticoagulant Reversal
entries.nodeLabel: STEP 2/3 — Unstable / massive GIB: agent-specific reversal in parallel with resuscitation and urgent endoscopy
entries.text:
STEP 2/3 — Unstable / massive GIB: agent-specific reversal in parallel with resuscitation and urgent endoscopy — • Lower GIB with ongoing bleeding: CT angiography first to localise the source
• Select reversal pathway according to the agent below — For haemodynamically unstable or massive bleeding, reversal is not deferred until after resuscitation and endoscopy — all three run in parallel, because the time to definitive haemostasis is what the reversal agent is trying to buy. For ongoing lower GI bleeding with instability, CT angiography is obtained first to localise the bleeding source before an endoscopic or radiological intervention is chosen, and brisk haematochezia with instability should also prompt consideration of an upper GI source. — The specific agent reversed depends entirely on which anticoagulant the patient is on, which is why this step hands off into four separate, agent-specific pathways below rather than a single generic reversal step. Across those pathways the same general preferences recur: 4F-PCC with IV vitamin K for VKA reversal, idarucizumab for dabigatran, and andexanet alfa or 4F-PCC for factor Xa inhibitors — a pattern also reflected in the 2020 ACC expert consensus pathway on bleeding in patients on oral anticoagulants. — four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate — A plasma-derived concentrate of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X (plus proteins C and S), used to rapidly replace the vitamin-K-dependent factors suppressed by a VKA, or as a fallback when a specific DOAC antidote is unavailable. — idarucizumab — A humanised monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with very high affinity, neutralising its anticoagulant effect within minutes. The specific reversal agent for dabigatran. — andexanet alfa — A modified, catalytically inactive recombinant factor Xa decoy protein that binds and sequesters factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban), restoring endogenous factor Xa activity. Carries the highest thrombotic risk among the reversal agents covered here. — computed tomography angiography — Contrast-enhanced CT imaging of the vasculature, used here to localise an ongoing lower GI bleeding source before an endoscopic or interventional-radiology procedure is chosen.

entries.title: Anticoagulant Reversal
entries.text:
VKA / warfarin — • 4F-PCC, INR- and weight-based dose (Table 2) + IV vitamin K 5–10 mg
• Recheck INR at 30 min and 6–8 h
• If PCC unavailable: FFP 10–15 mL/kg + vitamin K — Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC) replaces the vitamin-K-dependent clotting factors a VKA suppresses far faster than fresh frozen plasma (FFP) can, and is dosed by INR tier and body weight (25 IU/kg for INR 2–4, 35 IU/kg for INR 4–6, 50 IU/kg capped at 5,000 IU above INR 6). Intravenous vitamin K is given alongside every dose, not instead of it, because 4F-PCC's effect on clotting factor levels wanes over hours while vitamin K takes 6–12 hours to restore the liver's own synthesis — without it, the INR tends to rebound. The INR is rechecked at 30 minutes and again at 6–8 hours to confirm correction holds. — A randomized, plasma-controlled trial found 4F-PCC achieved rapid INR correction in 62% of patients versus 10% with plasma, and a GI-bleeding-specific cohort found no active bleeding at endoscopy in any patient reversed with PCC versus 35% of those given FFP, with a shorter emergency-department stay. A meta-analysis comparing 4F-PCC with FFP found lower thrombosis (2.5% vs 6.4%) and no significant mortality difference, and a large propensity-matched study of 1,119 pairs found no excess thrombotic risk at 45 days and lower mortality with 4F-PCC. Three-factor PCC, which lacks meaningful factor VII content, is substantially inferior for VKA reversal and should not be substituted. Weight- and INR-based dosing, as used here, more reliably reaches an INR below 1.5 than fixed-dose regimens, though fixed dosing is faster to administer. — INR 2–4 — 4F-PCC 25 IU/kg IV — INR 4–6 — 4F-PCC 35 IU/kg IV — INR >6 — 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg IV (max 5,000 IU) — With every dose — IV vitamin K 5–10 mg, infused over 30 minutes — If 4F-PCC unavailable — FFP 10–15 mL/kg + IV vitamin K — Vitamin K is not optional alongside 4F-PCC — omitting it risks the INR rebounding once the concentrate's own effect wanes. — Three-factor PCC is not an acceptable substitute for 4F-PCC in VKA reversal; its factor VII content is absent or trace. — FFP carries materially higher rates of transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI), circulatory overload (TACO) and transfusion-transmitted infection than 4F-PCC — a further reason it is listed here only as a fallback. — four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate — A plasma-derived concentrate of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X (plus proteins C and S), used to rapidly replace the vitamin-K-dependent factors suppressed by a VKA, or as a fallback when a specific DOAC antidote is unavailable. — fresh frozen plasma — Plasma containing all clotting factors at roughly normal plasma concentration. Slower to correct an elevated INR than 4F-PCC and carries materially higher rates of TRALI, TACO and transfusion-transmitted infection, so it is used here only when PCC is unavailable. — international normalised ratio — A standardised measure of the extrinsic/common coagulation pathway, used to monitor and dose VKA (warfarin) therapy and to track the response to its reversal. — transfusion-related acute lung injury — A serious, potentially fatal acute lung injury that can follow plasma or blood-product transfusion — occurs at materially higher rates with FFP than with 4F-PCC. — transfusion-associated circulatory overload — Acute pulmonary oedema from volume overload during or shortly after transfusion — particularly relevant in elderly anticoagulated patients with pre-existing cardiopulmonary disease, who make up much of this population, and occurs more often with FFP than with 4F-PCC.

entries.title: Anticoagulant Reversal
entries.text:
Dabigatran — • Idarucizumab 5 g IV (2 × 2.5 g, ≤15 min)
• If unavailable: aPCC or 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg
• Activated charcoal if last dose 2–6 h prior — Idarucizumab is a humanised monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with very high affinity — roughly 350 times that of thrombin itself — neutralising its anticoagulant effect within minutes of the two 2.5 g vials being given. Where it is not available, activated prothrombin complex concentrate (aPCC) or 4F-PCC at 50 IU/kg is used instead, and activated charcoal can still reduce further drug absorption if the last dose was taken within the last 2–6 hours and the patient can swallow safely. — The full RE-VERSE AD cohort confirmed idarucizumab's efficacy, with thrombotic events in 4.8% of participants at 30 days — attributed to the underlying thrombotic disease and the anticoagulant interruption itself, not to any prothrombotic property of the antibody fragment. Even so, the 2022 ACG/CAG guideline advises against routine idarucizumab use for GI bleeding specifically, reserving it for bleeding that is life-threatening or associated with haemodynamic instability — exactly the branch of this algorithm this pathway sits in. — First-line — Idarucizumab 5 g IV (two 2.5 g vials, given no more than 15 minutes apart) — If idarucizumab unavailable — aPCC 50 IU/kg IV or 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg IV — Last dose 2–6 h ago — Activated charcoal, if the patient can swallow safely — Renal impairment prolongs dabigatran's own effect and may warrant extended post-reversal monitoring for rebound anticoagulation. — Idarucizumab is not recommended as a routine measure for GI bleeding in general — it is reserved for life-threatening or haemodynamically unstable bleeding, which is the context this box applies in. — four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate — A plasma-derived concentrate of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X (plus proteins C and S), used to rapidly replace the vitamin-K-dependent factors suppressed by a VKA, or as a fallback when a specific DOAC antidote is unavailable. — activated prothrombin complex concentrate — A prothrombin complex concentrate containing activated clotting factors (chiefly factor VIIa alongside the others), used as a dabigatran- or factor-Xa-inhibitor-reversal fallback when the specific antidote is unavailable. — idarucizumab — A humanised monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with very high affinity, neutralising its anticoagulant effect within minutes. The specific reversal agent for dabigatran.

entries.title: Anticoagulant Reversal
entries.text:
Apixaban / rivaroxaban / edoxaban — • Andexanet alfa, low/high dose (Table 2), if available
• If unavailable or cost-prohibitive: 4F-PCC or aPCC 50 IU/kg
• Activated charcoal within 2–6 h (apixaban) or 6–8 h (rivaroxaban) — Andexanet alfa is a modified, catalytically inactive recombinant factor Xa decoy that binds and sequesters factor Xa inhibitors, restoring endogenous factor Xa activity. Dosing is tiered by which drug, what dose, and how recently it was taken — a low-dose regimen (400 mg bolus plus 480 mg over 2 hours) for apixaban ≤5 mg or rivaroxaban ≤10 mg, or when more than 8 hours have passed since the last dose, and a high-dose regimen (800 mg bolus plus 960 mg over 2 hours) otherwise. Where andexanet is unavailable or cost-prohibitive, 4F-PCC or aPCC at 50 IU/kg is used instead, and activated charcoal remains useful if the last dose was recent enough. — The full ANNEXA-4 study report established andexanet's haemostatic efficacy for factor Xa inhibitor-associated bleeding. But its thrombotic burden is the highest of the agents on this page — a 2024 meta-analysis reported thrombotic events in 14% of patients (95% CI 10–19%), with observational series reporting rates as high as 27%, and andexanet also carries a recognised procoagulant off-target effect. Real-world, GI-bleeding-specific cohorts support 4F-PCC as an effective, more available and less expensive alternative: one reported 72.6% haemostatic efficacy and a second reported 66.7%, both with lower reported thrombosis than andexanet series. A UK-wide audit of DOAC-bleeding patients found a higher 30-day stroke rate with andexanet than 4F-PCC in a GI-bleeding-matched subgroup (4.5% vs 0%), even though 90-day mortality was similar. Reflecting this balance, the 2022 ACG/CAG guideline suggests against routine andexanet or PCC use in GI bleeding, reserving reversal for refractory haemodynamic instability — most DOAC-associated GI bleeding is managed with resuscitation and endoscopy alone. — Low dose (apixaban ≤5 mg, rivaroxaban ≤10 mg, or >8 h since last dose) — Andexanet alfa 400 mg bolus + 480 mg over 2 hours — High dose (apixaban >5 mg, rivaroxaban >10 mg, within 8 h) — Andexanet alfa 800 mg bolus + 960 mg over 2 hours — If andexanet unavailable / cost-prohibitive — 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg IV or aPCC 50 IU/kg IV — Activated charcoal — Within 2–6 h of last dose for apixaban, or 6–8 h for rivaroxaban, if able to swallow safely — Andexanet alfa carries the highest observed thrombotic risk of the reversal agents covered on this page — this is a direct trade-off against its haemostatic efficacy, not an incidental side effect. — The 2022 ACG/CAG guideline suggests against routine andexanet or PCC use for GI bleeding specifically, reserving reversal for refractory haemodynamic instability rather than applying it by default to every factor Xa inhibitor-associated bleed. — four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate — A plasma-derived concentrate of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X (plus proteins C and S), used to rapidly replace the vitamin-K-dependent factors suppressed by a VKA, or as a fallback when a specific DOAC antidote is unavailable. — activated prothrombin complex concentrate — A prothrombin complex concentrate containing activated clotting factors (chiefly factor VIIa alongside the others), used as a dabigatran- or factor-Xa-inhibitor-reversal fallback when the specific antidote is unavailable. — direct oral anticoagulant — An oral anticoagulant that directly inhibits a single clotting factor — dabigatran inhibits thrombin (factor IIa); apixaban, rivaroxaban and edoxaban inhibit factor Xa — as opposed to a VKA, which suppresses the hepatic synthesis of several factors at once. — andexanet alfa — A modified, catalytically inactive recombinant factor Xa decoy protein that binds and sequesters factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban), restoring endogenous factor Xa activity. Carries the highest thrombotic risk among the reversal agents covered here.

entries.title: Anticoagulant Reversal
entries.text:
UFH / LMWH — • UFH: protamine 1 mg per 100 IU (max 50 mg)
• LMWH: protamine, partial reversal (~60%)
• Infuse slowly (hypotension / bradycardia) — Protamine sulfate is a strongly basic protein that binds unfractionated heparin (UFH) ionically, neutralising its anticoagulant effect essentially completely. Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) binds protamine less completely because a larger share of its anticoagulant activity comes from anti-factor Xa inhibition, which protamine neutralises poorly — so reversal with protamine is only partial, on the order of 60%. — The dosing shown here follows the authored protocol's own regimen; the manuscript's Table 2 does not cite a specific source for it. An independent emergency-medicine review of anticoagulation reversal confirms the same general approach — protamine dosed against the amount of heparin given and the time elapsed since the last dose, with LMWH reversal capped at roughly 60–75% of its anti-factor Xa activity because of protamine's weaker binding to the drug's smaller, more heavily sulfated chains. — UFH — Protamine sulfate 1 mg per 100 IU of UFH given in the last 2–3 hours (maximum 50 mg IV) — LMWH — Protamine 1 mg per 1 mg of enoxaparin — partial reversal only, roughly 60% — Protamine must be infused slowly — rapid administration can cause hypotension, bradycardia and anaphylactoid reactions, which are more frequent with faster infusion rates. — Reversal of LMWH is only ever partial; a persistently prolonged aPTT or ongoing bleeding after protamine does not necessarily mean the dose was inadequate. — protamine sulfate — A strongly basic protein that binds heparin ionically to neutralise its anticoagulant effect — essentially completely for unfractionated heparin, only partially (around 60%) for low-molecular-weight heparin. — unfractionated heparin — An injectable anticoagulant that potentiates antithrombin's inhibition of both thrombin and factor Xa. Fully neutralised by protamine sulfate, unlike LMWH. — low-molecular-weight heparin — A heparin derivative (e.g. enoxaparin) with more selective anti-factor-Xa activity than unfractionated heparin. Protamine reverses only around 60% of its anticoagulant effect.

entries.title: Anticoagulant Reversal
entries.text:
STEP 4 — Endoscopy and haemostasis — • Upper or lower GI endoscopy with endoscopic haemostasis (injection, thermal, mechanical) as indicated
• Target INR ≤1.5–2.0 is generally acceptable for most procedures in VKA-treated patients
• Reassess haemostasis clinically (vital signs, overt bleeding, serial haemoglobin) when DOAC-specific assays are unavailable — This is the point every pathway above converges on: definitive source control by endoscopy, with injection, thermal or mechanical haemostatic technique chosen as the lesion demands. For patients reversed from a VKA, an INR of 1.5–2.0 or below is generally acceptable to proceed rather than waiting for full normalisation. Because routine DOAC-specific coagulation assays (calibrated anti-Xa, diluted thrombin time, ecarin-based assays) are not available around the clock in most emergency departments, haemostatic adequacy for DOAC-treated patients is judged clinically — stabilising vital signs, cessation of overt bleeding, and stable or improving serial haemoglobin — with endoscopic confirmation of haemostasis as the reference standard. — Waiting for a fully normalised INR or a DOAC level before scoping would needlessly delay the one intervention — endoscopic haemostasis — that actually stops the bleeding; a modestly elevated INR is an acceptable trade-off against that delay for most lesions. Standard screening coagulation tests (PT/INR, aPTT) are unreliable for quantifying DOAC effect and should not be used alone to decide whether it is safe to proceed, which is why clinical and simple laboratory endpoints are used instead when specific assays are unavailable. — A normal PT/INR or aPTT does not exclude a clinically relevant residual DOAC effect — these tests were not designed to measure it and can look falsely reassuring. — international normalised ratio — A standardised measure of the extrinsic/common coagulation pathway, used to monitor and dose VKA (warfarin) therapy and to track the response to its reversal. — direct oral anticoagulant — An oral anticoagulant that directly inhibits a single clotting factor — dabigatran inhibits thrombin (factor IIa); apixaban, rivaroxaban and edoxaban inhibit factor Xa — as opposed to a VKA, which suppresses the hepatic synthesis of several factors at once.

entries.title: Anticoagulant Reversal
entries.nodeLabel: STEP 5 — Post-haemostasis monitoring and resumption planning
entries.text:
STEP 5 — Post-haemostasis monitoring and resumption planning — • Monitor for thromboembolic complications (highest with andexanet alfa)
• Assess for rebound anticoagulant activity (e.g., dabigatran after idarucizumab)
• High-dose PPI after endoscopic haemostasis (upper GIB)
• Plan anticoagulant resumption once haemostasis is secure, generally between 7 days and 6 weeks (risk-stratified, multidisciplinary; see Section 11) — Once bleeding is controlled, attention shifts to the risks the reversal itself created or revealed. Thrombotic complications are monitored for, particularly after andexanet alfa given its higher observed rate; rebound anticoagulant activity is watched for, notably in dabigatran-treated patients after idarucizumab; a high-dose proton pump inhibitor (PPI) is continued after endoscopic haemostasis for upper GI bleeding; and — the step that most shapes long-term outcome — a plan for resuming anticoagulation is made, generally somewhere between 7 days and 6 weeks after the bleed, individualised to the patient's competing bleeding and thrombotic risk and decided with the relevant specialties. — Both premature resumption and prolonged or permanent cessation of anticoagulation carry real harm: resuming too early raises rebleeding risk, while stopping for too long — or for good — raises thromboembolic and stroke risk. A meta-analysis found that resuming anticoagulation after GI bleeding is consistently associated with less thromboembolism and lower mortality than permanent cessation, at the cost of more recurrent bleeding, particularly when restarted within the first 2–3 weeks; most thromboembolic events occur beyond 2 weeks of interruption, and risk modelling suggests an optimal window of roughly 3–6 weeks for warfarin specifically. The ESGE recommends resuming as soon as bleeding is controlled, preferably within or soon after 7 days, and the BSG/ESGE guideline supports earlier resumption — with heparin bridging where appropriate — in patients at high thrombotic risk. Validated tools such as HAS-BLED (bleeding risk) and CHA₂DS₂-VASc (thromboembolic risk in atrial fibrillation) support this individualised decision. — Neither resuming immediately nor withholding anticoagulation indefinitely is a neutral default — each carries a distinct, serious failure mode (rebleeding versus thromboembolism), which is why this decision is explicitly individualised rather than protocolised to a single fixed interval. — Rebound anticoagulant activity after idarucizumab is a recognised phenomenon in dabigatran-treated patients and is a specific reason for continued clinical and, where available, laboratory reassessment rather than assuming reversal is durable. — idarucizumab — A humanised monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with very high affinity, neutralising its anticoagulant effect within minutes. The specific reversal agent for dabigatran. — andexanet alfa — A modified, catalytically inactive recombinant factor Xa decoy protein that binds and sequesters factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban), restoring endogenous factor Xa activity. Carries the highest thrombotic risk among the reversal agents covered here. — proton pump inhibitor — An acid-suppressing drug given at high dose after endoscopic haemostasis for upper GI bleeding, to create a less acidic environment that stabilises clot formation over the treated lesion. — HAS-BLED score — A bleeding-risk score (hypertension, abnormal renal/liver function, stroke history, bleeding history or predisposition, labile INR, elderly age, drugs/alcohol) used alongside a thromboembolic-risk score to individualise the decision to resume anticoagulation. — CHA₂DS₂-VASc score — A thromboembolic-risk score for atrial fibrillation (congestive heart failure, hypertension, age ≥75, diabetes, prior stroke/TIA/thromboembolism, vascular disease, age 65–74, sex category), used alongside a bleeding-risk score to individualise anticoagulant-resumption timing.

entries.title: The Adult with Obesity
entries.text: The Adult with Obesity In Emergency and Critical Care

entries.title: The Adult with Obesity
entries.nodeLabel: STEP 1 — TRIGGER: BMI ≥ 30 kg/m² activates the obesity care bundle
entries.text:
STEP 1 — TRIGGER: BMI ≥ 30 kg/m² activates the obesity care bundle — • Measure height and weight rather than estimating them; calculate predicted body weight (PBW) from height and sex and record it.
• Weight-rated trolley, bed and hoist; correctly sized blood-pressure cuffs; extra-long procedural equipment.
• Confirm CT table weight and gantry limits before transfer; ultrasound-guided vascular access as default, early intraosseous access if peripheral attempts fail.
• Early pharmacist review of every weight-based dose, with the weight descriptor recorded alongside the dose.
• Any patient taking a GLP-1 receptor agonist is managed as having a full stomach. — A single, simple threshold — BMI ≥30 kg/m² — opens a bundle of logistical and safety checks that have nothing to do with drug dosing yet: measured (not guessed) anthropometrics, weight-rated equipment, imaging-table limits, vascular access planning, a pharmacist safety net on every subsequent weight-based dose, and a standing assumption that a GLP-1 receptor agonist means delayed gastric emptying. None of this is drug-dose scaling — that question is deliberately deferred to Step 2, domain by domain. — Separating the trigger bundle from the dosing decisions keeps the two kinds of error apart: missing a weight-rated bed or an oversized BP cuff is an equipment failure, not a pharmacology one, and bundling both into a single BMI-triggered checklist means neither gets forgotten while the clinical team is focused on the other. — glucagon-like peptide-1 — A hormone class targeted by drugs (receptor agonists) that slow gastric emptying — the reason patients taking one are managed as having a full stomach regardless of reported fasting time.

entries.title: The Adult with Obesity
entries.nodeLabel: STEP 2 — SCALE EACH DECISION TO ITS OWN PHYSIOLOGICAL DESCRIPTOR, NOT TO BMI
entries.text: STEP 2 — SCALE EACH DECISION TO ITS OWN PHYSIOLOGICAL DESCRIPTOR, NOT TO BMI — The nine domains below (A–I) are not steps in a sequence and do not branch from one another — they apply concurrently, to the same patient, for as long as the obesity care bundle is active. Each domain answers one narrow question: for this particular drug, device setting, or target, which body-weight descriptor (lean, total, predicted, ideal/adjusted, or none at all) should the number actually be calculated from. BMI itself is never the scaling variable for any individual decision — it is only the trigger that activates the bundle in Step 1. — A single "obesity dose adjustment" rule of thumb would be wrong in at least half of these domains, because the physiological reason obesity changes a given decision is different for each one — volume of distribution for induction agents, lung size for tidal volume, renal clearance for antimicrobials, and so on. Scaling every domain to the descriptor that actually tracks the relevant physiology, rather than to a single body-size number, is the review's central organising idea.

entries.title: The Adult with Obesity
entries.text:
A. Airway and preoxygenation — • Anticipate difficult laryngoscopy and a short safe apnoea time.
• Ramped or head-up position, external auditory meatus level with the sternal notch.
• Positive-pressure (non-invasive ventilation) preoxygenation plus apnoeic oxygenation.
• Videolaryngoscope as the first device. — Obesity reduces functional residual capacity and increases oxygen consumption, so a patient with obesity desaturates faster once apnoeic than a patient of normal weight — the safe window for a failed first attempt is genuinely shorter, not just theoretically so. The ramped or head-up position and ear-to-sternal-notch alignment are positioning fixes aimed at restoring a view that excess chest-wall and neck soft tissue otherwise obscures in the standard supine sniffing position, and were shown in a randomized crossover comparison to improve the laryngoscopic view compared with the standard sniffing position. Positive-pressure preoxygenation combined with an alveolar recruitment manoeuvre around intubation, rather than plain tidal breathing on a facemask, was shown in a randomized trial to improve oxygenation during and after intubation in patients with morbid obesity. — Naming videolaryngoscopy as the first device, not a rescue device, reflects that direct laryngoscopy is disproportionately harder in obesity for anatomical reasons that don't resolve with extra attempts — escalating to it only after a failed direct view costs time the shortened apnoea tolerance in this population may not allow.

entries.title: The Adult with Obesity
entries.text:
B. Induction and neuromuscular blockade — • Propofol induction bolus on lean body weight; titrate to effect.
• Succinylcholine (suxamethonium) on total body weight.
• Rocuronium for RSI: avoid under-dosing (≥ 1.2 mg/kg; no default fixed 100 mg); sugammadex should be available.
• Blocker infusions on ideal body weight, titrated to train-of-four. — The four drugs in this domain are scaled to four different weight descriptors because each tracks a different pharmacokinetic property. A pharmacokinetic study in morbidly obese subjects found that scaling the propofol induction dose to lean rather than total body weight avoided over-dosing while still achieving reliable anaesthetic effect, since the induction effect depends on the dose reaching the brain fast, which tracks lean rather than fat mass. A separate pharmacokinetic study found succinylcholine's onset depends on plasma cholinesterase activity and extracellular distribution, both of which scale with total body weight, so underdosing by lean weight risks an inadequately paralysed, harder airway. Rocuronium for rapid sequence induction is deliberately flagged against a fixed 100 mg dose, because a fixed adult dose under-doses a larger patient exactly when a fast, reliable onset matters most; an observational non-inferiority study comparing ideal- and total-body-weight rocuronium dosing in obesity supports that general under-dosing concern, and sugammadex availability is named alongside the higher dose as the reversal safety net. Ongoing blocker infusions, by contrast, are titrated to a measured endpoint (train-of-four) on ideal body weight as a starting point, because a continuous infusion can be adjusted against real-time monitoring in a way a single bolus cannot. — Giving each drug its own descriptor rather than one blanket "reduce the dose in obesity" instruction prevents the two most common obesity-anaesthesia errors in opposite directions at once: over-sedating on an induction agent dosed by total body weight, and under-paralysing a succinylcholine or rocuronium dose scaled down too far. — A nerve-stimulator monitoring pattern used to titrate ongoing neuromuscular blocker infusions to a measured depth of paralysis, rather than to a fixed infusion rate.

entries.title: The Adult with Obesity
entries.text:
C. Mechanical ventilation — • Low tidal volume, about 6 mL/kg PBW, with or without ARDS; never actual body weight.
• Individualise PEEP (oesophageal manometry or electrical impedance tomography).
• Keep driving pressure ≤ 15 cmH₂O; prone if PaO₂/FiO₂ < 150. — Lung size, and therefore safe tidal volume, tracks height and sex far more closely than it tracks total body weight — adipose tissue does not need ventilating. The landmark ARDS Network trial established scaling tidal volume to predicted rather than actual body weight as the lung-protective standard; scaling to actual body weight in a patient with obesity delivers a volume calculated for lungs much larger than the ones actually being ventilated, risking volutrauma, regardless of whether the patient also has ARDS. Because obesity raises intra-abdominal and chest-wall pressure, a randomized trial in obese surgical patients found that an individualised, higher-PEEP strategy with recruitment manoeuvres reduced postoperative pulmonary complications compared with a low, fixed PEEP level — which is why this domain calls for individualising PEEP against a direct measurement (oesophageal manometry) or a bedside imaging surrogate (electrical impedance tomography) rather than a fixed number. Driving pressure (plateau pressure minus PEEP) and proning at a PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio below 150 both extend standard ARDS lung-protective practice — a pooled analysis linking driving pressure to survival, and the PROSEVA trial's own enrolment threshold for proning — into this population rather than replacing it. — Pairing "never actual body weight" directly with the tidal-volume instruction closes off the most common and most consequential scaling error in this domain — a volume that looks conservative relative to the patient's real weight can still be a volutrauma-generating volume relative to their actual lung size. — acute respiratory distress syndrome — Severe, diffuse acute lung injury causing hypoxaemia. Low-tidal-volume, lung-protective ventilation principles apply with or without a formal ARDS diagnosis in patients with obesity. — positive end-expiratory pressure — Pressure maintained in the airway at the end of expiration to keep alveoli open. Individualised in obesity because chest-wall and abdominal pressure change how much PEEP is actually needed. — Plateau airway pressure minus PEEP — a marker of lung stress during mechanical ventilation. Kept at or below 15 cmH₂O as an extension of standard lung-protective ventilation targets.

entries.title: The Adult with Obesity
entries.text:
D. Circulation and fluids — • Initial crystalloid bolus on adjusted or ideal body weight.
• Move early to dynamic assessment of fluid responsiveness.
• Vasopressors non-weight-based (micrograms/min), titrated to mean arterial pressure. — An initial fluid bolus calculated on actual body weight in a patient with obesity can substantially over-deliver volume, since circulating blood volume and extracellular fluid do not expand in proportion to fat mass — adjusted or ideal body weight is used instead as a closer approximation of the compartment actually being filled. Moving early to a dynamic measure of fluid responsiveness, rather than continuing fixed-volume boluses, matters more in this population because raised intra-abdominal pressure and reduced chest-wall compliance make standard dynamic indices themselves harder to interpret in obesity, not just static measures. Vasopressors are dosed in absolute micrograms per minute, titrated to a measured mean arterial pressure target, rather than on any weight-based scale at all, because their endpoint is directly observable at the bedside in a way a fluid bolus's effect is not. — This is the domain the review rates with the least confidence of the nine. A literature search for this page did not find a trial establishing that adjusted- or ideal-body-weight fluid dosing specifically improves outcomes in critically ill patients with obesity — one retrospective study on body-weight-adjusted fluid dosing in sepsis found an association between mortality and under-dosing by actual body weight, not evidence favouring adjusted or ideal weight, and cautioned against departing from standard practice without further study. That gap in the literature is itself consistent with the review's very-low-certainty rating for this domain.

entries.title: The Adult with Obesity
entries.nodeLabel: E. Kidney function and renal replacement
entries.text:
E. Kidney function and renal replacement — • Creatinine-based GFR estimates are unreliable in obesity.
• CRRT: target a delivered effluent dose of 20–25 mL/kg/h; state the weight descriptor used and avoid the very large absolute doses produced by actual body weight. — Serum creatinine is generated by muscle, not fat, and most GFR-estimating equations assume a body composition that no longer holds once fat mass is substantially elevated — the result can look reassuringly normal while true clearance is actually reduced, or vice versa. For continuous renal replacement therapy, a large randomized trial found no outcome benefit from a higher (40 mL/kg/h) effluent dose over a lower one (25 mL/kg/h), and the KDIGO acute kidney injury guideline's own rationale discussion cites that trial evidence in settling on roughly 20–25 mL/kg/h as the target delivered dose. Applying that target to actual body weight in a patient with severe obesity can generate an absolute prescribed dose far above what is clinically intended or deliverable, which is why the domain specifically calls for stating which weight descriptor the dose was calculated from. — Flagging the weight descriptor alongside every CRRT prescription, rather than just the final mL/h number, is what lets a second clinician catch a scaling error before it compounds — an effluent dose that looks plausible in isolation can still be calculated from the wrong starting weight. — glomerular filtration rate — A measure of kidney filtering capacity. Creatinine-based estimates of it are unreliable in obesity because serum creatinine generation depends on muscle mass, not fat mass. — continuous renal replacement therapy — Continuous (rather than intermittent) dialysis used in critically ill patients, typically dosed by a target effluent (filtered fluid) rate per kilogram per hour.

entries.title: The Adult with Obesity
entries.text:
F. Antimicrobials — • Loading dose on total body weight; never reduce the first dose for body size.
• Maintenance guided by clearance and therapeutic drug monitoring. — A loading dose exists to fill the entire volume of distribution quickly, and that volume is larger — not just the lean-tissue fraction of it — in a patient with obesity, so scaling the first dose down for body size risks subtherapeutic early concentrations at exactly the point in sepsis management when source control has not yet happened. A narrative review of antimicrobial dosing in obesity argues against simple linear total-body-weight correlations for ongoing dosing specifically, and instead calls for maintenance to be guided by measured clearance and therapeutic drug monitoring where available — the loading dose and the maintenance dose are different pharmacokinetic problems, and this domain treats them as such. — Splitting "never reduce the first dose" from "maintenance guided by clearance" into two separate instructions prevents the single most common antimicrobial-dosing error in obesity — treating the loading dose and the maintenance dose as the same scaling problem, when the pharmacokinetic principle behind each is different.

entries.title: The Adult with Obesity
entries.text:
G. Thromboprophylaxis — • Fixed standard doses become sub-prophylactic as BMI rises.
• Enoxaparin 40 mg twice daily or about 0.5 mg/kg daily; verify with anti-factor Xa where available.
• Unfractionated heparin 7500 units three times daily if renal function is poor or bleeding risk high. — A fixed once- or twice-daily low-molecular-weight heparin dose was established in trial populations of average body size; an observational study in critically ill patients found that a fixed-dose approach to thrombosis chemoprophylaxis becomes progressively less adequate as patient weight rises — a dose that is genuinely prophylactic at a normal BMI can become sub-prophylactic in obesity without any dosing error having occurred, the dose simply didn't scale. The two named regimens (weight-adjusted or higher fixed-dose enoxaparin; thrice-daily unfractionated heparin when renal function or bleeding risk makes a longer-acting agent less attractive) are both ways of correcting for that, with anti-factor Xa monitoring offered as a direct check on whether the chosen dose actually achieved a prophylactic level in that specific patient. — Stating explicitly that fixed doses "become" sub-prophylactic, rather than simply listing a higher dose, makes the point that this is a dose-response problem that gets silently worse as BMI increases — not a threshold a clinician either crosses or doesn't. — A blood test measuring the activity of low-molecular-weight heparin, used to confirm that a thromboprophylaxis dose is actually achieving a prophylactic level rather than assuming it from the dose alone.

entries.title: The Adult with Obesity
entries.text:
H. Nutrition and body composition — • High-protein hypocaloric feeding: 11–14 kcal/kg actual body weight/day; protein 2.0–2.5 g/kg ideal body weight/day.
• Look for sarcopenic obesity (CT or muscle ultrasound); interpret bioimpedance cautiously in oedema.
• Bariatric history: thiamine before glucose. — A society clinical guideline for nutrition support in hospitalized adults with obesity recommends hypocaloric, high-protein feeding — deliberately under-delivering calories relative to actual body weight, since much of that weight is energy-dense fat that does not need replacing acutely, while protecting lean mass with a protein target calculated on ideal body weight, which tracks the muscle actually at risk of catabolism. Sarcopenic obesity — reduced muscle mass hidden inside a high overall BMI — is actively screened for with imaging-based tools (CT or muscle ultrasound) because it changes the nutrition and mobility plan even though the patient looks well-nourished by weight alone; bioimpedance is flagged as unreliable in the presence of oedema because fluid shifts distort its electrical measurements independent of true body composition. A systematic review of Wernicke encephalopathy after bariatric surgery found that intravenous glucose given without prior thiamine was a contributing factor in a substantial minority of cases, supporting the practice of giving thiamine before glucose in a patient with that history. — Grouping calorie target, protein target, body-composition screening, and the thiamine-before-glucose rule into one domain reflects that all four are really the same underlying problem — a high BMI can conceal rather than rule out malnutrition, and each instruction corrects for a different way that concealment can go wrong.

entries.title: The Adult with Obesity
entries.text: I. Liberation from mechanical ventilation — Extubate onto prophylactic non-invasive ventilation — the only intervention here supported by an adequately powered randomised trial in a critically ill population with obesity. — Reduced functional residual capacity and a higher closing volume make a patient with obesity more prone to post-extubation atelectasis and reintubation than a patient of normal weight, independent of the reason they were ventilated in the first place. The EXTUB-OBESE trial — a multicentre, pragmatic randomised trial across 39 French ICUs in critically ill patients with obesity — found that planning extubation directly onto prophylactic non-invasive ventilation, rather than reactively starting it only if the patient deteriorated afterward, reduced extubation failure. It is the specific adequately-powered RCT this domain refers to. — Calling this out as the single adequately-powered-RCT-backed recommendation in the table is itself an important piece of information for a reader — it tells them where to hold a practice firmly versus where the rest of the domains are reasoned extrapolation from physiology and lower-certainty evidence.

entries.title: The Adult with Obesity
entries.nodeLabel: Cardiac arrest: follow the standard ALS/ACLS algorithm. Obesity-specific considerations (firm surface, early compressor rotation, mechanical compression devices, defibrillation energy) inform training and equipment planning; see Section 3.6.
entries.text: Cardiac arrest: follow the standard ALS/ACLS algorithm. Obesity-specific considerations (firm surface, early compressor rotation, mechanical compression devices, defibrillation energy) inform training and equipment planning; see Section 3.6. — This note deliberately sits outside the nine numbered domains: cardiac arrest management in a patient with obesity is not a variant algorithm, it is the standard ALS/ACLS algorithm, with a short list of logistical and training considerations layered on top rather than a different resuscitation pathway. A firm surface and earlier compressor rotation address the extra physical effort of generating adequate chest compression depth through a larger chest wall; mechanical compression devices and defibrillation energy are named as equipment and dosing questions to plan for in advance rather than improvise during the arrest itself. A 2024 ILCOR scoping review looked specifically for trial evidence behind adjustments like these and found too little to clearly support or refute any of them — which is itself why this box is framed as training and equipment planning rather than as a trial-backed instruction. — Keeping this as a dashed-border aside rather than a tenth domain reflects how the source table itself presents it — a cross-reference to a fuller discussion elsewhere in the review (Section 3.6, not available to this page), not a physiological-descriptor decision of the same kind as A–I.

entries.title: Dapagliflozin / SGLT2 Inhibitor
entries.text: Dapagliflozin / SGLT2 Inhibitor Overdose & Acute Illness Management

entries.title: Dapagliflozin / SGLT2 Inhibitor
entries.nodeLabel: Patient taking dapagliflozin presents unwell, OR suspected overdose
entries.text: Patient taking dapagliflozin presents unwell, OR suspected overdose — Two different presentations are deliberately funnelled into one pathway here: a patient on long-term dapagliflozin who has simply become unwell (an intercurrent illness, reduced oral intake, a surgical admission), and a patient who has taken — or is suspected of having taken — a supratherapeutic or intentional overdose. Both share the same first problem: a drug that can precipitate ketoacidosis without raising the blood glucose is easy to miss on a standard glucose-led assessment. — Treating "unwell on dapagliflozin" and "overdose of dapagliflozin" as one starting point, rather than two separate algorithms, reflects that the dangerous complication in both scenarios is the same — euglycaemic ketoacidosis — and the same first-line workup (ketones regardless of glucose) answers the question either way. — A near-normal blood glucose. Ketoacidosis is usually suspected because of a very high glucose reading; "euglycaemic" ketoacidosis has a normal or only mildly raised glucose instead, which is what makes it easy to miss without deliberately checking ketones.

entries.title: Dapagliflozin / SGLT2 Inhibitor
entries.nodeLabel: Mechanism: how dapagliflozin produces its effects
entries.text:
Mechanism: how dapagliflozin produces its effects — Blocks SGLT2 in the proximal tubule → Glycosuria
Osmotic diuresis and natriuresis → Volume loss
Falling insulin to glucagon ratio → Ketogenesis
Insulin-independent action → No hypoglycaemia — Dapagliflozin blocks the SGLT2 transporter in the proximal renal tubule, the site that normally reabsorbs almost all filtered glucose. Blocking it spills glucose into the urine (glycosuria), which in turn drags water and sodium out with it by osmotic diuresis and natriuresis. Separately, the resulting glycosuria shifts the body toward a relatively fasted hormonal state — the insulin-to-glucagon ratio falls — which promotes lipolysis and ketogenesis even when the blood glucose itself is normal or only mildly elevated. Its glucose-lowering action does not depend on stimulating insulin secretion the way a sulfonylurea's does, which is the pharmacological basis for not expecting hypoglycaemia from the drug alone — though one narrative review notes the picture is not perfectly clean: by lowering plasma glucose, SGLT2 inhibition can modestly reduce endogenous insulin secretion as a secondary effect, which is a different thing from acting "independent of insulin." — This mechanism panel is placed early because it explains, in one place, why the rest of the algorithm asks the questions it does: why ketones are checked regardless of the glucose reading (ketogenesis is glucose-independent), why volume status matters (natriuresis and osmotic diuresis), and why hypoglycaemia is not expected from the drug itself — so that a later finding of hypoglycaemia is read as a signal to look elsewhere, not as confirmation of dapagliflozin toxicity. — sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 — A protein in the proximal renal tubule responsible for reabsorbing almost all filtered glucose back into the blood. Dapagliflozin and the other drugs in its class block this transporter, causing glucose (and, with it, sodium and water) to be excreted in the urine instead. — Glucose appearing in the urine — the direct, intended effect of SGLT2 blockade, and the starting point for most of this drug's other effects, wanted and unwanted. — Increased sodium excretion in the urine. Here it travels together with the glucose being excreted, which is why SGLT2 inhibition produces a mild diuretic-like effect on blood pressure and volume status. — The liver's production of ketone bodies (including beta-hydroxybutyrate) from fat, normally switched on during fasting. SGLT2 inhibition can switch this on even without true fasting or hyperglycaemia, by lowering the insulin-to-glucagon ratio — the mechanism behind euglycaemic ketoacidosis.

entries.title: Dapagliflozin / SGLT2 Inhibitor
entries.nodeLabel: Three effects genuinely attributable to the drug
entries.text:
Three effects genuinely attributable to the drug — • Genital mycotic infection — ~3× increase vs control. Common but usually mild. → Treat with antifungals. Do not stop the drug.
• Ketoacidosis (often euglycaemic) — ~2× from a very low baseline in T2D; higher in T1D. → Measure ketones whatever the glucose reading shows.
• Volume depletion — Modest in trials; matters in frail, diuretic-treated patients. → Sick-day rules. Review diuretic dose. — Of the adverse effects reported with SGLT2 inhibitors, these three have randomised-trial evidence specifically linking them to the drug rather than to the background population taking it. Genital mycotic infection is the most common and least dangerous — glycosuria feeds local yeast overgrowth — and is managed with antifungal treatment rather than stopping an otherwise-working drug; the "~3×" figure as given matches class-wide SGLT2-inhibitor meta-analyses, though dapagliflozin's own pooled trial data show a larger effect, roughly 5- to 9-fold. Ketoacidosis is uncommon in absolute terms but increases from an already-low baseline — a multi-society consensus report gives a relative risk around 2 (meta-analyses of randomised trials and of observational studies both cluster near 2-fold, though dapagliflozin's own cardiovascular-outcomes trial shows a nominally larger, roughly 3-fold difference) — and is frequently euglycaemic, which is the reason this entire algorithm checks ketones independent of the glucose value. The risk is clearly higher still in type 1 diabetes, where SGLT2 inhibitors are used off-label. Volume depletion is the mildest signal in trial populations but becomes clinically relevant in patients who are frail or already on a diuretic, which is why "sick-day" guidance (temporarily withholding the drug during acute illness or reduced intake) and diuretic-dose review are the specific actions attached to it. — Framing these as the effects "genuinely attributable to the drug" — rather than listing every adverse event reported in a trial database — keeps the clinical picture honest: it tells a reader which signals are drug-specific and actionable, rather than background noise from the population studied. — sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 — A protein in the proximal renal tubule responsible for reabsorbing almost all filtered glucose back into the blood. Dapagliflozin and the other drugs in its class block this transporter, causing glucose (and, with it, sodium and water) to be excreted in the urine instead. — Glucose appearing in the urine — the direct, intended effect of SGLT2 blockade, and the starting point for most of this drug's other effects, wanted and unwanted. — A near-normal blood glucose. Ketoacidosis is usually suspected because of a very high glucose reading; "euglycaemic" ketoacidosis has a normal or only mildly raised glucose instead, which is what makes it easy to miss without deliberately checking ketones.

entries.title: Dapagliflozin / SGLT2 Inhibitor
entries.nodeLabel: Airway, breathing, circulation · IV access · capillary glucose
entries.text:
Airway, breathing, circulation · IV access · capillary glucose — History: time and quantity ingested, and — decisively — any CO-INGESTANT
(insulin, sulphonylurea, antihypertensive, cardiotoxic agent) — The initial survey is standard first-hour poisoning assessment, with one deliberately emphasised item: identifying a co-ingestant. Because dapagliflozin alone does not cause hypoglycaemia or cardiovascular collapse, any hypoglycaemia, arrhythmia, or haemodynamic instability found later in this patient is far more likely to come from something taken alongside it — a sulfonylurea, exogenous insulin, an antihypertensive, or a cardiotoxic agent — than from the dapagliflozin itself. — "Decisively" is the operative word in the source material: in an isolated SGLT2 inhibitor ingestion the drug's own toxicity is limited, so the single history question most likely to change management in the first hour is not the dapagliflozin dose, but what else was taken with it. — sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 — A protein in the proximal renal tubule responsible for reabsorbing almost all filtered glucose back into the blood. Dapagliflozin and the other drugs in its class block this transporter, causing glucose (and, with it, sodium and water) to be excreted in the urine instead. — Another substance taken at the same time as the drug in question. Central to this algorithm because dapagliflozin's own toxicity is limited — most of the danger in a mixed or large ingestion comes from what else was taken.

entries.title: Dapagliflozin / SGLT2 Inhibitor
entries.nodeLabel: Blood β-hydroxybutyrate · venous gas with anion gap · Na⁺, K⁺, Mg²⁺ · renal function · urinalysis
entries.text: Blood β-hydroxybutyrate · venous gas with anion gap · Na⁺, K⁺, Mg²⁺ · renal function · urinalysis — Measure ketones REGARDLESS of the blood glucose value — This panel exists to catch euglycaemic ketoacidosis, which a glucose-led assessment misses by design: capillary or point-of-care glucose can be entirely normal while blood ketones are already pathologically elevated. Beta-hydroxybutyrate is the dominant ketone body in DKA and is measured directly — a multi-society consensus report notes blood beta-hydroxybutyrate levels at or above 3.0 mmol/L correlate well with the acid–base changes of ketoacidosis, and that the hyperglycaemia/diabetes criterion applies irrespective of the presenting glucose value, which is exactly the euglycaemic-DKA scenario this box is built to catch. The venous gas with anion gap is included as a supportive finding — the same consensus report is explicit that a raised anion gap is not, on its own, a recommended first-line diagnostic criterion, since mixed acid–base disorders occur in roughly a third of DKA presentations. Electrolytes and renal function anticipate both the dehydration from osmotic diuresis and the potassium shifts that insulin treatment, if ketoacidosis is confirmed, will provoke. — This is the single instruction the whole algorithm is built around, and it is stated as its own emphasised line for that reason: a clinician anchored on a normal glucose reading has no other prompt in this pathway to think of ketoacidosis at all, so the instruction to check ketones is written to override that anchor explicitly rather than leaving it implicit in a decision rule. — A near-normal blood glucose. Ketoacidosis is usually suspected because of a very high glucose reading; "euglycaemic" ketoacidosis has a normal or only mildly raised glucose instead, which is what makes it easy to miss without deliberately checking ketones. — β-hydroxybutyrate — The dominant ketone body produced in ketoacidosis, measurable directly from a blood sample (point-of-care or laboratory) rather than inferred from urine ketone strips, which detect a different, minor ketone and lag behind the true picture. — A calculated gap between measured positive and negative blood electrolytes. A raised gap is consistent with an unmeasured acid — such as ketones — being present, but current guidance treats it as a supportive finding rather than a stand-alone first-line diagnostic criterion, since mixed acid–base disorders are common in DKA.

entries.title: Dapagliflozin / SGLT2 Inhibitor
entries.nodeLabel: Ketones ≥ 3.0 mmol/L and/or raised anion gap acidosis?
entries.text: Ketones ≥ 3.0 mmol/L and/or raised anion gap acidosis? — This is the branch point of the whole algorithm: whether the patient has biochemical ketoacidosis, regardless of what the glucose reading shows. The blood-ketone threshold matches current consensus guidance directly. The "and/or" framing is a lower bar than the literature's own first-line recommendation, which treats the raised anion gap as a supportive rather than independently sufficient criterion — this algorithm accepts either finding alone as a trigger for the ketoacidosis pathway, rather than requiring the guideline's preferred combination. — Using an "and/or" gate, rather than requiring both findings together, is a deliberately low bar: missing euglycaemic DKA because a single criterion fell just short of a strict combined threshold is a worse failure mode than over-treating a borderline case along the ketoacidosis pathway. — A near-normal blood glucose. Ketoacidosis is usually suspected because of a very high glucose reading; "euglycaemic" ketoacidosis has a normal or only mildly raised glucose instead, which is what makes it easy to miss without deliberately checking ketones. — A calculated gap between measured positive and negative blood electrolytes. A raised gap is consistent with an unmeasured acid — such as ketones — being present, but current guidance treats it as a supportive finding rather than a stand-alone first-line diagnostic criterion, since mixed acid–base disorders are common in DKA.

entries.title: Dapagliflozin / SGLT2 Inhibitor
entries.text:
KETOACIDOSIS — may be euglycaemic — • Stop dapagliflozin
• IV fluid resuscitation
• Fixed-rate insulin infusion
• Give IV dextrose from the outset if normoglycaemic
• Replace K⁺; monitor Mg²⁺
• Identify and treat the precipitant — This bundle matches current multi-society consensus guidance closely. Stopping the SGLT2 inhibitor on admission, fixed-rate IV insulin (started at 0.1 unit/kg/hour), and identifying/treating the precipitant are all explicit recommendations. The dextrose instruction is the one deliberate modification from ordinary hyperglycaemic-DKA management: for euglycaemic DKA specifically, current guidance has dextrose started at the same time as the initial fluids rather than withheld until glucose falls to a treatment threshold, because the insulin infusion is what actually switches off ketogenesis, and dextrose is run alongside it so insulin can continue at a ketone-clearing rate without causing hypoglycaemia. Potassium replacement once levels fall below 5.0 mmol/L, targeting 4–5 mmol/L, is likewise explicit in current guidance. — The instruction to dextrose-cover from the outset, rather than after a glucose threshold is crossed, is the single clinical point that most distinguishes this pathway from ordinary DKA management, and is the direct consequence of the mechanism established earlier: ketogenesis here is driven by the falling insulin:glucagon ratio, not by hyperglycaemia, so treatment has to target the ketosis without being gated by a glucose number that may never rise. — sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 — A protein in the proximal renal tubule responsible for reabsorbing almost all filtered glucose back into the blood. Dapagliflozin and the other drugs in its class block this transporter, causing glucose (and, with it, sodium and water) to be excreted in the urine instead. — The liver's production of ketone bodies (including beta-hydroxybutyrate) from fat, normally switched on during fasting. SGLT2 inhibition can switch this on even without true fasting or hyperglycaemia, by lowering the insulin-to-glucagon ratio — the mechanism behind euglycaemic ketoacidosis. — A near-normal blood glucose. Ketoacidosis is usually suspected because of a very high glucose reading; "euglycaemic" ketoacidosis has a normal or only mildly raised glucose instead, which is what makes it easy to miss without deliberately checking ketones.

entries.title: Dapagliflozin / SGLT2 Inhibitor
entries.text:
NO KETOACIDOSIS — • IV crystalloid to clinical need and urine output
• Correct K⁺ and Mg²⁺
• Recheck renal function — usually prerenal
• Antiemetics as required — If ketoacidosis is excluded, the presentation is treated as volume depletion from the drug's expected osmotic diuresis and natriuresis, compounded by whatever acute illness brought the patient in. Dapagliflozin's own product labelling specifically recommends temporary interruption of treatment for patients who develop volume depletion, until the condition is corrected, which is the same logic behind titrating fluid to clinical need and urine output here rather than giving a fixed bolus. Renal function is rechecked because an acute rise in creatinine in this setting is usually a prerenal pattern from volume loss, which should improve with rehydration, rather than intrinsic renal injury. — This pathway exists because excluding ketoacidosis does not mean excluding dapagliflozin-related illness altogether — the drug's own osmotic-diuretic mechanism is enough on its own to explain dehydration and a reversible creatinine rise, and this box gives that presentation a specific, proportionate treatment plan rather than defaulting to "nothing to do here." — Increased sodium excretion in the urine. Here it travels together with the glucose being excreted, which is why SGLT2 inhibition produces a mild diuretic-like effect on blood pressure and volume status. — A pattern of acute kidney function decline caused by reduced blood flow to otherwise-healthy kidneys (e.g. from dehydration), rather than direct injury to the kidney tissue itself — typically reversible with fluid replacement.

entries.title: Dapagliflozin / SGLT2 Inhibitor
entries.text: Hypoglycaemia present? — Having addressed the ketoacidosis question, the algorithm checks glucose in the other direction. This is placed deliberately after, not before, the ketoacidosis branch, because a normal or low glucose earlier in the workup should not have been reassuring — it is only at this point, once ketoacidosis has been assessed on its own terms, that a genuinely low glucose becomes informative in its own right. — Sequencing the hypoglycaemia question after the ketoacidosis question, rather than screening for both in parallel at triage, keeps the earlier instruction to "measure ketones regardless of glucose" unambiguous: glucose is not ignored, it is simply not allowed to gate the ketone workup.

entries.title: Dapagliflozin / SGLT2 Inhibitor
entries.nodeLabel: Actively seek a CO-INGESTANT (sulphonylurea or insulin).
entries.text: Actively seek a CO-INGESTANT (sulphonylurea or insulin). — Hypoglycaemia is NOT expected from an isolated SGLT2 inhibitor overdose. — Dapagliflozin's glucose-lowering action is not insulin-secretagogue the way a sulfonylurea's is, so it is not expected to drive the blood glucose low enough to cause hypoglycaemia, even in overdose.
