This is borne out in practice: a 13-poison-centre review of 88 single-substance SGLT2 inhibitor exposures — including intentional overdoses, one involving 6000 mg of an SGLT2 inhibitor — found no hypoglycaemia in any case, and a published human dose-escalation study found no apparent change in glycaemic parameters at doses up to 500 mg. A sulfonylurea or exogenous insulin, by contrast, is well established to cause hypoglycaemia as its defining overdose toxicity. Finding hypoglycaemia in this patient is therefore treated as a positive finding pointing elsewhere, not a feature of dapagliflozin toxicity — the history taken in the first box ("any co-ingestant") is revisited here with that specific question in mind. — Stating explicitly that hypoglycaemia is "NOT expected" closes off the most likely diagnostic error at this step: attributing a low glucose to the presenting drug simply because the patient is known to be diabetic and to have taken "too much" of a diabetes medication, when the pharmacology and the real-world case evidence both say this particular medication could not have caused it alone. — sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 — A protein in the proximal renal tubule responsible for reabsorbing almost all filtered glucose back into the blood. Dapagliflozin and the other drugs in its class block this transporter, causing glucose (and, with it, sodium and water) to be excreted in the urine instead. — Another substance taken at the same time as the drug in question. Central to this algorithm because dapagliflozin's own toxicity is limited — most of the danger in a mixed or large ingestion comes from what else was taken.

entries.title: Dapagliflozin / SGLT2 Inhibitor
entries.nodeLabel: DO NOT attempt haemodialysis or haemoperfusion for drug removal
entries.text: DO NOT attempt haemodialysis or haemoperfusion for drug removal — (Vd ≈ 118 L, ~91% protein-bound). Activated charcoal is not routinely indicated. — The two figures given are classic pharmacokinetic reasons to expect extracorporeal removal to be of little use. A large apparent volume of distribution means most of the drug has already left the bloodstream and distributed into tissue, so even efficient blood-side clearance would remove only a small fraction of the total body burden. High protein binding — approximately 91%, confirmed directly in dapagliflozin's own FDA prescribing information — means the fraction of drug free in plasma, the only fraction a dialysis membrane can actually clear, is small to begin with. It is worth being precise about what is and isn't directly established here: the FDA label itself does not say dialysis has been shown ineffective — it says plainly that "the removal of dapagliflozin by hemodialysis has not been studied." The instruction on this page not to attempt it is therefore standard pharmacokinetic reasoning applied to those two parameters (the same reasoning used for many other highly protein-bound, large-volume-of-distribution drugs), not a tested or guideline-stated conclusion. No source discussing activated charcoal specifically for dapagliflozin overdose could be located either. — This box is phrased as an explicit prohibition, in a protocol that otherwise phrases its boxes as instructions to act, because the realistic error here is not omission but a well-intentioned but likely futile intervention: a clinician faced with a large or intentional ingestion may reach for dialysis as an intuitive "get the drug out" response, and the pharmacokinetic parameters — even without a direct removal study to confirm it — give good reason to expect it will not meaningfully help. — apparent volume of distribution (Vd) — A pharmacokinetic value describing how far a drug spreads from the bloodstream into body tissue. A large Vd means most of the drug has left the blood, so even efficient blood-side removal (dialysis) can only ever clear a small fraction of the total dose. — plasma protein binding — The proportion of a drug circulating attached to plasma proteins rather than free in solution. Only the free fraction can cross a dialysis membrane, so a highly protein-bound drug is poorly cleared by dialysis regardless of its concentration.

entries.title: Dapagliflozin / SGLT2 Inhibitor
entries.text: OBSERVATION — extend beyond 4–6 h. — Observe ≥ 12–24 h after significant intentional ingestion with repeat ketones and electrolytes; longer if renal function is impaired on arrival, because the pharmacodynamic effect outlasts the plasma half-life of approximately 13 hours. — The plasma half-life of approximately 13 hours (12.9 hours by the FDA label) is directly confirmed. The specific "12–24 hour" observation window as given is this algorithm's own clinical judgement rather than a published fixed-duration guideline — no consensus toxicology source states that exact figure for SGLT2-inhibitor overdose specifically. Real-world data give a mixed picture: a poison-centre case series found actual follow-up ranged from 1 to 42 hours with a median of only 6 hours, while an isolated severe-overdose case report needed extended ICU observation well beyond 24 hours — though that case was confounded by large co-ingested doses of an antihypertensive and a calcium-channel blocker, not attributable to the SGLT2 inhibitor alone. Given the roughly 13-hour half-life and the persistence of glycosuria for as long as meaningful drug levels remain, extending observation beyond the standard short ED window is a reasonable extrapolation, particularly for a large or intentional ingestion or where renal function (the clearance route) is already impaired — but it should be read as clinical extrapolation, not a cited fixed rule. — "Extend beyond 4–6 h" is written as a correction to a default reflex: a patient who looks well after a few hours of standard observation, with reassuring first-pass bloods, is exactly the patient at risk of being discharged before a delayed ketoacidosis has had time to declare itself. — sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 — A protein in the proximal renal tubule responsible for reabsorbing almost all filtered glucose back into the blood. Dapagliflozin and the other drugs in its class block this transporter, causing glucose (and, with it, sodium and water) to be excreted in the urine instead. — Glucose appearing in the urine — the direct, intended effect of SGLT2 blockade, and the starting point for most of this drug's other effects, wanted and unwanted.

entries.title: Dapagliflozin / SGLT2 Inhibitor
entries.nodeLabel: Contact a regional poisons centre for large or mixed ingestions.
entries.text: Contact a regional poisons centre for large or mixed ingestions. — Arrange psychiatric assessment for every intentional overdose, in parallel with medical care. Do not restart the drug until the patient is metabolically stable and eating normally. — Three separate disposition actions are gathered here. Contacting a poisons centre for large or mixed ingestions is well-established general toxicology practice — a regional resource particularly suited to cases where, as this algorithm has established, co-ingestant toxicity rather than the dapagliflozin itself is likely to dominate the clinical picture. Psychiatric assessment running in parallel with, rather than after, medical treatment matches current national self-harm guidance directly: it specifically instructs that psychosocial assessment should not be delayed until medical treatment is complete, and that physical and mental healthcare should be delivered concurrently so neither is deprioritised. The restart criterion closes the loop back to the mechanism established earlier: a UK regulatory safety communication and a national position statement both support not restarting the drug until the patient's condition has stabilised (and, after a confirmed DKA episode, not restarting at all unless a clear alternative precipitant is identified) — restarting into a still-reduced oral intake would recreate the exact precipitant, relative fasting driving the insulin:glucagon ratio down, that triggers SGLT2-inhibitor-associated ketoacidosis in the first place. The added criterion of "eating normally," specifically, could not be traced to a primary SGLT2-inhibitor-specific guideline in the same way the "stable" criterion could — it appears in secondary patient-education material, and at least one source applies that exact phrasing to other diabetes drug classes rather than to SGLT2 inhibitors. — Ending the algorithm on the restart criterion, rather than on the acute treatment, matters because the single most preventable recurrence in this condition is restarting the drug too early during an ongoing illness — the same "sick-day" logic introduced in the adverse-effects panel at the top of this page, now stated as a discharge-safety instruction rather than a general caution. — sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 — A protein in the proximal renal tubule responsible for reabsorbing almost all filtered glucose back into the blood. Dapagliflozin and the other drugs in its class block this transporter, causing glucose (and, with it, sodium and water) to be excreted in the urine instead. — Another substance taken at the same time as the drug in question. Central to this algorithm because dapagliflozin's own toxicity is limited — most of the danger in a mixed or large ingestion comes from what else was taken.

entries.title: Lidocaine vs Prilocaine
entries.text: Lidocaine vs Prilocaine Local Anaesthesia for Laceration Repair

entries.title: Lidocaine vs Prilocaine
entries.nodeLabel: Laceration requiring local anaesthesia for repair
entries.text: Laceration requiring local anaesthesia for repair — The entry point for this tool: a traumatic wound that needs to be numbed before it can be explored, irrigated and closed. Everything downstream is about choosing and delivering that anaesthesia, not about wound closure technique itself. — Local anaesthesia underpins every step of wound care, and the injection itself is often reported as the most painful part of the whole encounter — which is why so much of this algorithm is about reducing that pain, not just achieving numbness.

entries.title: Lidocaine vs Prilocaine
entries.nodeLabel: Assess the wound and the patient
entries.text:
Assess the wound and the patient — Wound: site, length, depth, contamination, age of wound, need for deep exploration
Patient: age and weight (maximum dose), pregnancy, anaemia, cardiopulmonary disease, G6PD deficiency or methaemoglobinaemia, oxidising drugs (dapsone, nitrates, sulfonamides), amide allergy — Before choosing an agent, two separate sets of factors matter: what the wound itself needs (a deep, contaminated or several-hours-old wound behaves differently under anaesthesia than a clean, fresh, superficial one) and what the patient can safely tolerate (age/weight for dosing, and specifically the list of features that make prilocaine a worse choice). — Inflammation and local acidosis reduce the efficacy of amide local anaesthetics generally, so an old, deep or contaminated wound is already working against anaesthesia before the choice of agent even comes into play. Age/weight-based maximum dosing and a history of amide allergy are standard safety checks before any local anaesthetic is given. — One structural class of local anaesthetics (lidocaine and prilocaine both belong to it, along with bupivacaine and ropivacaine), distinguished from the older ester class by how the drug is metabolised and by a much lower rate of true allergy.

entries.title: Lidocaine vs Prilocaine
entries.nodeLabel: Contraindication or high-risk feature for prilocaine?
entries.text: Contraindication or high-risk feature for prilocaine? — Young infant (<6 months), pregnancy, methaemoglobinaemia or G6PD deficiency, oxidising drugs, significant anaemia or cardiopulmonary disease — Prilocaine's distinctive risk is methaemoglobinaemia: its hepatic metabolite o-toluidine oxidises haemoglobin so it can no longer carry oxygen. This question screens for the patients in whom that risk is least acceptable — before the next question (wound suitability) is even asked. — A 242-episode summary of local-anaesthetic methaemoglobinaemia recommends avoiding prilocaine in infants younger than 6 months and in pregnancy, and dose-reducing with oxidising drugs such as dapsone, nitrates and sulfonamides. That same summary is also why G6PD deficiency belongs on this list: it is a relative contraindication to methylene blue, the usual antidote, because methylene blue's own mechanism depends on an NADPH-generating pathway that G6PD-deficient red cells cannot run properly — so a patient who develops prilocaine-induced methaemoglobinaemia and happens to be G6PD-deficient is harder to treat safely, not necessarily more likely to develop it in the first place. Significant anaemia or cardiopulmonary disease is supported more generally: conditions that already limit oxygen transport can turn an otherwise low-grade methaemoglobinaemia symptomatic. Neither point rests on a prilocaine-specific primary study, so it is flagged rather than over-cited. — A state in which haemoglobin is oxidised to a form (methaemoglobin) that cannot carry oxygen. Prilocaine's liver metabolite, o-toluidine, is a potent oxidiser of haemoglobin, making this prilocaine's signature toxicity. — glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency — An inherited enzyme deficiency that limits a red cell's ability to regenerate the antioxidant glutathione, leaving it less able to defend against oxidative stressors — including the methaemoglobin-forming effect of prilocaine.

entries.title: Lidocaine vs Prilocaine
entries.text:
Avoid prilocaine — Use lidocaine-based anaesthesia:
• LET gel for small facial or scalp wounds (children)
• Lidocaine infiltration otherwise — When any contraindication is present, the pathway simplifies to lidocaine: LET (lidocaine–epinephrine–tetracaine) gel for small facial or scalp wounds in children, where it out-performs the eutectic cream, and lidocaine infiltration for everything else. — Two studies in children found LET gel more reliably produced adequate wound anaesthesia without needing a top-up injection, with similar repair pain, procedure time and complication rates to the lidocaine–prilocaine cream — the basis for preferring LET generally in children. Neither study specifically isolated facial or scalp wounds as the subgroup where LET's advantage is clearest; narrowing the recommendation to that particular context is the review's own clinical synthesis, preserved here as authored rather than independently re-confirmed. — lidocaine–epinephrine–tetracaine gel — A topical anaesthetic gel used mainly in children's facial and scalp lacerations; in several trials it anaesthetises small wounds better than the lidocaine–prilocaine eutectic mixture.

entries.title: Lidocaine vs Prilocaine
entries.nodeLabel: Small, superficial, clean wound AND 45–60 min available before repair?
entries.text: Small, superficial, clean wound AND 45–60 min available before repair? — This is the practical gate on using a topical agent at all: the eutectic cream needs real time to work, and it only performs comparably to infiltration in exactly the kind of wound it was tested in — small, superficial and clean. A deep, contaminated or time-critical wound skips straight to infiltration. — The eutectic lidocaine–prilocaine mixture needs 45–60 minutes under an occlusive dressing to reach adequate onset and depth of anaesthesia. Deeper dermatologic procedures have shown the cream giving less complete anaesthesia than infiltration, and inflammation/acidosis in an older or contaminated wound further undermines any topical agent — both reasons topical treatment is reserved for superficial, clean wounds with time to spare.

entries.title: Lidocaine vs Prilocaine
entries.text:
Lidocaine infiltration (default) — • Lidocaine 1% or 2%, with adrenaline where appropriate (safe in digits)
• Reduce injection pain: buffer, warm, 27–30 G needle, slow subdermal injection through wound edges
• Consider a regional or digital nerve block
• Injected prilocaine offers no advantage for wound infiltration — This is the evidence-based default across the whole algorithm: no randomized trial in two decades has found injected prilocaine to beat injected lidocaine for wound infiltration, and in the one direct comparison available, lidocaine was actually better tolerated. — No adverse event was reported in the small trials that have tested adding adrenaline/epinephrine to lidocaine for digital nerve blocks, which is why many clinicians now consider it acceptable — though that evidence base is thin enough that it disproves the old absolute contraindication more than it positively proves safety. Buffering, warming, a fine needle and slow subdermal injection through the wound edges each have their own supporting trial; the review's own synthesis judges this body of technique evidence stronger than the evidence for switching anaesthetic agent, since no trial of agent-switching for laceration infiltration exists at all. In the one direct skin-infiltration comparison identified, lidocaine with epinephrine caused less pain and was better tolerated than prilocaine with felypressin; a dental Cochrane review's pooled analysis of 2 of its 123 trials similarly found prilocaine-felypressin modestly less effective than lidocaine-epinephrine for achieving anaesthetic success — indirect evidence, from different tissues, but pointing the same way. — A synthetic vasoconstrictor (an analogue of vasopressin) used instead of epinephrine in some prilocaine dental cartridges, chosen for patients in whom epinephrine's cardiac effects are unwanted.

entries.title: Lidocaine vs Prilocaine
entries.text:
Topical lidocaine–prilocaine cream — • Apply at triage under an occlusive dressing for 45–60 min
• Keep the total dose conservative: absorption is higher in an open wound
• Where LET is available, prefer LET for paediatric wounds — For the small, clean, superficial wound where time allows, the needle-free eutectic cream is a reasonable alternative to infiltration — applying it as early as triage turns otherwise-dead waiting time into anaesthesia time. — In the most directly applicable randomized trial, applying the cream at triage in the emergency department did not prolong length of stay, and gave procedural pain statistically similar to lidocaine infiltration. Because an open wound absorbs the agents two- to four-fold more than intact skin in animal pharmacokinetic studies, the total applied dose should stay conservative, particularly in large wounds, small children and patients on oxidising drugs. Where LET is stocked, it remains preferred for paediatric facial/scalp wounds specifically (see "Avoid prilocaine" above) even outside the contraindication pathway. — lidocaine–epinephrine–tetracaine gel — A topical anaesthetic gel used mainly in children's facial and scalp lacerations; in several trials it anaesthetises small wounds better than the lidocaine–prilocaine eutectic mixture.

entries.title: Lidocaine vs Prilocaine
entries.text: Extensive hand or forearm injury? — Intravenous regional anaesthesia (Bier block) with prilocaine 0.5% is preferred in many centres because of its wider systemic safety margin — A single, specific exception to the lidocaine-first pattern: for a Bier block covering an extensive hand or forearm injury, prilocaine's safety margin is why many centres choose it over lidocaine for this particular technique — not because it anaesthetises any better. — A systematic review of Bier block complications (ref 20) found seizures reported at lower cumulative lidocaine doses than prilocaine, and cardiac arrests during IVRA reported with lidocaine and bupivacaine but not with prilocaine — the actual basis for this recommendation. A second trial (ref 19) is included only as supporting context on prilocaine's pharmacokinetics in this technique, since it compares prilocaine with ropivacaine, not lidocaine. Either way, this is a safety margin, not an efficacy advantage, which is why this note sits beside wound infiltration rather than replacing it. — intravenous regional anaesthesia (Bier block) — A technique for anaesthetising an entire limb by injecting local anaesthetic into a vein after applying a tourniquet, used for procedures on the hand or forearm.

entries.title: Lidocaine vs Prilocaine
entries.nodeLabel: Adequate anaesthesia on testing the wound edges?
entries.text: Adequate anaesthesia on testing the wound edges? — Before exploring or closing, the wound edge is tested rather than assumed numb — topical anaesthesia in particular can be patchy or incomplete, so this check is what decides whether infiltration needs to be added before proceeding. — This is a bedside verification step rather than a result drawn from a specific study in this review; no primary source for the testing technique itself was identified, so it is flagged rather than attached to a citation that doesn't actually support it.

entries.title: Lidocaine vs Prilocaine
entries.text: Supplement with lidocaine — Infiltrate through the anaesthetised wound edges — When the topical cream hasn't fully numbed the wound, lidocaine is infiltrated through the already-anaesthetised edges — using the partial numbness the cream achieved to reduce the pain of the top-up injection itself. — Topical lidocaine–prilocaine has been shown to give less complete anaesthesia than infiltration in deeper dermatologic procedures, so a supplementary injection is the expected fallback rather than a sign the topical step failed; injecting through already-numbed tissue is one of the specific technique points shown to reduce injection pain.

entries.title: Lidocaine vs Prilocaine
entries.nodeLabel: Explore, irrigate and close the wound
entries.text: Explore, irrigate and close the wound — The convergence point: whichever route got the patient here — avoiding prilocaine entirely, infiltrating by default, or using (and if needed supplementing) the topical cream — wound exploration, irrigation and closure proceed the same way from here. — Local anaesthesia is a means to this end, not the end itself; every pathway above exists only to get the wound safely and adequately numb for this step.

entries.title: Lidocaine vs Prilocaine
entries.text:
Monitor during and after anaesthesia — After prilocaine: cyanosis or SpO2≈85% not improving with oxygen → suspect methaemoglobinaemia → confirm by co-oximetry → methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV
Either agent: perioral numbness, tinnitus, agitation, seizures or arrhythmia → suspect local anaesthetic systemic toxicity → stop injection, secure airway, give 20% lipid emulsion — Two distinct toxicities to watch for, with different triggers and different antidotes: methaemoglobinaemia is specific to prilocaine (and worsens with dose and the risk factors screened for earlier), while local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) can occur with either agent, usually from inadvertent intravascular injection or an excessive dose. — Methaemoglobinaemia is dose-related and predictable; pulse oximetry is unreliable because it reads a blend of oxy- and methaemoglobin rather than true oxygen saturation, and a 242-episode case summary found an oximetry/arterial-oxygen mismatch in 91.8% of episodes. Co-oximetry is the diagnostic test, and methylene blue is the specific antidote — unless the patient is G6PD-deficient, in which case methylene blue itself becomes relatively contraindicated (see the contraindication-screening box) and alternatives such as exchange transfusion or ascorbic acid, with specialist input, become the fallback. Current ASRA guidance is the standard for recognising and managing LAST, including early use of 20% lipid emulsion. The specific "SpO2≈85%" figure traces to a classic experimental (canine) study showing pulse oximetry plateauing at a characteristic ~84–86% reading as methaemoglobin rises — an animal finding extrapolated here to the bedside teaching point, not a direct human measurement, so the exact number is flagged rather than treated as independently confirmed in people. — If the patient is known to be G6PD-deficient, avoid or use extreme caution with methylene blue for suspected methaemoglobinaemia — it can precipitate haemolysis instead of correcting the methaemoglobin, and alternative treatment should be discussed with a toxicologist or haematologist. — A state in which haemoglobin is oxidised to a form (methaemoglobin) that cannot carry oxygen. Prilocaine's liver metabolite, o-toluidine, is a potent oxidiser of haemoglobin, making this prilocaine's signature toxicity. — Multi-wavelength blood-gas analysis that can distinguish methaemoglobin from normal oxyhaemoglobin, unlike standard two-wavelength pulse oximetry — the test that actually confirms methaemoglobinaemia. — local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) — A dose-related, potentially life-threatening toxicity from excessive local-anaesthetic blood levels (usually inadvertent intravascular injection or an excessive total dose), causing neurological symptoms progressing to seizures and, at the highest levels, cardiac arrhythmia or arrest. — A 20% fat emulsion given intravenously as the specific rescue treatment for local anaesthetic systemic toxicity, thought to act partly by sequestering the lipophilic anaesthetic away from the heart and brain.

entries.title: Lidocaine vs Prilocaine
entries.nodeLabel: Evidence base (GRADE low to very low)
entries.text: Evidence base (GRADE low to very low) — Topical lidocaine–prilocaine vs lidocaine infiltration gave similar procedural pain, below the MCID (d≈0.5; 1.3/10), and abolished the pain of anaesthetic delivery; no trial since 2006 has compared injected prilocaine with lidocaine in traumatic lacerations. — A plain-language summary of how strong the evidence behind this whole algorithm actually is: good enough to support the topical-cream option for small clean wounds, but built on a small, heterogeneous evidence base — not the kind of certainty a fixed drug-dosing table would carry. — Pooling the four eligible randomized trials (one ED laceration trial, three perineal-repair trials; n=492) gave Hedges' g −0.31 (95% CI −1.03 to 0.40) with considerable heterogeneity (I²=94%) driven by one open-label trial; excluding it removed the heterogeneity and gave g 0.06 (95% CI −0.15 to 0.27) — both estimates fall below the minimal clinically important difference (MCID). No randomized trial published between 2006 and 2026 has compared injected prilocaine with injected lidocaine for traumatic lacerations, which is why every recommendation above about injected prilocaine rests on indirect evidence (dental, oculoplastic, regional-anaesthesia studies) rather than a laceration-specific trial. — A standardized effect size, similar to Cohen's d but adjusted for small-study bias, used here to compare pain scores measured on different scales across different trials. — minimal clinically important difference — The smallest change in an outcome (here, roughly 1.3 points on a 0–10 pain scale, or a standardized effect size of about 0.5) that a patient would consider meaningful — used to judge whether a statistically real difference actually matters clinically.

entries.title: Reperfusion Therapy
entries.text: Reperfusion Therapy In Acute Pulmonary Thromboembolism

entries.title: Reperfusion Therapy
entries.text: Confirmed acute pulmonary embolism — The entry point for this tool: a patient with imaging-confirmed acute PE, where the question is no longer diagnosis but which reperfusion strategy — if any — should sit on top of anticoagulation. — Anticoagulation is the therapeutic foundation for the overwhelming majority of patients with PE; this flowchart exists only to identify the minority — those with obstructive shock or with right ventricular dysfunction and impending decompensation — who may benefit from added pharmacological or mechanical reperfusion.

entries.title: Reperfusion Therapy
entries.text: Haemodynamically unstable? — Cardiac arrest, obstructive shock, or persistent hypotension not explained by another cause — The single most important branch point in the whole algorithm: haemodynamic instability — not clot burden on a scan — is what defines high-risk PE and justifies accepting a far higher bleeding risk from full-dose systemic fibrinolysis. — The ESC framework classifies a patient as high risk precisely when haemodynamic instability — cardiac arrest, obstructive shock, or persistent hypotension not explained by another cause — is present. This definition, carried verbatim into the box above, is the first of four sequential questions this review proposes for selecting candidates for reperfusion: is the patient unstable now; if not, is there RV dysfunction with myocardial injury; if so, are there further signals of a trajectory towards decompensation; and what is the bleeding risk.

entries.title: Reperfusion Therapy
entries.text: HIGH-RISK PE — AHA/ACC category E; ESC high risk. Reperfusion is indicated unless futile [4,5] — Haemodynamic instability alone reclassifies the patient as highest-acuity: AHA/ACC category E (established cardiopulmonary failure) under the 2026 five-tier scheme, equivalent to the older ESC high-risk tier — and in this group the default shifts from 'consider reperfusion' to 'reperfuse unless it would be futile.' — Systemic fibrinolysis is recommended by all major guidelines for haemodynamically unstable PE, a recommendation resting on physiological plausibility, registry data reporting 90-day mortality exceeding 50% in massive PE, and a small number of randomised patients rather than one large dedicated trial — an absolute-risk argument, not a relative one: even a substantial bleeding risk is judged acceptable against mortality this high. — The highest-acuity tier (established cardiopulmonary failure) of the 2026 AHA/ACC five-category clinical classification (A to E) for acute PE, intended to characterise severity more finely than the older low/intermediate/high-risk taxonomy.

entries.title: Reperfusion Therapy
entries.text: NORMOTENSIVE PE — Assess right ventricular function and cardiac troponin — The much larger group of patients, where the question shifts from 'reperfuse now' to 'how closely should this patient be watched, and is there already evidence they are failing on anticoagulation alone?' — RV dysfunction on imaging and elevated troponin are the two findings the ESC framework uses to separate intermediate-risk PE from low-risk PE, and both are checked together before any further severity assessment — the second of this review's four sequential questions ('if not unstable, is there objective RV dysfunction with myocardial injury?').

entries.title: Reperfusion Therapy
entries.text: Absolute contraindication to systemic fibrinolysis? — Apply the structured checklist in Table 2 — Before full-dose lysis is given to a crashing patient, the absolute contraindications — prior haemorrhagic stroke, recent major trauma or surgery, active bleeding, suspected aortic dissection, and similar — have to be actively ruled out, not merely assumed absent. — Contraindications should be applied as a structured checklist rather than recalled from memory, and their weight scaled to the indication: in cardiac arrest from confirmed PE a relative contraindication such as recent surgery may reasonably be overridden, since the alternative is death, whereas in a normotensive patient the same finding should usually preclude systemic lysis and redirect the discussion towards catheter-based or mechanical options. The absolute contraindications themselves — prior haemorrhagic stroke or stroke of unknown origin, ischaemic stroke within 6 months, CNS neoplasm/arteriovenous malformation/aneurysm, major trauma/surgery/head injury within 3 weeks, active bleeding, known bleeding diathesis, and suspected aortic dissection — derive largely from the acute coronary and stroke literature and have been carried into PE guidance with little PE-specific validation.

entries.title: Reperfusion Therapy
entries.nodeLabel: RV dysfunction on imaging AND elevated troponin?
entries.text: RV dysfunction on imaging AND elevated troponin? — The formal definition of intermediate-high-risk PE. The figure's own caption is explicit about what happens next: a patient positive for both findings passes directly to the severity-criteria question below, and 'anticoagulation alone' is reached only when at least one of the two is absent. — A structural ambiguity in an earlier draft of this figure (only a NO arrow was drawn from this box, with a 'YES' label sitting on the arrow leading onward from 'Anticoagulation alone') was identified and checked against this review's own text, which states the definition plainly: intermediate-high risk is 'normotensive but has both RV dysfunction on imaging and elevated cardiac troponin', usually with PESI class III-V or sPESI ≥1. The corrected figure's own caption now states this explicitly — patients with both findings pass directly to the severity-criteria assessment, and anticoagulation alone is an endpoint only for those in whom RV dysfunction and troponin elevation are not both present — confirming the correction. — Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index — An externally validated clinical score built from 11 patient variables, used to estimate 30-day mortality risk in PE and to help identify patients (class I-II) suitable for outpatient or early-discharge management. — simplified Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index — A simplified 6-item version of the PESI score; an sPESI of 0 identifies patients at low enough short-term risk to be considered for outpatient treatment.

entries.title: Reperfusion Therapy
entries.text: Anticoagulation alone — Consider early discharge if PESI class I-II, sPESI 0, or Hestia <1 [5] — Without both RV dysfunction and troponin elevation, this patient is low- or intermediate-low-risk, and anticoagulation alone — the therapeutic foundation for the large majority of PE patients — is correct management; a subset identified by validated clinical scores are well enough for outpatient treatment rather than admission. — PESI, simplified PESI (sPESI) and the Hestia criteria are validated clinical decision rules used by major guidelines to identify PE patients at low enough short-term risk to be considered for early discharge or fully outpatient management rather than routine admission. This review's own text does not itself re-derive or re-validate these scores or discuss the Hestia criteria specifically; the early-discharge thresholds shown here follow the figure as authored and are flagged for the reader as established guideline-level practice rather than a primary finding verified within this particular review. — Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index — An externally validated clinical score built from 11 patient variables, used to estimate 30-day mortality risk in PE and to help identify patients (class I-II) suitable for outpatient or early-discharge management. — simplified Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index — A simplified 6-item version of the PESI score; an sPESI of 0 identifies patients at low enough short-term risk to be considered for outpatient treatment. — An alternative 11-item European checklist — rather than a numeric score — used to identify PE patients safe for outpatient or early-discharge management. A patient with none of the Hestia exclusion criteria present is sometimes described as "Hestia-negative" or "Hestia <1."

entries.title: Reperfusion Therapy
entries.text: Full-dose systemic fibrinolysis — Alteplase 100 mg over 2 h, or 0.6 mg/kg over 15 min (max 50 mg) [4,15] — With no absolute contraindication, full-dose systemic alteplase is the default for high-risk PE — the one place in this entire algorithm where the evidence and the risk-benefit balance clearly favour this regimen as first-line therapy over a reduced dose or a catheter-based approach. — Alteplase is given as a 100 mg infusion over two hours, with an accelerated 0.6 mg/kg regimen (maximum 50 mg) reserved for situations such as cardiac arrest where immediate effect is required — standard dosing across guidelines and this review's own pharmacology table. Systemic fibrinolysis is recommended by all major guidelines for haemodynamically unstable PE, resting on physiological plausibility, registry mortality data and a small number of randomised patients rather than one large dedicated high-risk-PE trial. — Standard — Alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours — Accelerated (e.g. cardiac arrest, immediate effect required) — Alteplase 0.6 mg/kg IV over 15 minutes (maximum 50 mg)

entries.title: Reperfusion Therapy
entries.text: Catheter-based or surgical reperfusion — CDT, mechanical thrombectomy, embolectomy, or VA-ECMO as a bridge [24,35] — When an absolute contraindication rules out systemic lysis but the patient is still crashing, the alternatives are local or mechanical: catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) using a fraction of the systemic dose, purely mechanical thrombectomy avoiding lytic drugs altogether, open surgical embolectomy, or VA-ECMO used as a bridge to one of these. — A 2022 ESC/EAPCI clinical consensus statement recommended CDT be considered for high-risk PE with a contraindication to systemic thrombolysis or when it has failed, while explicitly noting no technique has been shown superior to another. Surgical embolectomy is indicated for high-risk PE when thrombolysis is contraindicated or has failed, for right heart thrombus in transit, and for paradoxical embolism through a patent foramen ovale; VA-ECMO can stabilise the failing right ventricle or bridge to one of these other options, though its evidence base remains observational. — catheter-directed thrombolysis — Delivery of a fraction — roughly one-fifth to one-tenth — of the systemic thrombolytic dose directly into the pulmonary-artery thrombus through a catheter, with or without adjunctive ultrasound energy, aiming for local clot lysis while limiting systemic bleeding risk. — venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation — A form of mechanical circulatory support that can stabilise a failing right ventricle, buy time for clot resolution, or bridge a patient to surgical or catheter-based reperfusion in refractory shock or cardiac arrest.

entries.title: Reperfusion Therapy
entries.text: Two or more severity criteria? — Systolic BP <=110 mmHg; respiratory rate >20/min; heart rate >=100/min; SpO2 <90% on air [7,13] — RV dysfunction and troponin elevation alone identify a large, heterogeneous group in which only a small fraction will actually decompensate; adding these bedside markers of physiological stress enriches for the smaller subgroup in whom a reperfusion trial has actually shown benefit. — Post hoc analysis of the PEITHO population showed that adding simple bedside markers of physiological stress to RV dysfunction and troponin elevation identifies a subgroup at appreciably higher short-term risk, an enrichment strategy subsequently adopted by HI-PEITHO, which required RV dysfunction and elevated troponin plus at least two of the four criteria shown above. One nuance worth flagging here: HI-PEITHO's own published enrolment criteria combined respiratory rate above 20/min and SpO2 below 90% into a single composite item, so the trial actually required two of three independent criteria, not two of four fully independent ones as this box (following the source figure) presents them. The underlying clinical substance — more physiological-stress markers identifies higher-risk patients — is unaffected by this simplification, but it is worth knowing the exact trial threshold differs slightly from how it is drawn here.

entries.title: Reperfusion Therapy
entries.text: Anticoagulation and close monitoring — Reassess frequently; rescue reperfusion if the patient deteriorates [4] — With RV dysfunction and troponin elevation but fewer than two additional severity criteria, this patient is intermediate-high risk but not in the enriched subgroup HI-PEITHO studied — the correct default remains anticoagulation, with frequent reassessment rather than routine reperfusion. — Systemic fibrinolysis is explicitly not recommended as first-line therapy for intermediate-high-risk PE, in whom close monitoring with rescue reperfusion on deterioration is preferred; the ESC framework is built around this contingency, and this review states plainly that for most intermediate-risk patients the correct answer remains anticoagulation with close observation and a clear escalation plan.

entries.title: Reperfusion Therapy
entries.nodeLabel: If lysis fails or arrest occurs
entries.text: If lysis fails or arrest occurs — Escalate to catheter-based or surgical reperfusion, and continue resuscitation for 60-90 min after the lytic is given [24,58] — Persistent or recurrent instability after full-dose systemic lysis defines failed thrombolysis. Repeating the systemic dose is generally discouraged because it compounds bleeding risk, so the next step is catheter-based or surgical reperfusion instead, with resuscitation continued for an extended period because thrombolytic effect during cardiac arrest can be delayed. — Guidelines and consensus statements support proceeding to catheter-based reperfusion or surgical embolectomy after failed systemic lysis, ideally with mechanical circulatory support where the patient is in refractory shock. Where thrombolysis is given during cardiac arrest specifically, a systematic review and meta-analysis restricted to PE-related arrest found higher rates of return of spontaneous circulation but no significant difference in survival to discharge, and the broader literature supports continuing resuscitation for at least 60 to 90 minutes before termination, since delayed responses to thrombolysis during arrest are well described.

entries.title: Reperfusion Therapy
entries.text: Activate PERT and consider reperfusion — Catheter-directed thrombolysis reduced 7-day decompensation without excess bleeding (HI-PEITHO) [7]. Full-dose systemic lysis is not first-line [4,5] — This is the enriched intermediate-risk subgroup — RV dysfunction, troponin elevation, and two or more severity criteria — in which a randomised trial has, for the first time, shown that catheter-based reperfusion improves a clinical outcome. A multidisciplinary pulmonary embolism response team (PERT) is the recommended way to weigh that option against the default of anticoagulation alone. — HI-PEITHO enrolled 544 patients meeting exactly this profile and found the seven-day composite of PE-related death, cardiorespiratory decompensation or collapse, and symptomatic recurrent PE occurred in 4.0% of the catheter-directed-thrombolysis group versus 10.3% of the anticoagulation-alone group (relative risk 0.39, P=0.005, number needed to treat approximately 16), with no significant difference in major bleeding. Two caveats this review's own discussion raises are worth stating alongside that headline result: the benefit was driven almost entirely by less cardiorespiratory decompensation, a softer composite component than mortality — PE-related death was rare and, while not significantly different, numerically higher in the catheter-directed-thrombolysis arm (0.4% versus 1.1% with anticoagulation alone) — and the trial was open-label, so decompensation, though blindly adjudicated, was still ascertained in an unblinded clinical environment. Full-dose systemic lysis is explicitly not recommended as first-line therapy in this population, which is why this box specifies catheter-directed treatment rather than systemic thrombolysis. The 2026 multisociety guideline elevates PERT activation itself to a Class 1 recommendation for intermediate- and high-risk PE. — pulmonary embolism response team — A multidisciplinary team — emergency medicine, cardiology, pulmonology, critical care, haematology, interventional radiology and cardiac surgery — convened for rapid consultation on intermediate- and high-risk PE. The 2026 multisociety guideline elevates its activation to a Class 1 recommendation. — The number of patients who would need to receive an intervention for one additional patient to benefit, compared with the control. HI-PEITHO's number needed to treat of approximately 16 means roughly 1 in 16 patients treated with catheter-directed thrombolysis instead of anticoagulation alone avoided the seven-day composite outcome.

entries.title: Reperfusion Therapy
entries.nodeLabel: At any point, haemodynamic deterioration on adequate anticoagulation is an indication for rescue reperfusion [4,35]
entries.text: At any point, haemodynamic deterioration on adequate anticoagulation is an indication for rescue reperfusion [4,35] — A floating safety-net reminder that applies across every branch of this algorithm, not only the two explicit 'reassess and rescue' boxes above: a patient's risk category on presentation is a starting point, not a fixed label, and any trajectory towards decompensation — wherever it is first noticed — should prompt reconsidering reperfusion. — Guidelines and consensus statements consistently build rescue reperfusion into the management of patients who deteriorate on anticoagulation, regardless of their initial risk category; the ESC framework in particular is explicitly structured around this contingency. The source figure places this note disconnected from the rest of the diagram, with no arrows in or out, for exactly this reason: it is not one more step in a sequence but a standing condition that overrides the sequence whenever it applies.

entries.title: LMWH Selection & Renal Dosing
entries.text: LMWH Selection & Renal Dosing In Unstable Angina / NSTEMI

entries.title: LMWH Selection & Renal Dosing
entries.nodeLabel: Adult with unstable angina or NSTEMI
entries.text:
Adult with unstable angina or NSTEMI — Aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor started
Assess ischaemic and bleeding risk (e.g., CRUSADE score) — The starting point for this algorithm: a patient with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTE-ACS) — unstable angina or NSTEMI — who has already been started on dual antiplatelet therapy and is now being assessed for a parenteral anticoagulant alongside it. — Parenteral anticoagulation added to antiplatelet therapy is a core, guideline-recommended component of initial NSTE-ACS management, reducing early ischaemic events on top of aspirin alone. Formal bleeding-risk scoring such as the CRUSADE score at this point helps balance that ischaemic benefit against the bleeding risk the chosen anticoagulant and its dose will carry. — A validated bleeding-risk score for NSTE-ACS, derived and validated in a registry of nearly 18,000 patients, used to estimate a patient's baseline risk of major in-hospital bleeding before an anticoagulant is chosen. — non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome — The umbrella term for unstable angina and non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) together — acute coronary syndromes that, unlike STEMI, do not show ST-segment elevation on the presenting ECG.

entries.title: LMWH Selection & Renal Dosing
entries.text: Invasive angiography planned within 24 hours? — The anticoagulant choice in current guidelines turns on management strategy: whether the patient is going for early invasive angiography (within 24 hours) or being managed with a more conservative, delayed-or-no-angiography approach. — Current European and American guidance frames the anticoagulant choice around this same branch point — unfractionated heparin for patients proceeding to early invasive management, fondaparinux (or, if unavailable, an LMWH) when early angiography is not planned — reflecting each agent's practical fit with the periprocedural setting rather than a difference in NSTE-ACS-specific trial evidence between the two strategies themselves. — non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome — The umbrella term for unstable angina and non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) together — acute coronary syndromes that, unlike STEMI, do not show ST-segment elevation on the presenting ECG.

entries.title: LMWH Selection & Renal Dosing
entries.text:
Unfractionated heparin preferred — 60–70 IU/kg IV bolus (max 5,000 IU), then 12–15 IU/kg/h (aPTT 1.5–2.5 × control); 70–100 IU/kg at PCI
If already on SC enoxaparin: continue it through PCI; do not switch — When early invasive management is planned, unfractionated heparin (UFH) — not an LMWH — is the preferred anticoagulant, dosed and monitored to a weight-based bolus/infusion regimen with aPTT targets, plus a separate weight-based bolus at the time of PCI itself. — UFH's short half-life and reversibility fit the periprocedural setting, and current guidelines name it the preferred agent when angiography is imminent. The 'do not switch' instruction reflects this review's own synthesis and direct trial evidence: in the SYNERGY PCI substudy, crossing over between anticoagulants during the same admission sharply increased bleeding in both directions, which is part of why switching between UFH and an LMWH — or between LMWHs — during one admission is specifically discouraged throughout this algorithm. — IV bolus — 60–70 IU/kg (max 5,000 IU) — Infusion — 12–15 IU/kg/h, titrated to aPTT 1.5–2.5 × control — At PCI — 70–100 IU/kg — If a patient is already established on subcutaneous enoxaparin, continuing it through PCI rather than switching to UFH avoids exactly the crossover-related bleeding increase described above.

entries.title: LMWH Selection & Renal Dosing
entries.text:
Fondaparinux preferred — 2.5 mg SC once daily (lowest bleeding risk vs enoxaparin)
If unavailable or not chosen: use an LMWH (below) — When early invasive management is not planned, fondaparinux is the preferred anticoagulant — a fixed-dose, once-daily factor Xa inhibitor with the lowest bleeding risk of any agent compared head-to-head with enoxaparin in a large trial. Where fondaparinux is unavailable or not chosen, an LMWH is the fallback, which is what the rest of this algorithm addresses. — In OASIS-5, fondaparinux was non-inferior to enoxaparin for the ischaemic composite at 9 days and nearly halved major bleeding (2.2% vs 4.1%); subsequent meta-analyses have confirmed the lower-bleeding finding at every time point measured. This is the single strongest, most consistent piece of comparative evidence anywhere in this algorithm — considerably more robust than the LMWH-vs-LMWH evidence that follows below. — Fondaparinux — 2.5 mg SC once daily

entries.title: LMWH Selection & Renal Dosing
entries.nodeLabel: If an LMWH is used, prefer the agent with most outcome data; use each agent only at its own tested regimen
entries.text: If an LMWH is used, prefer the agent with most outcome data; use each agent only at its own tested regimen — This is the central practical conclusion of the systematic review this algorithm is built from: among enoxaparin, nadroparin and dalteparin, choose the one with the most outcome data behind it, and whichever is used, give it at its own specific, independently validated dose — never at another agent's dose. — The review found no randomised evidence of a clinically important difference among the three LMWHs in unstable angina or NSTEMI, but the trials comparing them head-to-head were few, small and mostly at high risk of bias — nowhere near large enough to prove the agents are equivalent either. Absence of proven difference is not evidence of interchangeability: the pooled enoxaparin-vs-dalteparin confidence interval alone spans from a moderate benefit of enoxaparin to a real deficit, and the three agents differ pharmacologically (manufacturing process, molecular weight, anti-Xa:anti-IIa ratio) in ways that plausibly matter clinically even without trial proof yet. — anti-factor Xa activity — A laboratory measure of how strongly a heparin-based anticoagulant is inhibiting factor Xa, used both as a dosing target (particularly for enoxaparin) and, in some of the trials behind this algorithm, as a pharmacodynamic trial endpoint in its own right. — Shorthand, throughout this algorithm, for a difference judged large enough to matter to patients — operationalised in the review behind this tool as a standardised effect size (Cohen's d) of at least 0.20. A result can fail to reach this threshold, fall short of it, or have a confidence interval too wide to rule it in or out, all of which are different from the two agents being proven equivalent.

entries.title: LMWH Selection & Renal Dosing
entries.text:
First choice — Enoxaparin
1 mg/kg SC every 12 h
Largest RCT evidence and only LMWH named in ESC/ACC-AHA guidance — Enoxaparin is the default LMWH choice: the only one of the three with a large, modern randomised trial programme behind it, and the only one specifically named in current European and American NSTE-ACS guidelines. — Enoxaparin was superior to UFH in its pivotal trials and, across a systematic overview of six trials and nearly 22,000 patients, reduced 30-day death or MI (OR 0.91) without a significant increase in major bleeding or transfusion. A larger 12-trial, roughly 49,000-patient meta-analysis found the same ischaemic benefit at the cost of more major bleeding, with net clinical benefit neutral in NSTE-ACS specifically (as opposed to the full acute coronary syndrome spectrum, where it was clearly favourable). No comparable trial programme exists for dalteparin or nadroparin, which is the main reason current guidelines name enoxaparin specifically. — Enoxaparin — 1 mg/kg SC every 12 h — non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome — The umbrella term for unstable angina and non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) together — acute coronary syndromes that, unlike STEMI, do not show ST-segment elevation on the presenting ECG.

entries.title: LMWH Selection & Renal Dosing
entries.text:
Alternative — Dalteparin
120 IU/kg SC every 12 h (max 10,000 IU)
No proven difference vs enoxaparin — Dalteparin, at its own weight-based dose, is an acceptable alternative where formulary or availability constraints require it — not because it has been shown equivalent to enoxaparin, but because no head-to-head trial has shown it to be worse. — Three small trials compared enoxaparin with dalteparin directly; pooling the two with comparable composite endpoints gave an odds ratio of 0.74 (95% CI 0.37–1.47) — favouring enoxaparin numerically but falling short of a clinically important difference, with a confidence interval wide enough to be compatible with either agent being meaningfully better. No trial found a significant difference in bleeding between the two. This genuinely is 'no proven difference' rather than 'proven equivalence' — the distinction the whole algorithm is built around. — Dalteparin — 120 IU/kg SC every 12 h (max 10,000 IU) — Shorthand, throughout this algorithm, for a difference judged large enough to matter to patients — operationalised in the review behind this tool as a standardised effect size (Cohen's d) of at least 0.20. A result can fail to reach this threshold, fall short of it, or have a confidence interval too wide to rule it in or out, all of which are different from the two agents being proven equivalent.

entries.title: LMWH Selection & Renal Dosing
entries.text:
Alternative — Nadroparin
86 IU/kg SC every 12 h
Lower early anti-Xa than enoxaparin; ask about prior heparin skin reactions — Nadroparin, at its own weight-based dose, is the second alternative — again not proven equivalent to enoxaparin, and with one real pharmacodynamic difference worth knowing about: it produces measurably lower early anticoagulant activity at its recommended dose. — In a small pharmacodynamic trial, mean anti-Xa activity 3 hours after the first dose was more than twice as high with enoxaparin as with nadroparin (0.65 vs 0.30 IU/mL), and the therapeutic target was reached in 66.7% of enoxaparin-treated versus only 10.0% of nadroparin-treated patients. This shows the two agents produce different early pharmacodynamic profiles at their respective recommended doses — evidence against treating them as interchangeable — but because clinical outcomes were not reported in that trial, it cannot by itself prove a difference in clinical efficacy. A separate trial of enoxaparin and nadroparin, both given alongside tirofiban, found similar in-hospital major adverse cardiac events (19% vs 15%, OR 1.30, 95% CI 0.37–4.60) — again a wide, inconclusive interval, not evidence of equivalence. — Nadroparin — 86 IU/kg SC every 12 h — Nadroparin carries by far the highest reported risk of heparin-induced delayed-type cutaneous hypersensitivity among the anticoagulants compared in pooled safety data (odds ratio 30.2) — worth asking about before choosing it, even though this is a non-haemorrhagic safety signal rather than an efficacy difference. — anti-factor Xa activity — A laboratory measure of how strongly a heparin-based anticoagulant is inhibiting factor Xa, used both as a dosing target (particularly for enoxaparin) and, in some of the trials behind this algorithm, as a pharmacodynamic trial endpoint in its own right. — MACE — A composite outcome combining death, myocardial infarction, and other serious cardiac events, used as a trial endpoint in several of the head-to-head LMWH comparisons behind this algorithm.

entries.title: LMWH Selection & Renal Dosing
entries.nodeLabel: Check renal function (CrCl) and body weight; recalculate dose (never unit-for-unit)
entries.text: Check renal function (CrCl) and body weight; recalculate dose (never unit-for-unit) — Before continuing any LMWH, renal function and body weight need to be checked and the dose recalculated for that specific agent — never simply carried over milligram-for-milligram or unit-for-unit from another LMWH, or left at a standard dose that hasn't been adjusted for this patient. — All three LMWHs are cleared predominantly by the kidney, and dose-related bleeding risk in renal impairment is best documented for enoxaparin specifically. In a population pharmacokinetic study, enoxaparin clearance fell with declining creatinine clearance and patients with low clearance had a 3.8-fold higher risk of major haemorrhage; a separate meta-analysis confirmed higher anti-Xa levels and more major bleeding with unadjusted therapeutic-dose enoxaparin in severe renal impairment, while data for dalteparin in the same setting were explicitly insufficient to draw conclusions. In real-world practice this step is often skipped: a national survey found LMWH doses were not adjusted for renal failure in 71% of hospitals. — anti-factor Xa activity — A laboratory measure of how strongly a heparin-based anticoagulant is inhibiting factor Xa, used both as a dosing target (particularly for enoxaparin) and, in some of the trials behind this algorithm, as a pharmacodynamic trial endpoint in its own right.

entries.title: LMWH Selection & Renal Dosing
entries.text: CrCl 15-29 mL/min — Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC once daily; other LMWHs: reduce dose per product label — In moderate-to-severe renal impairment, enoxaparin's dose interval changes from twice daily to once daily at the same per-kilogram dose; dalteparin and nadroparin should likewise be reduced from their standard regimen, following their own product labelling rather than enoxaparin's once-daily rule. — This step-down reflects the accumulation risk documented for enoxaparin at full twice-daily dosing as renal function falls, and the general principle — repeated throughout this algorithm — that each LMWH's renal dose adjustment has to be looked up for that specific agent rather than inferred from another one's label. — Enoxaparin (CrCl 15–29 mL/min) — 1 mg/kg SC once daily

entries.title: LMWH Selection & Renal Dosing
entries.text: CrCl <15 mL/min — or dialysis: use UFH with aPTT monitoring; avoid LMWHs — Below a creatinine clearance of 15 mL/min, or in a patient on dialysis, no LMWH dose adjustment is considered safe enough — the recommendation switches back to unfractionated heparin with aPTT monitoring, the same reversible, non-renally-cleared agent used for patients going for early angiography. — Accumulation and bleeding risk in severe renal impairment are best documented for enoxaparin, where a meta-analysis found an excess of major bleeding with unadjusted therapeutic dosing; data for dalteparin and nadroparin in this setting are sparse rather than reassuring, which is part of why this algorithm does not attempt to offer a reduced LMWH dose at this level of renal function at all.

entries.title: LMWH Selection & Renal Dosing
entries.text: Special populations — Weight >150 kg, frailty or unstable renal function: anti-Xa 3-4 h after dose (enoxaparin 0.5-1.2 IU/mL) — At the extremes of body weight, in frailty, or when renal function is changing from day to day, weight-based dosing formulas become less reliable — so anti-Xa level monitoring, rather than the dose formula alone, is used to confirm the patient is actually in a safe and effective range. — Enoxaparin dosing by actual body weight appears appropriate up to moderate obesity, and a SYNERGY substudy and a recent meta-analysis both found obesity did not meaningfully change enoxaparin's efficacy or bleeding risk — but these reassuring findings come from studies of obesity alone, not the combination of obesity with renal impairment or genuine frailty that this box is aimed at, where monitoring rather than formula-trust is the more cautious approach. — Anti-Xa target (enoxaparin), measured 3–4 h post-dose — 0.5–1.2 IU/mL — anti-factor Xa activity — A laboratory measure of how strongly a heparin-based anticoagulant is inhibiting factor Xa, used both as a dosing target (particularly for enoxaparin) and, in some of the trials behind this algorithm, as a pharmacodynamic trial endpoint in its own right.

entries.title: LMWH Selection & Renal Dosing
entries.text:
All patients — Continue until revascularisation or discharge (maximum about 8 days); stop after uncomplicated PCI.
Avoid switching between UFH and LMWH, or between LMWHs, during the same admission.
Double-check weight-based doses: excess dosing accounts for a substantial share of major bleeding. — Three rules apply regardless of which anticoagulant pathway was taken: there is a natural stopping point (revascularisation, discharge, or roughly 8 days, whichever comes first, and earlier still after an uncomplicated PCI), the chosen agent should not be swapped for a different one mid-admission, and every weight-based dose is worth double-checking before it is given. — The 'no switching' rule is grounded directly in trial evidence: the SYNERGY PCI substudy showed bleeding rose sharply in both directions whenever patients crossed over between anticoagulants. The dosing-error warning is grounded just as directly: in a large North American registry, excess dosing of antithrombotic agents — more common in older patients, women, and those with renal insufficiency — was estimated to account for 15% of major bleeding in that population, a preventable share of harm that has nothing to do with which anticoagulant was chosen in the first place.

entries.title: Ketamine in Head Injury
entries.text: Ketamine in Head Injury Safety Analysis & Complication Management

entries.title: Ketamine in Head Injury
entries.nodeLabel: Head-injured patient requiring induction/RSI, sedation or analgesia
entries.text: Head-injured patient requiring induction/RSI, sedation or analgesia — The entry point to this algorithm: any head-injured patient for whom ketamine is being considered for one of three distinct roles — induction/rapid sequence intubation, ongoing ICU sedation, or analgesia in a conscious patient. — Traumatic brain injury carries a very large global burden, with an estimated 69 million people sustaining one every year, and outcome is shaped as much by secondary insults in the hours afterward as by the primary impact. Contemporary severe-TBI guidelines place the choice of sedative, analgesic and induction agent within the first tier of intracranial-pressure management, which is why that choice gets its own structured algorithm rather than being left to habit or the historical (and, as the rest of this tool sets out, outdated) reflex to avoid ketamine in head injury altogether.

entries.title: Ketamine in Head Injury
entries.text: Initial assessment: — GCS, pupils/herniation signs, SBP/MAP, heart rate, shock index (HR/SBP), SpO2, EtCO2; start resuscitation (airway, oxygenation, haemorrhage control) — Before any ketamine decision is made, a baseline primary survey is completed, including the shock index (heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure) — the single bedside number this algorithm uses later to decide how much to reduce the induction dose and whether to pre-empt hypotension with a vasopressor. — Hypotension is one of the most powerful, modifiable predictors of death after TBI: in a large prehospital cohort, every 10 mmHg increase in the lowest prehospital systolic blood pressure was associated with an 18.8% reduction in the adjusted odds of death, with no safe lower threshold identified between 40 and 119 mmHg. The Glasgow Coma Scale anchors every downstream severity and reassessment decision in this algorithm, and the shock index specifically is the one physiological number shown to predict which patients will become hypotensive after ketamine induction. — heart rate ÷ systolic blood pressure — A simple bedside ratio, normally well below 1, that rises before systolic blood pressure itself falls. Used throughout this algorithm as the trigger for a reduced ketamine induction dose and pre-emptive vasopressor readiness, since post-induction hypotension is concentrated almost entirely in patients with a shock index ≥0.9.

entries.title: Ketamine in Head Injury
entries.text: Indication for ketamine? — This is not a yes/no gate but a three-way fork: the same drug is being considered for three pharmacologically distinct roles, each with its own dose range and its own safety considerations, so the algorithm splits here into pathways A, B and C below. — Ketamine's unusual pharmacological profile — dissociative anaesthesia, potent analgesia, generally preserved airway reflexes and spontaneous ventilation, and blood-pressure support through sympathomimetic effects — is what makes a single drug plausible across all three roles (induction, sedation and analgesia) in the first place, rather than being restricted to one of them.

entries.title: Ketamine in Head Injury
entries.text: A. Induction / RSI — The first of the three indication pathways: ketamine used as the induction agent for rapid sequence intubation. — Large modern trials of emergency intubation in critically ill adults have specifically compared ketamine with etomidate for this exact role, which is why RSI is treated as its own pathway with its own dosing logic below rather than folded into general sedation dosing.

entries.title: Ketamine in Head Injury
entries.text:
Shock index ≥0.9 or SBP <100 mmHg? — YES: resuscitate first (fluids/blood); prepare vasopressor; ketamine 0.5–1 mg/kg IV (esketamine: half dose)

NO: ketamine 1–2 mg/kg IV (esketamine 0.5–1 mg/kg) + neuromuscular blocker — The induction dose is split by the shock-index/SBP check performed at initial assessment: a haemodynamically compromised patient gets resuscitated first and a reduced dose with a vasopressor on standby, while a haemodynamically normal patient gets a full conventional induction dose plus a neuromuscular blocker. Esketamine, being roughly twice as potent as racemic ketamine, is dosed at half the corresponding racemate dose throughout. — A shock index ≥0.9 is the specific threshold at which ketamine-associated hypotension becomes common: in a prehospital cohort, hypotension occurred in 26% of patients with a shock index ≥0.9 but in only 2% of those below that threshold, where systolic pressure actually rose after induction. Conventional full doses of 1–2 mg/kg IV were used in the major contemporary intubation trials comparing ketamine with etomidate. The complication-management literature behind this algorithm explicitly recommends calculating the shock index before induction, reducing the dose and preparing a vasopressor in advance when it is ≥0.9, rather than reacting to hypotension only after it occurs. — Ketamine is preferable to propofol in haemodynamically unstable patients, while the choice between ketamine and etomidate should be individualised — weighing ketamine's small excess risk of peri-intubation cardiovascular collapse against etomidate's adrenal suppression — rather than treated as a fixed rule. — heart rate ÷ systolic blood pressure — A simple bedside ratio, normally well below 1, that rises before systolic blood pressure itself falls. Used throughout this algorithm as the trigger for a reduced ketamine induction dose and pre-emptive vasopressor readiness, since post-induction hypotension is concentrated almost entirely in patients with a shock index ≥0.9. — S(+)-ketamine — The S(+)-enantiomer of ketamine, roughly twice as potent as the racemic mixture used elsewhere in this algorithm — doses are halved whenever esketamine is substituted — and associated with somewhat fewer cognitive disturbances on emergence.

entries.title: Ketamine in Head Injury
entries.text: B. ICU sedation (ventilated) — The second pathway: ketamine as a continuous-infusion adjunct to standard ICU sedation in a mechanically ventilated patient, rather than a single induction dose. — Ketamine's ICP and complication profile has mostly been studied in exactly this setting — ventilated, co-sedated neurocritical care patients — which is why controlled ventilation and co-sedation are written directly into this pathway's content rather than left implicit.

entries.title: Ketamine in Head Injury
entries.nodeLabel: Ketamine 0.5–3 mg/kg/h as adjunct to propofol or midazolam
entries.text:
Ketamine 0.5–3 mg/kg/h as adjunct to propofol or midazolam — Controlled ventilation, normocapnia (PaCO2 35–45 mmHg)

ICP/CPP monitoring where available; consider ≥1.15 mg/kg/h only in trials targeting spreading depolarisations — An infusion dose range spanning a low, sub-anaesthetic adjunct dose up to a higher physiological-target dose, always alongside — never instead of — a standard sedative, with ventilation controlled to a normal carbon-dioxide target. The higher end of the suppression-of-spreading-depolarisation dose range is explicitly marked as a research-only use, not routine practice. — Adjunctive ketamine at around 0.5 mg/kg/h has reduced propofol and fentanyl requirements without changing ICP or CPP, while a 3 mg/kg/h infusion targeted at physiological endpoints transiently increased CPP and lowered ICP. No included study demonstrated a sustained, clinically important ICP increase when ketamine was given with controlled ventilation and co-sedation; this is the mechanistic basis for the box's wording. Suppression of spreading depolarisations — waves of neuronal depolarisation linked to worse TBI outcome — has only been shown at doses of at least 1.15 mg/kg/h in a small randomised crossover trial, which is why this algorithm restricts that higher dose to trial settings rather than offering it as routine sedation. — The only adequately designed pilot RCT testing a high-dose, physiological-target ketamine infusion with a functional endpoint did not demonstrate an improvement in 3-month functional outcome (GOS-E) compared with saline, and the overall effect of ketamine on functional recovery remains uncertain — the ≥1.15 mg/kg/h dose is for depolarisation-suppression trials specifically, not a general-purpose escalation. — Waves of near-complete neuronal depolarisation that occur in more than half of patients with severe TBI and are independently associated with worse outcome. Ketamine suppresses them in a dose-dependent manner — the rationale, still investigational, for the higher infusion doses used only in trials targeting this mechanism. — Glasgow Outcome Scale–Extended — An 8-point scale measuring longer-term functional recovery after brain injury, used as the main outcome in trials testing whether ketamine's effects on ICP or vasopressor requirement actually translate into better patient-centred recovery — so far without a clearly demonstrated benefit.

entries.title: Ketamine in Head Injury
entries.text: C. Analgesia (conscious patient) — The third pathway: low-dose, titrated ketamine analgesia in a patient who is conscious and not being sedated or intubated — typically mild head injury with a co-existing painful extracranial injury. — This is the one pathway where the patient's own neurological examination is actively ongoing throughout treatment, which is why documentation and reassessment timing (rather than a dose table alone) are the content of this pathway's box.

entries.title: Ketamine in Head Injury
entries.text:
Sub-dissociative ketamine 0.1–0.3 mg/kg IV (titrated) — Opioid-sparing for extracranial injuries

Document dose time; repeat GCS after psychotomimetic effects resolve — A low, titrated dose well below the dissociative range, used to reduce opioid requirements for painful extracranial injuries without sedating the patient — with an explicit instruction to document when the dose was given and to wait for its transient psychiatric side effects to pass before trusting the next neurological exam. — Intravenous subdissociative-dose ketamine (around 0.1–0.3 mg/kg) has shown analgesia comparable to morphine in emergency-department trials and systematic reviews, with an opioid-sparing effect that is attractive in head-injured patients where opioid-induced sedation would otherwise confound the neurological exam. At these lower doses, transient dysphoria and disorientation can still complicate the serial Glasgow Coma Scale assessments that mild-to-moderate TBI management depends on — the reason this box explicitly calls for documenting dose timing and reassessing only once those effects have resolved.

entries.title: Ketamine in Head Injury
entries.nodeLabel: Continuous monitoring: SBP/MAP, HR, SpO2, EtCO2, ICP/CPP, sedation depth, EEG if comatose
entries.text: Continuous monitoring: SBP/MAP, HR, SpO2, EtCO2, ICP/CPP, sedation depth, EEG if comatose — Regardless of which of the three pathways above was used, the same continuous physiological and neuromonitoring applies afterward — this is the single point all three branches converge on before any complication is managed. — These are the core first-tier physiological targets in contemporary severe-TBI management guidelines. Continuous EEG is specified for comatose patients in particular because it is how spreading depolarisations — independently linked to worse outcome and suppressible by ketamine in a dose-dependent manner — are actually detected and followed in practice. — Waves of near-complete neuronal depolarisation that occur in more than half of patients with severe TBI and are independently associated with worse outcome. Ketamine suppresses them in a dose-dependent manner — the rationale, still investigational, for the higher infusion doses used only in trials targeting this mechanism.

entries.title: Ketamine in Head Injury
entries.text: Complication recognised → manage — A second branch point, not sequential with the first: at any point during monitoring, if one of the specific complications below is recognised, management jumps directly to that complication's own box. The source figure draws only two arrows out of this decision — to the top box of each column below — with the remaining four complication boxes in each column listed underneath as a grouped set rather than individually arrowed; that grouping is preserved exactly as drawn. — Structuring complication management as a recognise-then-jump decision, rather than a linear checklist, reflects how these complications actually present clinically — independently and at unpredictable times — rather than in the fixed order they happen to be listed in.

entries.title: Ketamine in Head Injury
entries.text: Hypotension / cardiovascular collapse: — vasopressor (noradrenaline or push-dose agent), fluids/blood, reduce or stop further doses; keep SBP ≥100–110 mmHg — The management pathway for ketamine-associated hypotension or peri-intubation cardiovascular collapse: vasopressor support, volume resuscitation, cutting back or stopping further ketamine dosing, and a blood-pressure target to manage toward. — Hypotension is the principal safety signal for ketamine in this evidence base: a meta-analysis found more hypotension episodes in TBI cohorts receiving ketamine (risk ratio 1.47), and large intubation trials in critically ill adults found more cardiovascular collapse with ketamine than etomidate (22.1% vs 17.0%; network-meta-analysis odds ratio 1.44). This risk concentrates specifically in patients with a high shock index, who are thought to be relatively catecholamine-depleted and therefore unable to mount the sympathomimetic response ketamine's blood-pressure support ordinarily depends on — which is why dose reduction and advance vasopressor preparation (set up already at the shock-index check in pathway A) are the first-line response here, alongside the same systolic blood pressure target used in general TBI management guidelines. — heart rate ÷ systolic blood pressure — A simple bedside ratio, normally well below 1, that rises before systolic blood pressure itself falls. Used throughout this algorithm as the trigger for a reduced ketamine induction dose and pre-emptive vasopressor readiness, since post-induction hypotension is concentrated almost entirely in patients with a shock index ≥0.9.

entries.title: Ketamine in Head Injury
entries.text: Emergence reaction / agitation: — midazolam 0.03 mg/kg IV; calm environment; use lowest effective dose; consider esketamine — The management pathway for dysphoric emergence phenomena and agitation on recovery from ketamine: a small prophylactic/treatment dose of midazolam, a calm recovery environment, minimising the ketamine dose used, and esketamine as an alternative with a somewhat better emergence profile. — Prophylactic midazolam at 0.03 mg/kg has been shown in a randomised trial to reduce recovery agitation from 25% to 8%. Hallucinations and nightmares after ketamine are dose-related, which is the basis for using the lowest effective dose; a large perioperative trial found ketamine did not reduce delirium but that hallucinations and nightmares increased with higher doses. Esketamine causes comparatively fewer cognitive disturbances than the racemate, supporting it as a substitution option when emergence reactions are a particular concern. — S(+)-ketamine — The S(+)-enantiomer of ketamine, roughly twice as potent as the racemic mixture used elsewhere in this algorithm — doses are halved whenever esketamine is substituted — and associated with somewhat fewer cognitive disturbances on emergence.

entries.title: Ketamine in Head Injury
entries.text: Seizure: — benzodiazepine, antiseizure medication, continuous EEG; ketamine may be an adjunct in refractory status epilepticus — Standard first-line seizure management (benzodiazepine and antiseizure medication, with continuous EEG), plus the specific point that ketamine itself has a role as an adjunct treatment in refractory status epilepticus rather than being something to stop reflexively if a seizure occurs during its use. — In super-refractory status epilepticus, adjunctive ketamine achieved at least a 50% reduction in seizure burden within 24 hours in 81% of patients, with stable mean arterial pressure and no adverse effect on ICP, cerebral blood flow or CPP in the monitored subgroup — the evidence base for treating ketamine as a potential adjunct rather than a drug to avoid once a seizure occurs.
