Continuous EEG monitoring is the same modality used elsewhere in this algorithm to track spreading depolarisations, so a single monitoring strategy serves both purposes in a comatose or heavily sedated patient. — One TBI cohort reported more seizure activity among patients exposed to ketamine (3.1% vs 1.0%); given the small number of events and the likelihood of confounding by indication — sicker patients were more likely to receive both ketamine and to have seizures — this signal requires confirmation rather than being treated as a reason to avoid ketamine. — Waves of near-complete neuronal depolarisation that occur in more than half of patients with severe TBI and are independently associated with worse outcome. Ketamine suppresses them in a dose-dependent manner — the rationale, still investigational, for the higher infusion doses used only in trials targeting this mechanism.

entries.title: Ketamine in Head Injury
entries.text: ICP rise: — check EtCO2/ventilation, sedation depth, head-up positioning and venous drainage; apply tier-1 ICP measures; do not stop ketamine reflexively — If intracranial pressure rises while a patient is on ketamine, the response is to work through the standard first-tier ICP checklist — ventilation adequacy, sedation depth, head positioning, venous drainage — rather than assuming ketamine itself is the cause and stopping it immediately. — No study in this review's evidence base demonstrated a sustained, clinically important ICP increase when ketamine was given with controlled ventilation and co-sedation; several studies even reported ICP reductions, plausibly through improved sedation depth, reduced metabolic demand, or suppression of spreading depolarisations. First-tier ICP measures — normocapnia, normoxia, head-of-bed elevation, adequate venous drainage, normothermia and euglycaemia — remain the foundation of care regardless of which sedative is used, and a transient rise after a ketamine bolus should prompt a check of these fundamentals before concluding ketamine is to blame. — Waves of near-complete neuronal depolarisation that occur in more than half of patients with severe TBI and are independently associated with worse outcome. Ketamine suppresses them in a dose-dependent manner — the rationale, still investigational, for the higher infusion doses used only in trials targeting this mechanism.

entries.title: Ketamine in Head Injury
entries.text: Laryngospasm / hypersalivation: — jaw thrust, positive-pressure ventilation with 100% O2; neuromuscular blocker if refractory; atropine for excess secretions — The airway-complication management pathway: first-line manual airway manoeuvres and positive-pressure ventilation with 100% oxygen, escalating to a neuromuscular blocker only for a refractory laryngospasm, with atropine reserved for troublesome secretions rather than given routinely. — Laryngospasm during ketamine sedation is rare and idiosyncratic — 22 cases among 8,282 sedations in a large individual-patient-data meta-analysis — and was not predictable from patient or procedural factors, which is why the response is a standard airway-rescue sequence rather than a specific preventive drug. Atropine reduces vomiting compared with glycopyrrolate but neither anticholinergic reduces the rate of laryngospasm or apnoea itself, which is the basis for using atropine specifically for excess secretions rather than as laryngospasm prophylaxis; these findings fed directly into the 2011 update of the emergency-department ketamine dissociative-sedation practice guideline.

entries.title: Ketamine in Head Injury
entries.nodeLabel: Reassess and document: GCS, pupils, MAP/CPP, ICP, adverse events; adjust dose to haemodynamic status
entries.text: Reassess and document: GCS, pupils, MAP/CPP, ICP, adverse events; adjust dose to haemodynamic status — The closing step after any complication is managed — and, more generally, the standing instruction running through the whole algorithm: repeat the core neurological and haemodynamic checks, document what happened, and titrate the ketamine dose to how the patient is actually responding rather than to a fixed protocol number. — This closing box restates the algorithm's own central organising principle: doses throughout are indicative and explicitly meant to be adjusted to haemodynamic status, age and comorbidity, and the Glasgow Coma Scale — the same scale used at initial assessment — remains the reference point for tracking whether a patient is improving, stable, or deteriorating after any intervention or complication.

entries.title: Midazolam versus Clonazepam
entries.text: Midazolam versus Clonazepam Seizures, Acute Agitation & Anxiety

entries.title: Midazolam versus Clonazepam
entries.nodeLabel: Airway, breathing, circulation; oxygen; glucose; monitoring.
entries.text: Airway, breathing, circulation; oxygen; glucose; monitoring. — Note the time of onset and of each dose. — The entry point to Panel A: a convulsive seizure that has already lasted five minutes or more, or a seizure cluster — the point at which guidelines classify ongoing seizure activity as status epilepticus and recommend starting first-line drug treatment rather than continuing to wait. — Status epilepticus is defined operationally as a seizure that has outlasted the point at which spontaneous termination becomes unlikely, set at five minutes for generalised tonic-clonic activity, with a risk of long-term neuronal injury once seizures continue beyond roughly thirty minutes. Because the probability of pharmacological seizure termination falls as seizure duration increases, the interval between onset and the first effective dose is the main modifiable determinant of outcome — which is why both the time of onset and the time of each dose are written into this box rather than left to recall afterward. — A seizure that has outlasted the point at which spontaneous termination becomes unlikely — set at five minutes for a generalised convulsive seizure — carrying a risk of long-term neuronal injury once activity continues beyond roughly thirty minutes.

entries.title: Midazolam versus Clonazepam
entries.text: Intravenous access already established? — The fork this review's own evidence is organised around: whether a vein is already open decides which drug and route come next, because midazolam's non-intravenous routes have strong trial support and clonazepam's evidence is almost entirely intravenous. — For practice, the choice can be organised around venous access and setting. Where access is absent, as in most prehospital, home and many paediatric presentations, midazolam by the intramuscular, buccal or intranasal route is supported by multiple trials and meta-analyses and is endorsed by guidelines; clonazepam has no comparable non-intravenous evidence. Where access is already established, intravenous clonazepam at an adequate dose is a reasonable first-line agent with randomised evidence of efficacy, and it may be preferred when a sustained effect is wanted and monitoring is available.

entries.title: Midazolam versus Clonazepam
entries.text:
MIDAZOLAM, non-intravenous — IM 10 mg (>40 kg) or 5 mg (13 to 40 kg)
or buccal / intranasal 0.2 mg/kg (max 10 mg)
Do not delay to obtain a vein — When no vein is open, midazolam is given by whichever non-intravenous route is fastest to hand — intramuscular, buccal or intranasal — rather than delaying treatment to cannulate first. — In RAMPART, 893 children and adults in prehospital status epilepticus were randomised to intramuscular midazolam by autoinjector or intravenous lorazepam; seizures were absent on arrival without rescue therapy in 73.4% versus 63.4%, a difference that met both non-inferiority and superiority criteria. The advantage was driven by speed of delivery: median time to treatment was 1.2 minutes for the intramuscular route against 4.8 minutes for the intravenous route. In the one head-to-head trial against clonazepam, intramuscular midazolam 10 mg was non-inferior to intravenous clonazepam 1 mg for seizure cessation and stopped seizures sooner after administration. A systematic review found buccal midazolam superior to rectal diazepam with moderate-quality evidence when no intravenous access is available. — A shorter latency with intramuscular midazolam than with intravenous clonazepam is unexpected on pharmacokinetic grounds; until replicated, the finding should be read as showing midazolam 10 mg IM is not slower than clonazepam 1 mg IV, which is sufficient to support its use when a vein is not immediately available, rather than as proof that the intramuscular route is intrinsically faster. — A seizure that has outlasted the point at which spontaneous termination becomes unlikely — set at five minutes for a generalised convulsive seizure — carrying a risk of long-term neuronal injury once activity continues beyond roughly thirty minutes.

entries.title: Midazolam versus Clonazepam
entries.text:
CLONAZEPAM IV 1 mg (about 0.015 mg/kg) — or IV lorazepam / diazepam per local protocol
Clonazepam if sustained effect is wanted and monitoring is available — When a vein is already open, intravenous clonazepam at an adequately weight-informed dose is a reasonable first-line choice, particularly when its much longer duration of action is itself wanted — or, per local protocol, an alternative intravenous benzodiazepine such as lorazepam or diazepam. — The principal randomised data for clonazepam alone come from the control arm of the SAMUKeppra trial: convulsions stopped within 15 minutes in 57 of 68 patients (84%) given intravenous clonazepam 1 mg with placebo, a rate at least as high as those reported for other first-line benzodiazepines. In a registry of 251 adult episodes, the median loading dose given in routine practice was 0.010 mg/kg — below the 0.015 mg/kg usually recommended — and doses at or above that recommended level were not associated with better seizure control but were associated with more intubation for airway protection, which is why this box states the per-kilogram target explicitly rather than leaving the 1 mg dose unanchored to weight. — A multicentre cohort found clonazepam an effective alternative to both lorazepam and midazolam as first-line therapy for status epilepticus, with lorazepam associated with more refractory status than clonazepam after adjustment — a finding the review attributes largely to frequent underdosing of lorazepam and to differences between centres, not to any inherent advantage of clonazepam. — A seizure that has outlasted the point at which spontaneous termination becomes unlikely — set at five minutes for a generalised convulsive seizure — carrying a risk of long-term neuronal injury once activity continues beyond roughly thirty minutes.

entries.title: Midazolam versus Clonazepam
entries.text: Still seizing after 5 minutes? — A reassessment point five minutes after the first dose: if the seizure has stopped, the pathway moves to observation; if it continues, the same drug is repeated once and the escalation ladder begins. — Guideline-based status epilepticus protocols build in a fixed reassessment interval after the first benzodiazepine dose precisely because both under-treatment (waiting too long before escalating) and over-treatment (stacking doses on a seizure that has already stopped) carry their own risks — recognised in this review's own finding that excessive benzodiazepine dosing was associated with substantially higher odds of respiratory depression and intubation. — A seizure that has outlasted the point at which spontaneous termination becomes unlikely — set at five minutes for a generalised convulsive seizure — carrying a risk of long-term neuronal injury once activity continues beyond roughly thirty minutes.

entries.title: Midazolam versus Clonazepam
entries.nodeLabel: Observe; monitor airway and respiration; look for and treat the cause
entries.text: Observe; monitor airway and respiration; look for and treat the cause — Once the seizure has stopped, management shifts from drug escalation to monitoring for delayed respiratory compromise and investigating why the seizure happened in the first place. — Across first-line trials in adults, respiratory depression occurred in 6.4% to 10.6% of patients given active benzodiazepine treatment, but was more frequent still in those given placebo — evidence that untreated seizures, not the benzodiazepine that stopped them, are the greater respiratory hazard, which is why airway and respiratory monitoring continues after cessation rather than stopping once the convulsion is visibly over.

entries.title: Midazolam versus Clonazepam
entries.text: Evidence — Midazolam IM vs clonazepam IV: non-inferior and faster after dosing (1 RCT, n = 64; low certainty) — A standing evidence note attached beside this part of the algorithm, not a step in the sequence: it summarises the single head-to-head trial this entire seizure pathway's comparative claim rests on, and flags plainly how thin that evidence base is. — Of the 76 reports this review included, only one — a double-blind, double-dummy non-inferiority trial of 64 prehospital patients — directly compared midazolam with clonazepam for seizures. Treatment success occurred in 75.0% of patients given midazolam against 62.5% given clonazepam (a small, imprecise difference whose confidence interval includes both no difference and a moderate benefit), while the interval from drug administration to seizure cessation was shorter with midazolam, a large standardised effect. GRADE certainty for both outcomes was rated low, chiefly for imprecision from relying on one small trial — the reason this box reads 'low certainty' rather than presenting the comparison as settled. — A structured system for rating how much confidence to place in a body of evidence for a specific outcome — from high down to very low — based on risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias. — A trial designed to show that a new treatment is not unacceptably worse than an existing one by more than a prespecified margin, rather than to show it is better — the design used for this review's one direct midazolam-versus-clonazepam comparison.

entries.title: Midazolam versus Clonazepam
entries.nodeLabel: Repeat the same benzodiazepine once. Obtain IV access.
entries.text: Repeat the same benzodiazepine once. Obtain IV access. — Avoid both underdosing and cumulative excess. — If the seizure is still going at five minutes, the same drug already given is repeated once — not switched — while intravenous access is obtained if it has not been already, so that further escalation (second-line therapy) can be given intravenously if needed. — A systematic review of guideline deviations found that underdosing and delay were associated with prolonged seizures, while excessive benzodiazepine dosing was associated with 5.8-fold higher odds of respiratory depression and intubation — a finding that applies to both drugs in this algorithm and is the direct basis for this box's explicit instruction to avoid both failure modes rather than defaulting toward either caution or aggression.

entries.title: Midazolam versus Clonazepam
entries.nodeLabel: Still seizing: second-line antiseizure medication IV
entries.text: Still seizing: second-line antiseizure medication IV — (levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate) — If the seizure persists despite a repeated benzodiazepine dose, management moves beyond benzodiazepines altogether to an intravenous second-line antiseizure medication. — The choice among levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate at this stage is supported by a large randomised trial (ESETT) that is independent of which benzodiazepine was given initially, finding the three agents similarly effective as second-line treatment for benzodiazepine-refractory status epilepticus — which is why this box lists all three as interchangeable options rather than ranking them. — A seizure that has outlasted the point at which spontaneous termination becomes unlikely — set at five minutes for a generalised convulsive seizure — carrying a risk of long-term neuronal injury once activity continues beyond roughly thirty minutes.

entries.title: Midazolam versus Clonazepam
entries.text: Refractory: intensive care, continuous EEG, — midazolam infusion or other anaesthetic (clonazepam not studied) — If second-line therapy also fails, the seizure is now refractory status epilepticus: management escalates to intensive care with continuous EEG monitoring and an anaesthetic-dose infusion — a stage where, among the two drugs this review compares, only midazolam has evidence at all. — For refractory status epilepticus only midazolam has been studied, as a continuous infusion; no study of clonazepam at this stage was identified anywhere in this review's searches. Systematic reviews of anaesthetic infusions found more breakthrough seizures but less hypotension with midazolam than with pentobarbital, and no clear influence of the choice of anaesthetic agent on mortality. In a small paediatric trial, midazolam and diazepam infusions controlled refractory status equally often, but seizures recurred more frequently with midazolam (57% versus 16%) once the infusion was stopped — the basis for continuing continuous EEG monitoring through this stage rather than relying on clinical observation alone. — A seizure that has outlasted the point at which spontaneous termination becomes unlikely — set at five minutes for a generalised convulsive seizure — carrying a risk of long-term neuronal injury once activity continues beyond roughly thirty minutes.

entries.title: Midazolam versus Clonazepam
entries.text: Predominant problem? — Panel B's single branch point: whether the presenting problem is severe agitation needing parenteral sedation, or acute anxiety/panic — two clinical situations this review found no comparative evidence connecting, so each is handled as its own, separately-reasoned pathway. — No study comparing midazolam with clonazepam for acute agitation was found, and a systematic review of intravenous medication for acute disturbance identified no eligible data for intravenous clonazepam at all — so the comparison in both branches below is entirely indirect, built from each drug's own separate trial literature rather than from any head-to-head evidence.

entries.title: Midazolam versus Clonazepam
entries.text: Severe agitation needing parenteral sedation — The first of the two Panel B pathways: a patient whose agitation requires rapid parenteral (injected) sedation rather than an oral, sustained-effect agent. — Across controlled trials, parenteral midazolam consistently sedates agitated patients faster than antipsychotic-based regimens, which is the evidence base this pathway draws on; clonazepam's controlled evidence in this setting is limited to small, older trials in acute mania rather than undifferentiated agitation.

entries.title: Midazolam versus Clonazepam
entries.text: Acute anxiety or panic — The second Panel B pathway: a patient whose predominant problem is acute anxiety or a panic attack rather than agitation requiring sedation. — Clonazepam, not midazolam, has the controlled evidence base for this indication — it is an established oral treatment of panic disorder with trial support over weeks and some evidence for an acute effect within hours of a single dose, which is why this pathway is organised around clonazepam rather than mirroring the agitation pathway's midazolam-first logic.

entries.title: Midazolam versus Clonazepam
entries.nodeLabel: MIDAZOLAM 5 mg IM, or 2.5 to 5 mg IV increments, in a monitored setting; consider combining with droperidol or an antipsychotic.
entries.text:
MIDAZOLAM 5 mg IM, or 2.5 to 5 mg IV increments, in a monitored setting; consider combining with droperidol or an antipsychotic. — Expect faster sedation but more rescue doses and airway events.
Reduce or avoid in older adults.
Clonazepam: one small trial only — Parenteral midazolam, given intramuscularly or titrated intravenously in a monitored setting, optionally combined with droperidol or another antipsychotic — with an explicit expectation that it will sedate faster than those comparators but at the cost of more rescue dosing and airway events, and a specific instruction to reduce or avoid it in older adults. — In TREC-Rio, 301 agitated or aggressive patients were randomised to intramuscular midazolam or haloperidol plus promethazine; 89% versus 67% were tranquil or asleep at 20 minutes, though the advantage had narrowed by 40 minutes and disappeared by one hour. Other trials qualify the speed advantage: in one, half of patients given midazolam 5 mg needed rescue sedation compared with one in ten given droperidol, and in the DORM study midazolam produced more adverse effects from oversedation than droperidol (28% versus 6%). As an adjunct, droperidol or olanzapine added to intravenous midazolam shortened time to sedation by four to five minutes. The only controlled parenteral clonazepam data in agitation is a single trial comparing it with haloperidol in manic patients, in which haloperidol acted more quickly. — Among older adults treated for severe agitation, adverse events occurred in 53% of those given midazolam, with more than five times the odds of an adverse event relative to haloperidol — the basis for this box's explicit instruction to reduce or avoid midazolam in that population rather than using the standard adult dose.

entries.title: Midazolam versus Clonazepam
entries.nodeLabel: Discharge planned, sustained effect wanted: oral CLONAZEPAM, short course (trial doses 1 to 2 mg/day).
entries.text:
Discharge planned, sustained effect wanted: oral CLONAZEPAM, short course (trial doses 1 to 2 mg/day). — Titratable sedation needed (palliative care, severe distress): MIDAZOLAM, titrated to effect.
No midazolam trials for anxiety — Two different agents for two different goals within the same anxiety/panic pathway: oral clonazepam as a short, sustained-effect course when the patient is being discharged, or titrated midazolam when the goal is titratable sedation for severe distress — most relevant in palliative care — rather than treatment of anxiety as such. — In a fixed-dose trial of 413 patients with panic disorder, daily clonazepam doses of 1 to 4 mg were clearly superior to placebo, with 1 to 2 mg offering the best balance of benefit and tolerability — the direct basis for the discharge-course dose range in this box. Midazolam has no trial evidence for anxiety outside procedural and palliative settings; in palliative care it is among the most frequently used drugs for anxiety, agitation, seizures and sedation at the end of life, which is why it appears here only for titratable sedation in severe distress, not as a treatment aimed at the anxiety itself. — A patient with an acute panic attack who is to be discharged and a patient with terminal restlessness or severe distress requiring titratable sedation are different clinical situations calling for different drugs for different reasons — presenting clonazepam and midazolam here as interchangeable alternatives to be ranked against each other would misrepresent the evidence.

entries.title: Vasopressor Agent Selection
entries.text: Vasopressor Agent Selection Aminergic Agents in Shock States

entries.title: Vasopressor Agent Selection
entries.text: Reassess — If shock is not confirmed, the algorithm does not apply — the patient is reassessed rather than started on vasopressors, since hypotension alone is not the trigger. — Treating a blood pressure number rather than a perfusion deficit risks unnecessary vasopressor exposure, which carries its own harms (arrhythmia, digital/skin ischaemia, excess myocardial oxygen demand). The same shock-recognition framework that triggers this algorithm also governs when to step back from it.

entries.title: Vasopressor Agent Selection
entries.text: Patient in SHOCK? — The entry point: a bedside judgement that the patient has life-threatening circulatory failure with evidence of inadequate tissue perfusion, not simply a low blood pressure reading on its own. — Shock is defined by cellular and tissue hypoxia from reduced oxygen delivery, impaired oxygen utilisation, or both — recognised clinically by a combination of systemic hypotension, altered mental status, oliguria, and skin mottling or delayed capillary refill, backed by biochemical markers such as a rising lactate. Confirming shock before committing to a vasopressor pathway matters because the interventions downstream (norepinephrine first-line, dose escalation, rescue agents) are not benign and are not indicated for isolated hypotension without a perfusion deficit.

entries.title: Vasopressor Agent Selection
entries.text: Identify Shock Type & Resuscitate — Once shock is confirmed, the next step is simultaneous: classify which of the four physiological shock categories is driving it, while beginning resuscitation (fluids, source control, airway/oxygenation as indicated) rather than waiting for classification to finish before acting. — The four-category framework — distributive/vasodilatory (septic being the dominant cause), cardiogenic, hypovolaemic/haemorrhagic, and obstructive — is the standard taxonomy used to decide initial vasopressor strategy, because the physiological lesion differs fundamentally between them: vasoplegia with preserved or high cardiac output in septic shock versus pump failure in cardiogenic shock versus inadequate preload in haemorrhagic/obstructive shock. A structured organ-dysfunction score such as SOFA can support this classification and severity-tracking step, though it was developed as a research and prognostic tool rather than a bedside diagnostic instrument in its own right. Early, protocolised initiation of this resuscitation sequence is itself associated with lower mortality: both delayed vasopressor initiation and later timing relative to fluid loading have been independently linked to worse outcomes in septic shock, a relationship also described specifically in the emergency-department setting where this algorithm is most often first applied. — Sequential Organ Failure Assessment — A six-organ-system scoring tool (respiratory, coagulation, hepatic, cardiovascular, neurological, renal) originally developed to track organ dysfunction over time in critically ill patients; an increase of 2 or more points is part of the Sepsis-3 definition of sepsis. — Pathological loss of vascular smooth-muscle tone causing profound vasodilation and hypotension despite normal or high cardiac output — the physiological lesion behind distributive shock, most commonly from sepsis but also seen with anaphylaxis, neurogenic injury, or certain drugs.

entries.title: Vasopressor Agent Selection
entries.text:
SEPTIC /
VASODILATORY — Distributive shock from pathological vasodilation and loss of vascular tone — sepsis being its most common cause in this algorithm's emergency/critical-care setting, but the same physiology applies to anaphylactic, neurogenic or drug-induced vasoplegia. — Sepsis-3 defines septic shock as sepsis with persisting hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) of 65 mmHg or above, together with a serum lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation — a definition built specifically around the need for vasopressor support, which is why this category leads directly into a norepinephrine-first pathway below. — mean arterial pressure — The average pressure driving blood flow through the arterial system over a full cardiac cycle (roughly diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure). It is the vasopressor-titration target throughout this algorithm, with 65 mmHg as the initial threshold. — Pathological loss of vascular smooth-muscle tone causing profound vasodilation and hypotension despite normal or high cardiac output — the physiological lesion behind distributive shock, most commonly from sepsis but also seen with anaphylaxis, neurogenic injury, or certain drugs. — Shock caused by inappropriate vasodilation and maldistribution of blood flow rather than a primary deficit of volume or cardiac pump function — septic shock is its most common cause in critical care.

entries.title: Vasopressor Agent Selection
entries.text:
Norepinephrine
(first-line) — ± Vasopressin add-on — Norepinephrine is started as the first-line vasopressor for septic/vasodilatory shock, with vasopressin available as an early add-on rather than a last resort. — Norepinephrine is recommended as the first-choice vasopressor for septic shock by the Surviving Sepsis Campaign (and summarised in a companion highlights review for practising clinicians) on the strength of head-to-head trial evidence: compared with dopamine, norepinephrine carries a lower risk of arrhythmia and, in the septic-shock subgroup specifically, lower mortality, a finding a subsequent meta-analysis reproduced. Norepinephrine also outperformed phenylephrine as initial support in a randomised trial — consistent with phenylephrine's narrower, largely alpha-1-mediated profile seen in other settings where the two agents have been compared head-to-head — and broad systematic reviews of vasopressor choice in septic shock converge on the same first-line recommendation. Starting norepinephrine early rather than late is itself tied to outcome: delayed initiation, and initiation more than an hour after fluid loading, have each been independently associated with higher mortality in large cohorts, and a trial of protocolised early norepinephrine (CENSER) improved shock control. An epinephrine-versus-norepinephrine comparison in a broader critically ill population found the two agents similarly effective at achieving haemodynamic targets, which is part of why epinephrine is kept available as a later, septic-shock-specific alternative in this algorithm rather than a routine first-line option. Vasopressin is addressed in its own node below as the second-line step once the MAP target is not met on norepinephrine alone. — Low-dose dopamine does not protect the kidney and should not be used for this purpose — a landmark placebo-controlled trial found no benefit on renal function or outcome, and dopamine use itself has been linked to worse outcomes in large observational shock cohorts. — mean arterial pressure — The average pressure driving blood flow through the arterial system over a full cardiac cycle (roughly diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure). It is the vasopressor-titration target throughout this algorithm, with 65 mmHg as the initial threshold.

entries.title: Vasopressor Agent Selection
entries.text: CARDIOGENIC — Shock from primary pump failure — the heart cannot generate adequate cardiac output despite adequate or even elevated filling pressures. — Cardiogenic shock spans a spectrum of severity, formalised in the SCAI staging system (A through E) that predicts mortality and guides escalation; sepsis-induced cardiac dysfunction (septic cardiomyopathy) can also mimic or compound this picture, which is part of why shock classification and ongoing reassessment, not a single snapshot, drive this algorithm. — Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions — Professional society whose staging system classifies cardiogenic shock severity from Stage A (at risk) to Stage E (extremis), used to predict mortality and guide how aggressively to escalate support.

entries.title: Vasopressor Agent Selection
entries.text:
Norepinephrine
(first-line) — + Inotrope if needed — Norepinephrine remains the first-line vasopressor in cardiogenic shock too, with an inotrope (e.g. dobutamine) added when low cardiac output — not vasoplegia — is the dominant problem. — In the SOAP II trial's prespecified cardiogenic-shock subgroup, norepinephrine was associated with lower mortality than dopamine, and a general pharmacotherapy review of vasopressors and inotropes in the ICU supports norepinephrine as the default pressor across shock types, reserving inotropic support for when contractility itself is impaired. An individual-data meta-analysis found epinephrine use in cardiogenic shock associated with worse short-term survival compared with other agents, reinforcing norepinephrine (± a dedicated inotrope) rather than epinephrine as the routine first step here; a trial of vasopressin versus norepinephrine after cardiac surgery, and a network meta-analysis of vasopressor/inotrope regimens in infarct-related cardiogenic shock, inform the same choice in this specific subgroup. — Sepsis-induced cardiac dysfunction can complicate the distinction between septic and cardiogenic physiology — reassess the dominant lesion rather than anchoring on the initial category. — Pathological loss of vascular smooth-muscle tone causing profound vasodilation and hypotension despite normal or high cardiac output — the physiological lesion behind distributive shock, most commonly from sepsis but also seen with anaphylaxis, neurogenic injury, or certain drugs.

entries.title: Vasopressor Agent Selection
entries.text:
HAEMORRHAGIC /
HYPOVOLAEMIC — Shock from an absolute deficit of circulating volume — blood loss or severe fluid/electrolyte loss — in which the primary lesion is inadequate preload, not vasoplegia or pump failure. — Because the physiological problem is volume, not vascular tone or contractility, vasopressors are an adjunct to, never a substitute for, source control and volume replacement in this category, which is why the algorithm explicitly orders "volume first" before naming norepinephrine as a bridge. — Pathological loss of vascular smooth-muscle tone causing profound vasodilation and hypotension despite normal or high cardiac output — the physiological lesion behind distributive shock, most commonly from sepsis but also seen with anaphylaxis, neurogenic injury, or certain drugs.

entries.title: Vasopressor Agent Selection
Vasopressor Agent Selection
entries.text: OBSTRUCTIVE — Shock from a mechanical obstruction to circulation or cardiac filling — massive pulmonary embolism, cardiac tamponade, or tension pneumothorax are the classic causes. — As with hypovolaemic shock, the primary lesion in obstructive shock is mechanical, not vascular tone or contractility, so this category is kept distinct from both septic/vasodilatory and cardiogenic shock even though its bridging pharmacological support looks similar.

entries.title: Vasopressor Agent Selection
Vasopressor Agent Selection
entries.text:
MAP ≥ 65 mmHg
achieved? — Across all four shock categories, the pathways converge here: has the initial vasopressor strategy achieved a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg? — A MAP target of 65 mmHg is the standard initial resuscitation goal in septic shock, directly supported by the SEPSISPAM trial, which found no outcome benefit from targeting a higher MAP (80-85 mmHg) in the general septic-shock population, at the cost of more atrial fibrillation — though a prespecified subgroup with chronic hypertension needed less renal-replacement therapy at the higher target. A broader systematic review of vasopressor blood-pressure targets across critically ill adults with hypotension, and a trial testing reduced vasopressor exposure specifically in older patients with vasodilatory hypotension, support individualising the target around this same 65 mmHg anchor rather than a fixed one-size-fits-all number, which current international guidelines also adopt as the initial target. — mean arterial pressure — The average pressure driving blood flow through the arterial system over a full cardiac cycle (roughly diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure). It is the vasopressor-titration target throughout this algorithm, with 65 mmHg as the initial threshold. — Dialysis or haemofiltration used to substitute for failing kidney function — referenced here both as an outcome that vasopressor strategy can influence and as a clinical context (patients already receiving it) in which angiotensin II has specifically been studied.

entries.title: Vasopressor Agent Selection
entries.text: Continue & titrate — Monitor perfusion — If the MAP target is met, the current vasopressor strategy is continued and titrated to the lowest dose that sustains perfusion, with ongoing monitoring rather than a fixed, set-and-forget dose. — Meeting a MAP number is a necessary but not sufficient endpoint — ongoing reassessment of perfusion (lactate clearance, capillary refill, urine output, and where available less invasive haemodynamic monitoring) is what distinguishes adequate circulatory support from a pressure target met at the expense of tissue perfusion. — mean arterial pressure — The average pressure driving blood flow through the arterial system over a full cardiac cycle (roughly diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure). It is the vasopressor-titration target throughout this algorithm, with 65 mmHg as the initial threshold. — The rate at which blood lactate falls toward normal with treatment — a marker of improving tissue perfusion used alongside blood pressure to judge whether a vasopressor strategy is actually restoring adequate circulation, not just the numbers.

entries.title: Vasopressor Agent Selection
entries.text:
Add 2nd-line agent: — Vasopressin 0.03 U/min
or Epinephrine (septic only) — If the MAP target is not met on the first-line agent, a fixed low-dose vasopressin infusion (0.03 U/min) is added — or, specifically in septic shock, epinephrine may be used instead — rather than simply escalating the norepinephrine dose indefinitely. — Current guidelines recommend adding vasopressin to norepinephrine once the norepinephrine dose is in the moderate range, rather than waiting for very high doses, a strategy supported by the VASST trial's fixed low-dose vasopressin protocol (0.01-0.03 U/min) and the subsequent VANISH trial, which also found less progression to renal-replacement therapy with earlier vasopressin exposure. Individual-patient-data and aggregate meta-analyses of vasopressin add-on therapy support a renal-sparing and catecholamine-sparing effect, though vasopressin's addition is not free of risk: it has been associated with a higher incidence of new atrial fibrillation in a large meta-analysis, and with ischaemic digital/skin lesions at higher or prolonged doses, which is why the dose given here is capped rather than open-ended. The timing of this add-on step also matters on its own: later vasopressin initiation relative to catecholamine dose and lactate trajectory has been linked to higher mortality. Epinephrine as the alternative second-line agent in septic shock specifically is supported by a landmark trial finding it comparable to norepinephrine plus dobutamine. — Vasopressin's narrow benefit (renal-sparing, catecholamine-sparing) comes with real harms at higher exposure — digital/skin ischaemia and new atrial fibrillation — which is the rationale for the fixed, capped 0.03 U/min dose rather than titrating it upward like a catecholamine. — mean arterial pressure — The average pressure driving blood flow through the arterial system over a full cardiac cycle (roughly diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure). It is the vasopressor-titration target throughout this algorithm, with 65 mmHg as the initial threshold. — A treatment effect that reduces the dose of catecholamine vasopressors (such as norepinephrine) needed to maintain the same blood pressure target — relevant because high catecholamine doses carry their own dose-dependent harms. — Dialysis or haemofiltration used to substitute for failing kidney function — referenced here both as an outcome that vasopressor strategy can influence and as a clinical context (patients already receiving it) in which angiotensin II has specifically been studied.

entries.title: Vasopressor Agent Selection
entries.text: Refractory shock? — If the second-line agent still does not control shock, the algorithm asks whether this has become refractory (catecholamine-resistant) shock, which changes the treatment goal from escalating the same agents further to adding a rescue strategy. — Very high vasopressor requirements identify a sicker population with a materially worse prognosis, and the cumulative norepinephrine-equivalent dose itself is increasingly used as a severity marker rather than simply a number to keep pushing upward — reinforcing that recognising refractoriness, not indefinite dose escalation on the same agents, is the decision point this node represents.

entries.title: Vasopressor Agent Selection
entries.text:
Angiotensin II
or Terlipressin (HRS) — Consider MCS (cardiogenic) — For refractory shock, a non-catecholamine rescue vasopressor is considered: angiotensin II for refractory vasodilatory/septic shock broadly, terlipressin specifically where the refractory picture is hepatorenal syndrome, or mechanical circulatory support (MCS) when the refractory physiology is cardiogenic. — The ATHOS-3 trial established angiotensin II as an effective third-line vasopressor in catecholamine-resistant vasodilatory shock, including a prespecified subgroup already on renal-replacement therapy; subsequent safety reviews and narrative reviews have further characterised its role and limits as a rescue agent. Terlipressin, a vasopressin analogue, has trial-level support specifically in hepatorenal syndrome, reflected in two independent meta-analyses of its renal and vasoactive effects there. Mechanical circulatory support is the parallel rescue option when the refractory picture is cardiogenic rather than vasodilatory, consistent with how cardiogenic shock reviews frame escalation once pharmacological support alone is failing. — These are rescue options for refractory shock, not first- or second-line agents — reach for them once the earlier steps in this algorithm have been tried and have failed, not as a shortcut. — mechanical circulatory support — Devices that mechanically augment or replace cardiac output — intra-aortic balloon pumps, percutaneous ventricular assist devices, or extracorporeal life support — used as a rescue option in cardiogenic shock once pharmacological support alone is failing. — Progressive kidney failure occurring in patients with advanced liver disease and portal hypertension, driven by splanchnic and systemic vasodilation rather than intrinsic kidney damage — which is why a vasoconstrictor such as terlipressin, rather than renal-specific therapy, is part of its treatment. — Shock that persists despite first- and second-line vasopressor therapy at adequate doses — also called catecholamine-resistant shock. Reaching this point shifts the decision from escalating the same agents further to adding a rescue strategy (a non-catecholamine agent, or mechanical support). — Dialysis or haemofiltration used to substitute for failing kidney function — referenced here both as an outcome that vasopressor strategy can influence and as a clinical context (patients already receiving it) in which angiotensin II has specifically been studied.

entries.title: Vasopressor Agent Selection
entries.nodeLabel:
Stabilised — wean vasopressors
gradually; monitor closely
entries.text:
Stabilised — wean vasopressors
gradually; monitor closely — If shock resolves without becoming refractory, vasopressors are weaned gradually rather than stopped abruptly, with continued close monitoring through the wean. — The same perfusion-monitoring principle that governs the "continue & titrate" step applies at the other end of the course: a gradual, monitored wean avoids rebound hypotension and lets perfusion markers, not simply the clock, pace de-escalation.

entries.title: Whole-Body CT in Traumatic Shock
entries.text: Whole-Body CT in Traumatic Shock A Stepwise Decision Algorithm

entries.title: Whole-Body CT in Traumatic Shock
entries.text: ADULT MAJOR TRAUMA - SUSPECTED HAEMORRHAGE — Primary survey with monitored resuscitation; eFAST; chest and pelvic radiographs; arterial blood gas with lactate and base excess — The entry point: an adult with major trauma and a clinical suspicion of significant haemorrhage, worked up with the standard primary-survey bundle before any decision about whole-body CT is made. — eFAST, chest/pelvic radiographs and an arterial blood gas with lactate and base excess are fast, bedside tests that can be done without leaving the resuscitation bay, and together they start to answer the two questions the rest of the algorithm depends on: is bleeding immediately uncontrolled, and is the patient physiologically in shock. Nothing here commits the patient to WBCT — it is the data this algorithm reasons from at every later step. — extended focused assessment with sonography for trauma — A rapid bedside ultrasound protocol used during the primary survey to detect free fluid in the abdomen, pericardium and pleural spaces, plus pneumothorax, in an unstable trauma patient — fast enough to perform without leaving the resuscitation bay. A negative scan does not exclude significant injury, which is why persistent shock despite a negative eFAST is itself an indication for WBCT in this algorithm. — whole-body computed tomography — A single contrast-enhanced CT acquisition from vertex to pubic symphysis, imaging the head, neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis in one pass — the subject of this algorithm's whole decision pathway.

entries.title: Whole-Body CT in Traumatic Shock
entries.nodeLabel: STEP 1 Is an immediately life-threatening state present?
entries.text:
STEP 1 Is an immediately life-threatening state present? — • Peri-arrest or cardiopulmonary resuscitation in progress
• Uncontrolled external or cavitary haemorrhage
• SBP < 60 mmHg unresponsive to resuscitation and blood products
• One obvious source of exsanguination requiring control now — Checks for a state so unstable that the patient cannot survive the journey to, or time inside, a CT scanner — peri-arrest physiology, uncontrolled bleeding, or one obvious source of exsanguination that needs immediate control rather than imaging. — WBCT takes minutes the patient may not have, and the scanner itself removes the team from an environment equipped for immediate haemostatic intervention. Any one of these four features means the correct next step is stopping the bleeding — in theatre, with REBOA, or with external control — not characterising it on CT first. This is a gate, not a scoring system: a single present feature is enough to exit to immediate haemostasis. — resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta — A catheter-based technique that temporarily occludes the aorta with an inflatable balloon to control torso and junctional haemorrhage and preserve perfusion to the heart and brain while definitive haemostasis is arranged — a bridge, not a treatment in itself. — whole-body computed tomography — A single contrast-enhanced CT acquisition from vertex to pubic symphysis, imaging the head, neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis in one pass — the subject of this algorithm's whole decision pathway.

entries.title: Whole-Body CT in Traumatic Shock
entries.text: CONTRAINDICATED - DO NOT SCAN — Immediate haemostasis: theatre, resuscitative thoracotomy or REBOA, pelvic binder and packing. Selective imaging only. WBCT after bleeding control. — The outcome when Step 1 is positive: WBCT is withheld entirely, and the patient goes straight to the intervention that can actually stop the bleeding. — In a peri-arrest or uncontrollably haemorrhaging patient, time spent transferring to and acquiring a WBCT is time taken directly from definitive haemostatic control, and mortality in this group is dominated by minutes, not by diagnostic completeness. "Selective imaging only" means a focused study — a single body region, or imaging performed in a hybrid theatre already equipped for intervention — once bleeding is controlled, not a blanket deferral of all imaging. — whole-body computed tomography — A single contrast-enhanced CT acquisition from vertex to pubic symphysis, imaging the head, neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis in one pass — the subject of this algorithm's whole decision pathway.

entries.title: Whole-Body CT in Traumatic Shock
entries.nodeLabel: STEP 2 Confirm shock physiologically, not by blood pressure alone
entries.text: STEP 2 Confirm shock physiologically, not by blood pressure alone — ALL THREE required: SBP < 100 mmHg AND lactate > 2.2 mmol/L AND base excess < -2 mmol/L (base deficit >= 2) — Replaces a single blood-pressure threshold with a three-part physiological definition of shock — a low systolic pressure plus biochemical evidence of impaired perfusion (raised lactate, a negative base excess) — all three required together. — Blood pressure alone is an unreliable marker of shock in trauma: young, compensated patients can maintain a near-normal SBP despite significant blood loss, while others run a lower baseline SBP without hypoperfusion. Requiring lactate and base excess alongside SBP anchors the definition in tissue perfusion rather than a single haemodynamic number, which is also why Step 2 exists as its own gate separate from Step 1's pure life-threat screen. — systolic blood pressure — The peak arterial pressure during cardiac systole — the upper number in a blood pressure reading, and the first of the three physiological criteria this algorithm requires to confirm shock.

entries.title: Whole-Body CT in Traumatic Shock
entries.text: HYPOTENSION WITHOUT METABOLIC SHOCK — About half of hypotensive trauma patients. Manage as haemodynamically stable: WBCT by standard institutional criteria. — The outcome when SBP is low but lactate and base excess do not confirm a perfusion deficit — the patient is hypotensive without being in metabolic shock by this algorithm's definition. — Routing this large group — roughly half of hypotensive trauma presentations — back to standard institutional WBCT criteria rather than down the shock-specific pathway avoids over-applying shock-tier urgency (the under-30-minute door-to-scan target, mandatory bay-adjacent scanning) to patients who do not need it, while still allowing WBCT exactly as it would be used in a stable major-trauma workup. — systolic blood pressure — The peak arterial pressure during cardiac systole — the upper number in a blood pressure reading, and the first of the three physiological criteria this algorithm requires to confirm shock. — whole-body computed tomography — A single contrast-enhanced CT acquisition from vertex to pubic symphysis, imaging the head, neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis in one pass — the subject of this algorithm's whole decision pathway.

entries.title: Whole-Body CT in Traumatic Shock
entries.nodeLabel: STEP 3 Is the environment safe to scan? ALL FOUR required
entries.text:
STEP 3 Is the environment safe to scan? ALL FOUR required — • Scanner in or adjacent to the resuscitation bay, transfer under 5 minutes
• Interventional radiology immediately available
• Operating theatre activated and immediately available
• Monitored transfer with resuscitation and blood products continued — With shock confirmed, this checks whether the institution can actually deliver safe, rapid WBCT and immediate haemostatic intervention if the scan identifies a bleeding source — not whether the patient should be imaged in principle, but whether the environment can support it right now. — A shocked patient who deteriorates inside or in transit to the scanner needs an immediate route back to intervention. All four conditions — proximity, IR availability, an activated theatre, and a monitored transfer — must hold together, because any single missing link (a scanner across the hospital, IR on call rather than in-house, no theatre slot) turns the scan into the most dangerous part of the patient's care rather than the fastest route to finding the bleeding source. — interventional radiology — The radiology subspecialty providing image-guided, catheter-based treatment — principally angioembolisation for arterial bleeding identified on CT — as an alternative or adjunct to open surgical haemostasis. — whole-body computed tomography — A single contrast-enhanced CT acquisition from vertex to pubic symphysis, imaging the head, neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis in one pass — the subject of this algorithm's whole decision pathway.

entries.title: Whole-Body CT in Traumatic Shock
entries.text: DEFER WBCT — Damage-control resuscitation with selective imaging. Achieve definitive haemostasis first, then delayed WBCT once the patient responds. — The outcome when any one of Step 3's four environment conditions is absent: WBCT is deferred, not cancelled, while damage-control resuscitation and selective (not whole-body) imaging continue. — This is a logistics-driven deferral, not a clinical judgement that imaging is unnecessary — the shocked patient still needs source control and resuscitation, achieved first through damage-control principles, with WBCT revisited once haemostasis is secured and the environment can support it safely. — whole-body computed tomography — A single contrast-enhanced CT acquisition from vertex to pubic symphysis, imaging the head, neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis in one pass — the subject of this algorithm's whole decision pathway.

entries.title: Whole-Body CT in Traumatic Shock
entries.nodeLabel: PROCEED: SINGLE-PASS CONTRAST-ENHANCED WBCT, VERTEX TO PUBIC SYMPHYSIS
entries.text: PROCEED: SINGLE-PASS CONTRAST-ENHANCED WBCT, VERTEX TO PUBIC SYMPHYSIS — Split-bolus, dose-optimised protocol | target door-to-scan under 30 minutes | trauma team and blood products remain with the patient | radiologist reporting at the console | abort the scan and go to theatre if physiology deteriorates — The scan itself: one contrast-enhanced acquisition covering vertex to pubic symphysis, run as a monitored extension of resuscitation rather than a stand-alone radiology test. — Keeping the trauma team and blood products physically with the patient, having the radiologist report at the console rather than later from a workstation, and setting an explicit abort threshold all treat the scanner as part of the resuscitation space, not a handoff away from it — the door-to-scan target exists because the diagnostic value of WBCT is time-limited in a shocked patient. — whole-body computed tomography — A single contrast-enhanced CT acquisition from vertex to pubic symphysis, imaging the head, neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis in one pass — the subject of this algorithm's whole decision pathway.

entries.title: Whole-Body CT in Traumatic Shock
entries.text: INTERPRET AND ACT WITHIN MINUTES — The scan's findings are triaged into one of three action pathways immediately, at the console — WBCT in this pathway is a decision-making tool embedded in ongoing resuscitation, not a diagnostic study awaited passively. — A finding that changes management — active extravasation, peritoneal violation, a non-haemorrhagic cause of instability — needs to drive the next intervention within minutes of acquisition, which is why reporting happens at the console (see PROCEED) and why the three outcome pathways below are framed as immediate actions, not differential diagnoses. — whole-body computed tomography — A single contrast-enhanced CT acquisition from vertex to pubic symphysis, imaging the head, neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis in one pass — the subject of this algorithm's whole decision pathway.

entries.title: Whole-Body CT in Traumatic Shock
entries.nodeLabel: Arterial extravasation or solid organ injury; transient responder
entries.text: Arterial extravasation or solid organ injury; transient responder — Angioembolisation, or haemostasis in a hybrid room. Protocolised non-operative management with defined follow-up imaging. — WBCT identifies a solid-organ or arterial bleeding source in a patient who responded, even if only transiently, to resuscitation — the pathway most likely to be managed without an operation. — A "transient responder" who re-shows a bleeding source on CT is the population angioembolisation and non-operative management were developed for: haemodynamically controllable enough to tolerate a targeted procedure instead of a laparotomy, provided follow-up imaging and clear thresholds for escalation are built into the plan rather than treating non-operative management as the end of surveillance. — whole-body computed tomography — A single contrast-enhanced CT acquisition from vertex to pubic symphysis, imaging the head, neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis in one pass — the subject of this algorithm's whole decision pathway. — A trauma-resuscitation response category: a patient whose vital signs improve with initial fluid or blood product administration but who then deteriorates again, as opposed to a "responder" (sustained improvement) or "non-responder" (no improvement at all) — implying ongoing bleeding that has not yet been controlled, not a resolved problem.

entries.title: Whole-Body CT in Traumatic Shock
entries.nodeLabel: Peritoneal violation, hollow viscus or diaphragm injury; ongoing bleeding
entries.text: Peritoneal violation, hollow viscus or diaphragm injury; ongoing bleeding — Targeted operation: laparotomy, thoracotomy or laparoscopy. Damage control if coagulopathic, acidotic or hypothermic. — WBCT identifies an injury that angioembolisation cannot fix — a breached peritoneum, hollow viscus or diaphragm injury, or bleeding that is ongoing rather than a single arterial point — and the three outcome pathways converge here before moving to definitive care. — These findings need source control through an operation, not interventional radiology; whether that operation is a full definitive repair or an abbreviated damage-control procedure is governed by the same physiological triad used throughout trauma surgery — coagulopathy, acidosis and hypothermia — rather than by the CT findings alone. — whole-body computed tomography — A single contrast-enhanced CT acquisition from vertex to pubic symphysis, imaging the head, neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis in one pass — the subject of this algorithm's whole decision pathway.

entries.title: Whole-Body CT in Traumatic Shock
entries.nodeLabel: Non-haemorrhagic cause: severe TBI, high cord injury, tamponade, tension pneumothorax
entries.text: Non-haemorrhagic cause: severe TBI, high cord injury, tamponade, tension pneumothorax — Treat the identified cause. Avoid futile torso exploration and non-therapeutic laparotomy. — WBCT shows that the instability is not primarily haemorrhagic at all — a severe head or high spinal cord injury, cardiac tamponade, or tension pneumothorax — redirecting management toward that specific cause. — One of WBCT's main values in the undifferentiated shocked trauma patient is ruling bleeding out as the dominant problem, not just ruling it in; exploring the abdomen or chest surgically when the real driver of shock lies elsewhere delays the treatment that would actually help and adds operative risk with no therapeutic benefit. — whole-body computed tomography — A single contrast-enhanced CT acquisition from vertex to pubic symphysis, imaging the head, neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis in one pass — the subject of this algorithm's whole decision pathway.

entries.title: Whole-Body CT in Traumatic Shock
entries.text: AFTER DEFINITIVE CARE — Tertiary survey for missed injury | record cumulative effective dose | document incidental findings and hand over a defined follow-up plan | audit door-to-scan and door-to-haemostasis intervals — The algorithm's closing step, reached once bleeding is controlled: a structured tertiary survey, formal accounting of radiation dose and incidental findings, and an audit of how long the pathway actually took. — A single-pass WBCT performed under resuscitation pressure can miss injuries that only become apparent once the patient is stable, and incidental findings — along with the cumulative radiation dose of a technique explicitly built around rapid, repeatable imaging — need a documented plan rather than disappearing into the acute record; auditing the door-to-scan and door-to-haemostasis intervals is how the time targets set earlier in the pathway are actually enforced over time. — whole-body computed tomography — A single contrast-enhanced CT acquisition from vertex to pubic symphysis, imaging the head, neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis in one pass — the subject of this algorithm's whole decision pathway.

entries.title: Whole-Body CT in Traumatic Shock
entries.nodeLabel: SUMMARY: INDICATIONS, USE AND CONTRAINDICATIONS OF WBCT IN TRAUMATIC SHOCK
entries.text: SUMMARY: INDICATIONS, USE AND CONTRAINDICATIONS OF WBCT IN TRAUMATIC SHOCK — A reference summary alongside the decision pathway above — not a further step in the sequence, but a consolidated account of when WBCT is indicated, how it should be performed, and when it should not be done at all. — These three panels restate and extend points already embedded in the stepwise algorithm — the Step 1 contraindications, the Step 3 environment checks, the PROCEED protocol detail — as a single quick-reference block, useful on its own without re-tracing the whole decision pathway. — whole-body computed tomography — A single contrast-enhanced CT acquisition from vertex to pubic symphysis, imaging the head, neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis in one pass — the subject of this algorithm's whole decision pathway.

entries.title: Whole-Body CT in Traumatic Shock
entries.text:
INDICATIONS — • High-energy blunt or penetrating multisystem trauma
• Transient or stable responder to resuscitation
• Confirmed shock with no single identified bleeding source
• Persistent shock despite a negative eFAST
• Depressed consciousness preventing reliable examination
• Need to define an embolisation target or to justify non-operative management
• Suspected occult thoracic, retroperitoneal or vascular injury — The clinical situations in which WBCT adds genuine value — mechanism, resuscitation response, diagnostic uncertainty, or the need for a specific procedural target rather than a general survey. — Several of these indications exist precisely because another test's negative result is not reassuring enough on its own — a negative eFAST does not exclude retroperitoneal, thoracic or hollow-viscus injury, and depressed consciousness removes the clinical examination as a safety net — which is why WBCT functions as a confirmatory, not a first-line, test in several of these scenarios. — extended focused assessment with sonography for trauma — A rapid bedside ultrasound protocol used during the primary survey to detect free fluid in the abdomen, pericardium and pleural spaces, plus pneumothorax, in an unstable trauma patient — fast enough to perform without leaving the resuscitation bay. A negative scan does not exclude significant injury, which is why persistent shock despite a negative eFAST is itself an indication for WBCT in this algorithm. — whole-body computed tomography — A single contrast-enhanced CT acquisition from vertex to pubic symphysis, imaging the head, neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis in one pass — the subject of this algorithm's whole decision pathway.

entries.title: Whole-Body CT in Traumatic Shock
entries.text:
USE - HOW TO DO IT — • Single pass, vertex to pubic symphysis
• Split-bolus technique; arterial phase if extravasation suspected
• Dose-optimised acquisition with iterative reconstruction
• Iso-osmolar contrast; do not withhold for creatinine alone
• Scanner adjacent to the bay; theatre and IR on standby
• Immediate radiologist reporting at the console
• Door-to-scan under 30 minutes; abort if physiology deteriorates — The technical and logistical detail behind PROCEED and Step 3, gathered into one place: the acquisition technique, the contrast protocol, and the standby resources the scan depends on. — "Do not withhold for creatinine alone" is a deliberate instruction: delaying a potentially life-saving trauma scan over a theoretical contrast-nephropathy risk is a worse trade than the risk itself in an actively bleeding patient, which is why the contrast decision is framed as a default to proceed rather than a default to wait for renal results.

entries.title: Whole-Body CT in Traumatic Shock
entries.text:
CONTRAINDICATIONS — • Cardiac arrest or peri-arrest state
• Refractory hypotension, SBP < 60 mmHg, despite resuscitation and blood
• Obvious single source of exsanguination requiring immediate control
• Scanner remote, or transfer time exceeding physiological reserve
• Interventional radiology or theatre not immediately available
• Inability to monitor and resuscitate during transfer and acquisition
• Known severe anaphylaxis to iodinated contrast (relative) — The mirror image of Steps 1 and 3 above, collected as a standalone checklist: the situations in which WBCT should not be attempted, whether because of the patient's physiology or the environment's readiness. — Listing the contraindications separately from the stepwise gates gives a fast single-glance check — useful, for instance, when deciding whether to accept a transfer for WBCT at a receiving centre, where Steps 1-3 as written assume the patient is already in the resuscitation bay. The one relative contraindication — known severe anaphylaxis to iodinated contrast — is flagged as relative rather than absolute, consistent with the "do not withhold for creatinine alone" instruction in USE: this algorithm treats radiological risk as something to manage, not a default reason to withhold a potentially life-saving scan. — whole-body computed tomography — A single contrast-enhanced CT acquisition from vertex to pubic symphysis, imaging the head, neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis in one pass — the subject of this algorithm's whole decision pathway.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited Contemporary Decision-Making Algorithm

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: ANAPHYLAXIS — This lane covers epinephrine's use in acute systemic anaphylaxis — the one indication in this entire algorithm where the evidence for epinephrine is unequivocal and uncontested. — Anaphylaxis is mediated by histamine, tryptase and prostaglandin release, producing vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, bronchospasm and mucosal oedema. Epinephrine is the only agent that addresses all four mechanisms at once: α1-mediated vasoconstriction reverses vasodilation and vascular leak, β2-mediated bronchodilation relieves bronchoconstriction, β1 chronotropy/inotropy supports cardiac output, and α1-mediated mucosal constriction reduces laryngeal oedema. No other single agent recapitulates this breadth, which is why antihistamines and corticosteroids — frequently misused as primary treatment — are relegated to secondary roles with no demonstrated mortality benefit.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text:
Epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg IM — anterolateral thigh
(auto-injector) — Intramuscular epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh (vastus lateralis), by auto-injector where available, is the singular first-line intervention for anaphylaxis endorsed by both the WAO 2020 guidance and the 2020 AAAAI/ACAAI practice parameter. — IM injection into the vastus lateralis gives reliable absorption with a time to maximum concentration of roughly 8 minutes — substantially faster and more predictable than the subcutaneous route, which the guidelines regard as inadequate in acute reactions. The 1:1000 (1 mg/mL) solution is mandatory for IM use; inadvertent use of the 1:10,000 solution delivers a tenfold underdose. Auto-injector needle length needs attention in obesity: standard 15 mm needles may fail to penetrate subcutaneous fat above BMI 30 kg/m², and an extended-length (25 mm) device should be prescribed instead. Patients should also be trained to avoid directing auto-injectors toward the digits, since inadvertent intra-arterial injection into the digital arteries of the thumb has caused finger ischaemia. — Needle length: standard 15 mm devices may not reach muscle in patients with BMI > 30 kg/m² — prescribe a 25 mm extended-length auto-injector instead. — Never give the 1:10,000 (0.1 mg/mL) resuscitation concentration IM in place of the 1:1000 (1 mg/mL) anaphylaxis concentration — a tenfold underdose. — Avoid directing an auto-injector toward a digit — inadvertent intra-arterial injection has caused finger ischaemia. — World Allergy Organization — International body whose 2020 anaphylaxis guidance underpins first-line IM epinephrine dosing. — American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology — US allergy/immunology society; co-issued the 2020 anaphylaxis practice parameter with the ACAAI. — American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology — US allergy/immunology college; co-issued the 2020 anaphylaxis practice parameter with the AAAAI. — intramuscular — Route of epinephrine administration in anaphylaxis (anterolateral thigh).

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: Response adequate? — A reassessment gate after the initial IM dose, determining whether the patient moves to a period of observation or needs a repeat dose / escalation to IV infusion for refractory anaphylaxis. — This gate matters because epinephrine is substantially underused in practice: meta-analytic data show it is administered in only 38–62% of confirmed anaphylactic episodes in emergency departments, with clinicians disproportionately reaching for antihistamines instead — a pattern associated with progression to biphasic reactions, ICU admission and preventable death. A structured reassessment step is a deliberate counter to that pattern of undertreatment. — intramuscular — Route of epinephrine administration in anaphylaxis (anterolateral thigh). — intravenous — Route of epinephrine administration in cardiac arrest and shock states, and for refractory anaphylaxis infusion.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: Observe ≥4–6 h — Watch for biphasic reaction — Following an adequate response, guidelines recommend a minimum observation period of 4–6 hours, extended to 24 hours after a severe or biphasic reaction, because a single resolved episode does not rule out recurrence. — Biphasic anaphylaxis affects 5–20% of patients, typically within 1–72 hours of the initial reaction, from incomplete mast-cell mediator suppression or a mediator re-release phenomenon. Premature discharge after a single epinephrine injection without adequate observation is a recognised, preventable patient-safety risk in international adverse-event reporting. — A recurrence of anaphylactic symptoms after apparent resolution, typically within 1–72 hours, affecting 5–20% of patients — the reason for post-treatment observation.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.nodeLabel: Repeat IM dose or IV infusion
entries.text: Repeat IM dose or IV infusion — (refractory anaphylaxis) — If the initial IM dose is inadequate, the next step is a repeat IM dose (guideline-supported at 5–15 minute intervals) or escalation to an IV epinephrine infusion for refractory anaphylaxis. — A second IM dose is required in a substantial minority of cases (reported at up to roughly one-third), underscoring that under-dosing — not over-dosing — is the dominant clinical error in anaphylaxis management. Continuous IV infusion is reserved for patients who remain refractory to repeated IM dosing. — intramuscular — Route of epinephrine administration in anaphylaxis (anterolateral thigh). — intravenous — Route of epinephrine administration in cardiac arrest and shock states, and for refractory anaphylaxis infusion.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: CARDIAC ARREST — This lane covers epinephrine's standard-dose role in cardiac arrest resuscitation, where its benefit is real but — unlike anaphylaxis — ethically and neurologically more complicated. — Epinephrine's role in cardiac arrest derives from its α1-adrenergic effect: peripheral vasoconstriction raises aortic diastolic pressure and thereby coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure during CPR. This rationale was codified into resuscitation protocols from 1960s experimental models, well before rigorous randomised-trial evidence existed — evidence that has since substantially qualified, without overturning, the original assumption.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text:
Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO — every 3–5 min
(AHA 2020 / ERC 2021) — The guideline-standard dose in cardiac arrest is 1 mg IV or IO, repeated every 3–5 minutes, per both AHA 2020 and ERC 2021 advanced life support guidance. — The PARAMEDIC2 trial — a double-blind RCT of 8,014 out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients — confirmed that this standard 1 mg dose significantly increases 30-day survival (OR 1.39, 95% CI 1.06–1.82) versus placebo, though without improving the rate of favourable neurological outcome among survivors. Historical high-dose regimens (2–5 mg or 0.1–0.2 mg/kg) conferred no survival benefit over standard dosing and were associated with post-resuscitation myocardial dysfunction, arrhythmia and excess mortality — a now-settled question that is universally reflected in current guidelines, even though case reports of high-dose administration continue to surface in practice. When IV access fails, intraosseous delivery is an accepted alternative, though a systematic review found IO administration associated with lower ROSC rates in some observational analyses, raising unresolved questions about pharmacokinetic equivalence during low-flow states. — High-dose epinephrine (2–5 mg, or 0.1–0.2 mg/kg) has no survival benefit over the standard 1 mg dose and carries excess harm — this is a settled historical pitfall, not a dosing option. — Intraosseous access is an accepted alternative when IV access cannot be established rapidly, but the evidence base for its pharmacokinetic equivalence to IV is predominantly observational. — American Heart Association — US professional body issuing advanced cardiovascular life support guidelines, most recently updated in 2020. — European Resuscitation Council — European counterpart to the AHA issuing resuscitation guidelines, most recently updated in 2021. — intravenous — Route of epinephrine administration in cardiac arrest and shock states, and for refractory anaphylaxis infusion. — intraosseous — Alternative route to IV in cardiac arrest when venous access cannot be rapidly established. — return of spontaneous circulation — Restoration of a perfusing rhythm after cardiac arrest; post-ROSC myocardial dysfunction is a recognised epinephrine-related complication. — Double-blind RCT (n=8,014) of IV epinephrine vs placebo in OHCA; showed improved 30-day survival (OR 1.39) but no improvement in favourable neurological outcome.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: Shockable rhythm? — (VF / pVT) — The timing of epinephrine relative to defibrillation is rhythm-dependent, which is why this gate — not present in anaphylaxis or the shock-state lane — asks specifically whether the arrest rhythm is shockable (VF/pVT) before deciding when to give epinephrine. — Timing evidence shows the two rhythm categories pull in opposite directions: in non-shockable rhythms (PEA/asystole), earlier epinephrine is associated with improved survival, whereas in shockable rhythms (VF/pVT), giving epinephrine before defibrillation may be harmful. This is what current AHA 2020 and ERC 2021 guidance encode — epinephrine as soon as feasible in non-shockable rhythms, but defibrillation must never be delayed for epinephrine in shockable rhythms. — American Heart Association — US professional body issuing advanced cardiovascular life support guidelines, most recently updated in 2020. — European Resuscitation Council — European counterpart to the AHA issuing resuscitation guidelines, most recently updated in 2021. — ventricular fibrillation — A shockable cardiac arrest rhythm; defibrillation, not epinephrine, is the immediate priority. — pulseless ventricular tachycardia — A shockable cardiac arrest rhythm, managed identically to VF in the algorithm. — pulseless electrical activity — A non-shockable cardiac arrest rhythm in which early epinephrine (not defibrillation) is the priority.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: Defibrillate first — Epinephrine after 3rd shock — In VF/pVT, defibrillation takes priority; epinephrine is given after the rhythm has had further shock attempts, not instead of or before prompt defibrillation. — A systematic review/meta-analysis examining epinephrine timing relative to the first shock found that early epinephrine before shock delivery in VF/pVT was not beneficial — reinforcing that in a shockable rhythm, restoring a perfusing rhythm electrically is the immediate priority. — ventricular fibrillation — A shockable cardiac arrest rhythm; defibrillation, not epinephrine, is the immediate priority. — pulseless ventricular tachycardia — A shockable cardiac arrest rhythm, managed identically to VF in the algorithm.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text:
Epinephrine ASAP — (PEA / asystole)
Early timing critical — In non-shockable rhythms (PEA or asystole), epinephrine should be given as soon as feasible — here, early administration is itself the intervention, since there is no shockable rhythm to prioritise instead. — Two independent analyses (Panchal et al. and Okubo et al.) found that earlier epinephrine administration is associated with improved survival specifically in non-shockable rhythms, and that delay is harmful in this context — the mechanistic rationale being that, absent a shockable rhythm to treat first, epinephrine's α1-mediated support of coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure is the primary lever available during the arrest. — pulseless electrical activity — A non-shockable cardiac arrest rhythm in which early epinephrine (not defibrillation) is the priority.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: SHOCK STATES — This lane covers epinephrine's role across the three major shock subtypes — septic (distributive), cardiogenic, and obstructive — where, unlike anaphylaxis and cardiac arrest, the risk-benefit balance is sharply different in each subtype and cannot be generalised across them. — The unifying theme of the underlying review is that epinephrine's risk-benefit calculus is highly indication-specific: haemodynamically appropriate but metabolically costly in septic shock, and a drug of last resort in cardiogenic shock, with obstructive shock requiring the underlying obstruction to be treated rather than papered over with a vasopressor. Clinicians who treat shock as a monolithic class — "epinephrine is a vasopressor, therefore use it in shock" — are exposed to the full spectrum of preventable epinephrine-related harm this lane is built to prevent.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: Identify shock subtype — (distributive / cardiogenic / obstructive) — Before any vasopressor decision is made, the shock subtype must be identified, because epinephrine's appropriate role — second-line, last-resort, or actively contraindicated — depends entirely on which subtype is present. — This triage step is the structural core of the shock-states lane: the same drug, at the same dose, is haemodynamically reasonable second-line therapy in septic shock, a drug reserved for refractory cases as a bridge to mechanical support in cardiogenic shock, and a drug whose tachycardic and afterload effects can actively worsen obstructive shock if given without first addressing the underlying obstruction.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
