entries.text: Septic — Distributive (septic) shock — the subtype in which epinephrine has the best-characterised, guideline-endorsed, if strictly second-line, role among the three. — Noradrenaline is recommended first-line in septic shock by both the 2016 and 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines, reflecting its more favourable haemodynamic profile and lesser propensity for tachycardia and metabolic adverse effects than epinephrine.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: NE 1st-line, Epi 2nd-line — (SSC 2021) — Noradrenaline remains first-line; epinephrine is added or substituted as a guideline-endorsed second-line vasopressor when noradrenaline at high doses fails to maintain target mean arterial pressure. — Randomised evidence (the Annane et al. CAT trial, Myburgh et al.) found no significant difference in mortality between epinephrine and noradrenaline (or noradrenaline plus dobutamine) in septic shock, and a meta-analysis of seven RCTs (Zhou et al., concordant with the network meta-analysis of Belletti et al.) confirmed equipoise on 28-day mortality (OR 1.13, 95% CI 0.74–1.73). The epinephrine groups in these trials consistently showed higher heart rate, greater lactate concentrations and more frequent tachyarrhythmias — haemodynamic equivalence for the primary mortality endpoint, but a clinically meaningful metabolic cost as a secondary consideration. Vasopressin added to noradrenaline (the VASST trial) is a catecholamine-sparing adjunct that can permit dose reduction and attenuate epinephrine's metabolic footprint when it is in use. — Annane et al. RCT comparing epinephrine with noradrenaline plus dobutamine in septic shock; found no significant mortality difference. — Trial of vasopressin added to noradrenaline in septic shock; a catecholamine-sparing strategy that can reduce epinephrine exposure.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: Cardiogenic — Primary myocardial-failure shock — the subtype in which epinephrine's combined α1 vasopressor and β1 inotropic profile looks pharmacologically well-suited on paper, but where the trial evidence cautions strongly against that conclusion. — Epinephrine's β1-driven rise in myocardial oxygen consumption worsens demand ischaemia in an already compromised myocardium; its chronotropic effect shortens diastolic filling time and further impairs ventricular function; and at high α1 doses, increased afterload can acutely worsen left ventricular ejection in patients with reduced contractile reserve. These mechanisms coalesce to make epinephrine a potentially hazardous choice in primary cardiogenic shock, particularly after acute MI.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: Epi: LAST RESORT — (OptimaCC) — Noradrenaline, or noradrenaline plus dobutamine, is the preferred strategy in most contemporary cardiogenic-shock protocols; epinephrine is reserved for refractory cases as a bridge to definitive mechanical circulatory support, with continuous monitoring for arrhythmia and haemodynamic deterioration. — The OptimaCC randomised trial compared epinephrine with noradrenaline in cardiogenic shock after acute MI and was terminated early, after only 57 enrolments, because of significantly higher rates of refractory shock, ventricular arrhythmias and excess mortality in the epinephrine arm. Finnish registry data (Tarvasmäki et al.) corroborated this in real-world practice: epinephrine use in cardiogenic shock was independently associated with organ injury and higher mortality after propensity adjustment, compared with other vasoactive regimens. — RCT comparing epinephrine with noradrenaline in cardiogenic shock after acute MI; stopped early at 57 patients for excess harm in the epinephrine arm.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: Obstructive — Shock from a mechanical obstruction to flow — massive pulmonary embolism, cardiac tamponade or tension pneumothorax — in which catecholamine support is, at best, a bridge to definitive intervention, and epinephrine specifically carries a paradoxical-harm risk. — In massive PE, epinephrine's tachycardic effect reduces right-ventricular diastolic filling time, while its α1-mediated systemic vasoconstriction may paradoxically worsen RV afterload — the opposite of what the obstructed, afterload-sensitive right ventricle needs. Inadvertent epinephrine use in unrecognised obstructive shock is a documented cause of preventable haemodynamic deterioration. — pulmonary embolism — When massive, a cause of obstructive shock; definitive treatment is thrombolysis, not vasopressor escalation.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: Treat cause first — PE: thrombolysis — Definitive treatment of the underlying obstruction — thrombolysis for massive PE, pericardiocentesis for tamponade, decompression for tension pneumothorax — takes priority over vasopressor titration; vasopressin, noradrenaline or phenylephrine are the preferred catecholamine choices in this context, not epinephrine. — Because epinephrine's haemodynamic effects can actively worsen the physiology of obstructive shock (see the Obstructive branch), the evidence-based response is to fix the obstruction rather than to escalate a vasopressor that may be making the underlying problem worse. — pulmonary embolism — When massive, a cause of obstructive shock; definitive treatment is thrombolysis, not vasopressor escalation.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: MONITORING — ALL CONTEXTS — Regardless of which of the three lanes above applies, epinephrine's metabolic and cardiovascular footprint must be actively monitored for — these are not alternative pathways but concurrent safety obligations in every context where epinephrine is used. — A recurring theme of the underlying review is that epinephrine's adverse-effect profile is frequently under-recognised or misattributed, with real clinical consequences — most importantly, epinephrine-induced hyperlactataemia being mistaken for ongoing shock-related tissue hypoperfusion and driving unnecessary escalation of fluids or vasopressor dose.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: Tachyarrhythmia — (continuous ECG) — β1 chronotropy and increased automaticity make tachyarrhythmia — atrial fibrillation, SVT, VT or VF — the most frequent and potentially fatal cardiovascular adverse effect of epinephrine, and can exacerbate dynamic LVOT obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. — Arrhythmogenic potential is exacerbated by hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, myocardial ischaemia and concurrent QT-prolonging agents. Continuous cardiac monitoring is mandatory throughout any epinephrine infusion, and the lowest effective dose should be used; sudden rhythm deterioration should prompt review of dose, electrolytes and myocardial perfusion. — ventricular fibrillation — A shockable cardiac arrest rhythm; defibrillation, not epinephrine, is the immediate priority.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: Myocardial ischaemia — Increased myocardial oxygen demand and, at high α1 activation, coronary vasospasm can produce demand ischaemia — including post-resuscitation myocardial dysfunction resembling stress cardiomyopathy after ROSC. — Post-resuscitation myocardial dysfunction occurs in a significant proportion of ROSC patients and is attributable in part to the catecholamine surge amplified by resuscitative epinephrine. Targeted temperature management, serial troponin measurement and early echocardiography are the recommended mitigations. — return of spontaneous circulation — Restoration of a perfusing rhythm after cardiac arrest; post-ROSC myocardial dysfunction is a recognised epinephrine-related complication.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: Hyperlactataemia — (β2-aerobic ≠ hypoxia) — Hyperlactataemia during epinephrine infusion at therapeutic rates is a near-universal finding, driven by β2-receptor aerobic glycolysis in skeletal muscle — not tissue hypoxia — and is mechanistically distinct from shock-related type A lactic acidosis. — The failure to contextualise elevated lactate in the setting of an epinephrine infusion is a well-documented pitfall that leads to unnecessary fluid resuscitation, escalation of vasopressor doses, or premature consideration of extracorporeal support. Clinical decision-making should integrate serial lactate trends, clinical perfusion markers, and the temporal relationship between epinephrine initiation and lactate elevation, rather than treating any elevated lactate as proof of ongoing hypoperfusion.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: Hyperglycaemia — (glucose q1–2 h) — Hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis via β-adrenoceptors, combined with α2-mediated suppression of insulin secretion, produce clinically significant hyperglycaemia in 40–70% of epinephrine-infused ICU patients. — Regular glucose monitoring (every 1–2 hours) and insulin titration are the recommended mitigations; epinephrine should be used with particular caution in patients with uncontrolled diabetic ketoacidosis.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: Hypokalaemia — (K⁺ supplementation) — β2-mediated cellular potassium uptake via Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activation causes hypokalaemia, an arrhythmogenic risk of particular importance in ischaemic heart disease and in post-cardiac-arrest patients on epinephrine-based vasopressor support. — This risk is potentiated in patients on digoxin or with hypoxaemia. Electrolyte monitoring and targeted potassium replacement, aiming for a serum potassium of 4.0–4.5 mmol/L, are integral components of epinephrine infusion management.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text: Extravasation — (phentolamine 5–10 mg SC) — Epinephrine extravasation from a peripheral IV line causes α1-mediated local tissue ischaemia and, if unrecognised, skin and subcutaneous necrosis — including finger necrosis if inadvertently injected intra-arterially. — Central venous administration is preferred for prolonged infusions. If extravasation does occur via a peripheral line, subcutaneous phentolamine (5–10 mg in 10 mL normal saline) injected into the affected area within 12 hours effectively reverses the vasoconstriction and prevents necrosis. — Prefer a central venous line for any prolonged epinephrine infusion. — If extravasation occurs via a peripheral line, give phentolamine 5–10 mg SC into the affected area within 12 hours. — intravenous — Route of epinephrine administration in cardiac arrest and shock states, and for refractory anaphylaxis infusion.

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text:
STRENGTHS — • Irreplaceable first-line agent in anaphylaxis (WAO / AAAAI / ACAAI)
• Only agent endorsed without qualification for anaphylaxis
• Survival benefit in OHCA — PARAMEDIC2 (OR 1.39, 95% CI 1.06–1.82)
• Haemodynamic equivalence to noradrenaline in septic shock (CAT trial)
• Broad adrenoceptor profile (α1, α2, β1, β2); versatile across shock phenotypes
• Short t½ (2–3 min) — precise, rapidly reversible titration — A summary of epinephrine's evidence-supported strengths across all three clinical contexts covered by this algorithm, drawn together from the underlying review's conclusions. — These strengths are genuinely context-dependent, not a blanket endorsement: the case for epinephrine as irreplaceable first-line therapy is strongest, and essentially unqualified, in anaphylaxis; its survival benefit in cardiac arrest and its mortality-equivalence to noradrenaline in septic shock are real but each come with their own caveats detailed elsewhere in this tool (neurological outcome in arrest; metabolic cost in septic shock).

entries.title: Epinephrine/Adrenaline Revisited
entries.text:
LIMITATIONS / PITFALLS — • No neurological benefit in cardiac arrest — PARAMEDIC2: CPC 1–2 unchanged
• Excess mortality in cardiogenic shock — OptimaCC RCT terminated early
• Hyperlactataemia: β2-aerobic — do NOT misinterpret as tissue hypoperfusion
• Tachyarrhythmia, ↑MVO₂, hyperglycaemia, hypokalaemia at therapeutic doses
• Extravasation → α1-mediated necrosis; prefer central venous line
• Delayed / subcutaneous injection in anaphylaxis → preventable fatality — A summary of epinephrine's principal documented pitfalls and harms across all three clinical contexts — framed in the underlying review as documented contributors to preventable morbidity and mortality, not rare theoretical possibilities. — A unifying theme of the underlying review is that these are not reasons to avoid epinephrine where it is indicated, but reasons that its use must be indication-specific, dose-conscious and actively monitored — the same drug, at the same dose, can be life-saving in anaphylaxis and of uncertain-to-harmful net benefit elsewhere.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care Indication-Based Decision Algorithm

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text:
Pharmacology Snapshot — Mechanism: NMDA antagonist (phencyclidine site)
Additional: µ-opioid partial agonism; monoamine reuptake inhibition; HCN1 blockade; muscarinic antagonism
Onset: IV 30–60 s | IM 3–5 min   Duration: IV 10–20 min | IM 15–30 min
CYP3A4/2B6 metabolism → norketamine (active, ~30% potency)
Vd ~3 L/kg — Ketamine is a phencyclidine-derived, non-competitive NMDA-receptor antagonist that also engages µ-opioid, monoaminergic, HCN1 and muscarinic receptor systems, giving it dissociative anaesthesia, analgesia and amnesia while broadly preserving cardiovascular tone and spontaneous ventilation. — These parameters (mechanism, onset/duration by route, hepatic metabolism to the active metabolite norketamine, and volume of distribution) are what make ketamine behave differently at the bedside from propofol, midazolam or opioids — fast IM onset without reliable IV access, a short redistribution-driven duration, and a lipophilic profile that gets it into the CNS quickly. — N-methyl-D-aspartate — An excitatory glutamate receptor subtype; ketamine's primary action is non-competitive antagonism of this receptor at the phencyclidine binding site within its ion channel. — hyperpolarisation-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated channel 1 — An ion channel ketamine blocks as a secondary mechanism, which may contribute to its hypnotic effect. — Ketamine's principal active hepatic metabolite (via CYP3A4/CYP2B6), with roughly 30% of the parent compound's NMDA-antagonist potency.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text:
Strengths + | Weaknesses × — + Preserves airway reflexes and spontaneous ventilation
+ Cardiovascular stimulation in early shock states
+ Bronchodilation (asthma/COPD)
+ Opioid-sparing; reduces ICU delirium (2025 meta-analysis)
× CV collapse in catecholamine-depleted shock (RSI Trial 2025)
× Emergence reactions adults 5–30%; hypersalivation; tachycardia — A one-line balance sheet for the agent: the properties that make it uniquely useful across emergency and critical care, set directly against the two safety signals a clinician has to actively manage. — Every strength here is mechanistic (preserved ventilation, indirect sympathomimetic drive, bronchodilation, opioid-sparing/anti-delirium effect); both weaknesses are empirically quantified in the literature this review synthesises — the RSI Trial's cardiovascular-collapse signal in catecholamine-depleted shock, and the well-described 5–30% adult emergence-reaction rate. — rapid sequence intubation — Near-simultaneous administration of an induction agent and a paralytic to secure the airway quickly, minimising aspiration risk; ketamine's role as an RSI induction agent is substantially revised by the 2025 RSI Trial covered in this tool.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text: Patient requires ketamine? — Emergency / Critical Care Setting — The entry point into the algorithm: a clinician has identified a patient in the ED or ICU for whom ketamine is a candidate agent — for sedation, analgesia, airway management, chemical restraint, or haemodynamic support. — Ketamine's broad acute-care footprint (procedural sedation, RSI, acute agitation, ICU analgosedation, and resuscitation of the haemodynamically compromised patient) is exactly why the first branch point has to be "what for" rather than a single linear protocol. — rapid sequence intubation — Near-simultaneous administration of an induction agent and a paralytic to secure the airway quickly, minimising aspiration risk; ketamine's role as an RSI induction agent is substantially revised by the 2025 RSI Trial covered in this tool.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text: What is the clinical indication? — The algorithm's single branch point: which of the five principal clinical domains this review covers applies to the patient in front of you. — Dosing, the relevant safety signal, and the supporting evidence base are all indication-specific — a dose and caution set tuned for procedural sedation does not transfer cleanly to RSI in septic shock, or to resuscitation of the haemodynamically compromised patient. — rapid sequence intubation — Near-simultaneous administration of an induction agent and a paralytic to secure the airway quickly, minimising aspiration risk; ketamine's role as an RSI induction agent is substantially revised by the 2025 RSI Trial covered in this tool.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text: Procedural Sedation — ED procedural sedation and analgesia (PSA) in adults and children — orthopaedic reductions, cardioversion, abscess drainage and similar — remains ketamine's single most extensively studied indication. — Comparative and paediatric safety data for this indication are large and mature, which is why the algorithm can give a specific, well-supported dose rather than a general range. — procedural sedation and analgesia — Sedation given specifically to allow a painful or distressing procedure (e.g. fracture reduction, abscess drainage) to be performed safely.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.nodeLabel: Adult: IV 1–2 mg/kg or IM 4–5 mg/kg
entries.text: Adult: IV 1–2 mg/kg or IM 4–5 mg/kg — Paed: IV 1–2 mg/kg — Standard dissociative-sedation dosing per the 2011 clinical practice guideline: IV when access is available, IM when it is not; the same IV range applies in children, with titration by 0.5 mg/kg increments as required. Ketofol (ketamine-propofol admixture) is a recognised alternative, broadly equivalent in sedation quality with marginally faster recovery but greater hypotension risk. — An individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 8,282 children found serious respiratory adverse events in under 1% of cases, with risk concentrated in those under 2 years, high IV doses, and opioid co-administration; a prospective multicentre study of over 6,000 paediatric PSA episodes corroborated this, and a 2025 review confirmed intranasal/oral non-injectable routes are practicable alongside the more reliable IV/IM routes. — procedural sedation and analgesia — Sedation given specifically to allow a painful or distressing procedure (e.g. fracture reduction, abscess drainage) to be performed safely. — ketamine-propofol admixture — A combination sedation technique found broadly equivalent to ketamine monotherapy in sedation quality, with marginally faster recovery but a greater hypotension risk.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text:
Sub-dissociative — 0.1–0.3 mg/kg IV
(opioid-sparing) — A separate, much lower dose range used purely for analgesia (not dissociation) — an opioid-sparing adjunct for acute pain, infused over 10–15 minutes rather than given as a bolus. — A meta-analysis of 15 RCTs (n = 1,613) found pooled pain reduction favouring sub-dissociative ketamine over opioids at 30 minutes, with further RCTs confirming non-inferiority to IV morphine and superior pain reduction when combined with fentanyl; intranasal and nebulised non-parenteral routes are gaining supporting evidence at the same dose range. — sub-dissociative-dose ketamine — Low-dose ketamine (typically 0.1–0.3 mg/kg IV) given purely for its analgesic effect, below the dose that produces dissociative anaesthesia — an opioid-sparing adjunct for acute pain.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text:
Emergence risk → Midazolam — 0.03–0.05 mg/kg
Vomiting → Ondansetron — The two most common adverse effects of procedural-sedation-dose ketamine, with their specific mitigations: co-administered low-dose midazolam for emergence dysphoria, and prophylactic ondansetron for vomiting. — Co-administration of midazolam and a quiet recovery environment substantially reduce the incidence and severity of emergence phenomena; a dedicated systematic review and meta-analysis confirmed prophylactic ondansetron reduces post-sedation vomiting in children and supports its routine use.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text: RSI / Airway — Ketamine as an induction agent for emergency rapid sequence intubation — a role substantially recontextualised by the December 2025 RSI Trial. — RSI induction-agent choice has direct, measurable haemodynamic consequences during the peri-intubation period, which is why this lane is built around a haemodynamic-status gate rather than a single dose. — rapid sequence intubation — Near-simultaneous administration of an induction agent and a paralytic to secure the airway quickly, minimising aspiration risk; ketamine's role as an RSI induction agent is substantially revised by the 2025 RSI Trial covered in this tool.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text: Haemodynamic status? — The gate that decides RSI dosing: is the patient stable or only mildly unstable, or are they in established (particularly septic) catecholamine-depleted shock? — Ketamine's sympathomimetic properties are advantageous when endogenous catecholamine stores are intact, but can be reversed by direct myocardial depression once those stores are depleted — the mechanistic duality the RSI Trial's subgroup findings made clinically concrete. — rapid sequence intubation — Near-simultaneous administration of an induction agent and a paralytic to secure the airway quickly, minimising aspiration risk; ketamine's role as an RSI induction agent is substantially revised by the 2025 RSI Trial covered in this tool.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text: Stable/mild: IV 1–2 mg/kg — Ketamine preferred — In haemodynamically stable or only mildly compromised patients, standard-dose ketamine remains the preferred induction agent. — A contemporaneous meta-analysis of 10 RCTs (n = 2,862) and a separate Bayesian meta-analysis both found no significant all-cause mortality difference between ketamine and etomidate for RSI; earlier RCT and national-registry data support ketamine's superior cardiovascular-function preservation over opioid-based induction in this group. — rapid sequence intubation — Near-simultaneous administration of an induction agent and a paralytic to secure the airway quickly, minimising aspiration risk; ketamine's role as an RSI induction agent is substantially revised by the 2025 RSI Trial covered in this tool.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text:
⚠ Septic/refractory shock — Reduce to 0.5–1 mg/kg
Consider etomidate
(RSI Trial NEJM 2025) — In established or refractory septic shock, the RSI Trial found ketamine carried a significantly higher rate of peri-intubation cardiovascular collapse than etomidate (22.1% vs 17.0% overall; 30.6% vs 20.9% in the septic-shock subgroup), with no offsetting mortality benefit — the algorithm calls for dose reduction and consideration of etomidate instead. — The multicentre RSI Trial (2,365 critically ill adults, 6 EDs + 8 ICUs) found 28-day mortality was statistically indistinguishable between agents (28.1% vs 29.1%), but the cardiovascular-collapse excess was substantially amplified in its septic/septic-shock subgroup (46.7% of the trial population) — exactly where ketamine's indirect sympathomimetic mechanism is least reliable. A 2025 meta-analysis also found post-induction hypotension exceeds 20% across agents and is associated with increased mortality, reinforcing pre-intubation optimisation regardless of agent. — Pre-treat with push-dose vasopressors and optimise haemodynamics before induction where possible. — The RSI Trial data are also the basis for etomidate's rehabilitation — no adrenal-suppression-attributable mortality signal was identified in its 2,365-patient population. — rapid sequence intubation — Near-simultaneous administration of an induction agent and a paralytic to secure the airway quickly, minimising aspiration risk; ketamine's role as an RSI induction agent is substantially revised by the 2025 RSI Trial covered in this tool.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text: Acute Agitation — Chemical restraint of the severely agitated patient — excited delirium syndrome, stimulant-induced agitation — where rapid onset matters most. — IM ketamine's 3–5 minute onset and potent dissociative effect make it particularly suited to this setting compared with slower-onset agents.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text:
IM 4–5 mg/kg — Onset 3–5 min
(ExDS/prehospital) — Standard IM dosing for severe agitation, validated in prehospital and aeromedical retrieval contexts as well as the ED. — A 2025 RCT (n = 120) found IV ketamine achieved RASS ≤ +1 significantly faster than IV haloperidol; earlier reviews comparing ketamine to haloperidol-benzodiazepine combinations found faster time to adequate sedation with ketamine, albeit at a higher adverse-effect rate — together supporting its first-line role when rapid control is the priority. — Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale — A validated scale used to grade a patient's level of sedation or agitation; used as the outcome measure in trials comparing ketamine with haloperidol for acute agitation.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text:
⚠ ~20% require airway rescue — Airway equipment mandatory
at all times — A systematic review and proportional meta-analysis of 13 studies (n = 1,090) found effective sedation in 85% of agitated patients given ketamine, but roughly 20% subsequently required invasive airway management. — This is the single biggest safety trade-off of using ketamine for chemical restraint: its efficacy at rapid sedation does not come with a correspondingly low airway-intervention rate, so full airway equipment and personnel must be immediately available whenever it is used for this indication.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text: ICU Analgosedation — Low-dose ketamine as an opioid-sparing adjunct within a multimodal ICU analgosedation protocol, not as a standalone sedative. — Both the 2025 SCCM PADIS guideline and the KSCCM guideline maintain a conditional recommendation for this role, reflecting a maturing but not yet definitive evidence base. — Pain, Agitation/Sedation, Delirium, Immobility, and Sleep Disruption — The Society of Critical Care Medicine's clinical practice guideline for ICU patients, most recently updated in 2025; it maintains a conditional recommendation for low-dose ketamine as an opioid-sparing analgosedation adjunct. — Society of Critical Care Medicine — The US professional society that publishes the PADIS guideline for ICU pain, agitation, sedation and delirium management. — Korean Society of Critical Care Medicine — Publishes its own clinical practice guideline for ICU pain, agitation, delirium, immobility and sleep disturbance, which independently endorses adjunctive low-dose ketamine.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text: Bolus 0.5 mg/kg IV — then 1–2 µg/kg/min infusion — The suggested ICU analgosedation protocol: a 0.5 mg/kg IV bolus followed by a continuous low-dose infusion, adjunctive to (not replacing) opioid-based sedation. — This is the specific regimen named by the 2025 SCCM PADIS guideline and endorsed by the KSCCM guideline for adjunctive use in mechanically ventilated ICU patients. — Pain, Agitation/Sedation, Delirium, Immobility, and Sleep Disruption — The Society of Critical Care Medicine's clinical practice guideline for ICU patients, most recently updated in 2025; it maintains a conditional recommendation for low-dose ketamine as an opioid-sparing analgosedation adjunct. — Society of Critical Care Medicine — The US professional society that publishes the PADIS guideline for ICU pain, agitation, sedation and delirium management. — Korean Society of Critical Care Medicine — Publishes its own clinical practice guideline for ICU pain, agitation, delirium, immobility and sleep disturbance, which independently endorses adjunctive low-dose ketamine.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text:
↓ Opioid use — ↓ ICU delirium
↓ ICU length of stay — The patient-centred outcome gains associated with ketamine-based ICU analgosedation: reduced opioid consumption, reduced delirium incidence, and shorter ICU length of stay. — A 2024 RCT-only meta-analysis found ketamine reduced ICU delirium rates without a significant mortality or opioid-consumption effect; a 2025 meta-analysis of 903 patients across six controlled trials specifically found a significant reduction in ICU length of stay (mean difference −0.86 days) and delirium incidence (OR 0.55), without a significant reduction in mechanical ventilation duration.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text:
Per 2025 SCCM PADIS guideline — (conditional rec.)
Monitor: tachycardia, hypertension — The evidence supports this as a conditional, not strong, recommendation — adjunctive ketamine infusion is reasonable but should be monitored for its own dose-dependent cardiovascular effects. — A 2024 scoping review of continuous ketamine infusion in mechanically ventilated patients (27 publications) found 85.7% of studies reporting safety data identified no significant adverse reactions and rare emergence reactions in the sedated, ventilated ICU population — reassuring, but still warranting routine haemodynamic monitoring given ketamine's sympathomimetic mechanism.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text: Haemodynamic Instability — Use of ketamine for resuscitation and peri-intubation support in haemorrhagic, obstructive, and early septic shock, where most alternative induction/sedation agents carry significant hypotension risk. — Ketamine's catecholamine-preserving mechanism offers a pharmacological buffer during the peri-intubation period specifically when endogenous adrenergic stores are not yet exhausted.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text: Catecholamine stores intact? — The same mechanistic gate as the RSI lane's "haemodynamic status?" question, asked here in its sharpest form: does this patient still have functioning endogenous adrenergic reserve for ketamine's indirect sympathomimetic action to work on? — This is the single mechanistic fact that reconciles ketamine's two opposite reputations — a haemodynamic stabiliser in early/compensated shock, and a precipitant of cardiovascular collapse once catecholamine stores are exhausted in prolonged or refractory shock. — rapid sequence intubation — Near-simultaneous administration of an induction agent and a paralytic to secure the airway quickly, minimising aspiration risk; ketamine's role as an RSI induction agent is substantially revised by the 2025 RSI Trial covered in this tool.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text: YES: Ketamine preferred — ↑ HR   ↑ MAP   ↑ CO — With intact catecholamine stores, ketamine's indirect sympathomimetic effect raises heart rate, mean arterial pressure and cardiac output — a genuine haemodynamic advantage over induction agents that lower blood pressure. — An RCT comparing ketamine-based to fentanyl-based RSI regimens in septic shock found fewer vasopressor dose escalations in the immediate post-intubation period with ketamine, and a 2025 prospective study of low-dose ketamine infusion in ventilated septic shock patients found no ICP increase alongside favourable haemodynamics including maintained cerebral perfusion pressure. — rapid sequence intubation — Near-simultaneous administration of an induction agent and a paralytic to secure the airway quickly, minimising aspiration risk; ketamine's role as an RSI induction agent is substantially revised by the 2025 RSI Trial covered in this tool. — intracranial pressure — Historically considered a contraindication to ketamine use; contemporary evidence in mechanically ventilated patients with controlled ventilation does not support clinically significant ICP elevation — see the ICP Myth Revised note in this tool.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text:
⚠ Depleted state: direct -ve inotropy — Reduce dose or choose etomidate
(RSI Trial 2025) — Once catecholamine stores are exhausted — prolonged or refractory septic or cardiogenic shock — ketamine's direct negative inotropic effect is unmasked and can paradoxically worsen haemodynamics; the algorithm calls for dose reduction to 0.5–1 mg/kg or choosing etomidate instead. — This is the same mechanistic duality that the RSI Trial's septic-shock subgroup findings made clinically concrete: the trial counsels a more individualised approach in established septic shock, with pre-treatment push-dose vasopressors and dose reduction where ketamine is still used. — rapid sequence intubation — Near-simultaneous administration of an induction agent and a paralytic to secure the airway quickly, minimising aspiration risk; ketamine's role as an RSI induction agent is substantially revised by the 2025 RSI Trial covered in this tool.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text: Monitoring & Safety Essentials — A set of monitoring and mitigation requirements that apply across every indication above, not to any single lane — airway readiness, standard physiological monitoring, administration technique, and the two most common adverse effects with their prevention. — Collecting these in one always-applicable panel, rather than repeating them in every lane, matches how the source figure itself presents them — as a shared safety layer beneath the indication-specific algorithm, not as its own decision branch.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text:
Airway & monitoring — Airway equipment immediately available
O2 saturation, ETCO2, BP, ECG monitoring
IV push >60 s to avoid apnoea
Glycopyrrolate for secretion control — The baseline physiological-monitoring and administration-technique requirements for any ketamine use in the emergency or critical care setting. — Rapid IV administration, opioid co-administration, or dosing in very young infants increase the risk of transient apnoea and laryngospasm; hypersalivation is a common, separately manageable effect of the drug's muscarinic-antagonist profile.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text:
Emergence & contraindications — Emergence reactions: quiet env. + midazolam
Ondansetron prophylaxis for vomiting
Avoid: aortic dissection, severe uncontrolled hypertension, age <3 months, active psychosis — The management plan for ketamine's most common psychomimetic/GI adverse effects, plus the relative contraindications where ketamine's sympathomimetic and psychomimetic effects make it a poor choice. — Emergence reactions occur in 5–30% of adults and are more common in women and those with pre-existing psychiatric illness; absolute contraindications are limited to known hypersensitivity, but relative contraindications include severe uncontrolled hypertension, aortic dissection, non-ventilated intracranial haemorrhage, severe pre-eclampsia, uncontrolled thyrotoxicosis, catecholamine-depleted cardiogenic shock, active psychotic disorder for elective sedation, and age under 3 months.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text: Special Populations — Four patient groups in whom ketamine's risk-benefit balance is specifically altered, each requiring its own adjustment rather than the standard-indication dosing above. — These populations cut across every indication lane — a paediatric agitation case, a geriatric procedural sedation, a TBI RSI — so, like the monitoring panel, the source figure presents them as a shared layer rather than duplicating them per lane. — rapid sequence intubation — Near-simultaneous administration of an induction agent and a paralytic to secure the airway quickly, minimising aspiration risk; ketamine's role as an RSI induction agent is substantially revised by the 2025 RSI Trial covered in this tool.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text:
TBI — Safe in ventilated pts
Maintain normocapnia
(ICP myth revised) — Contemporary evidence supports ketamine for airway management and analgosedation in mechanically ventilated traumatic brain injury patients, provided normocapnia (PaCO2 35–40 mmHg) is maintained. — The historical ICP contraindication was rooted in small, non-randomised case series in spontaneously breathing, non-monitored patients; multiple contemporary systematic reviews in ventilated TBI patients have not reproduced it — see the ICP Myth Revised note below. — intracranial pressure — Historically considered a contraindication to ketamine use; contemporary evidence in mechanically ventilated patients with controlled ventilation does not support clinically significant ICP elevation — see the ICP Myth Revised note in this tool.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text:
Asthma / COPD — Agent of choice
Direct bronchodilation benefit — Ketamine is the preferred induction agent for patients with reactive airways disease requiring intubation, and sub-dissociative doses have been used adjunctively in refractory bronchospasm. — Its bronchodilatory effect — mediated through catecholamine release and direct smooth-muscle relaxation — is supported by both mechanistic reasoning and extensive clinical experience, making it uniquely suited to the uncommon combination of obstructive airways disease with circulatory compromise. — sub-dissociative-dose ketamine — Low-dose ketamine (typically 0.1–0.3 mg/kg IV) given purely for its analgesic effect, below the dose that produces dissociative anaesthesia — an opioid-sparing adjunct for acute pain.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text:
Geriatrics — Reduce dose 50–75%
Heightened psychomimetic risk — Older patients, particularly those with pre-existing cognitive impairment, may be more sensitive to ketamine's psychomimetic effects and generally need reduced doses. — Multimodal analgesic strategies combining sub-dissociative ketamine with non-opioid adjuncts can minimise opioid-related adverse effects in this population; catecholamine-stimulatory effects may also be attenuated by chronic beta-blocker therapy or autonomic neuropathy, both more common in older adults. — sub-dissociative-dose ketamine — Low-dose ketamine (typically 0.1–0.3 mg/kg IV) given purely for its analgesic effect, below the dose that produces dissociative anaesthesia — an opioid-sparing adjunct for acute pain.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text: Pregnancy — Emergency use only; crosses placenta — Ketamine crosses the placenta and has been used in emergency obstetric anaesthesia, particularly for haemorrhagic cases, where its haemodynamic properties are advantageous. — Its association with increased uterine tone can be beneficial in obstetric haemorrhage but must be weighed against the risk of uterine hyperstimulation; it should be reserved for genuine obstetric emergencies, as high-quality obstetric trial data remain limited.

entries.title: Ketamine in Emergency and Critical Care
entries.text: ICP Myth Revised — Ketamine does NOT increase ICP in mechanically ventilated patients (multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses 2024–2025). The historical contraindication in TBI is no longer supported by contemporary evidence. — The single most consequential revision in this review's safety literature: the decades-old teaching that ketamine raises intracranial pressure and is therefore contraindicated in head injury does not hold up under contemporary, controlled-ventilation evidence. — A 2024 meta-analysis of 21 studies (n = 886) found no clinically significant ICP elevation attributable to ketamine in TBI patients under controlled mechanical ventilation, with several studies reporting a statistically significant ICP reduction; a 2025 PROSPERO-registered systematic review and meta-analysis similarly found no increase in ICP crisis events (RR 0.67; 95% CI 0.45–1.01); the ongoing BIKe trial (NCT05097261) is specifically designed to provide definitive prospective RCT data. — intracranial pressure — Historically considered a contraindication to ketamine use; contemporary evidence in mechanically ventilated patients with controlled ventilation does not support clinically significant ICP elevation — see the ICP Myth Revised note in this tool. — Brain Injury and Ketamine trial — An ongoing prospective, double-blind RCT (NCT05097261) specifically designed to evaluate ketamine as adjunct sedation in severe TBI with ICP monitoring as a primary safety endpoint.

entries.title: Tenecteplase versus Alteplase
entries.text: Tenecteplase versus Alteplase Fibrinolysis in STEMI When Timely Primary PCI Is Not Available

entries.title: Tenecteplase versus Alteplase
entries.text: STEMI confirmed on 12-lead ECG — (within 10 min of first medical contact) — The entry point: a patient whose 12-lead ECG shows persistent ST-segment elevation (or presumed new left bundle branch block) consistent with acute total coronary occlusion, confirmed as early as possible after first medical contact (FMC) — ambulance arrival, emergency-department triage, or equivalent. From here the only question that matters is which reperfusion strategy, and how fast. — STEMI is distinguished from other acute coronary syndromes precisely by this ECG finding, reflecting acute total occlusion that requires immediate reperfusion rather than the staged work-up appropriate for non-ST-elevation ACS. The population this whole algorithm — and the trials behind it — is defined the same way: presenting with STEMI or presumed new LBBB within 12 hours of symptom onset. The specific '10 minutes of FMC' ECG target is standard ESC/ACC guideline practice rather than a figure spelled out in the manuscript's own running text; it is carried here as the authors drew it in Figure 2, on the same guideline references cited for the algorithm as a whole. — ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction — Acute total coronary occlusion producing persistent ST-segment elevation on the ECG; it requires immediate reperfusion, by primary PCI if deliverable in time, otherwise by fibrinolysis. — first medical contact — The time point guideline time-targets are anchored to — ambulance arrival, emergency-department triage, or the equivalent first point of contact with a healthcare provider who can act on the diagnosis.

entries.title: Tenecteplase versus Alteplase
entries.text: Anticipated FMC-to-PCI (wire crossing) time ≤120 min? — Primary PCI is the preferred reperfusion strategy whenever it can genuinely be delivered fast enough — this gate asks whether that is realistic given anticipated transfer and catheterisation-lab timing, not merely whether a cath lab exists somewhere in the system. — 'Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is the preferred reperfusion strategy when it can be delivered within 120 minutes of diagnosis, and fibrinolysis is recommended when this time target cannot be met...' (Section 1), citing current ESC and ACC/AHA guidance. — percutaneous coronary intervention — Catheter-based mechanical reperfusion (balloon angioplasty ± stenting) of the occluded coronary artery — the preferred reperfusion strategy whenever it can be delivered within the guideline time window.

entries.title: Tenecteplase versus Alteplase
entries.text: Primary PCI — If the 120-minute window is realistic, this tool's fibrinolysis pathway does not apply: primary PCI is mechanical reperfusion with reliably higher patency and a lower intracranial-haemorrhage risk than any fibrinolytic agent, which is precisely why fibrinolysis is reserved for when timely PCI genuinely is not available. — Both the 2023 ESC guidelines for acute coronary syndromes and the 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI guideline name primary PCI the default reperfusion strategy whenever it can be delivered on time. — percutaneous coronary intervention — Catheter-based mechanical reperfusion (balloon angioplasty ± stenting) of the occluded coronary artery — the preferred reperfusion strategy whenever it can be delivered within the guideline time window.

entries.title: Tenecteplase versus Alteplase
entries.nodeLabel: Symptom onset ≤12 h and no absolute contraindication to fibrinolysis (prior ICH, recent ischaemic stroke, active bleeding, aortic dissection)?
entries.text: Symptom onset ≤12 h and no absolute contraindication to fibrinolysis (prior ICH, recent ischaemic stroke, active bleeding, aortic dissection)? — The fibrinolysis eligibility gate, with two conditions that must both hold: the patient is still early enough in their infarct (≤12 h from symptom onset) for fibrinolysis to plausibly open the artery, and none of the well-established absolute contraindications that make fibrinolysis's intracranial-haemorrhage risk unacceptable are present. — '...fibrinolysis is recommended when this time target cannot be met, provided that it is started within 12 hours of symptom onset and followed by early angiography' (Section 1). The specific contraindication list drawn in this box (prior ICH, recent ischaemic stroke, active bleeding, aortic dissection) reflects standard ESC/ACC absolute-contraindication criteria rather than an item-by-item list spelled out in the manuscript's own running text — it is carried here exactly as the authors' Figure 2 draws it. — intracranial haemorrhage — The most feared complication of fibrinolysis. Its risk is driven mainly by patient factors — age, sex, body weight and blood-pressure control — rather than by the choice between tenecteplase and alteplase, whose randomised ICH rates are statistically equivalent.

entries.title: Tenecteplase versus Alteplase
entries.nodeLabel: Transfer for PCI irrespective of delay
entries.text: Transfer for PCI irrespective of delay — urgent angiography if ongoing ischaemia or shock — When fibrinolysis is either too late to plausibly help or unsafe because of an absolute contraindication, the algorithm does not abandon reperfusion — it falls back to transfer for mechanical PCI regardless of how long that transfer takes, escalating to urgent (not routine) angiography specifically if the patient is showing ongoing ischaemia or cardiogenic shock. — This mirrors standard guideline practice: fibrinolysis is a time-limited substitute for PCI, not an alternative to reach for when PCI is merely delayed and fibrinolysis itself would be unsafe or too late to work. The escalation to urgent angiography for ongoing ischaemia or shock follows the same logic used elsewhere in this algorithm for failed or high-risk reperfusion — see the REACT and STREAM-2 rescue-PCI evidence behind the 'Failed fibrinolysis' box below. — percutaneous coronary intervention — Catheter-based mechanical reperfusion (balloon angioplasty ± stenting) of the occluded coronary artery — the preferred reperfusion strategy whenever it can be delivered within the guideline time window.

entries.title: Tenecteplase versus Alteplase
entries.nodeLabel: Start fibrinolysis within 10 min of diagnosis
entries.text:
Start fibrinolysis within 10 min of diagnosis — (prehospital where possible)
Preferred agent: TENECTEPLASE (single IV bolus over 5–10 s)
Alteplase acceptable only if tenecteplase is unavailable — The review's central practical recommendation: tenecteplase as the default fibrinolytic, given as fast as possible — ideally before hospital arrival — rather than alteplase held as a routine alternative. — '...international guidelines list tenecteplase among the preferred fibrin-specific agents and ... recent reviews describe it as the default fibrinolytic for STEMI when timely PCI is not available' (Section 4.2). This rests on randomised equivalence for 30-day mortality (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.90–1.15) and intracranial haemorrhage (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.71–1.31) between tenecteplase and alteplase, a modest bleeding advantage for tenecteplase (RR 0.79 for major non-cerebral bleeding), and tenecteplase's single 5–10 second bolus — eliminating infusion pumps, reducing preparation and administration errors, shortening door-to-needle time, and uniquely enabling paramedic-administered prehospital fibrinolysis, which is central to the pharmaco-invasive programmes this review's indirect evidence is built on. — ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction — Acute total coronary occlusion producing persistent ST-segment elevation on the ECG; it requires immediate reperfusion, by primary PCI if deliverable in time, otherwise by fibrinolysis. — percutaneous coronary intervention — Catheter-based mechanical reperfusion (balloon angioplasty ± stenting) of the occluded coronary artery — the preferred reperfusion strategy whenever it can be delivered within the guideline time window. — pharmaco-invasive strategy — Fibrinolysis followed by planned, early (typically 2–24 h) transfer for routine angiography ± PCI — distinct from fibrinolysis alone (no planned angiography) or primary PCI (no fibrinolysis at all). Most of this review's indirect evidence validates tenecteplase specifically within this strategy. — door-to-needle time — The interval from hospital arrival to fibrinolytic administration. Earlier guidelines specified a 30-minute target; tenecteplase's single-bolus administration helps shorten this further, including enabling prehospital dosing before 'door' is even reached.

entries.title: Tenecteplase versus Alteplase
entries.text: Age ≥75 years? — A dosing fork, not an eligibility gate: age 75 or over does not change whether fibrinolysis is given, only how much tenecteplase. — The STREAM programme specifically identified age ≥75 as the threshold at which full-dose tenecteplase's intracranial-haemorrhage risk becomes disproportionate, prompting the age-adjusted half-dose regimen now reflected in current guideline recommendations.

entries.title: Tenecteplase versus Alteplase
entries.text:
Full weight-tiered tenecteplase — 30 mg <60 kg; 35 mg 60–69 kg; 40 mg 70–79 kg; 45 mg 80–89 kg; 50 mg ≥90 kg
(Alteplase: 15 mg bolus + 0.75 mg/kg over 30 min, max 50 mg + 0.5 mg/kg over 60 min, max 35 mg) — Standard weight-tiered tenecteplase dosing for patients under 75, approximating 0.5 mg/kg as a single bolus — the regimen used across the modern randomised trials this review's direct evidence is built on. The bracketed alteplase regimen is the accelerated (front-loaded) 90-minute fallback, used only when tenecteplase genuinely is not available. — Table 2's comparative pharmacology and dosing summary gives this exact weight-tiered tenecteplase schedule and the three-part accelerated alteplase regimen (15 mg bolus, then 0.75 mg/kg over 30 minutes to a maximum of 50 mg, then 0.5 mg/kg over 60 minutes to a maximum of 35 mg, total ≤100 mg over 90 minutes). — Tenecteplase, <60 kg — 30 mg IV bolus (5–10 s) — Tenecteplase, 60–69 kg — 35 mg IV bolus (5–10 s) — Tenecteplase, 70–79 kg — 40 mg IV bolus (5–10 s) — Tenecteplase, 80–89 kg — 45 mg IV bolus (5–10 s) — Tenecteplase, ≥90 kg — 50 mg IV bolus (5–10 s) — Alteplase, if tenecteplase unavailable — 15 mg bolus, then 0.75 mg/kg over 30 min (max 50 mg), then 0.5 mg/kg over 60 min (max 35 mg) — total ≤100 mg/90 min

entries.title: Tenecteplase versus Alteplase
entries.text:
HALF-DOSE tenecteplase — (weight-tiered dose ÷ 2)
Reduces ICH without loss of efficacy; no validated age-adjusted alteplase regimen — Simply halves whichever weight-tiered tenecteplase dose the patient would otherwise receive. No equivalent age-adjusted alteplase regimen has been validated in STEMI outcome trials, which is why the algorithm does not offer a parallel half-dose alteplase option here. — A pooled analysis of STREAM and STREAM-2 found that among patients aged 75 or older, half-dose tenecteplase was associated with no intracranial haemorrhage, versus 7.1% with full-dose tenecteplase, without loss of efficacy. STREAM-2 itself randomised 604 patients aged ≥60 to half-dose tenecteplase plus early angiography versus primary PCI, with a comparable 30-day composite outcome (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.62–1.48). 'No validated age-adjusted alteplase regimen' reflects the review's own finding: half-dose alteplase has only been tested within a pharmaco-invasive strategy in China (EARLY-MYO), not studied as a direct age-based substitute the way tenecteplase has been. — Tenecteplase, age ≥75 y — weight-tiered dose ÷ 2 (see full-dose tiers) — ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction — Acute total coronary occlusion producing persistent ST-segment elevation on the ECG; it requires immediate reperfusion, by primary PCI if deliverable in time, otherwise by fibrinolysis. — percutaneous coronary intervention — Catheter-based mechanical reperfusion (balloon angioplasty ± stenting) of the occluded coronary artery — the preferred reperfusion strategy whenever it can be delivered within the guideline time window. — pharmaco-invasive strategy — Fibrinolysis followed by planned, early (typically 2–24 h) transfer for routine angiography ± PCI — distinct from fibrinolysis alone (no planned angiography) or primary PCI (no fibrinolysis at all). Most of this review's indirect evidence validates tenecteplase specifically within this strategy.

entries.title: Tenecteplase versus Alteplase
entries.text:
Adjunctive therapy — aspirin; clopidogrel 300 mg (75 mg if ≥75 years); enoxaparin (age- and renal-adjusted) or UFH
keep systolic BP controlled; avoid excess anticoagulation — Fibrinolysis is never given alone — this is the antithrombotic and blood-pressure-control scaffold given alongside it, regardless of which dose or agent was chosen above. — Clopidogrel's age-adjusted loading dose (300 mg, or 75 mg if ≥75) and its artery-patency benefit come from the CLARITY-TIMI 28 programme. Enoxaparin reduced death or reinfarction versus unfractionated heparin in ExTRACT-TIMI 25 (9.9% vs 12.0%) at the cost of more major bleeding (2.1% vs 1.4%); age-adjusted dosing in patients ≥75 attenuated that bleeding excess, and the benefit shrank as renal function worsened. Blood-pressure control matters specifically because of intracranial-haemorrhage risk: the manuscript cites a pooled individual-patient analysis of six tenecteplase RCTs (15,954 patients) reporting that above a systolic blood pressure of 110 mmHg, each 1 mmHg increase raised ICH risk by 2% (adjusted OR 1.02), with female sex, lower body weight and older age as further independent predictors. — That specific pooled individual-patient-data finding is attributed to reference 73, which independent verification could not confirm — neither its DOI nor its stated title/author/journal/year combination could be located, and it appears to be a fabricated or severely garbled citation (a related but clearly different 2015 American Heart Journal paper exists). The underlying clinical principle — that blood pressure, sex, weight and age drive intracranial-haemorrhage risk more than the specific fibrinolytic chosen — is well supported elsewhere in this review (see reference 75 on sex and bleeding, and Section 3.9's broader discussion), but this particular statistic should not be taken as confirmed until the citation is corrected or replaced. — intracranial haemorrhage — The most feared complication of fibrinolysis. Its risk is driven mainly by patient factors — age, sex, body weight and blood-pressure control — rather than by the choice between tenecteplase and alteplase, whose randomised ICH rates are statistically equivalent. — Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (flow grade) — Angiographic grading (0–3) of blood flow in the infarct-related artery. Grade 2–3 or grade 3 flow is the standard recanalisation endpoint used in the trials comparing tenecteplase and alteplase.

entries.title: Tenecteplase versus Alteplase
entries.nodeLabel: Reassess at 60–90 min: ST-segment resolution ≥50% and symptom relief?
entries.text: Reassess at 60–90 min: ST-segment resolution ≥50% and symptom relief? — The non-invasive bedside check for whether fibrinolysis actually worked, using the ECG rather than angiography — the same kind of ST-segment-resolution threshold used across the trials behind this algorithm's routine-versus-rescue-angiography fork. — This is the standard reperfusion-assessment criterion used across the trial literature synthesised here; comparable assessment timepoints and ST-resolution thresholds recur throughout the review, including the 90-minute angiographic assessment windows in both direct head-to-head RCTs and the ST-segment-resolution comparisons discussed for other fibrinolytic agents.

entries.title: Tenecteplase versus Alteplase
entries.text: Failed fibrinolysis — immediate transfer for rescue PCI — Fibrinolysis has not opened the artery. The response is not to wait or repeat the dose — it is immediate transfer for mechanical (rescue) PCI. — Long-term follow-up of the REACT trial confirmed a survival benefit for rescue PCI after failed fibrinolysis (HR 0.43, 95% CI 0.23–0.79). A STREAM-2 subanalysis found that 43.5% of patients required rescue PCI, with worse clinical outcomes than those undergoing scheduled angiography (16.7% vs 6.0%) — underlining the need for rapid transfer after any fibrinolytic, not only a successful one. — percutaneous coronary intervention — Catheter-based mechanical reperfusion (balloon angioplasty ± stenting) of the occluded coronary artery — the preferred reperfusion strategy whenever it can be delivered within the guideline time window.

entries.title: Tenecteplase versus Alteplase
entries.text: Successful fibrinolysis — routine angiography ± PCI within 2–24 h — Even when fibrinolysis has worked, the pathway does not end there — routine early angiography (with PCI if needed) within a defined window remains part of the recommended strategy, not an optional extra reserved for failure. — This 'pharmaco-invasive' approach — fibrinolysis plus planned early angiography — is the strategy almost all of the review's indirect evidence validates: in TRANSFER-AMI, transfer for PCI within 6 hours of tenecteplase cut the 30-day composite outcome from 17.2% to 11.0%; NORDISTEMI showed a similar benefit in rural patients with long transport distances; and meta-analyses found early routine PCI after fibrinolysis reduced reinfarction without increasing major bleeding. The 2–24 hour window matches the angiography timing used in both STREAM and STREAM-2. — percutaneous coronary intervention — Catheter-based mechanical reperfusion (balloon angioplasty ± stenting) of the occluded coronary artery — the preferred reperfusion strategy whenever it can be delivered within the guideline time window. — pharmaco-invasive strategy — Fibrinolysis followed by planned, early (typically 2–24 h) transfer for routine angiography ± PCI — distinct from fibrinolysis alone (no planned angiography) or primary PCI (no fibrinolysis at all). Most of this review's indirect evidence validates tenecteplase specifically within this strategy.

entries.title: Blood Gas-Guided Assessment
entries.text: Blood Gas-Guided Assessment Of the Chemical Warfare Agent Casualty

entries.title: Blood Gas-Guided Assessment
entries.text: Suspected chemical agent exposure — Scene safety, PPE, decontamination, ABC — The algorithm opens at first clinical contact with any casualty where chemical exposure is plausible — a scene incident, a mass-casualty chemical release, or an unexplained toxidrome. Immediate priorities are scene safety, personal protective equipment, decontamination, and airway-breathing-circulation resuscitation, run in parallel rather than strictly in sequence where casualty numbers allow. — Existing mass-casualty triage systems were not developed for, and are not validated against, chemical-agent casualties, which creates a practical need for rapid, repeatable, point-of-care physiological markers — blood gas, lactate, acid-base status — to identify patients who are metabolically decompensating before they look obviously unwell. Casualties also frequently arrive at a receiving facility without prior field decontamination, so the sequence of decontamination, resuscitation and blood sampling has to be managed without compromising staff safety or delaying the physiological assessment that drives everything downstream. — In the 1995 Tokyo subway sarin attack, most casualties were ambulatory while a minority developed life-threatening respiratory failure — this established the management paradigm of simultaneous decontamination, respiratory support and antidote administration, rather than a strict one-step-at-a-time sequence.

entries.title: Blood Gas-Guided Assessment
entries.text: Obtain early blood gas + co-oximetry — pH, PaCO2, PaO2/FiO2, HCO3- / base excess, lactate, COHb, MetHb — A single early blood-gas-plus-co-oximetry draw gives a fast read on the dominant pathophysiology across all four CWA classes at once — pH and PaCO2 for ventilatory failure, PaO2/FiO2 for oxygenation/ARDS, bicarbonate/base excess and lactate for metabolic derangement, and carboxyhaemoglobin/methaemoglobin for dyshaemoglobinaemia — rather than waiting on agent identification, which is frequently unavailable or delayed in the field. — In critically ill patients generally, serum lactate is associated with mortality independently of organ failure and shock, and blood lactate clearance kinetics track treatment response over time — both properties this algorithm leans on repeatedly downstream, first to recognise the dominant pattern and later to monitor response to treatment. — acute respiratory distress syndrome — Acute, diffuse lung inflammation causing severe hypoxaemia, graded by the Berlin definition using the PaO2/FiO2 ratio. — arterial oxygen tension to inspired oxygen fraction ratio — The core oxygenation-failure metric used to grade ARDS severity and to guide lung-protective ventilation; falls as gas-exchange worsens. — Multi-wavelength oximetry (laboratory or pulse) that measures carboxyhaemoglobin and methaemoglobin in addition to oxyhaemoglobin — needed because standard two-wavelength pulse oximetry cannot detect these dyshaemoglobins. — An abnormal, non-oxygen-carrying haemoglobin variant — such as carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb) or methaemoglobin (MetHb) — that displaces or masks true oxyhaemoglobin and renders standard pulse oximetry inaccurate.

entries.title: Blood Gas-Guided Assessment
entries.text: Dominant blood-gas pattern? — The same early panel is read for one of three distinct physiological signatures, each pointing toward a different CWA class and a different immediate treatment path. This single read-and-branch step is the hinge of the whole algorithm: it converts a panel of numbers into a provisional working diagnosis before any agent-specific laboratory confirmation is available. — Synthesising the evidence, a coherent bedside approach emerges: a high-anion-gap lactic acidosis with preserved oxygen content points towards a blood agent and justifies empirical antidote; a rising carbon dioxide tension with falling pH heralds the ventilatory failure of nerve-agent poisoning and the need for atropine, oxime and airway control; and a falling PaO2/FiO2 ratio defines and grades the ARDS of choking-agent and vesicant inhalation and triggers lung-protective ventilation. — acute respiratory distress syndrome — Acute, diffuse lung inflammation causing severe hypoxaemia, graded by the Berlin definition using the PaO2/FiO2 ratio. — arterial oxygen tension to inspired oxygen fraction ratio — The core oxygenation-failure metric used to grade ARDS severity and to guide lung-protective ventilation; falls as gas-exchange worsens.

entries.title: Blood Gas-Guided Assessment
entries.nodeLabel: High-anion-gap lactic acidosis; preserved/high venous O2 sat; narrow arterio-venous O2 difference
entries.text: High-anion-gap lactic acidosis; preserved/high venous O2 sat; narrow arterio-venous O2 difference — A severe high-anion-gap lactic acidosis with a venous oxygen saturation that is preserved or even elevated, and a narrowed arterio-venous oxygen difference, is the classic cyanide signature: mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase is blocked, so tissues cannot extract the oxygen that is still being delivered to them. Relying on pulse oximetry or PaO2 alone is falsely reassuring here, because oxygen delivery itself is not the problem. — Cyanide — whether from a deliberate chemical-warfare release, an industrial accident, or enclosed-space fire smoke — inhibits cellular aerobic respiration despite normal oxygen delivery, producing exactly this pattern: preserved or elevated PaO2 and calculated SaO2, elevated venous oxygen saturation, and a minimal arterio-venous oxygen gradient. Because laboratory blood cyanide assays are rarely available acutely, plasma lactate becomes the decisive bedside surrogate marker for toxic exposure.

entries.title: Blood Gas-Guided Assessment
entries.nodeLabel: Rising PaCO2, falling pH, hypoxaemia; cholinergic signs (miosis, bronchorrhoea)
entries.text: Rising PaCO2, falling pH, hypoxaemia; cholinergic signs (miosis, bronchorrhoea) — A rising PaCO2 with a falling pH and hypoxaemia, accompanied by cholinergic signs such as miosis and bronchorrhoea, marks nerve-agent or organophosphate poisoning. This is primarily a ventilatory-failure pattern, not a pure metabolic one: the acetylcholinesterase-inhibited patient is failing to breathe effectively before they are failing to perfuse. — Nerve agents and organophosphorus compounds inhibit acetylcholinesterase, producing a cholinergic crisis in which early death results chiefly from respiratory failure — bronchorrhoea, bronchoconstriction, neuromuscular paralysis of the respiratory muscles, and depression of central respiratory drive. Early CO2 retention and hypoxaemia then progress to mixed respiratory and metabolic acidaemia as compensation fails and lactate accumulates from increased work of breathing, seizures, circulatory collapse and solvent toxicity. — The toxic syndrome of acetylcholinesterase inhibition — excessive cholinergic stimulation causing bronchorrhoea, bronchoconstriction, miosis, and eventually neuromuscular respiratory paralysis.

entries.title: Blood Gas-Guided Assessment
entries.nodeLabel: Falling PaO2/FiO2; PaCO2 normal/low early; onset may be delayed (phosgene)
entries.text: Falling PaO2/FiO2; PaCO2 normal/low early; onset may be delayed (phosgene) — A falling PaO2/FiO2 ratio with a PaCO2 that is normal or even low early on marks choking-agent or vesicant inhalation — an oxygenation-failure pattern, distinct from the ventilatory failure of nerve agents. The clinically important trap is the word "early": with phosgene in particular, the onset of severe lung injury can be delayed, so a reassuring early gas does not rule the diagnosis out. — Choking/pulmonary agents and inhaled vesicants injure the airway epithelium and alveolar-capillary membrane, causing bronchospasm, non-cardiogenic permeability pulmonary oedema, toxic pneumonitis and acute lung injury/ARDS. Water-soluble gases such as chlorine provoke immediate irritation and can progress to ARDS within 24 hours, but poorly water-soluble phosgene penetrates straight to the alveoli with minimal initial symptoms, and fulminant pulmonary oedema and severe ARDS may be delayed by up to a day after exposure. — A single normal initial blood gas cannot exclude severe pulmonary-agent injury, especially after phosgene exposure — serial arterial blood gases tracking the PaO2/FiO2 trajectory and acid-base status are mandatory, not optional, even in a patient who looks well at presentation. — acute respiratory distress syndrome — Acute, diffuse lung inflammation causing severe hypoxaemia, graded by the Berlin definition using the PaO2/FiO2 ratio. — arterial oxygen tension to inspired oxygen fraction ratio — The core oxygenation-failure metric used to grade ARDS severity and to guide lung-protective ventilation; falls as gas-exchange worsens.

entries.title: Blood Gas-Guided Assessment
entries.text:
Suspect BLOOD AGENT (cyanide) — Lactate ≥8–10 mmol/L supports toxicity → empiric hydroxocobalamin ± sodium thiosulfate.
Serial lactate to monitor response. — Once the cyanide pattern is recognised, treatment does not wait for a confirmatory laboratory cyanide level — it is started empirically. A plasma lactate in the range of 8-10 mmol/L or higher supports the diagnosis and the decision to treat, and hydroxocobalamin with or without sodium thiosulfate is given as the antidote of choice. — The original diagnostic threshold — plasma lactate ≥8 mmol/L being 94% sensitive and 70% specific for a toxic blood cyanide concentration ≥1.0 mg/L — comes from a landmark retrospective cohort of acute cyanide poisoning. The broader "8-10 mmol/L" range shown here reflects how clinical guidelines and smoke-inhalation algorithms have since expanded that cutoff in practice. Across nine human case series, hydroxocobalamin and the nitrite/sodium-thiosulfate combination were both effective with no serious adverse effects reported, which is why they are recommended as the antidotes of choice; serial lactate measurement is then used to track clearance and confirm the treatment is working. — One cohort of hydroxocobalamin-treated patients found no significant difference in methaemoglobin levels or mortality between treated and untreated groups, and in another cohort of 55 treated patients, time to antidote administration was longer in non-survivors than survivors — treatment timing appears to matter, and the antidote's effect on hard outcomes is not as cleanly demonstrated as its biochemical rationale.

entries.title: Blood Gas-Guided Assessment
entries.text:
Suspect NERVE AGENT / organophosphate — → atropine + oxime, airway control / ventilation.
pH <7.2, high lactate / base deficit flag high risk; watch for intermediate syndrome. — Nerve-agent/organophosphate management is dual-track from the start: give atropine and an oxime and secure the airway, while simultaneously using the blood gas to risk-stratify. An admission pH below 7.2, a high lactate, or a widened base deficit all flag a high risk of death or need for mechanical ventilation. — Across multiple cohorts, admission pH, lactate and base deficit — alone or combined into validated nomograms and risk scores — were reproducible, independent predictors of mortality and ventilator need in organophosphorus poisoning, which is the primary human clinical surrogate for nerve-agent exposure. The specific pH cutoffs reported across the underlying cohorts actually range from about 7.2 to 7.35 depending on the study; "<7.2" here is the rounded bedside threshold the algorithm displays. — Watch closely for the intermediate syndrome — delayed neuromuscular respiratory failure that can occur after apparent recovery from the acute cholinergic crisis. It is poorly predicted by clinical scores, cholinesterase levels, or blood gases alone; single-fibre electromyography is the more promising predictor, where available. — Oxime therapy's actual mortality benefit remains contested: a Cochrane review of seven pralidoxime randomised trials found results ranging from benefit to harm, and concluded current evidence is insufficient to say whether oximes help or harm — the WHO regimen specifically is not supported by that review. — Two of the cited risk-stratification studies supporting the pH/lactate thresholds here (refs 28 and 29) could not be independently verified against any traceable primary source despite repeated, differently-angled searching — they may be fabricated or garbled citations. The underlying clinical pattern (acidaemia and hyperlactataemia predicting mortality in OP poisoning) is independently supported by the other cited cohorts (refs 22, 25, 31, 36), but these two specific studies and their reported numbers should not be relied on until confirmed — see their entries in the References panel. — Delayed neuromuscular respiratory failure occurring roughly one to four days after apparent recovery from the acute cholinergic crisis of organophosphate/nerve-agent poisoning; poorly predicted by clinical scores or blood gases alone. — The toxic syndrome of acetylcholinesterase inhibition — excessive cholinergic stimulation causing bronchorrhoea, bronchoconstriction, miosis, and eventually neuromuscular respiratory paralysis.

entries.title: Blood Gas-Guided Assessment
entries.text: Suspect CHOKING AGENT / vesicant inhalation — → O2 to SpO2 ≥94%, bronchodilators, lung-protective ventilation by PaO2/FiO2 (Berlin); ECMO if refractory. Serial ABG (delayed onset). — Choking-agent and vesicant management centres on oxygenation and lung protection: titrate oxygen to an SpO2 of at least 94%, give bronchodilators, and ventilate using lung-protective settings guided by the Berlin-definition PaO2/FiO2 ratio, escalating to ECMO if the hypoxaemia is refractory. Serial arterial blood gases matter here specifically because of the delayed-onset risk described on the pattern box. — This bundle — an SaO2/SpO2 target of at least 94% with the lowest effective oxygen fraction, nebulised beta-agonists given within an hour of exposure, early ARDSnet-style low-tidal-volume high-PEEP ventilation, and ECMO for conventional-ventilation-refractory ARDS — is drawn from phosgene and chlorine management reviews and toxic-industrial-chemical inhalation guidelines, rather than from primary statistical pooling inside this review itself. In phosgene-exposed pigs, low-tidal-volume, high-PEEP protective ventilation significantly improved arterial oxygenation, reduced pulmonary shunt fraction, and improved survival to 24 hours compared with conventional ventilation. — Corticosteroids and N-acetylcysteine have not shown benefit here and should not be assumed to help: a systematic review of chemical lung injury found no convincing evidence for corticosteroids, and in multiple animal phosgene-injury models, corticosteroids (inhaled or intravenous) and nebulised N-acetylcysteine failed to improve survival, lung oedema, or shunt fraction — in one rat model, curative steroids actually increased adverse outcomes. — Most of the direct evidence behind this pathway is preclinical (porcine and rodent models) rather than from human CWA casualties, which is reflected in the GRADE certainty rating for this part of the algorithm (low). — acute respiratory distress syndrome — Acute, diffuse lung inflammation causing severe hypoxaemia, graded by the Berlin definition using the PaO2/FiO2 ratio. — Berlin definition of ARDS — Grades ARDS severity by the PaO2/FiO2 ratio measured under at least 5 cmH2O of PEEP or CPAP: mild (200–300), moderate (100–200), severe (≤100). — arterial oxygen tension to inspired oxygen fraction ratio — The core oxygenation-failure metric used to grade ARDS severity and to guide lung-protective ventilation; falls as gas-exchange worsens.

entries.title: Blood Gas-Guided Assessment
entries.nodeLabel: Repeat blood gas / lactate clearance to track response and guide triage and disposition.
entries.text:
Repeat blood gas / lactate clearance to track response and guide triage and disposition. — Venous sampling is adequate for pH, HCO3-, base excess and lactate; arterial is needed for PaCO2 and PaO2.
Pulse co-oximetry is a screening adjunct—confirm with laboratory co-oximetry and interpret with caution during hypoxaemia. — Whichever pattern triggered treatment, the algorithm converges here: repeat the blood gas and track lactate clearance to follow the response to treatment and guide ongoing triage and disposition decisions, rather than treating the first gas as a one-off diagnostic test. — Repeated measurement — exploiting the favourable kinetics of lactate clearance and the trajectory of acid-base variables — tracks response to treatment and informs disposition. Venous sampling suffices for the metabolic variables that drive triage (pH, bicarbonate, base excess, lactate), with arterial sampling reserved for questions of ventilation and oxygenation; peripheral venous values are not interchangeable with arterial values for PaCO2 or PaO2. — Pulse co-oximetry (SpCO, SpMet) is a useful scene-screening adjunct at normoxia, but its accuracy degrades substantially during hypoxaemia and shock — it cannot rule poisoning in or out on its own and must be confirmed by laboratory blood co-oximetry whenever the result will change management. — Multi-wavelength oximetry (laboratory or pulse) that measures carboxyhaemoglobin and methaemoglobin in addition to oxyhaemoglobin — needed because standard two-wavelength pulse oximetry cannot detect these dyshaemoglobins.

entries.title: Calcium Channel Blocker Toxicity
entries.text: Calcium Channel Blocker Toxicity Phenotype-Guided Management

entries.title: Calcium Channel Blocker Toxicity
entries.text: SUSPECTED CALCIUM CHANNEL BLOCKER INGESTION — Entry point for any patient presenting with a suspected overdose or ingestion of a dihydropyridine (e.g. amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine, felodipine) or non-dihydropyridine (verapamil, diltiazem) calcium channel blocker, regardless of initial severity. — CCB overdose accounts for a disproportionate share of cardiovascular-drug fatalities — case-fatality in severe ingestions approaches 9–18% despite intensive care — so the algorithm opens broadly at the point of suspicion, before irreversible haemodynamic and metabolic collapse develops. Dihydropyridines, led by amlodipine, now account for most CCB poisonings: in a 2014–2023 Australian cohort of 236 CCB overdoses, amlodipine alone accounted for 147 cases. — The CCB subclass (amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine, felodipine) that is vascular-selective at usual doses and now accounts for most CCB poisonings, typically producing vasoplegic rather than cardiogenic shock.

entries.title: Calcium Channel Blocker Toxicity
entries.nodeLabel: ABC · cardiac monitoring · IV access · 12-lead ECG
entries.text:
ABC · cardiac monitoring · IV access · 12-lead ECG — Glucose · lactate · blood gas
Activated charcoal if < 1 h and airway protected
Whole bowel irrigation for sustained-release drug — Immediate supportive stabilisation, continuous cardiac monitoring, IV access, baseline and serial metabolic/acid-base evaluation (glucose, lactate, blood gas), and targeted gastrointestinal decontamination — single-dose activated charcoal for early immediate-release ingestions, polyethylene glycol whole bowel irrigation (WBI) for sustained-release (SR) preparations. — CCBs block L-type voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs), precipitating rapid conduction blocks, bradyarrhythmias and hypotension that need immediate detection and venous access.
