The same VGCC blockade impairs pancreatic beta-cell insulin release, producing hyperglycaemia and relative insulinopenia that starve the myocardium of glucose, while hypoperfusion and mitochondrial dysfunction raise lactate — so baseline and serial glycaemia/acid-base checks both index severity and set up later HIE dosing. SR formulations have delayed peak concentrations and a prolonged absorption window that WBI can meaningfully shorten; immediate-release formulations peak quickly, so charcoal only helps within the first hour. — Activated charcoal — 1 g/kg within 1 h of ingestion (ext. guideline, ref 2) — SR toxicokinetics behind WBI — peak concentration delayed 6–18 h; toxicity can evolve over 24–48 h — The manuscript's own Section 8 describes this step more narrowly — cardiac monitoring, IV access, and serial BP/heart-rate/glycaemia/acid-base assessment — without separately naming ABC or a 12-lead ECG, and its charcoal recommendation (Section 7.3) is explicitly restricted to immediate-release formulations, a qualifier the figure box itself doesn't repeat. — voltage-gated calcium channel — The L-type calcium channel that CCBs block — in vascular smooth muscle this causes vasodilation, and in cardiac SA/AV nodal and myocardial tissue it depresses conduction and contractility. — hyperinsulinaemia–euglycaemia therapy — High-dose insulin with dextrose co-infusion, used as a metabolic/inotropic adjunct in cardiogenic-phenotype CCB shock; acts as an inodilator, which is why it's withheld in isolated vasoplegia unless LV dysfunction is proven.

entries.title: Calcium Channel Blocker Toxicity
entries.text: Bradycardia, hypotension or conduction abnormality? — Triage diamond separating asymptomatic patients after suspected CCB exposure (No) from symptomatic patients with any cardiovascular manifestation of toxicity — bradycardia, hypotension, or SA/AV nodal conduction delay or block (Yes). — Asymptomatic ingestions — particularly modest immediate-release or unintentional extra doses — frequently never progress to severe toxicity and can be safely observed, whereas any sign of bradycardia, hypotension or conduction abnormality marks active VGCC blockade requiring immediate pharmacological resuscitation. Among 436 unintentional supratherapeutic ingestions of a patient's own beta-blocker or CCB, symptoms developed in only 10.1% and just 7.3% required hospital admission. — voltage-gated calcium channel — The L-type calcium channel that CCBs block — in vascular smooth muscle this causes vasodilation, and in cardiac SA/AV nodal and myocardial tissue it depresses conduction and contractility.

entries.title: Calcium Channel Blocker Toxicity
entries.text:
Observe with monitoring — Immediate-release: ≥ 6 h
Sustained-release: 12–24 h — Clinical observation with serial haemodynamic and cardiac monitoring for patients with no bradycardia, hypotension or conduction abnormality at presentation, with the observation window stratified by formulation. — Immediate-release preparations peak quickly, so an asymptomatic patient after a modest ingestion needs only a limited window; sustained-release formulations delay peak concentration and prolong absorption, so severe toxicity can still emerge many hours after an initially reassuring presentation. — Immediate-release observation — ≥ 6 h — Sustained-release observation — 12–24 h (ext. guideline, refs 2, 3) — The manuscript text itself doesn't state a ≥ 6 h figure for immediate-release observation — only that modest immediate-release ingestions "may be managed with observation alone". There is also an internal tension on the sustained-release window: this box and Section 8 say 12–24 h, while Section 3.1 separately says SR toxicity "may evolve over 24–48 hours", a wider figure.

entries.title: Calcium Channel Blocker Toxicity
entries.text:
INITIAL RESUSCITATION (all symptomatic patients) — IV calcium, repeated · cautious fluids · atropine
Monitor ionised calcium · early toxicology advice — First-line bedside stabilisation for every symptomatic CCB-poisoned patient: repeated IV calcium with serial ionised-calcium monitoring, cautious fluid resuscitation, atropine, and early clinical toxicology consultation. — Raising the extracellular calcium gradient partially overcomes competitive VGCC blockade; calcium chloride is preferred over calcium gluconate for faster ionisation and more elemental calcium per ampoule, though the effect is typically transient and needs serial ionised-calcium checks during repeat dosing. Early toxicology input is recommended by international expert consensus to guide the multimodal escalation that follows and to coordinate ECMO early if it turns out to be needed. — Calcium chloride (preferred) — 10 mL of 10% (1 g / 6.8 mmol elemental Ca²⁺) IV over 5–10 min, repeat q10–20 min PRN — Calcium gluconate (alternative) — 3 g IV, repeat q10–20 min PRN (ext. guideline, refs 2, 15) — "Cautious fluids" and "atropine" sit in this box but aren't actually recommended or dosed anywhere in the manuscript's own Section 6 or 8 text — "fluids" there only appears describing two paediatric case series' prior failed therapy, and "atropine" only appears describing an animal resuscitation model. — Section 8 also says urgent HIE preparation should start at this same step for every symptomatic patient — the figure instead defers HIE to the phenotype-specific boxes below, after echocardiography. — voltage-gated calcium channel — The L-type calcium channel that CCBs block — in vascular smooth muscle this causes vasodilation, and in cardiac SA/AV nodal and myocardial tissue it depresses conduction and contractility. — hyperinsulinaemia–euglycaemia therapy — High-dose insulin with dextrose co-infusion, used as a metabolic/inotropic adjunct in cardiogenic-phenotype CCB shock; acts as an inodilator, which is why it's withheld in isolated vasoplegia unless LV dysfunction is proven.

entries.title: Calcium Channel Blocker Toxicity
entries.text:
BEDSIDE ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY — Assess LV function early
Repeat as the picture evolves — Early point-of-care echocardiography to classify the patient into a vasoplegic (preserved LV) or cardiogenic (reduced LV) phenotype, repeated serially as the clinical picture evolves. — Dihydropyridines — now the majority of CCB poisonings — typically cause distributive/vasoplegic shock with preserved or hyperdynamic contractility, while verapamil and diltiazem cause cardiogenic shock with reduced contractility and bradycardia. Because high-dose insulin (HIE) is an inodilator that can worsen isolated vasoplegia, the haemodynamic phenotype — not the drug name — has to determine whether therapy is vasopressor-led or inotrope/HIE-led. Serial repetition matters because mixed phenotypes are common and can evolve over hours as sustained-release drug continues to be absorbed. — The figure routes every symptomatic patient from Initial Resuscitation through this diamond — including isolated bradycardia without shock — while the manuscript text (Section 8) specifically scopes bedside echo to "any CCB-poisoned patient with shock", a narrower population than the figure's own trunk implies. — hyperinsulinaemia–euglycaemia therapy — High-dose insulin with dextrose co-infusion, used as a metabolic/inotropic adjunct in cardiogenic-phenotype CCB shock; acts as an inodilator, which is why it's withheld in isolated vasoplegia unless LV dysfunction is proven.

entries.title: Calcium Channel Blocker Toxicity
entries.text:
VASOPLEGIC PHENOTYPE — Preserved or hyperdynamic LV · low SVR
Usually amlodipine
Norepinephrine first-line, MAP ≥ 65 mmHg
Add vasopressin if catecholamine-refractory
Repeat calcium · correct acidosis
Methylene blue or angiotensin II only if refractory
High-dose insulin only with proven LV dysfunction — Phenotype-directed management of vasodilatory/distributive CCB shock (low SVR, preserved or hyperdynamic LV, most often amlodipine or another dihydropyridine): norepinephrine first-line titrated to blood pressure, vasopressin added if catecholamine-refractory, repeated calcium and acidosis correction, methylene blue or exogenous angiotensin II reserved for refractory cases, and high-dose insulin withheld unless LV dysfunction is actually demonstrated. — Dihydropyridines selectively block vascular smooth-muscle VGCCs, causing peripheral vasodilation and reflex tachycardia. Norepinephrine and, if catecholamine-refractory, vasopressin restore systemic vascular resistance and coronary perfusion pressure — vasopressin acts through vascular V1a receptors via a calcium-independent pathway, so it can still work when adrenergic and calcium-channel signalling are both impaired. Methylene blue inhibits guanylyl cyclase to blunt nitric-oxide-mediated vasodilation, but the only controlled animal trial in amlodipine toxicity found it no better than saline and inferior to IVLE, and human evidence for both methylene blue and angiotensin II is limited to isolated case reports — hence "only if refractory". High-dose insulin is an inodilator, not a true antidote, and can itself worsen isolated vasoplegia; recent dihydropyridine cohorts show vasopressors doing most of the work, with HIE reserved for the minority who actually have documented LV dysfunction. — MAP target — ≥ 65 mmHg (figure-only — see caution below) — Vasopressin — 0.04 units/min IV infusion — Calcium repeat dosing — CaCl₂ 1 g IV (10 mL of 10%) or calcium gluconate 3 g IV, q10–20 min PRN — Methylene blue (preclinical) — 2 mg/kg IV in the negative rat trial vs. saline/IVLE — Two figure items in this box have no match anywhere in the manuscript's own text: the MAP ≥ 65 mmHg target, and "correct acidosis" as a named therapeutic step — the closest the text gets is a general mention of serially assessing acid-base status. — In an Australian multicentre series of 50 hypotensive dihydropyridine overdoses, only 20% received HIE (mostly those with LV dysfunction); in a separate single-centre cohort of 68 dihydropyridine exposures, 62% needed vasopressors and 15% received HIE — consistent with vasopressors, not HIE, being the mainstay here. — systemic vascular resistance — The resistance the left ventricle pumps against; low SVR with preserved contractility is the signature of vasoplegic/distributive CCB shock. — mean arterial pressure — The average arterial pressure over a cardiac cycle, used here as the resuscitation target for vasopressor titration in vasoplegic-phenotype shock. — hyperinsulinaemia–euglycaemia therapy — High-dose insulin with dextrose co-infusion, used as a metabolic/inotropic adjunct in cardiogenic-phenotype CCB shock; acts as an inodilator, which is why it's withheld in isolated vasoplegia unless LV dysfunction is proven. — intravenous lipid emulsion — A 20% lipid infusion used as salvage therapy for CCB shock refractory to calcium, vasopressors and HIE — proposed to work as a lipid sink and as a mitochondrial energy substrate; not first-line or prophylactic. — The CCB subclass (amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine, felodipine) that is vascular-selective at usual doses and now accounts for most CCB poisonings, typically producing vasoplegic rather than cardiogenic shock.

entries.title: Calcium Channel Blocker Toxicity
entries.text:
CARDIOGENIC PHENOTYPE — Reduced contractility · bradycardia · AV block
Usually verapamil or diltiazem
Hyperinsulinaemia–euglycaemia (HIE) therapy
Glucagon when bradycardia or AV block dominates,
and as a bridge while HIE is titrated
Norepinephrine for coexisting vasoplegia
Pacing for refractory bradycardia — Phenotype-directed management of myocardial pump and conduction failure (reduced LV contractility, bradycardia, AV block, classically verapamil or diltiazem): HIE as the primary inotropic/metabolic adjunct, IV glucagon when bradycardia or AV block dominates and as a fast bridge while HIE is titrated, norepinephrine for coexisting vasoplegia, and pacing for bradycardia refractory to drug therapy. — Non-dihydropyridines strongly block cardiac L-type VGCCs, depressing SA/AV nodal conduction and excitation–contraction coupling, while the same pancreatic beta-cell blockade starves the failing myocardium of glucose. HIE has the strongest cumulative evidence and international consensus backing as the preferred first-line adjunct: insulin activates myocardial GLUT-4 transporters to restore glucose uptake independently of blocked calcium channels and provides a non-calcium-mediated inotropic effect, with observational safety confirmed in both adults (46 cases over 7 years, 0 hypoglycaemic events) and children (36 patients over 25 years, 0 discontinuations for adverse events). Glucagon stimulates myocardial adenylyl cyclase independently of calcium channels and acts within minutes, whereas HIE's onset is delayed 15–45 minutes — so glucagon bridges that gap and targets dominant bradycardia/AV block specifically, even though it doesn't correct the underlying metabolic starvation and its clinical effects are modest and inconsistent. Norepinephrine is added because CCB shock often has a vasodilatory component too, and HIE itself is an inodilator. Pacing for refractory bradycardia follows the cardiogenic arm of the Mehrpour & Brent echo-guided flowchart this algorithm is built on. — HIE — insulin bolus — 1 unit/kg IV — HIE — insulin infusion — 0.5–1 unit/kg/h, titrated to haemodynamic response — HIE — dextrose — 25–50 g IV bolus, then continuous infusion — HIE — glucose target — 8–10 mmol/L (ext. guideline, ref 15) — HIE — potassium target — 3.0–3.5 mmol/L, hourly K⁺ checks — HIE onset — 15–45 min (also reported 15–60 min) — Glucagon bolus — 3–10 mg IV over 1–2 min — Glucagon infusion — 3–5 mg/h, titrated to response — Glucagon's 2017/2023 downgrade from first-line to a second-line/adjunctive option is sourced from external consensus guidelines the review cites (St-Onge 2017; 2023 AHA Focused Update, Class IIb, LOE C-LD), not from this review's own pooled analysis — and GRADE certainty for glucagon's chronotropic response and survival benefit is rated very low (⊕⊖⊖⊖). In the largest glucagon series (107 beta-blocker-overdose patients, 144 administrations), the heart-rate increase at 20 minutes was statistically significant but small (mean +4 bpm), with nausea, vomiting and hyperglycaemia as common side effects. — Table 2's "Agent / Dose" column actually states an 8–12 mmol/L glucose target, a small internal mismatch against the 8–10 mmol/L figure given in Section 6.1 and this box. — Pacing for refractory bradycardia is mentioned exactly once in the whole manuscript (Section 8, listing the Mehrpour & Brent flowchart's elements) — it isn't otherwise discussed. Levosimendan is also named in the Abstract as "a potential add-on" for refractory cardiogenic toxicity but doesn't appear in this or any other box of the figure. — hyperinsulinaemia–euglycaemia therapy — High-dose insulin with dextrose co-infusion, used as a metabolic/inotropic adjunct in cardiogenic-phenotype CCB shock; acts as an inodilator, which is why it's withheld in isolated vasoplegia unless LV dysfunction is proven. — Delayed or blocked electrical conduction between the atria and ventricles — a hallmark of cardiogenic-phenotype CCB toxicity from verapamil or diltiazem.

entries.title: Calcium Channel Blocker Toxicity
entries.nodeLabel: MIXED PHENOTYPE — treat both arms, reassess serially
entries.text:
MIXED PHENOTYPE — treat both arms, reassess serially — Common after massive dihydropyridine ingestion and in
β-blocker co-ingestion; may evolve as SR drug is absorbed — Recognition and simultaneous treatment of combined vasodilatory and cardiogenic shock — running both the vasoplegic-phenotype and cardiogenic-phenotype arms together — with serial clinical and echocardiographic reassessment, since the dominant pattern can shift over time. — At high plasma concentrations (massive or sustained-release dihydropyridine overdoses in particular), dihydropyridines lose their vascular selectivity and directly depress myocardial contractility and conduction on top of causing vasodilation. Mixed vasodilatory–cardiogenic shock is also frequent when a CCB is co-ingested with a beta-blocker, and can evolve dynamically over hours as a sustained-release tablet keeps being absorbed. Two patients with amlodipine ingestions exceeding 1000 mg needed norepinephrine requirements above 2 µg/kg/min; in one series of 28 IVLE-treated beta-blocker-poisoning patients, 13 had co-ingested a CCB. — In the figure, dashed (arrowhead-free) lines run from both phenotype boxes into this one, and the single solid arrow onward to the next decision comes from this box — visually this can read as though every patient passes through Mixed Phenotype on the way to the next step, rather than this being a conditional bridge specifically for patients showing features of both arms at once or in sequence. — intravenous lipid emulsion — A 20% lipid infusion used as salvage therapy for CCB shock refractory to calcium, vasopressors and HIE — proposed to work as a lipid sink and as a mitochondrial energy substrate; not first-line or prophylactic. — The CCB subclass (amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine, felodipine) that is vascular-selective at usual doses and now accounts for most CCB poisonings, typically producing vasoplegic rather than cardiogenic shock.

entries.title: Calcium Channel Blocker Toxicity
entries.nodeLabel:
Still unstable despite
maximal therapy above?
entries.text:
Still unstable despite
maximal therapy above? — Decision diamond evaluating whether the patient remains haemodynamically unstable after optimal phenotype-directed first- and second-line therapy (calcium, high-dose vasopressors/vasopressin, HIE, glucagon, pacing). — The evidence behind intravenous lipid emulsion is very-low certainty and comes from confounded case reports, so international consensus guidelines (EXTRIP, AHA, St-Onge) and recent reviews restrict it to patients who have already failed standard first-line and phenotype-directed therapy. Once that threshold of refractoriness is actually reached, though, giving it should not be delayed until deterioration becomes irreversible. — hyperinsulinaemia–euglycaemia therapy — High-dose insulin with dextrose co-infusion, used as a metabolic/inotropic adjunct in cardiogenic-phenotype CCB shock; acts as an inodilator, which is why it's withheld in isolated vasoplegia unless LV dysfunction is proven.

entries.title: Calcium Channel Blocker Toxicity
entries.text: Continue titrated therapy — Watch for late deterioration — For patients who stabilise on phenotype-directed therapy without needing salvage IVLE: maintain and carefully titrate the ongoing infusions (vasopressors, HIE, calcium, glucagon) while watching closely for delayed or recurrent decompensation. — Sustained-release CCB formulations have delayed peak absorption (6–18 h) and toxicity that can evolve over 24–48 h, and amlodipine's own elimination half-life runs 35–50 hours — all of which create real risk of late or recurrent deterioration after an apparently successful initial stabilisation. HIE infusions in particular often need to be maintained for a prolonged period. — SR peak delay / toxicity window — 6–18 h delay to peak; 24–48 h evolution — Amlodipine elimination half-life — 35–50 h (≈40 h in the manuscript's own table) — This box is drawn as a dead end in the figure, with no arrow onward to Post-Resuscitation Care — but patients who stabilise here, especially those still on HIE or after an intentional overdose, still need exactly that post-resuscitation monitoring and psychiatric assessment. — hyperinsulinaemia–euglycaemia therapy — High-dose insulin with dextrose co-infusion, used as a metabolic/inotropic adjunct in cardiogenic-phenotype CCB shock; acts as an inodilator, which is why it's withheld in isolated vasoplegia unless LV dysfunction is proven. — intravenous lipid emulsion — A 20% lipid infusion used as salvage therapy for CCB shock refractory to calcium, vasopressors and HIE — proposed to work as a lipid sink and as a mitochondrial energy substrate; not first-line or prophylactic.

entries.title: Calcium Channel Blocker Toxicity
entries.text:
SALVAGE: INTRAVENOUS LIPID EMULSION — Rescue only — not first-line, not prophylactic
Use after calcium, vasopressors and HIE have failed
Expect interference with CRRT and extracorporeal circuits,
lipaemic assay interference, hypertriglyceridaemia — 20% intravenous lipid emulsion (IVLE) given strictly as salvage for life-threatening instability refractory to calcium, vasopressors and HIE — while anticipating the lipid-related laboratory and extracorporeal-circuit complications it causes. — Proposed mechanisms: a "lipid sink" effect, where the infused oil compartment partitions lipophilic CCB away from target tissue (shown in vitro for verapamil at concentrations as low as 0.03%); direct mitochondrial energetic support, supplying fatty acids for beta-oxidation to counter ATP depletion; and vascular/cellular signalling effects shown in rat tissue. Why rescue-only: human evidence is entirely uncontrolled case reports and series (GRADE very low certainty, ⊕⊖⊖⊖) confounded by concurrent therapies, with 459 fatal IVLE cases recorded in the NPDS registry pointing to real publication bias — and while preclinical verapamil/diltiazem/nicardipine studies showed benefit, a controlled swine study of nifedipine shock showed none. That's why EXTRIP, the 2023 AHA update, St-Onge, and this review itself all restrict IVLE to salvage after standard therapy fails rather than early or prophylactic use. Why the circuit/lab warnings: concentrated lipid causes hypertriglyceridaemia, makes blood samples lipaemic (interfering with labs and plasma drug assays), and can clog or interfere with CRRT filters and extracorporeal circuits, as reported in a massive amlodipine poisoning case — on top of a real risk of fat-overload syndrome and pancreatitis. — 20% lipid emulsion bolus — 1.5 mL/kg IV over 1 min — Continuous infusion — 0.25 mL/kg/min for 30–60 min — Repeat bolus — once more, 1.5 mL/kg, if no response at 5 min (ext. guideline, refs 15–17) — Maximum cumulative dose — ~10–12 mL/kg of 20% emulsion — Reported haemodynamic improvement/survival across overlapping human case-report pools runs 74–89%, but because almost every one of those patients also received calcium, vasopressors and/or HIE, that figure reflects reported clinical response, not demonstrated IVLE efficacy on its own — the manuscript's own conclusion is explicit about this. — A poison-centre implementation gap is documented in the source review: HIE was actually instituted in only 42% of recommended cases, and IVLE in just 33% of those, despite 80% of poison-centre directors endorsing IVLE for verapamil cardiac arrest — a real gap between guideline endorsement and bedside use. — Unlike the superseded embedded figure in the manuscript file, this box deliberately doesn't print the numeric dosing regimen inline — the authors moved the numbers out to the manuscript's own Section 4.6 and Table 2. — hyperinsulinaemia–euglycaemia therapy — High-dose insulin with dextrose co-infusion, used as a metabolic/inotropic adjunct in cardiogenic-phenotype CCB shock; acts as an inodilator, which is why it's withheld in isolated vasoplegia unless LV dysfunction is proven. — intravenous lipid emulsion — A 20% lipid infusion used as salvage therapy for CCB shock refractory to calcium, vasopressors and HIE — proposed to work as a lipid sink and as a mitochondrial energy substrate; not first-line or prophylactic. — continuous renal replacement therapy — Continuous dialysis/filtration support, whose filters and circuits can be clogged or interfered with by the hypertriglyceridaemia that high-volume lipid emulsion therapy causes.

entries.title: Calcium Channel Blocker Toxicity
entries.text:
Refractory shock or
cardiac arrest? — Decision diamond assessing whether the patient remains in refractory shock or progresses to refractory cardiac arrest despite every pharmacological therapy including salvage IVLE (Yes), versus recovering enough to go straight to post-resuscitation care (No). — When maximal pharmacological support — calcium, vasopressors, HIE, glucagon, IVLE — fails to restore circulation or prevent impending or actual cardiac arrest, mechanical circulatory support via VA-ECMO is the only life-saving bridge left until the drug itself is metabolised and cleared. — The manuscript's own Section 6.5, Table 2 and Section 8 frame VA-ECMO's primary indication more narrowly, as cardiac arrest refractory to pharmacological treatment (activated once signs of impending cardiac collapse emerge) — this diamond is explicitly broader, including refractory shock short of arrest, which does match the case reports the review itself cites (Kuhn et al.; Fisher et al.) and the cardiogenic arm of the Mehrpour & Brent flowchart this figure is built on. — hyperinsulinaemia–euglycaemia therapy — High-dose insulin with dextrose co-infusion, used as a metabolic/inotropic adjunct in cardiogenic-phenotype CCB shock; acts as an inodilator, which is why it's withheld in isolated vasoplegia unless LV dysfunction is proven. — intravenous lipid emulsion — A 20% lipid infusion used as salvage therapy for CCB shock refractory to calcium, vasopressors and HIE — proposed to work as a lipid sink and as a mitochondrial energy substrate; not first-line or prophylactic. — veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation — Mechanical circulatory support bridging a patient through refractory shock or cardiac arrest until the body clears the ingested drug; does not remove the drug itself.

entries.title: Calcium Channel Blocker Toxicity
entries.text:
VA-ECMO / EXTRACORPOREAL LIFE SUPPORT — Activate the team early, before collapse is irreversible
Transfer if ECMO is unavailable on site
Bridges circulation; does not remove drug — Urgent initiation of veno-arterial ECMO to mechanically support systemic circulation and end-organ perfusion until the ingested CCB is hepatically/renally cleared, including early team activation and interfacility transfer to an ECMO-capable centre when needed. — VA-ECMO supports the circulation while the body clears the drug, but the circuit itself does not remove lipophilic CCB from the body. Activating the team before haemodynamic deterioration causes irreversible end-organ damage is associated with better outcomes. In two reported cases, early coordination between the ICU, toxicology, and a regional ECMO team allowed successful interfacility transfer for VA-ECMO in refractory CCB/beta-blocker overdose. — No specific ECMO flow or cannulation thresholds are given anywhere in the manuscript. A related but distinct number from the same section: in a separate 24-patient cohort treated with resin haemoadsorption rather than ECMO, MAP rose more by 48 hours despite a sicker baseline population — cited for context, not as part of this box's own pathway. — mean arterial pressure — The average arterial pressure over a cardiac cycle, used here as the resuscitation target for vasopressor titration in vasoplegic-phenotype shock. — veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation — Mechanical circulatory support bridging a patient through refractory shock or cardiac arrest until the body clears the ingested drug; does not remove the drug itself.

entries.title: Calcium Channel Blocker Toxicity
entries.text:
POST-RESUSCITATION CARE — Glucose and potassium management while HIE continues
Avoid negative inotropes · monitor ≥ 24 h
Psychiatric assessment after intentional ingestion — Post-stabilisation intensive care: continuous glucose and potassium monitoring/supplementation for as long as HIE continues, strict avoidance of negative-inotropic drugs, at least 24 hours of extended haemodynamic monitoring, and psychiatric evaluation after an intentional self-poisoning. — High-dose insulin drives both glucose and potassium into cells, so mandatory dextrose co-infusion and routine potassium supplementation prevent iatrogenic hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia during prolonged HIE. A recovering myocardium stays vulnerable to recurrent depression, and delayed redistribution or a long drug half-life means at least 24 hours of monitoring is needed after haemodynamic stabilisation. — Post-stabilisation monitoring — ≥ 24 h (ext. guideline, ref 15) — Glucose target during HIE — 8–10 mmol/L (8–12 mmol/L in one table) — Potassium target during HIE — 3.0–3.5 mmol/L, hourly checks — Psychiatric assessment after intentional ingestion isn't actually discussed anywhere in the manuscript's own prose or tables, even though intentional overdoses are mentioned in Section 4.4 case reports. — The superseded embedded figure's own closing box specified a longer SR-CCB monitoring window (≥ 48 h) than this one (≥ 24 h) — one more place the old and new figures disagree; this tool follows the standalone image's ≥ 24 h, consistent with the current Section 8 text. — hyperinsulinaemia–euglycaemia therapy — High-dose insulin with dextrose co-infusion, used as a metabolic/inotropic adjunct in cardiogenic-phenotype CCB shock; acts as an inodilator, which is why it's withheld in isolated vasoplegia unless LV dysfunction is proven.

entries.title: Haloperidol Adjunct Selection
entries.nodeLabel: Adult with hyperactive delirium with severe agitation
entries.text: Adult with hyperactive delirium with severe agitation — (e.g., RASS ≥ +3 or AMSS ≥ +2; danger to self or others) — Entry point for the algorithm: an adult meeting a validated threshold for severe agitation attributable to hyperactive delirium (classically termed excited delirium syndrome), posing danger to self or others. — Time to adequate sedation is a plausible surrogate for physiological rescue, not a convenience endpoint — continued physical struggle against restraint drives lactic acidosis, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemia, and cardiac arrest in this population characteristically occurs against a background of severe acidaemia. Neither the ICD nor the DSM recognises excited delirium as a formal diagnosis, and the label has been criticised as a post hoc justification for restraint-related deaths; the 2021 ACEP task force's descriptor “hyperactive delirium with severe agitation” (ACEP formally withdrew its 2009 white paper in 2023) reorients clinicians toward identifying and treating reversible underlying causes rather than treating sedation as an end in itself.

entries.title: Haloperidol Adjunct Selection
entries.text:
Immediate measures (in parallel) — Team approach; verbal de-escalation if feasible; minimise restraint time, never prone
Point-of-care glucose; SpO2, capnography (ETCO2) and temperature as soon as safe
Suction, bag-valve-mask and airway equipment at the bedside before sedation — Parallel, non-pharmacological and monitoring steps performed alongside — not instead of — pharmacological sedation. — None of this algorithm's 12 included comparative studies tested verbal de-escalation, prone-restraint avoidance, point-of-care glucose, or a pre-sedation airway checklist as a study intervention — these steps are adopted from external guidance (the 2024 ACEP clinical policy among others) rather than from the review's own charted trial data.

entries.title: Haloperidol Adjunct Selection
entries.nodeLabel: Haloperidol backbone at the lowest effective dose
entries.text: Haloperidol backbone at the lowest effective dose — (2.5–5 mg IV/IM in the included trials; obtain ECG/QTc when feasible) — Haloperidol — a butyrophenone dopamine D2 receptor antagonist and the default parenteral antipsychotic in many health systems for four decades — is the backbone every adjunct in this algorithm is added to. — Haloperidol monotherapy is comparatively slow in onset and frequently fails to achieve adequate sedation within clinically relevant windows: an individual-participant-data network meta-analysis of rapid tranquillisation found haloperidol monotherapy among the least effective options and associated with extrapyramidal side-effects, and in a placebo-controlled palliative-care RCT, haloperidol produced higher delirium symptom scores than placebo — so here it is used as agitation-directed therapy to control dangerous behaviour, not as delirium-directed therapy. Because monotherapy is frequently insufficient, combination regimens dominate real-world practice. — Dose in included combination trials — 2.5–5 mg IV/IM — Monitoring — ECG/QTc when feasible — This 2.5–5 mg range is the dose used in the midazolam/ketamine combination trials specifically — several of the review's other included studies used haloperidol comparator arms at 10 mg, or did not state the milligram dose used at all.

entries.title: Haloperidol Adjunct Selection
entries.text: Suspected sedative-hypnotic or ethanol withdrawal? — First branch point: is the agitation attributable to sedative-hypnotic or ethanol withdrawal, rather than to primary psychiatric illness, delirium of another cause, or sympathomimetic toxicity? — The adjunct choice for withdrawal states is driven by pharmacological mechanism, not by the comparative speed/safety trial data that drives the rest of this algorithm.

entries.title: Haloperidol Adjunct Selection
entries.text: Haloperidol + MIDAZOLAM — Benzodiazepine is mechanistically indicated in withdrawal states — In suspected sedative-hypnotic or ethanol withdrawal, midazolam is selected irrespective of the comparative sedation-speed data favouring ketamine elsewhere in this algorithm. — Midazolam, a short-acting benzodiazepine that potentiates GABA-A-mediated inhibition, directly treats the pharmacology of withdrawal — a benzodiazepine is mechanistically indicated here regardless of which adjunct sedates faster in the general population, because ketamine (an NMDA-receptor antagonist) does not address the withdrawal mechanism itself. — N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor — The receptor ketamine non-competitively blocks, producing dissociative sedation while relatively preserving airway reflexes and respiratory drive. — gamma-aminobutyric acid type A receptor — The inhibitory receptor midazolam potentiates, producing anxiolysis, amnesia and sedation — also the mechanism that makes a benzodiazepine mechanistically indicated in sedative-hypnotic and ethanol withdrawal.

entries.title: Haloperidol Adjunct Selection
entries.text: Older adult (≥ 65 years)? — Second branch point, for patients not in withdrawal: is the patient 65 years of age or older? — This threshold is not derived from the review's own included studies — participant ages across all 12 studies ranged from a mean/median of 29 to 53 years, with only one trial (mean age 52.8 ± 19.4 years) averaging over 50. The cutoff, and the guidance that follows it, is adopted from external geriatric-emergency-medicine and ACEP guidance rather than from stratified data within this review's own trials.

entries.title: Haloperidol Adjunct Selection
entries.text:
Avoid benzodiazepines where possible — (precipitate/prolong delirium)
Reduce doses of all agents; ketamine data sparse — choose by airway resources — In older adults, benzodiazepines are avoided where possible, doses of all agents are reduced, and the choice between remaining agents is guided by available airway resources rather than by the general-population speed/safety comparison. — A Geriatric Emergency Department Guidelines 2.0 systematic review found adverse events were most common among older patients receiving benzodiazepines, and benzodiazepines are independently associated with precipitating and prolonging delirium in this age group. Comparative evidence for ketamine specifically in older adults remains sparse, so the clinical rule here is: the argument against midazolam is stronger than the evidence base for ketamine as a confirmed alternative — hence dose reduction of all agents and airway-resource-guided selection, not a blanket switch to ketamine. — Comparative trial data for either adjunct in patients ≥ 65 years is sparse — this branch reflects geriatric-delirium and medication-safety guidance, not head-to-head trial evidence in this specific age group.

entries.title: Haloperidol Adjunct Selection
entries.text:
Haloperidol + MIDAZOLAM — (0.05 mg/kg IV or 5 mg IM in trials)
Watch: hypoventilation, SpO2 fall at 5–10 min; worse with ethanol/opioids — Where immediate airway rescue is not available, midazolam is the adjunct of choice. — Benzodiazepine-induced respiratory depression is gradual in onset and dose-dependent, and in the great majority of cases is reversible and manageable with positioning, supplemental oxygen and bag-valve-mask support — unlike laryngospasm, ketamine's main airway risk, which has the shortest interval to catastrophe of any adverse event in this algorithm and specifically requires immediate rescue capability. — Trial dosing — 0.05 mg/kg IV or 5 mg IM — Watch for hypoventilation and a SpO2 fall at 5–10 minutes; this effect is worse with co-ingested ethanol or opioids.

entries.title: Haloperidol Adjunct Selection
entries.nodeLabel: Capnography, airway expertise and immediate airway rescue available?
entries.text: Capnography, airway expertise and immediate airway rescue available? — Third branch point, for patients not in withdrawal and under 65: are capnography, airway expertise, and immediate airway rescue capability available at the bedside? — This question gates the ketamine option specifically. Ketamine's main advantage — relative preservation of respiratory drive — only translates into a net safety benefit if its principal airway risk, laryngospasm, can be rescued immediately; the algorithm defaults to midazolam wherever that capability isn't confirmed (e.g. a resource-limited prehospital service, remote facility, or isolated ward).

entries.title: Haloperidol Adjunct Selection
entries.text:
Haloperidol + KETAMINE — Faster control, less restraint (LOW certainty); favoured in sympathomimetic toxicity. 0.5 mg/kg IV in the direct RCT
Watch: hypersalivation, laryngospasm, emergence reactions — Where immediate airway rescue is available, ketamine is the adjunct of choice — a non-competitive NMDA-receptor antagonist producing dissociative sedation with relative preservation of airway reflexes and respiratory drive, acting within minutes even by the IM route. — In the one direct RCT (haloperidol 2.5 mg IV + ketamine 0.5 mg/kg IV vs haloperidol 2.5 mg IV + midazolam 0.05 mg/kg IV, n = 140, Aghili 2023), the ketamine arm showed significantly greater agitation-score reduction at 5, 10 and 15 minutes, a significantly shorter time to maximum effect, and significantly less need for physical restraint (p = 0.001). In the near-direct RCT (ketamine 5 mg/kg IM vs midazolam 5 mg + haloperidol 5 mg IM, n = 80, Barbic 2021), median time to adequate sedation was 5.8 vs 14.7 minutes (HR 2.43, 95% CI 1.43–4.12) — but converted to a standardised effect size this is d ≈ 0.49, sitting right at the boundary of this review's own prespecified MCID (d ≥ 0.50) rather than convincingly beyond it. Ketamine is specifically favoured where sympathomimetic toxicity is suspected, given its faster onset and lower respiratory-depressant burden. — Direct RCT dosing — 0.5 mg/kg IV — Watch for hypersalivation, laryngospasm, and emergence reactions. — A pooled meta-analysis of 18 prehospital studies (3,476 patients) found a 16% (95% CI 8–26%) intubation rate after prehospital ketamine for acute agitation — but that evidence comes from ketamine monotherapy at 4–5 mg/kg IM, five to ten times this algorithm's low-dose IV combination regimen, so its applicability here is uncertain and probably overstated. — Certainty of evidence for every outcome in this comparison is LOW at best (efficacy) and VERY LOW for every safety outcome — no outcome in the underlying review reached moderate or high certainty. — minimal clinically important difference — The smallest effect size judged clinically meaningful. This review set its MCID at Cohen's d ≥ 0.50, converting a hazard ratio to an approximate standardised mean difference where needed — the near-direct ketamine-vs-midazolam trial's effect (d ≈ 0.49) sits right at this boundary. — N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor — The receptor ketamine non-competitively blocks, producing dissociative sedation while relatively preserving airway reflexes and respiratory drive.

entries.title: Haloperidol Adjunct Selection
entries.nodeLabel: Reassess at 5, 10, 15 and 30 min: RASS/AMSS, SpO2, ETCO2, HR, BP, temperature
entries.text: Reassess at 5, 10, 15 and 30 min: RASS/AMSS, SpO2, ETCO2, HR, BP, temperature — Convergence point after any adjunct is given: structured reassessment on a fixed schedule, with a fixed parameter set, regardless of which branch was taken. — Every pathway through this algorithm reconvenes here before the next decision (adequate sedation vs. rescue) is made. — Reassessment schedule — 5, 10, 15 and 30 min — Parameters — RASS/AMSS, SpO2, ETCO2, HR, BP, temperature — Richmond Agitation–Sedation Scale — A validated 10-point scale (−5 to +4) used in several of this review's included trials to grade agitation severity and define “adequate sedation” as a target score (e.g. RASS ≤ −1). — Altered Mental Status Scale — A validated agitation-scoring instrument used in several included trials (e.g. an entry threshold of AMSS ≥ +2) as an alternative to RASS for grading agitation severity. — end-tidal carbon dioxide — The capnography reading used alongside SpO2 to monitor ventilation during and after sedation — recommended at the bedside before any sedative is given, and specifically what gates the ketamine option at the airway-resources decision point.

entries.title: Haloperidol Adjunct Selection
entries.text: Adequate sedation? — Is the patient now adequately sedated, by whichever validated instrument and threshold the treating team is using? — Definitions of “adequate sedation” varied across the review's 12 included studies — from RASS ≤ −1 to AMSS < +1 — reflecting genuine heterogeneity in how different trials operationalised this endpoint, not a single universal cutoff. — Richmond Agitation–Sedation Scale — A validated 10-point scale (−5 to +4) used in several of this review's included trials to grade agitation severity and define “adequate sedation” as a target score (e.g. RASS ≤ −1). — Altered Mental Status Scale — A validated agitation-scoring instrument used in several included trials (e.g. an entry threshold of AMSS ≥ +2) as an alternative to RASS for grading agitation severity.

entries.title: Haloperidol Adjunct Selection
entries.text: Rescue — Repeat adjunct; ketamine is effective for refractory agitation (airway ready) — If sedation remains inadequate, repeat the chosen adjunct rather than switching agents outright, then return to the reassessment cycle (5, 10, 15 and 30 minutes) — shown here as a dead end only because this diagram doesn't draw backward loops; in the authors' own figure this box loops back up to Reassess. — In a dedicated ED observational study, ketamine specifically evaluated as rescue therapy for patients who failed to sedate adequately with conventional agents achieved control in the great majority of refractory cases — supporting a clinical niche for ketamine as a second-line rescue agent even where it wasn't the first-line choice, provided the airway is confirmed ready. — Only use ketamine for rescue where the airway is confirmed ready, as at the original decision point.

entries.title: Haloperidol Adjunct Selection
entries.nodeLabel: Post-sedation care — sedation is the means, not the endpoint
entries.text:
Post-sedation care — sedation is the means, not the endpoint — Release restraints; continuous SpO2/ETCO2 and haemodynamic monitoring
Seek and treat the cause: hypoglycaemia, sepsis, intracranial lesion, sympathomimetic toxicity, withdrawal
Active cooling, IV fluids; check blood gas/lactate, potassium and creatine kinase — Sedation is the means to safe evaluation and treatment, not the endpoint of care — this closing box bundles the monitoring and diagnostic steps that follow adequate sedation. — Prolonged agitation and physical restraint delay essential diagnostic evaluation for reversible underlying causes, and the same physiological derangements that made rapid sedation urgent — lactic acidosis, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia — are exactly what this closing step screens for and treats. — Certainty of evidence across this entire algorithm is LOW at best for efficacy outcomes and VERY LOW for every safety outcome. — Where droperidol is available, droperidol + midazolam has the strongest supporting evidence of any regimen in the wider literature — this algorithm addresses the haloperidol-adjunct choice specifically, for settings where droperidol is not available. — Doses throughout this algorithm are those used in the included trials — follow your own institution's local protocol.

entries.title: Selection of a Neuromuscular Blocking Agent
entries.text: Selection of a Neuromuscular Blocking Agent Succinylcholine vs Rocuronium for Rapid Sequence Induction and Intubation

entries.title: Selection of a Neuromuscular Blocking Agent
entries.nodeLabel: Patient requires tracheal intubation with neuromuscular blockade
entries.text: Patient requires tracheal intubation with neuromuscular blockade — The entry point for this tool: a patient who needs a neuromuscular blocking agent (NMBA) to facilitate tracheal intubation during rapid sequence induction (RSI). Three sequential questions below decide which of the two agents in routine use — succinylcholine or rocuronium — fits this particular patient and situation. — RSI is the near-simultaneous administration of a hypnotic and a rapid-onset NMBA, with intubation attempted within about 60 seconds, designed to minimise the interval of unprotected airway and the risk of pulmonary aspiration of gastric contents. Succinylcholine and rocuronium remain the two NMBAs in routine use for RSI, and two decades of randomised and observational research have refined, but not settled, the choice between them — current European guidance explicitly declines to mandate either agent. — rapid sequence induction and intubation (RSI) — Near-simultaneous administration of a hypnotic and a rapid-onset neuromuscular blocking agent, with intubation attempted within about 60 seconds, designed to minimise the interval of unprotected airway and the risk of pulmonary aspiration. — neuromuscular blocking agent (NMBA) — A drug that paralyses skeletal muscle by blocking transmission at the neuromuscular junction, given alongside a hypnotic during RSI to achieve the muscle relaxation needed for laryngoscopy and intubation. Succinylcholine (depolarising) and rocuronium (non-depolarising) are the two in routine use.

entries.title: Selection of a Neuromuscular Blocking Agent
entries.nodeLabel: STEP 1 — Screen for contraindications to succinylcholine
entries.text: STEP 1 — Screen for contraindications to succinylcholine — The algorithm starts by ruling succinylcholine in or out, not by comparing the two drugs head to head — because succinylcholine's contraindications are closer to absolute than any property of rocuronium's. If any feature in the next box is present, rocuronium is simply the only option left. — Succinylcholine's distinctive liabilities — hyperkalaemia, raised intragastric and intraocular pressure, bradyarrhythmia in children and with repeat dosing, malignant hyperthermia susceptibility, and prolonged block in plasma cholinesterase deficiency — are what complicate its use in undifferentiated emergency patients. Screening for them first, before anything about airway-rescue strategy or sedation logistics, reflects that these are safety-critical exclusions rather than a preference to be weighed. — A rare, pharmacogenetic, life-threatening hypermetabolic reaction triggered by certain anaesthetic agents — including succinylcholine — causing rapid rises in temperature, carbon dioxide production and muscle rigidity. A personal or family history is an absolute contraindication to succinylcholine. — plasma (pseudo)cholinesterase deficiency — A reduced or absent ability to metabolise succinylcholine, due to an inherited enzyme variant or an acquired deficiency, that can prolong its usually brief block from minutes to hours.

entries.title: Selection of a Neuromuscular Blocking Agent
entries.nodeLabel: Hyperkalaemia or a condition predisposing to it - Denervation or immobility beyond 48-72 h - Burn injury beyond 24 h - Crush injury or rhabdomyolysis - Chronic myopathy or muscular dystrophy - Personal or family history of malignant hyperthermia - Known or suspected plasma cholinesterase deficiency
entries.text: Hyperkalaemia or a condition predisposing to it - Denervation or immobility beyond 48-72 h - Burn injury beyond 24 h - Crush injury or rhabdomyolysis - Chronic myopathy or muscular dystrophy - Personal or family history of malignant hyperthermia - Known or suspected plasma cholinesterase deficiency — Seven specific features that rule succinylcholine out. Most trace back to the same mechanism: succinylcholine briefly opens the neuromuscular junction's acetylcholine receptor before blocking it, and that initial depolarisation releases potassium from muscle — dangerous when receptors are already up-regulated (denervation, prolonged immobility, burns, crush injury, chronic myopathy) or when the rise can't be cleared safely. Malignant hyperthermia susceptibility and plasma cholinesterase deficiency are separate, non-potassium-related hazards: the first a pharmacogenetic trigger risk, the second a risk of a dramatically prolonged block from an inability to metabolise the drug. — The explicit hour cutoffs here (immobility/denervation beyond 48–72 h, burns beyond 24 h) are the authored figure's own operational translation — the manuscript's narrative text cites denervation, immobility and burn injury as general contraindications without attaching these specific windows, which is why this is flagged for the authors rather than presented as independently established. A retrospective ED cohort restricted to patients already hyperkalaemic at baseline (K+ > 5.5 mmol/L) found no mortality difference between rocuronium and succinylcholine in that population (10.0% vs 10.5%, p = 0.989) — but that cohort was itself overwhelmingly rocuronium-treated (310 of 434 patients), consistent with clinicians already screening this group away from succinylcholine rather than evidence that the screening doesn't matter. — A rare, pharmacogenetic, life-threatening hypermetabolic reaction triggered by certain anaesthetic agents — including succinylcholine — causing rapid rises in temperature, carbon dioxide production and muscle rigidity. A personal or family history is an absolute contraindication to succinylcholine. — plasma (pseudo)cholinesterase deficiency — A reduced or absent ability to metabolise succinylcholine, due to an inherited enzyme variant or an acquired deficiency, that can prolong its usually brief block from minutes to hours.

entries.title: Selection of a Neuromuscular Blocking Agent
entries.text: Any contraindication present? — A binary gate: if yes, the rest of the algorithm doesn't apply — rocuronium is used regardless of airway-rescue strategy or sedation readiness, because safety here overrides every other consideration downstream. — This question is deliberately asked before airway-rescue planning or analgosedation readiness, because a true succinylcholine contraindication isn't a trade-off to weigh against those later factors — it is a hazard to avoid outright, independent of everything the rest of the algorithm goes on to consider.

entries.title: Selection of a Neuromuscular Blocking Agent
entries.text: ROCURONIUM 1.2 mg/kg — Succinylcholine is not an option. Plan explicitly for 30-70 min of paralysis. — The contraindication pathway's endpoint: a full intubating dose of rocuronium, chosen specifically because at 1.2 mg/kg it reaches onset speed and intubating conditions close to succinylcholine's — but the clinician must now explicitly plan around 30–70 minutes of paralysis rather than succinylcholine's 8–10 minute window. — Rocuronium's clinical duration at intubating doses is 30–70 minutes, during which the patient cannot return to spontaneous ventilation and awareness is possible if sedation lapses. Across the literature rocuronium's onset is the fastest of any non-depolarising NMBA but still consistently 25–35 seconds slower than succinylcholine — a gap that high-dose rocuronium narrows as far as a non-depolariser realistically can. A stratified systematic review of 12 true-RSI trials and a network meta-analysis of RCTs both confirm the dose-dependence behind this specific 1.2 mg/kg figure: thiopental induction with conventional-dose rocuronium (0.6–0.7 mg/kg) was clearly inferior to succinylcholine for intubating conditions (RR 0.69), but raising the dose to 0.9–1.2 mg/kg restored equivalence (RR 0.99).

entries.title: Selection of a Neuromuscular Blocking Agent
entries.nodeLabel: STEP 2 — Define the airway rescue strategy
entries.text: STEP 2 — Define the airway rescue strategy — If succinylcholine isn't contraindicated, the next question isn't about the drug itself but about the backup plan: if intubation fails, does this patient's rescue plan actually depend on the paralysis wearing off on its own? — This is the algorithm's safety-net question. Rocuronium's own rescue mechanism — sugammadex reversal — sounds like it should make this question moot, but the evidence is explicit that rescue reversal is unreliable in a genuine cannot-intubate-cannot-oxygenate (CICO) crisis, because recognising the emergency, preparing and administering sugammadex, and waiting for recovery typically takes longer than the time to critical desaturation. So wherever spontaneous recovery really is the rescue plan, succinylcholine's intrinsically short duration is what actually protects the patient — not a reversal agent that may not arrive in time. — A modified cyclodextrin that selectively binds and reverses rocuronium (or vecuronium), given at 16 mg/kg to reverse a full intubating dose. It reliably reverses profound blockade within minutes under controlled conditions, but is not a dependable rescue in an evolving cannot-intubate-cannot-oxygenate emergency, where the time to prepare and administer it can exceed the time to critical desaturation. — cannot-intubate-cannot-oxygenate (CICO) — A failed-airway emergency in which neither tracheal intubation nor bag-mask/supraglottic ventilation is achieving oxygenation — the scenario this tool's Step 2 question is designed around, since it is the situation in which an agent's own duration of action, not a rescue drug, determines how long the patient has.

entries.title: Selection of a Neuromuscular Blocking Agent
entries.nodeLabel: Is return of spontaneous ventilation the primary rescue plan for a failed airway?
entries.text: Is return of spontaneous ventilation the primary rescue plan for a failed airway? — Asks whether this specific patient, in this specific setting, is relying on the paralytic wearing off as the actual rescue mechanism if intubation and ventilation both fail — not a hypothetical, but the real plan for this particular airway. — Modelling and clinical analyses of 'rescue reversal' with sugammadex show the time required to recognise a CICO emergency, prepare and administer sugammadex, and await recovery generally exceeds the time to critical desaturation. Cost, availability and the adverse-effect profile of sugammadex are additional practical considerations. Where spontaneous ventilation really is the backup plan, succinylcholine's 8–10 minute self-limiting block is the safer choice, independent of which agent would otherwise be preferred. — A modified cyclodextrin that selectively binds and reverses rocuronium (or vecuronium), given at 16 mg/kg to reverse a full intubating dose. It reliably reverses profound blockade within minutes under controlled conditions, but is not a dependable rescue in an evolving cannot-intubate-cannot-oxygenate emergency, where the time to prepare and administer it can exceed the time to critical desaturation.

entries.title: Selection of a Neuromuscular Blocking Agent
entries.text: SUCCINYLCHOLINE 1.0-1.5 mg/kg — Spontaneous recovery in 8-10 min; onset 25-35 s faster than rocuronium. — When spontaneous ventilation really is the rescue plan, succinylcholine is preferred for exactly the properties that otherwise read as limitations elsewhere in this algorithm: its short, self-terminating block, and its onset advantage. — Succinylcholine's spontaneous offset is roughly 8–10 minutes, and its onset is consistently 25–35 seconds faster than rocuronium across RCTs measuring onset time or time to intubation — both figures hold essentially independent of induction agent or rocuronium dose, unlike the intubating-conditions advantage, which is concentrated in thiopental-based inductions and narrows substantially with modern propofol- and high-dose-rocuronium regimens.

entries.title: Selection of a Neuromuscular Blocking Agent
entries.nodeLabel: STEP 3 — Test the post-intubation analgosedation system
entries.text: STEP 3 — Test the post-intubation analgosedation system — The final gate isn't about the intubation itself at all — it's about what happens in the minutes immediately after, because rocuronium's real downstream risk is a paralysed, inadequately sedated patient. — Across cohort after cohort, rocuronium is associated with delayed and lighter post-intubation analgosedation compared with succinylcholine, and a prospective cohort found rocuronium exposure carried a more than fivefold odds of awareness with paralysis. Whether a department can reliably close that gap is therefore as important to the agent choice as anything about the drugs' own pharmacology. — A patient's conscious recall of events while pharmacologically paralysed but inadequately sedated — a rare but severe harm specific to the period after a neuromuscular blocking agent is given, reported far more often in emergency intubation (3.3–7.4% of NMBA-exposed survivors in some cohorts) than in the operating room (0.1–0.2%).

entries.title: Selection of a Neuromuscular Blocking Agent
entries.nodeLabel: Are analgesia and sedation drawn up BEFORE the paralytic and reliably started within 5 min of tube confirmation?
entries.text: Are analgesia and sedation drawn up BEFORE the paralytic and reliably started within 5 min of tube confirmation? — A systems question, not a pharmacology question: does this department's workflow actually guarantee fast sedation, or does it only guarantee fast paralysis? The answer changes which agent's downside matters more. — This specific 5-minute operational threshold is the authored figure's own formulation; the manuscript's narrative text more generally states sedation should start 'immediately after tube confirmation', and a separate consensus MCID table defines 10 minutes as the threshold delay likely to be clinically perceptible — the figure's tighter, concrete 5-minute cutoff operationalises that same underlying concern rather than being a number drawn directly from a trial, which is why it is flagged for author confirmation. Three-ED cohort data (n = 2059) found rocuronium associated with a reduced hazard of timely sedation (adjusted HR 0.75) and analgesia (adjusted HR 0.73) relative to succinylcholine — but NEAR registry and quality-improvement data also show that bedside pharmacist presence and institutional protocols strongly attenuate these differences, which is exactly why this is framed here as a system check rather than a fixed agent property. — minimal clinically important difference — The smallest difference in an outcome that this review's authors judged a patient or clinician would consider meaningful — used throughout to distinguish a statistically significant finding from one large enough to actually change practice (for example, a consensus-defined 30-second threshold for onset time, or 10 minutes for delay to post-intubation sedation).

entries.title: Selection of a Neuromuscular Blocking Agent
entries.text: EITHER AGENT IS ACCEPTABLE — If rocuronium is chosen, dose at 0.9-1.2 mg/kg; intubating conditions are equivalent at this dose. — When a department can guarantee timely analgosedation, rocuronium's main downstream harms — delayed sedation and awareness with paralysis — are substantially neutralised, so the choice genuinely becomes a matter of preference rather than safety. — A network meta-analysis and the dose-stratified systematic review of 12 true-RSI trials both found that propofol induction with rocuronium 0.9–1.2 mg/kg produces intubating conditions statistically indistinguishable from succinylcholine (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.92–1.01) — the conventional-dose inferiority reported elsewhere in the literature is a dosing artefact rather than an intrinsic difference between the two agents. — A patient's conscious recall of events while pharmacologically paralysed but inadequately sedated — a rare but severe harm specific to the period after a neuromuscular blocking agent is given, reported far more often in emergency intubation (3.3–7.4% of NMBA-exposed survivors in some cohorts) than in the operating room (0.1–0.2%).

entries.title: Selection of a Neuromuscular Blocking Agent
entries.text: PREFER SUCCINYLCHOLINE 1.0-1.5 mg/kg — Shorter blockade limits the window for awareness with paralysis. — When timely sedation isn't guaranteed, rocuronium's longer block simply gives a bigger window for a paralysed, unsedated patient to be conscious — so succinylcholine's short duration becomes the safer default here, independent of intubating conditions. — A prospective cohort of 383 mechanically ventilated ED patients found an overall awareness-with-paralysis prevalence of 2.6%, with rocuronium exposure at any point carrying an unadjusted odds ratio of 5.1 (95% CI 1.30–20.1) for awareness — the single largest patient-centred signal identified anywhere in this review. Reported prevalence across emergency cohorts generally (3.3–7.4% among NMBA-exposed survivors) is far higher than the operating room's 0.1–0.2%, a gap attributed largely to emergency sedation practice rather than the drugs themselves — which is exactly why this box exists as the fallback for departments that haven't yet closed that gap.

entries.title: Selection of a Neuromuscular Blocking Agent
entries.text:
APPLIES TO EVERY PATHWAY — 1. Never dose rocuronium below 0.9 mg/kg for rapid sequence induction: the historical inferiority in intubating conditions is largely an artefact of 0.6 mg/kg dosing.
2. Induce with propofol or ketamine plus an opioid; the succinylcholine advantage in intubating conditions is confined to thiopental-based induction.
3. Start analgesia and sedation immediately after tube confirmation and record the interval from tube confirmation to first sedative dose as a quality indicator.
4. Dose succinylcholine on total body weight and rocuronium on ideal body weight; succinylcholine is the more frequently underdosed agent above 120 kg.
5. Sugammadex 16 mg/kg reverses profound rocuronium blockade within 2-3 min, but rescue reversal is unreliable in an evolving cannot-intubate-cannot-oxygenate crisis. — Five practical rules that hold regardless of which branch of the algorithm a patient ends up on — mostly about not undermining the algorithm's own logic through under-dosing, the wrong induction agent, or delayed sedation. In the source figure this box sits apart from the decision tree with no arrows connecting it to any other box — it is drawn as a standing footer, not a step reached by any particular branch, which is preserved here by giving this node no incoming or outgoing edge either (see METHODOLOGY.md). — Items 1 and 2 both address the same underlying finding: the historical succinylcholine advantage in intubating conditions is concentrated in thiopental-based inductions and conventional-dose rocuronium, and largely disappears with a modern induction regimen and adequate rocuronium dosing — a stratified systematic review of 12 true-RSI trials found thiopental plus conventional-dose rocuronium clearly inferior (RR 0.69) but thiopental plus high-dose rocuronium equivalent (RR 0.99), while propofol induction showed no meaningful difference at either dose. Item 3 operationalises the Step 3 sedation-timing concern as a trackable quality indicator, consistent with NEAR registry and quality-improvement literature on what actually narrows the sedation-delay gap. Item 4 reflects that succinylcholine and rocuronium are conventionally dosed on different weight scalars (total vs ideal body weight) and that succinylcholine specifically is the more frequently underdosed agent above 120 kg, where first-pass success falls to 76% (adjusted OR 0.2, 95% CI 0.1–0.5). Item 5 restates the Step 2 CICO-rescue caveat as a general rule: sugammadex reliably reverses profound rocuronium blockade within 2–3 minutes under controlled conditions (a rounded summary of trial data showing a median 168 s to 90% first-twitch recovery and 216 s to spontaneous ventilation), but that controlled-conditions speed does not translate reliably into an evolving cannot-intubate-cannot-oxygenate emergency. — A modified cyclodextrin that selectively binds and reverses rocuronium (or vecuronium), given at 16 mg/kg to reverse a full intubating dose. It reliably reverses profound blockade within minutes under controlled conditions, but is not a dependable rescue in an evolving cannot-intubate-cannot-oxygenate emergency, where the time to prepare and administer it can exceed the time to critical desaturation. — cannot-intubate-cannot-oxygenate (CICO) — A failed-airway emergency in which neither tracheal intubation nor bag-mask/supraglottic ventilation is achieving oxygenation — the scenario this tool's Step 2 question is designed around, since it is the situation in which an agent's own duration of action, not a rescue drug, determines how long the patient has. — A weight estimate derived from height and sex rather than measured directly — used for dosing rocuronium in this algorithm, in contrast to succinylcholine, which is dosed on total (actual) body weight. — Successful tracheal intubation on the first laryngoscopy attempt — a key procedural-ease outcome that, unlike intubating-conditions scores, showed no consistent difference between succinylcholine and rocuronium across the emergency and critical-care literature reviewed here.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.text: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients Geriatric Analgesic Decision Algorithm, Age 65+

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.text: Step 1 - Assess pain — NRS / VRS / PAINAD (if cognitive impairment) — Entry point: before any analgesic is started, characterise the pain (etiology, severity, quality, temporal pattern) with a validated self-report scale, or a behavioural pain scale in patients with dementia/cognitive impairment, alongside a full geriatric assessment (function, cognition, medication burden, hepatic/renal status, nutrition, psychosocial context). — Persistent pain affects more than half of community-dwelling older adults and more than 80% of institutionalised older adults, yet is routinely under-recognised and undertreated (oligoanalgesia) because of cognitive impairment, communication difficulties, underreporting in dementia, and atypical presentations. — The figure's VRS (Verbal Rating Scale) is never mentioned anywhere in the manuscript's prose or tables. Conversely, the manuscript text and Key Practice Point 1 list VAS (Visual Analogue Scale) and the Abbey Pain Scale, both of which are absent from the figure — the two sources name different, non-overlapping scales. — Verbal Rating Scale — A pain-scoring scale named only in the figure's own footer legend — it does not appear anywhere in the manuscript's prose or tables, which instead describe VAS and the Abbey Pain Scale. — Visual Analogue Scale — A validated self-report pain scale named in the manuscript's own text and Key Practice Point 1, but omitted from the figure, which lists VRS instead. — A behavioural pain-observation scale for patients with dementia, named in the manuscript's own text but omitted from the figure.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.nodeLabel: Step 2 - Exclude red flags / acute emergency
entries.text: Step 2 - Exclude red flags / acute emergency — Fracture - infection - malignancy - acute abdomen — Assess pain etiology and identify acute medical emergencies that need immediate intervention alongside prompt analgesia. — Uncontrolled severe acute pain is itself treated as a medical emergency in the manuscript's cited triage framework, where physiological and humanitarian imperatives mandate acting without delay. — The manuscript's own prose does not contain a dedicated red-flag screening step, and never names 'fracture', 'infection', or 'acute abdomen' anywhere in the text or tables — only malignancy/cancer pain and acute pancreatitis are discussed as clinical scenarios. — Prompt treatment of severe acute pain is linked in the text to the Australian Emergency Triage framework, which classifies uncontrolled severe pain at the highest urgency levels.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.text: Step 3 - Classify pain severity — NRS 1–3 mild - 4–6 moderate - 7–10 severe — Medication selection is stratified by patient-reported severity into mild, moderate, or severe tiers, adapting the WHO analgesic ladder (non-opioids for mild pain, weak opioids for moderate pain, strong opioids for severe pain, with adjuvants and non-pharmacological strategies integrated). — Preferences on medication in the elderly depend on self-reported severity balanced against organ failure, comorbidities, polypharmacy, and age-related pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic vulnerability. — Table 1 gives the same NRS cut-offs, but as table/figure data, not running prose — the manuscript's own narrative text never restates these numeric ranges. — The foundational severity ladder (mild → non-opioid; moderate-to-severe → weak then strong opioids plus adjuvants) is attributed to the WHO analgesic ladder, which the manuscript's introduction does not itself cite with a reference number. — Numeric(al) Rating Scale — A 0–10 (or here, 1–10) self-reported pain-intensity scale; this algorithm uses it to stratify patients into Mild (1–3), Moderate (4–6), and Severe (7–10) tiers at Step 3. — World Health Organization analgesic ladder — The foundational three-step severity-based framework (non-opioid → weak opioid → strong opioid, with adjuvants integrated throughout) this algorithm's Step 3 branch structure is adapted from.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.text: Non-opioid first-line — Paracetamol PO preferred — Non-opioid analgesics are prioritised first-line for mild (and mild-to-moderate nociceptive) pain in older adults, with oral paracetamol as first choice. — Paracetamol provides central COX inhibition and serotonergic modulation without the gastrointestinal, renal, cardiovascular, or respiratory-depressant hazards of NSAIDs and opioids — endorsed as first-line for mild-to-moderate nociceptive pain by both the AGS and WHO. — Non-pharmacological interventions are described in the manuscript as first-line for chronic pain, but are entirely absent from Figure 1.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.text:
Paracetamol — PO: 500–1000 mg q6–8h
Max 3 g/day (↓ if hepatic risk)
IV: same dose if NPO — Oral and intravenous paracetamol dosing and daily ceiling, with dose reduction when hepatic risk factors exist and IV use when the oral route is unavailable (NPO). — Age-related decline in hepatic mass/clearance, low body weight, malnutrition, hepatic impairment, or chronic alcohol use raise the risk of paracetamol hepatotoxicity; inadvertent supratherapeutic dosing also occurs via combination products. IV paracetamol gives equivalent analgesia when oral intake is contraindicated. — PO (Table 1) — 500–1000 mg q6–8h; max 3 g/day (reduce if hepatic impairment) — PO, AGS Panel wording (Section 5.A) — Max generally 4 g/day; 2000–3000 mg/day if low body weight, malnutrition, liver failure or alcoholism — PO, Section 5.A paragraph 3 & Table 2 — 325–650 mg q4–6h; max 3 g/day (2 g/day if hepatic impairment; Child-Pugh C contraindicated) — IV (Table 1 vs Table 2/3) — Figure: same dose if NPO. Text/Table 2–3: 1 g over 15 min, q6h (q6–8h in Table 1); <50 kg: 650 mg (Section 5.A) or 15 mg/kg (Table 3) — Renal adjustment (Section 5.A, not in this box) — Extend interval to every 8 hours if eGFR <30 mL/min — The figure's single oral dose/max (500–1000 mg q6–8h; max 3 g/day) does not match the manuscript's own two internally different statements of the daily maximum (4 g/day generally, 2–3 g/day if hepatic risk, in Section 5.A paragraph 2, versus 3 g/day generally, 2 g/day if hepatic impairment, in paragraph 3 and Table 2) — the manuscript itself is not fully self-consistent here. — The figure's 'IV: same dose if NPO' (implying 500–1000 mg q6–8h) does not match the manuscript's and Tables 2–3's IV dose of 1 g over 15 minutes. — Uncertain analgesic benefit and potential safety concerns in osteoarthritis specifically are also noted in the manuscript's own text. — estimated glomerular filtration rate — The lab-estimated kidney-function value this algorithm uses repeatedly (most often the <30 mL/min threshold) to decide which opioids, NSAIDs, or adjuvants are safe to use or must be avoided or dose-reduced. — nil per os (nothing by mouth) — The condition under which this algorithm switches paracetamol from the oral to the intravenous route. — A clinical scoring system (A/B/C) for the severity of liver disease, used in this algorithm to set paracetamol's maximum dose and to flag Child-Pugh C as a contraindication to paracetamol.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.text:
⚠ NSAIDs — use with caution — Ibuprofen PO: 200–400 mg q8h
Avoid if eGFR <30, HF, or PUD
Add PPI if GI risk; short course only — Oral NSAIDs (exemplified by low-dose, short-course ibuprofen) may be used for inflammatory/arthritic pain where paracetamol is insufficient, but require strict avoidance in severe renal impairment, heart failure, or peptic ulcer disease, plus PPI gastroprotection and minimal duration. — Competitive COX-1/COX-2 inhibition disrupts prostaglandin synthesis, causing age-enhanced gastrointestinal ulceration/perforation/haemorrhage, disruption of renal prostaglandin autoregulation (acute kidney injury, fluid retention), and cardiovascular events. Reduced albumin in frail/malnourished elderly also increases the free fraction of highly protein-bound NSAIDs. — Oral (Section 5.B & Table 2) — Ibuprofen 200–400 mg PO q8h, max 1200 mg/day; or celecoxib 100 mg once or twice daily — Short-course limit (text) — Not exceeding 10 days — Renal threshold — Avoid if eGFR <30 mL/min; extreme caution/dose reduction if eGFR 30–60 mL/min (2023 AGS Beers Criteria) — The manuscript's own text, Key Practice Point 4 and Table 1 emphasise avoiding systemic NSAIDs wherever possible and preferring topical NSAIDs (diclofenac gel 1% TID–QID) over oral formulations for localised osteoarthritis — this box omits the topical option entirely and lists only oral ibuprofen. — This box says 'Add PPI if GI risk', whereas the manuscript's own text states that concurrent PPI gastroprotection is mandatory whenever a systemic NSAID cannot be avoided, not conditional on an identified GI risk factor. — estimated glomerular filtration rate — The lab-estimated kidney-function value this algorithm uses repeatedly (most often the <30 mL/min threshold) to decide which opioids, NSAIDs, or adjuvants are safe to use or must be avoided or dose-reduced. — proton pump inhibitor — Gastroprotective co-therapy this algorithm calls for alongside systemic NSAID use in older adults — conditional on identified GI risk in the figure's own wording, but stated as mandatory whenever a systemic NSAID cannot be avoided in the manuscript's own text. — American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria — The 2023 updated expert-panel list of potentially inappropriate medications for older adults, cited repeatedly in this manuscript as the external source for renal-dosing thresholds, tramadol's and tertiary TCAs' inappropriateness, and opioid-associated delirium risk.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.text: Step-up: weak opioid ± — non-opioid combination — Escalation to a weak opioid alone or combined with a non-opioid analgesic (multimodal analgesia) for moderate pain (NRS 4–6). — Follows the second step of the WHO analgesic ladder and multimodal opioid-sparing principles when non-opioid monotherapy is insufficient — though the manuscript warns that fixed-dose opioid/paracetamol combination products (co-codamol, tramadol/paracetamol) frequently cause inadvertent supratherapeutic paracetamol dosing. — Table 1 lists transdermal buprenorphine patch (5 µg/h, titrate every 7 days) as the 'preferred opioid' for moderate pain — this is omitted from both the figure and the rest of the manuscript's prose. — Numeric(al) Rating Scale — A 0–10 (or here, 1–10) self-reported pain-intensity scale; this algorithm uses it to stratify patients into Mild (1–3), Moderate (4–6), and Severe (7–10) tiers at Step 3. — World Health Organization analgesic ladder — The foundational three-step severity-based framework (non-opioid → weak opioid → strong opioid, with adjuvants integrated throughout) this algorithm's Step 3 branch structure is adapted from.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.text:
⚠ Tramadol PO — 25–50 mg q6–8h; max 200 mg/day
Seizure risk; avoid MAOIs, CYP2D6 — Oral tramadol — a dual weak mu-opioid agonist and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor — used cautiously for moderate pain, watching for seizure threshold reduction and drug-drug interactions. — Tramadol lowers the seizure threshold, can precipitate potentially fatal serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic agents (MAOIs, SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans, linezolid), prolongs QTc, can cause hyponatremia/SIADH and delirium, and accumulates its active metabolite O-desmethyltramadol in renal impairment. — Figure & Table 1 — 25–50 mg q6–8h; max 200 mg/day — Section 5.C.7 & Table 2 — 25–50 mg twice daily (bd); max 100–200 mg/day — Renal/other thresholds (text, not in this box) — Avoid if eGFR <30 mL/min, epilepsy, or severe hepatic failure;
