extend interval if eGFR 30–60 mL/min — Tramadol is explicitly listed as potentially inappropriate in older adults in both the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria and STOPP/START criteria v3 — flagged in the manuscript's own Key Practice Point 7 — even though Figure 1 presents it as the main weak-opioid option. — This box's dosing interval ('q6–8h') does not match Section 5.C.7 and Table 2's 'twice daily (bd)' interval for the same drug. — estimated glomerular filtration rate — The lab-estimated kidney-function value this algorithm uses repeatedly (most often the <30 mL/min threshold) to decide which opioids, NSAIDs, or adjuvants are safe to use or must be avoided or dose-reduced. — monoamine oxidase inhibitors — A drug class that, combined with tramadol, raises the risk of serotonin syndrome — one of the named reasons for tramadol's caution in this algorithm. — American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria — The 2023 updated expert-panel list of potentially inappropriate medications for older adults, cited repeatedly in this manuscript as the external source for renal-dosing thresholds, tramadol's and tertiary TCAs' inappropriateness, and opioid-associated delirium risk. — A separate, explicit set of criteria (version 3, 2023) for potentially inappropriate prescribing and prescribing omissions in older people, cited alongside the AGS Beers Criteria for tramadol's and gabapentinoid/opioid combinations' inappropriateness. — The corrected QT interval on an ECG; this algorithm flags both tramadol and the antiemetics used for opioid-induced nausea (ondansetron, haloperidol) as QTc-prolonging.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.text:
Codeine PO (if tolerated) — 15–30 mg q4–6h; max 120 mg/day
⚠ poor metabolisers; constipation — Oral codeine as a weak-opioid prodrug subject to genetic CYP2D6 metabolic variability and opioid-induced constipation. — Codeine requires hepatic CYP2D6 activation to morphine; poor metabolisers get inadequate analgesia, while ultra-rapid metabolisers risk morphine toxicity, and all opioids cause constipation. — In the manuscript's own prose, codeine is placed under 'Opioid agents to avoid in the elderly', with no recommended dosing regimen given there at all, and the text separately states it should be avoided entirely in hepatic failure — the figure instead presents it as a usable 'if tolerated' option with a dosing ceiling. — The ceiling 'max 120 mg/day' shown in this box never appears anywhere in the manuscript's prose or tables. — No reference is specifically cited for this box in the source material beyond the figure's own overall citations. — cytochrome P450 2D6 — The hepatic enzyme that activates codeine to morphine and metabolises oxycodone and tramadol; genetic variability in its activity produces poor, normal, or ultra-rapid metabolisers, with correspondingly inadequate analgesia or toxicity risk.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.text:
± Adjuvant (neuropathic) — Gabapentin 100 mg nocte → titrate
Duloxetine 30 mg/day → 60 mg/day — Addition of a neuropathic adjuvant — a gabapentinoid (gabapentin) or an SNRI (duloxetine) — when neuropathic pain (e.g. postherpetic neuralgia, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, fibromyalgia, or mixed musculoskeletal pain) is present. — Gabapentin and duloxetine are preferred over tricyclic antidepressants in older adults because they lack potent anticholinergic effects (tertiary TCAs are flagged as potentially inappropriate for age ≥75 years in the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria). Slow nocturnal initiation and gradual titration reduce dizziness, somnolence, cognitive impairment, and fall risk. — Gabapentin titration (Section 5.D.1) — Start 100 mg nocte, titrate by 100 mg every 3–7 days to 300–1200 mg/day divided (max 2700 mg/day if renally tolerated) — Gabapentin renal caps (Table 2) — eGFR 30–60: max 600–1200 mg/day; eGFR 15–30: max 300 mg/day; eGFR <15: max 150 mg/day; haemodialysis: 200–300 mg post-dialysis — Duloxetine (Section 5.D.2 & Table 2) — 30 mg/day for 2 weeks, then 60 mg/day (30–60 mg/day); avoid if eGFR <30, ESRD, or severe hepatic failure; ECG monitoring if >60 mg/day — Placing this adjuvant only at the bottom of the Moderate column conflicts with the manuscript's own WHO-ladder description of integrating adjuvant therapies throughout, and with Clinical Case 1, which considers duloxetine/gabapentinoids without a weak opioid at all. — Pregabalin (25–50 mg nocte) and topical lidocaine/capsaicin are detailed in the manuscript as neuropathic options but are omitted from the figure entirely. — The manuscript separately reports CNS-active polypharmacy at 23% in nursing homes, with gabapentin the most frequent culprit, and the 2023 Beers Criteria caution against combining gabapentinoids with opioids. — estimated glomerular filtration rate — The lab-estimated kidney-function value this algorithm uses repeatedly (most often the <30 mL/min threshold) to decide which opioids, NSAIDs, or adjuvants are safe to use or must be avoided or dose-reduced. — American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria — The 2023 updated expert-panel list of potentially inappropriate medications for older adults, cited repeatedly in this manuscript as the external source for renal-dosing thresholds, tramadol's and tertiary TCAs' inappropriateness, and opioid-associated delirium risk. — end-stage renal disease — The most severe stage of chronic kidney disease, used in this algorithm's renal-dosing caveats for paracetamol, gabapentin, and duloxetine.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.text: Strong opioid required — Start low - titrate slow — Uncontrolled severe pain (NRS 7–10) requires prompt strong-opioid therapy, started at conservative geriatric doses with immediate-release formulations and titrated upward slowly based on response and tolerability. — Opioids are unmatched in efficacy for intense pain, but age-related reductions in hepatic clearance, renal excretion and respiratory reserve, plus heightened CNS opioid sensitivity, expose older adults to respiratory depression, sedation, delirium, falls, and opioid-induced neurotoxicity (reported in roughly 1 in 5 cancer patients) — demanding individualised conservative initiation rather than adult weight- or age-based formulae alone. — Starting dose rule (Section 5.C.1 & Key Practice Point 5) — For age ≥70 years: 25–50% of the standard adult dose, immediate-release, titrated every 4–6 hours initially — The manuscript also reports a real-world median morphine-equivalent daily dose of 19.6 mg/day (with a subgroup above 120 mg/day) in terminal cancer patients aged ≥90 years — a very different population from the general geriatric acute-pain patient this box addresses. — Numeric(al) Rating Scale — A 0–10 (or here, 1–10) self-reported pain-intensity scale; this algorithm uses it to stratify patients into Mild (1–3), Moderate (4–6), and Severe (7–10) tiers at Step 3.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.text:
Morphine — PO IR: 1–2.5 mg q4h (opioid-naive)
IV/SC: 1–2 mg q4h; titrate PRN
⚠ reduce dose if eGFR <30 — Immediate-release oral or parenteral morphine titration for severe pain in opioid-naive older adults, with strong renal precautions. — Morphine undergoes hepatic glucuronidation to morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G, inactive/neuroexcitatory, causing myoclonus and hyperalgesia) and morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G, a potent active analgesite). In renal impairment, M6G and M3G accumulate, causing prolonged sedation, neurotoxicity, and respiratory depression. — Figure — PO IR: 1–2.5 mg q4h (opioid-naive); IV/SC: 1–2 mg q4h, titrate PRN — Section 5.C.3, Table 1 & Table 2 — PO: 2.5–5 mg (q4–6h in Section 5.C.3/Table 2; q4h in Table 1); IV: 1–2 mg titrated (Table 1: 1–2.5 mg q4h titrated); Table 3 IV-PCA: bolus 1 mg, lockout 8 min, no basal — This box's own instruction — 'reduce dose if eGFR <30' — directly contradicts Box 6.1 (Renal impairment) in the SAME figure, which says 'Avoid morphine (M6G accumulation)' at the same threshold, and also contradicts Section 6.A, Table 1 and Table 2, which all state avoid/contraindicated below eGFR 30 mL/min (Table 2 places only 'reduce dose & extend interval' at eGFR 30–60). — The subcutaneous (SC) route for morphine is never mentioned anywhere in the manuscript's own text or tables — only subcutaneous hydromorphone is mentioned there. — This box's oral starting dose (1–2.5 mg) is lower than the 2.5–5 mg the manuscript's own Section 5.C.3, Table 1 and Table 2 all state. — estimated glomerular filtration rate — The lab-estimated kidney-function value this algorithm uses repeatedly (most often the <30 mL/min threshold) to decide which opioids, NSAIDs, or adjuvants are safe to use or must be avoided or dose-reduced. — morphine-6-glucuronide — Morphine's potent active glucuronide metabolite, which accumulates in renal impairment and drives prolonged sedation, neurotoxicity, and respiratory depression — the stated reason both for reducing morphine's dose and, elsewhere in the same figure, for avoiding it altogether below eGFR 30. — morphine-3-glucuronide — Morphine's inactive but neuroexcitatory glucuronide metabolite (implicated in myoclonus and hyperalgesia), which — like M6G — accumulates when renal clearance is reduced.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.text:
Oxycodone PO — IR: 2.5–5 mg q4–6h (opioid-naive)
CR: 5–10 mg q12h when stable
Preferred if renal impairment — Oral immediate-release oxycodone initiation for severe pain in opioid-naive older adults, transitioning to controlled-release once analgesic requirements are stable. — Extended-release preparations provide more stable plasma concentrations and reduce peak toxicity once requirements are established. Oxycodone is metabolised via hepatic CYP2D6 and CYP3A4. — IR — 2.5–5 mg q4–6h in opioid-naive elderly (Table 1 adds: titrate in 25–33% increments) — Hepatic adjustment (Section 5.C.6, Table 2) — In advanced hepatic failure, half-life extends to ~24 hours; reduce initial dose by 30–50% — The controlled-release dose shown here (5–10 mg q12h) appears only in Figure 1 — the manuscript's own Section 5.C.1 discusses extended-release formulations only conceptually, and Table 2 gives no milligram dose for the controlled-release step at all. — 'Preferred if renal impairment' is qualified in Table 1 as 'preferred if renal impairment moderate' specifically, while Table 2 instead warns 'reduce dose and extend interval if eGFR <30 mL/min — active metabolite oxymorphone accumulates — monitor closely in moderate-severe CKD', and Section 6.A omits oxycodone from its renal-impairment discussion entirely, naming fentanyl as the preferred opioid there instead (with hydromorphone preferred over morphine in moderate renal impairment). — estimated glomerular filtration rate — The lab-estimated kidney-function value this algorithm uses repeatedly (most often the <30 mL/min threshold) to decide which opioids, NSAIDs, or adjuvants are safe to use or must be avoided or dose-reduced. — cytochrome P450 2D6 — The hepatic enzyme that activates codeine to morphine and metabolises oxycodone and tramadol; genetic variability in its activity produces poor, normal, or ultra-rapid metabolisers, with correspondingly inadequate analgesia or toxicity risk.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.text:
Fentanyl (transdermal) — 12–25 mcg/h patch q72h
For stable opioid-tolerant patients
IV: 12.5–25 mcg q30min PRN — Sustained-release transdermal fentanyl every 72 hours, restricted to stable opioid-tolerant elderly patients (including those with dysphagia or renal failure), or titrated IV fentanyl for rapid-onset acute pain control. — Fentanyl is metabolised hepatically via CYP3A4 to inactive norfentanyl (roughly 90% inactive metabolites), making it safer in renal impairment. High lipophilicity prolongs its elimination half-life in elderly patients with increased adipose tissue, and starting transdermal fentanyl in an opioid-naive older adult is hazardous because of unpredictable absorption (especially with cachexia/fever) and life-threatening respiratory depression. — The manuscript's own text, Table 1, Table 2 and Clinical Case 2 specify only a 12 mcg/h starting patch dose every 72 hours — this box's upper bound of 25 mcg/h as a STARTING dose is never mentioned in the manuscript text or tables. — The manuscript and Table 2 state IV fentanyl as 25–50 mcg titrated, and Table 1 states 0.5–1 µg/kg bolus — neither the figure's '12.5–25 mcg' dose nor its 'q30min PRN' interval appears anywhere in the manuscript's text or tables. — The manuscript also notes non-opioid-mediated chest wall rigidity/vocal cord closure at non-routine or illicit fentanyl doses — a mechanism distinct from ordinary opioid overdose.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.text: Step 4 - Reassess at 24–72 h — Efficacy - ADRs - functional improvement — All three severity branches converge into mandatory follow-up to evaluate analgesic efficacy, adverse drug reactions, and functional recovery, guiding further titration, rotation, or deprescribing. — Pharmacokinetic variability, narrow therapeutic windows, heightened CNS/organ vulnerability, and oligoanalgesia in older adults require frequent clinical reassessment and retreatment adjustment rather than static prescribing. — While the manuscript repeatedly mandates 'frequent reassessments', 'frequent clinical review', and 'regular reassessment' of pain, ADRs, and function, the specific timeframe '24–72 h' shown in this box does not appear anywhere in the manuscript's own text or tables — it appears solely in the figure.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.text:
Step 5 - Monitor for opioid-specific ADRs — Constipation (prophylactic laxative from day 1) - Sedation - Respiratory depression
Nausea (ondansetron 4 mg IV/PO PRN) - Falls risk - Delirium - Urinary retention — Proactive prophylaxis and clinical surveillance for known opioid-induced adverse effects, including day-1 laxative co-prescription, antiemetic rescue, and monitoring of CNS, respiratory, fall, and urological complications. — Constipation is universally expected with opioids; mu-receptor suppression of hypercapnic ventilatory drive causes dose-dependent respiratory depression (compounded by COPD, sleep apnoea, benzodiazepines, or gabapentinoids); opioids impair balance/reaction time (raising fall risk), can precipitate or worsen delirium, and cause urinary retention (especially in older men with benign prostatic hypertrophy). — Constipation prophylaxis (text) — Prophylactic osmotic laxative — polyethylene glycol/macrogol or lactulose — from day 1 of any opioid — Respiratory depression rescue (text, not in this box) — Naloxone 0.04–0.1 mg IV, titrated cautiously to avoid acute withdrawal and sympathetic surge — This box's 'ondansetron 4 mg IV/PO PRN' does not match the manuscript's own Section 5.C.9, which specifies 'low-dose haloperidol (0.5 mg) or ondansetron (4 to 8 mg IV/SL)' — a different route (SL, not PO), a wider dose range, and an alternative drug (haloperidol) the figure omits. The manuscript separately cautions that both ondansetron and haloperidol prolong QTc. — This step sits on the single main trunk below Step 4, meaning even the Mild (non-opioid) pathway visually passes through 'Monitor for opioid-specific ADRs' even when no opioid was actually prescribed. — The 2023 AGS Beers Criteria formally added opioids to the drugs that precipitate or exacerbate delirium in older adults, and caution against concurrent opioid plus benzodiazepine/gabapentinoid respiratory depression. — American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria — The 2023 updated expert-panel list of potentially inappropriate medications for older adults, cited repeatedly in this manuscript as the external source for renal-dosing thresholds, tramadol's and tertiary TCAs' inappropriateness, and opioid-associated delirium risk. — The corrected QT interval on an ECG; this algorithm flags both tramadol and the antiemetics used for opioid-induced nausea (ondansetron, haloperidol) as QTc-prolonging.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.nodeLabel: Step 6 - Special considerations in the elderly
entries.text: Step 6 - Special considerations in the elderly — Tailoring analgesic agent choice, dose, and dosing interval to major geriatric comorbidities — renal impairment, hepatic impairment, and cognitive impairment. — Organ failure and cognitive impairment profoundly alter metabolite accumulation, drug clearance, CNS vulnerability, and pain reporting in elderly patients. — Visually, Step 6 appears after drug selection, reassessment, and ADR monitoring — but the manuscript's own text states renal, hepatic, and cognitive status must be assessed BEFORE selecting an analgesic, and a single patient may have multiple concurrent impairments (Clinical Case 2 combines hepatic and renal impairment). — The manuscript also discusses cardiac failure and respiratory failure/COPD as organ-based prescribing categories, both of which are omitted from Step 6 in the figure.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.text:
Renal impairment — Avoid morphine (M6G accumulation)
Prefer fentanyl or oxycodone
Paracetamol safe; avoid NSAIDs — Renal-specific drug-selection rules to prevent toxic metabolite accumulation and nephrotoxicity. — GFR declines by roughly 1 mL/min/year after age 40 (requiring Cockcroft-Gault or CKD-EPI estimation rather than serum creatinine alone, given low muscle mass). Renal impairment causes accumulation of M6G and M3G with morphine, whereas fentanyl is hepatically metabolised to inactive norfentanyl. NSAIDs block prostaglandin-mediated renal autoregulation, risking acute kidney injury and fluid retention. — This box's 'Avoid morphine' directly contradicts Box 3C.2 (morphine) in the SAME figure, which instead says 'reduce dose if eGFR <30'. — This box pairs oxycodone with fentanyl as preferred in renal failure, but the manuscript's own text names fentanyl alone as consistently preferred, restricts oxycodone's preference to MODERATE renal impairment only (Table 1), and states for oxycodone that dose should be reduced and the interval extended below eGFR 30 with its active metabolite oxymorphone accumulating (Table 2) — the text instead names hydromorphone for moderate renal impairment and specialist-supervised methadone as renally unaffected. — This box says 'Paracetamol safe', but the manuscript's own text and Table 2 specify that below eGFR 30 mL/min, paracetamol's dosing interval must be extended to every 8 hours because of accumulation risk in ESRD — not simply 'safe' without qualification. — The manuscript also mandates avoiding meperidine, tramadol (eGFR <30), and duloxetine (eGFR <30), and reducing gabapentinoid doses in renal impairment — all omitted from this box. — estimated glomerular filtration rate — The lab-estimated kidney-function value this algorithm uses repeatedly (most often the <30 mL/min threshold) to decide which opioids, NSAIDs, or adjuvants are safe to use or must be avoided or dose-reduced. — morphine-6-glucuronide — Morphine's potent active glucuronide metabolite, which accumulates in renal impairment and drives prolonged sedation, neurotoxicity, and respiratory depression — the stated reason both for reducing morphine's dose and, elsewhere in the same figure, for avoiding it altogether below eGFR 30. — morphine-3-glucuronide — Morphine's inactive but neuroexcitatory glucuronide metabolite (implicated in myoclonus and hyperalgesia), which — like M6G — accumulates when renal clearance is reduced. — end-stage renal disease — The most severe stage of chronic kidney disease, used in this algorithm's renal-dosing caveats for paracetamol, gabapentin, and duloxetine.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.text:
Hepatic impairment — Paracetamol max 2 g/day (Child-Pugh)
Use opioids with extended intervals
Avoid codeine / tramadol — Hepatic-specific dose ceilings, interval extensions, and drug exclusions in patients with liver disease/cirrhosis. — Hepatic blood flow, hepatocyte mass (declining up to 40% with age), CYP450 oxidative activity, first-pass metabolism, and albumin binding are all impaired in liver disease, reducing clearance and increasing the bioavailability and half-life of hepatically metabolised analgesics; prodrugs (codeine) and extensively metabolised drugs (tramadol) carry unpredictable efficacy or toxicity/encephalopathy risk. — Paracetamol — Max 2 g/day in hepatic impairment; Child-Pugh C contraindicated (Table 2); Clinical Case 2 illustrates Child-Pugh B — Opioids — 30–50% dose reduction for morphine in Child-Pugh B/C and for oxycodone in severe hepatic failure (where its half-life reaches ~24 hours), plus extended dosing intervals — Section 5.A paragraph 2 also mentions 2000–3000 mg/day for liver failure/malnutrition/alcoholism before paragraph 3 separately specifies 2 g/day — the same internal inconsistency already flagged under the Paracetamol box. — The manuscript also advises avoiding meperidine and NSAIDs in cirrhosis, and avoiding duloxetine in severe hepatic failure — none of which appear in this box. — A clinical scoring system (A/B/C) for the severity of liver disease, used in this algorithm to set paracetamol's maximum dose and to flag Child-Pugh C as a contraindication to paracetamol.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.text:
Cognitive impairment — Avoid tramadol (lowers seizure threshold)
Use PAINAD for pain scoring
Lowest effective opioid dose — Specific assessment and prescribing safeguards for older adults with dementia or cognitive impairment. — Pain is underreported in dementia, requiring behavioural observation scales (PAINAD or the Abbey Pain Scale). Analgesics are also the leading medication class implicated in drug-induced cognitive-impairment adverse events; CNS-active analgesics (opioids, tramadol, gabapentinoids, TCAs) can precipitate or worsen delirium and dementia symptoms, and tramadol additionally lowers the seizure threshold. — Starting dose — Lowest effective dose — 25–50% of the standard adult opioid dose for age ≥70 years — Avoidance of tramadol in older adults is linked in the manuscript to both the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria and STOPP/START criteria v3, and opioid-induced delirium exacerbation is separately linked to the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria. — Pain Assessment in Advanced Dementia — A behavioural observation scale for scoring pain in patients with dementia/cognitive impairment who cannot reliably self-report, used at Step 1 and again at the Cognitive impairment box. — A behavioural pain-observation scale for patients with dementia, named in the manuscript's own text but omitted from the figure. — American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria — The 2023 updated expert-panel list of potentially inappropriate medications for older adults, cited repeatedly in this manuscript as the external source for renal-dosing thresholds, tramadol's and tertiary TCAs' inappropriateness, and opioid-associated delirium risk. — A separate, explicit set of criteria (version 3, 2023) for potentially inappropriate prescribing and prescribing omissions in older people, cited alongside the AGS Beers Criteria for tramadol's and gabapentinoid/opioid combinations' inappropriateness.

entries.title: Pharmacological Pain Management in Elderly Patients
entries.nodeLabel: Core prescribing principles for the elderly
entries.text:
Core prescribing principles for the elderly — "Start low, go slow" - Regular rather than PRN dosing for chronic pain - Schedule bowel regimen with opioids
Review polypharmacy (anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, SNRIs) - Renal/hepatic dose adjustment mandatory
Reassess goal (comfort vs. function) - Deprescribe opioids when acute pain resolves — Overarching summary of safe geriatric analgesic prescribing, medication review, bowel prophylaxis, organ-based dosing, goal alignment, and opioid stewardship/deprescribing across all patients exiting the algorithm. — Physiological heterogeneity, reduced homeostatic reserve, high prevalence of polypharmacy (five or more concurrent medications, affecting up to 62.5% of elderly patients), synergistic fatal respiratory depression or anticholinergic/serotonergic toxicity from drug-drug interactions, universal opioid constipation, and community diversion/misuse risk from leftover acute opioid prescriptions all necessitate systematic prescribing and deprescribing safeguards. — 'Regular rather than PRN dosing for chronic pain' is never explicitly stated in the manuscript's own prose — Section 5.C.1 only mentions introducing extended-release opioids once requirements are established, and this phrase appears to derive from the figure's own cited external guidelines rather than the review's own text. — The explicit contrast 'comfort vs. function' in 'Reassess goal' appears only in the figure — the manuscript discusses functional assessment and end-of-life palliative comfort care separately, but never frames them as this explicit pair. — This box's 'Review polypharmacy' list omits gabapentinoids, even though the manuscript's own Abstract, Section 5.C.2, Section 8, and Table 2 repeatedly emphasise gabapentinoids alongside benzodiazepines as a high-risk fatal combination with opioids.

entries.title: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron
entries.text: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron Antiemetic Selection by Clinical Setting

entries.title: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron
entries.nodeLabel: Adult or child with nausea and/or vomiting in whom an antiemetic is considered
entries.text: Adult or child with nausea and/or vomiting in whom an antiemetic is considered — Entry point for any adult or child whose nausea and/or vomiting is significant enough that the clinician is considering an antiemetic drug — the point at which a choice between metoclopramide and ondansetron first arises. — Metoclopramide and ondansetron are the antiemetics most often prescribed in general medical practice, but the review's central finding is that they are not interchangeable: which one performs better depends on the emetic pathway actually driving the patient's vomiting. Where vomiting is driven by serotonin release from enterochromaffin cells activating vagal 5-HT3 receptors (chemotherapy, radionuclide therapy, gut inflammation in paediatric gastroenteritis, and surgery/anaesthesia), ondansetron clearly outperforms conventional-dose metoclopramide; where the trigger is heterogeneous or hormonal (undifferentiated adult ED nausea, hyperemesis gravidarum), the two drugs perform equivalently and the choice should instead be guided by tolerability, comorbidity and cost. — Serotonin type-3 receptor — A vagal-afferent and chemoreceptor-trigger-zone receptor activated by serotonin released from gut enterochromaffin cells. Ondansetron's antiemetic effect comes from blocking this receptor.

entries.title: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron
entries.text: Initial assessment — Identify and treat the underlying cause; correct fluid and electrolyte deficits (potassium, magnesium); exclude red flags requiring specific management (bowel obstruction, raised intracranial pressure, acute coronary syndrome, diabetic ketoacidosis, intoxication) — Before an antiemetic is chosen, identify and treat whatever is actually causing the nausea or vomiting, correct fluid and electrolyte deficits (particularly potassium and magnesium), and exclude red-flag diagnoses that need their own specific management rather than symptomatic antiemetic therapy. — Electrolyte correction here is not an isolated step: hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia are two of the three risk factors this same figure flags later, at the drug-specific safety check, as reasons to avoid or limit intravenous ondansetron — correcting them before an antiemetic is chosen directly reduces that downstream risk. — This box's content — treating the underlying cause, correcting potassium/magnesium, and excluding these specific red-flag diagnoses — does not appear anywhere in the systematic review's own extracted text. The review's scope is a head-to-head efficacy/safety comparison between metoclopramide and ondansetron, not a diagnostic work-up of nausea and vomiting; this box is general clinical background the figure adds independently of the review's own synthesis.

entries.title: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron
entries.text: What is the clinical setting? — The branch point: the review found that the relative performance of metoclopramide and ondansetron is setting-dependent, so the next step is identifying which of six clinical contexts the patient is in. — Each of the six settings below draws on a different subset of the review's 73 included reports, with its own certainty rating — which is why the recommendation differs from branch to branch rather than applying one single rule to every patient.

entries.title: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron
entries.text:
Emetogenic chemotherapy or
radionuclide therapy — Patients receiving emetogenic chemotherapy (e.g. cisplatin- or FAC-based regimens) or radionuclide therapy (e.g. radioiodine for differentiated thyroid cancer). — Cytotoxic chemotherapy and therapeutic radiation release serotonin from enterochromaffin cells in the gut wall, activating vagal afferent 5-HT3 receptors — the same pathway ondansetron blocks — producing the largest, most consistent advantage for ondansetron of any setting in this review. — Serotonin type-3 receptor — A vagal-afferent and chemoreceptor-trigger-zone receptor activated by serotonin released from gut enterochromaffin cells. Ondansetron's antiemetic effect comes from blocking this receptor.

entries.title: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron
entries.text:
Ondansetron preferred [GRADE: low] — Base prophylaxis on a 5-HT3 antagonist as per antiemetic guidelines;
conventional-dose metoclopramide is less effective (d 0.81 to 1.51). — Ondansetron (or another 5-HT3 antagonist) should form the basis of antiemetic prophylaxis in this setting; conventional-dose metoclopramide is a weaker option. — Six primary studies (seven reports) directly compared the drugs in oncology settings, all rated High risk of bias and predating modern triple/quadruple antiemetic prophylaxis standards. Effect sizes uniformly favoured ondansetron and exceeded the 0.5 MCID: complete acute vomiting control 93% vs 65% in FAC chemotherapy (Bosnjak, d = 1.10) [55]; complete suppression 65% vs 30% at low-dose cisplatin (Bhatia, d = 0.81) [56], with a similar advantage at the high dose and in the delayed phase [57]; complete acute emesis control 90% vs 36.7% with cisplatin and cyclophosphamide, both regimens combined with dexamethasone and lorazepam (Manusirivithaya, d = 1.51) [58]. Ondansetron also pulled ahead from the second chemotherapy course onward in a repeated-courses trial (Raynov) [59], and outperformed metoclopramide and pantoprazole for nausea (though neither prevented vomiting) after radioiodine therapy (Mirzababaee) [60], a finding echoed in a large non-randomised radioiodine cohort (Li, n = 1755) [61]. GRADE certainty for the core chemotherapy comparison is Low — rated down for risk of bias and indirectness, since the included trials predate current multi-agent prophylaxis regimens. — All six oncology comparator studies were rated High risk of bias (or Serious by ROBINS-I, for the one non-randomised cohort); none reflects current triple/quadruple antiemetic prophylaxis practice, so the effect sizes shown here describe ondansetron against metoclopramide specifically, not against modern standard-of-care combination prophylaxis. — This recommendation aligns with the ASCO Antiemetics Guideline Update (Hesketh et al., 2020) [8], which places 5-HT3 antagonists within triple/quadruple regimens and reserves metoclopramide for a secondary role — an external guideline the review cites rather than a finding from its own pooled comparative data. — Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation — A structured framework for rating how confident clinicians should be in a body of evidence, from very low to high certainty, based on risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias. — Minimal Clinically Important Difference — The smallest difference in an outcome that patients or clinicians would consider meaningful. This review uses a Cohen's d of 0.5 (half a standard deviation) as the cutoff, so a statistically significant finding below that threshold is not treated as clinically important. — Risk Of Bias In Non-randomised Studies - of Interventions — The companion tool to RoB 2 for assessing bias in non-randomised comparative studies; its ratings top out at ‘serious’ or worse because such studies cannot fully control for confounding by indication. — Serotonin type-3 receptor — A vagal-afferent and chemoreceptor-trigger-zone receptor activated by serotonin released from gut enterochromaffin cells. Ondansetron's antiemetic effect comes from blocking this receptor. — American Society of Clinical Oncology — The guideline body whose Antiemetics Guideline Update (2020) this review cites as recommending 5-HT3 antagonists within multi-agent chemotherapy prophylaxis regimens.

entries.title: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron
entries.text:
Perioperative period (PONV
prophylaxis) — Patients requiring antiemetic prophylaxis for postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) around the time of surgery. — Surgery and anaesthesia activate the same serotonergic emetic pathway as chemotherapy (gut and vagal afferent 5-HT3 receptors). This is the largest single evidence base in the review: 27 head-to-head trials and 6 syntheses. — Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting — Nausea and vomiting occurring after surgery and anaesthesia, usually within the first 24 hours — the single largest evidence base in this review (27 trials, 6 syntheses). — Serotonin type-3 receptor — A vagal-afferent and chemoreceptor-trigger-zone receptor activated by serotonin released from gut enterochromaffin cells. Ondansetron's antiemetic effect comes from blocking this receptor.

entries.title: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron
entries.text:
Ondansetron preferred [GRADE: moderate] — Modest advantage (pooled d 0.61; largest trials d ≈ 0.3). Metoclopramide
remains acceptable within multimodal prophylaxis. — Ondansetron (or another 5-HT3 antagonist) should form the basis of PONV prophylaxis, but the advantage over metoclopramide is real yet modest — metoclopramide remains an acceptable component of multimodal prophylaxis rather than a drug to avoid. — Across 24 head-to-head prophylaxis trials, 13 favoured ondansetron on at least one emetic outcome, 11 showed no significant difference, and none showed metoclopramide superior for emesis. A laparoscopic cholecystectomy meta-analysis reached the MCID (pooled d = 0.61, Wu) [89], but the two largest individual trials showed smaller effects (Krobbuaban d = 0.29 [71]; Bolton d = 0.31 [63]) — the ‘largest trials d ≈ 0.3’ this box cites — indicating the true advantage is real but modest. Metoclopramide 10 mg still reduced 24-hour PONV against control in its own 30-trial meta-analysis (De Oliveira, odds ratio 0.58) [95], supporting its continued place in multimodal regimens. GRADE certainty is Moderate, rated down for risk of bias across the 27 trials. — Routine combination of ondansetron plus metoclopramide is explicitly NOT supported by this review: a factorial paediatric adenotonsillectomy trial found a negative interaction between the two drugs when combined (Gunter) [64], whereas ondansetron plus dexamethasone performed best in a seven-group comparison (Leksowski) [83] — the evidence favours combining ondansetron with a drug from a different class, not with metoclopramide. — One trial in this evidence base (Quaynor, laparoscopic cholecystectomy, OND 8 mg vs MTC 20 mg) found metoclopramide associated with less postoperative pain than ondansetron, with no significant difference in PONV itself [78] — the review's only finding anywhere in the perioperative literature pointing toward a metoclopramide-favouring outcome, though it concerns pain rather than emesis. — This recommendation aligns with the Fourth Consensus Guidelines for the Management of PONV (Gan et al., 2020) [7], which places 5-HT3 antagonists at the centre of prophylaxis and reserves metoclopramide for a secondary role — an external guideline the review cites rather than a finding from its own pooled data. — Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation — A structured framework for rating how confident clinicians should be in a body of evidence, from very low to high certainty, based on risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias. — Minimal Clinically Important Difference — The smallest difference in an outcome that patients or clinicians would consider meaningful. This review uses a Cohen's d of 0.5 (half a standard deviation) as the cutoff, so a statistically significant finding below that threshold is not treated as clinically important. — Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting — Nausea and vomiting occurring after surgery and anaesthesia, usually within the first 24 hours — the single largest evidence base in this review (27 trials, 6 syntheses). — Serotonin type-3 receptor — A vagal-afferent and chemoreceptor-trigger-zone receptor activated by serotonin released from gut enterochromaffin cells. Ondansetron's antiemetic effect comes from blocking this receptor.

entries.title: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron
entries.text:
Child with acute
gastroenteritis — Children presenting with vomiting due to acute gastroenteritis. — Gut inflammation in paediatric gastroenteritis releases serotonin from enterochromaffin cells via the same 5-HT3 pathway as chemotherapy, favouring ondansetron. This is also the setting with the clearest practical stake, since controlling vomiting is what allows oral rehydration therapy to proceed instead of IV fluids or admission. — Serotonin type-3 receptor — A vagal-afferent and chemoreceptor-trigger-zone receptor activated by serotonin released from gut enterochromaffin cells. Ondansetron's antiemetic effect comes from blocking this receptor.

entries.title: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron
entries.text:
Ondansetron preferred (0.1 to 0.15 mg/kg)
[GRADE: low] — Facilitates oral rehydration; benefit exceeds MCID at 24 h (d 0.70 to 1.44).
Avoid routine metoclopramide (extrapyramidal effects ≈ 9%). — Ondansetron (0.1 to 0.15 mg/kg) should be preferred over metoclopramide, which should not be used routinely because of its extrapyramidal side-effect rate in children. — Early control at 1 hour is similar between the drugs, but ondansetron provides significantly more durable cessation of vomiting at 24 hours, with effect sizes exceeding the 0.5 MCID in two of three head-to-head trials: Epifanio found 96.6% vs 67.2% vomiting-free at 24 h (d = 1.44) [35], and Ahmad found 92.5% vs 77.5% (d = 0.70) [36]; Al-Ansari's single-IV-dose trial did not reach the MCID (d = 0.27) [34]. Five further syntheses support ondansetron: a Bayesian-updated Cochrane review found no evidence supporting metoclopramide at all [46,47], a 24-trial network meta-analysis (Niño-Serna) found ondansetron the only intervention that reduced vomiting, hospitalisation and IV rehydration versus placebo [48], and a 33-trial network meta-analysis (Alsabri) found IV ondansetron improved 24-hour vomiting cessation with fewer adverse events [50]. The extrapyramidal-effects figure this box cites (≈9%) comes from a dedicated paediatric metoclopramide safety meta-analysis, which also found a 6% sedation rate (Lau Moon Lin) [98]. GRADE certainty is Low, rated down for risk of bias and inconsistency across the 3 head-to-head trials. — Risk-of-bias ratings varied considerably across the three head-to-head trials behind this recommendation: RoB 2: Some concerns for Al-Ansari [34] and Epifanio [35], but RoB 2: High for Ahmad [36] — the single-blind trial that showed the larger, MCID-exceeding effect at 24 hours is also the more bias-prone one. — Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation — A structured framework for rating how confident clinicians should be in a body of evidence, from very low to high certainty, based on risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias. — Minimal Clinically Important Difference — The smallest difference in an outcome that patients or clinicians would consider meaningful. This review uses a Cohen's d of 0.5 (half a standard deviation) as the cutoff, so a statistically significant finding below that threshold is not treated as clinically important. — Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 — The standard Cochrane tool for assessing risk of bias in randomised trials, rating each trial as low risk, some concerns, or high risk across several bias domains. — NMA — A meta-analysis technique that combines direct and indirect trial comparisons to rank three or more treatments against each other even when not every pair has been tested head-to-head.

entries.title: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron
entries.text:
Pregnancy: hyperemesis
gravidarum — Pregnant patients with hyperemesis gravidarum, after first-line therapy has failed. — Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy is hormonally driven rather than following the serotonergic or dopaminergic pathways the other settings turn on — part of why efficacy here is equivalent between the two drugs rather than favouring one of them.

entries.title: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron
entries.nodeLabel:
Either drug as second-line therapy
[GRADE: moderate]

entries.title: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron
entries.nodeLabel:
Adult with undifferentiated
nausea in the ED
entries.text:
Adult with undifferentiated
nausea in the ED — Adults presenting with undifferentiated nausea and/or vomiting in the emergency department, where pain, opioids, vestibular disturbance, metabolic disorders and gastric stasis may all contribute.

entries.title: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron
entries.nodeLabel:
Either drug; choose by safety profile
[GRADE: moderate]
entries.text:
Either drug; choose by safety profile
[GRADE: moderate] — Differences below MCID; large placebo response. Ondansetron 4 mg IV or
metoclopramide 10 mg IV over 15 min; doses > 10 mg add no benefit. — Either drug is reasonable — symptom relief is indistinguishable between them and neither clearly beats placebo. Choose by safety profile: ondansetron 4 mg IV or metoclopramide 10 mg IV given over 15 minutes; raising the metoclopramide dose above 10 mg adds no benefit. — The two largest head-to-head trials found essentially no difference: Egerton-Warburton (n = 258) found a 27 mm vs 28 mm VAS fall at 30 minutes, neither exceeding the 23 mm placebo-arm fall (d = -0.04, negligible, MCID not reached) [26]; Feiz Disfani's mild-head-trauma trial found 23.6 vs 25.9 mm against a 31.9 mm placebo fall (d = 0.10, negligible) [29]. A Cochrane review of 8 trials (952 participants) found both drugs barely separated from placebo at 30 minutes [9], and a Bayesian network meta-analysis ranked oral ondansetron among the least effective options while IV ondansetron was the most likely to be free of significant adverse reactions [10]. The ‘doses above 10 mg add no benefit’ statement draws on two sources: no trial in medical (non-surgical) patients showed higher metoclopramide doses improving symptom relief, while 20 mg increased akathisia versus 10 mg (15% vs 9%) [26,27,97]. A 2009 narrative review had proposed ondansetron as first-line on safety grounds [6], an external recommendation the review's own head-to-head data do not clearly bear out for efficacy. GRADE certainty is Moderate (4 RCTs, n = 665, plus 2 syntheses), rated down for risk of bias. — Figure — Ondansetron 4 mg IV or metoclopramide 10 mg IV over 15 min; doses > 10 mg add no benefit — Table 1 (full range across included studies) — Ondansetron 4 mg (range 4 to 8 mg) IV, 8 to 24 mg orally; metoclopramide 10 mg (range 10 to 20 mg) IV or orally — One trial behind this box (Jokar, renal colic) was rated RoB 2: High, with the review itself noting: ‘Several trials were registered retrospectively, and in one the tabulated data were internally inconsistent’ [30]. — A borderline finding favoured metoclopramide in one trial — freedom from rescue medication (Egerton-Warburton, d = -0.49, small, borderline MCID) [26] — but the review notes this occurred at a 20 mg metoclopramide dose, which itself carries a higher akathisia risk than the 10 mg this box recommends [97]. — Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation — A structured framework for rating how confident clinicians should be in a body of evidence, from very low to high certainty, based on risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias. — Minimal Clinically Important Difference — The smallest difference in an outcome that patients or clinicians would consider meaningful. This review uses a Cohen's d of 0.5 (half a standard deviation) as the cutoff, so a statistically significant finding below that threshold is not treated as clinically important. — Visual Analogue Scale — A patient-reported symptom-intensity scale, typically a 100 mm line the patient marks between ‘none’ and ‘worst imaginable’, used throughout this review to quantify nausea severity and change over time. — Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 — The standard Cochrane tool for assessing risk of bias in randomised trials, rating each trial as low risk, some concerns, or high risk across several bias domains. — NMA — A meta-analysis technique that combines direct and indirect trial comparisons to rank three or more treatments against each other even when not every pair has been tested head-to-head. — A subjective, distressing sense of inner restlessness and inability to stay still — an extrapyramidal side effect of dopamine-blocking drugs like metoclopramide, easily mistaken for the nausea or agitation being treated.

entries.title: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron
entries.nodeLabel:
Opioid-induced, uraemic,
vestibular or palliative
nausea
entries.text:
Opioid-induced, uraemic,
vestibular or palliative
nausea — Nausea with a mixed or less common aetiology: opioid-induced (e.g. in cancer patients), uraemic, vestibular (acute vestibular neuritis), or palliative-care nausea of hepatic origin.

entries.title: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron
entries.nodeLabel:
No firm preference; individualise
[GRADE: very low]
entries.text:
No firm preference; individualise
[GRADE: very low] — Single small trials only. Trend favouring metoclopramide in opioid-induced
and ondansetron in uraemic nausea. — Neither drug has a firm advantage here — the evidence is limited to single small trials, so the choice should be individualised. What trend exists favours metoclopramide for opioid-induced nausea and ondansetron for uraemic nausea. — Pharmacologically, metoclopramide's prokinetic/D2-receptor-antagonist action has a rationale where gastric stasis or dopaminergic stimulation from opioids contributes, while a large effect favoured ondansetron in a small uraemia crossover trial. In opioid-induced cancer nausea, Hardy's multinational trial (stopped early after 92 patients due to slow recruitment) found complete nausea control numerically favouring metoclopramide (36% vs 17%, d = -0.56, moderate, technically reaching the MCID), but the confidence interval crossed zero and the difference was not significant [37]. In uraemia, Ljutić's small crossover trial (n = 10) found a large effect favouring ondansetron on both observer- and patient-rated scores (d = 2.42) [38] — a striking result, but from only 10 patients. In acute vestibular neuritis, ondansetron was associated with a shorter hospital stay (2.88 vs 4.5 days) in a 20-patient pilot trial, though nausea outcomes themselves were not reported [39]. In palliative-care hepatic-origin nausea, a non-randomised cohort (each arm also receiving dexamethasone, ROBINS-I: Serious) found no significant difference in improvement at day 7, with a lower post-treatment nausea score favouring metoclopramide (p = 0.002), an unadjusted comparison vulnerable to confounding by indication [40]. GRADE certainty is Very Low, rated down two levels for risk of bias and imprecision. — This is the lowest-certainty branch in the entire algorithm (GRADE: Very low) — three small RCTs (n = 122 total) and one non-randomised cohort across four distinct, mechanistically different causes of nausea, none large enough to support a confident recommendation either way. — Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation — A structured framework for rating how confident clinicians should be in a body of evidence, from very low to high certainty, based on risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias. — Minimal Clinically Important Difference — The smallest difference in an outcome that patients or clinicians would consider meaningful. This review uses a Cohen's d of 0.5 (half a standard deviation) as the cutoff, so a statistically significant finding below that threshold is not treated as clinically important. — Risk Of Bias In Non-randomised Studies - of Interventions — The companion tool to RoB 2 for assessing bias in non-randomised comparative studies; its ratings top out at ‘serious’ or worse because such studies cannot fully control for confounding by indication. — Dopamine type-2 receptor — The receptor metoclopramide blocks in the chemoreceptor trigger zone to produce its antiemetic and prokinetic effects — the same mechanism responsible for its extrapyramidal side effects.

entries.title: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron
entries.text: Before administration: drug-specific safety check — Before giving either drug, check for the specific risk factors that make one drug preferable to the other, regardless of which of the six clinical settings the patient is in.

entries.title: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron
entries.text:
Risk of QT prolongation? — Cardiac disease, hypokalaemia or hypomagnesaemia,
other QT-prolonging drugs
→ Avoid or limit IV ondansetron; prefer the oral route or
metoclopramide; obtain an ECG and correct electrolytes — In patients with cardiac disease, hypokalaemia or hypomagnesaemia, or on other QT-prolonging drugs, avoid or limit intravenous ondansetron: prefer the oral route or metoclopramide, obtain an ECG, and correct electrolytes first. — IV ondansetron 4 mg prolonged the QTc by a mean of 19.3 ms in hospitalised cardiovascular patients with torsades risk factors in a prospective observational study [25]. A post-marketing systematic review identified 60 arrhythmia reports associated with ondansetron: 80% followed IV administration, 83% involved significant medical history or a concomitant QT-prolonging drug, and none followed a single oral dose [12]. Reassuringly, zero arrhythmias were reported in any of the head-to-head trials in this review, though few of them performed ECG monitoring — meaning the trials were not designed to detect this risk, not that it doesn't exist. — The review's own stated limitations note that no included head-to-head trial was designed to detect arrhythmia, so the absence of reported events in trial data should not be read as reassurance equal in strength to the pharmacovigilance data above. — Corrected QT interval — The QT interval on the ECG adjusted for heart rate. Prolongation increases the risk of torsades de pointes — the mechanism behind this algorithm's intravenous-ondansetron caution.

entries.title: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron
entries.nodeLabel:
Risk of extrapyramidal effects or
sedation?
entries.text:
Risk of extrapyramidal effects or
sedation? — Children, young adults, previous dystonia or akathisia,
Parkinson's disease
→ Prefer ondansetron; if metoclopramide is used: 10 mg
infused over 15 min, lowest effective dose, short course — In children, young adults, patients with a previous dystonic reaction or akathisia, or Parkinson's disease, prefer ondansetron; if metoclopramide must be used, give 10 mg infused over 15 minutes, at the lowest effective dose, for the shortest course. — Metoclopramide's dopamine D2-receptor blockade in the chemoreceptor trigger zone — the same action behind its antiemetic effect — also produces its characteristic extrapyramidal side effects. Drowsiness/sedation ranged from 13.3% to 43.3% across trials, roughly double the ondansetron rate in several head-to-head comparisons, and was also higher with metoclopramide in FAC chemotherapy and in epidural caesarean delivery [28,41,55,62]; dry mouth was similarly about twice as frequent (23.8% vs 10.0%) [41,52]. Acute dystonia occurred in 5 of 60 patients on metoclopramide versus 0 on ondansetron in one head-trauma trial [28], though 0 extrapyramidal events were seen in three other trials [29,34,40]. Slowing the infusion is a specifically evidence-based mitigation: a 15-minute infusion reduced akathisia from 24.7% (after a 2-minute bolus) to 5.8% [24], and prophylactic diphenhydramine did not help — 12% akathisia in both arms [97] — so dose and infusion rate matter more than premedication. Long-term exposure carries a boxed regulatory warning for tardive dyskinesia, estimated at under 1%, though this is not relevant to the short courses used for acute nausea and vomiting [5,11]. — Figure — If metoclopramide is used: 10 mg infused over 15 minutes, lowest effective dose, short course — Section 3.2, Table 1 (full range) — 10 mg (range 10 to 20 mg) IV or orally, up to three or four times daily — The tardive dyskinesia boxed warning [5] concerns prolonged/long-term metoclopramide exposure and is not clinically relevant to the single or short-course acute dosing this algorithm addresses — the review includes it as a known regulatory fact about the drug class, not as a risk specific to acute antiemetic use. — Dopamine type-2 receptor — The receptor metoclopramide blocks in the chemoreceptor trigger zone to produce its antiemetic and prokinetic effects — the same mechanism responsible for its extrapyramidal side effects. — CTZ — A region in the brainstem, outside the blood–brain barrier, that senses circulating drugs and toxins and triggers vomiting when stimulated via dopamine D2 or serotonin 5-HT3 receptors — the shared anatomical target of both drugs in this review. — A subjective, distressing sense of inner restlessness and inability to stay still — an extrapyramidal side effect of dopamine-blocking drugs like metoclopramide, easily mistaken for the nausea or agitation being treated. — Sustained, involuntary muscle contraction (of the neck, jaw, or eyes, for instance) — another extrapyramidal reaction to dopamine blockade, distinct from akathisia. — A potentially irreversible movement disorder (repetitive, involuntary movements, often of the face and tongue) associated with prolonged dopamine-blocking drug exposure — the subject of metoclopramide's boxed regulatory warning, estimated at under 1% with long-term use.

entries.title: Metoclopramide versus Ondansetron
entries.text:
Reassess at 30 to 60 minutes — Controlled: continue or switch to the oral route. Persistent: add an agent
of a different class rather than escalating the dose, and reconsider
the diagnosis. — At 30 to 60 minutes: if symptoms are controlled, continue the current drug or switch to the oral route; if they persist, add an agent from a different pharmacological class rather than simply escalating the dose of the same drug, and reconsider whether the working diagnosis is correct. — The instruction to add a different class ‘rather than escalating the dose’ is consistent with the review's own dose-response findings for metoclopramide specifically: no evidence in medical patients that doses above 10 mg improve symptom relief, while 20 mg increases akathisia risk compared with 10 mg (15% vs 9%) [26,27,97] — escalating this particular drug's dose trades a higher side-effect rate for no proven extra benefit. — Like the Initial assessment box, this closing step does not appear in the systematic review's own extracted text — the review compares the two drugs' efficacy and safety, but does not describe a reassessment protocol or timeframe. This is general clinical practice the figure adds independently of the review's own synthesis. — A subjective, distressing sense of inner restlessness and inability to stay still — an extrapyramidal side effect of dopamine-blocking drugs like metoclopramide, easily mistaken for the nausea or agitation being treated.

entries.title: Needle Aspiration versus Tube Thoracostomy
entries.text: Needle Aspiration versus Tube Thoracostomy Symptom-Led Management of Spontaneous Pneumothorax

entries.title: Needle Aspiration versus Tube Thoracostomy
entries.text: Suspected spontaneous pneumothorax — Confirm on chest radiograph, CT or thoracic ultrasound — Initial diagnostic confirmation of suspected spontaneous pneumothorax (air in the pleural space without trauma or iatrogenic instrumentation) via imaging, and localisation of a safe site if pleural intervention turns out to be needed. — Because contemporary management rests on symptoms and high-risk characteristics rather than radiographic pneumothorax size, imaging's main role here is confirming the diagnosis and finding a safe procedural site, not triggering drainage on size alone. Thoracic ultrasonography is more sensitive than supine chest radiography with comparable specificity in trauma and critical-care populations, and handheld ultrasound is effective and safe for guiding pleural procedures. Automated deep-learning detection/notification, AI triage models predicting need for tube thoracostomy, and large-language-model chest radiograph evaluation all exist but remain unvalidated for autonomous clinical use. — CT is listed here and expanded in the figure's own caption ("CT, computed tomography"), but the manuscript prose never discusses the diagnostic role, indications or accuracy of CT for confirming suspected spontaneous pneumothorax — not stated in the manuscript. — spontaneous pneumothorax — Accumulation of air in the pleural space without trauma or iatrogenic instrumentation, occurring either without known lung disease (primary) or with it (secondary).

entries.title: Needle Aspiration versus Tube Thoracostomy
entries.text: Tension physiology or — haemodynamic instability? — Immediate clinical triage for life-threatening tension pneumothorax physiology or haemodynamic compromise, before any conservative, aspiration or ambulatory pathway is even considered. Tension pneumothorax was itself excluded from the systematic review's primary RCT comparison of aspiration versus tube thoracostomy. — Tension physiology or haemodynamic instability makes immediate pleural evacuation obligatory rather than discretionary; every aspiration-first or conservative strategy in this algorithm applies only to haemodynamically stable patients. — No numeric blood pressure, heart rate or shock-index cutoff for "instability" is given in the figure or anywhere in the manuscript text — not stated in the manuscript. — randomised controlled trial — A study design in which participants are randomly assigned to different interventions to minimise bias when comparing outcomes.

entries.title: Needle Aspiration versus Tube Thoracostomy
entries.text: IMMEDIATE — needle decompression, then tube thoracostomy — Urgent needle decompression to relieve tension physiology/instability, followed by definitive insertion of an indwelling intercostal drain (tube thoracostomy) connected to an underwater-seal/drainage system. — Tension physiology or haemodynamic instability mandates immediate decompression and continuous pleural evacuation via tube thoracostomy. — Needle gauge, the anatomical landmark used for tension decompression, and the subsequent tube's French size are not stated anywhere in the manuscript. — This box has no further arrow in the figure connecting it to drain-care, persistent-air-leak assessment or recurrence prevention, even though these patients go on to standard tube drainage like any other drained patient.

entries.title: Needle Aspiration versus Tube Thoracostomy
entries.text: Any high-risk — characteristic? — Screens haemodynamically stable patients for clinical or physiological high-risk features — established or presumed secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (SSP), bilateral involvement, blood in the pleural space, significant hypoxia, or positive-pressure ventilation — that rule out conservative observation or simple needle aspiration as the default therapy. — Patients with underlying parenchymal pathology (COPD, interstitial lung disease, cystic fibrosis, opportunistic infection) have limited physiological reserve, tolerate pleural air poorly, and account for nearly all in-hospital spontaneous-pneumothorax mortality. Significant hypoxia and bilateral pneumothorax are BTS guideline high-risk features requiring procedural drainage rather than symptom-led observation. Spontaneous haemopneumothorax is described as "a surgical emergency in which the balance of considerations shifts decisively towards immediate drainage and operative exploration." Positive-pressure ventilation and impaired physiological reserve (ICU, COVID-19, ARDS/ECMO settings) sharply reverse the risk-benefit calculus away from minimally invasive or conservative care and toward tube thoracostomy. — Figure-vs-text gap: in the figure, haemopneumothorax routes via "Yes" to the small-bore tube-thoracostomy box, but the manuscript's own text frames spontaneous haemopneumothorax as a surgical emergency favouring immediate drainage *and* operative exploration — small-bore preference isn't specifically endorsed there for this subgroup. — secondary spontaneous pneumothorax — Pneumothorax occurring in a patient with pre-existing lung disease (e.g. COPD, interstitial lung disease, cystic fibrosis) — carries poorer physiological reserve than primary spontaneous pneumothorax and is managed more cautiously throughout this algorithm. — spontaneous pneumothorax — Accumulation of air in the pleural space without trauma or iatrogenic instrumentation, occurring either without known lung disease (primary) or with it (secondary). — British Thoracic Society — The UK professional body whose pleural disease guideline (2023, and earlier 2010 version) is cited repeatedly in this algorithm for high-risk thresholds and procedural technique details not derived from the review's own randomised evidence.

entries.title: Needle Aspiration versus Tube Thoracostomy
entries.text: High-risk characteristics — Significant hypoxia · Bilateral pneumothorax · Underlying lung disease (SSP) · Haemopneumothorax · Age >50 with smoking history · Positive pressure ventilation — The defining list of "high-risk" features referred to by the decision box it's attached to. — Underlying lung disease (SSP) and age over 50 with a smoking history: patients with limited physiological reserve account for nearly all in-hospital spontaneous-pneumothorax mortality, although one RCT subgroup of 48 SSP patients showed shorter hospital stay with aspiration and a dedicated non-inferiority trial (PRINCE-SSP) is still ongoing — current guidance nonetheless continues to favour tube drainage as the provisional default in SSP. Significant hypoxia and bilateral pneumothorax are listed BTS guideline high-risk features. Haemopneumothorax is treated as a surgical emergency. Positive-pressure ventilation and impaired physiological reserve reverse the risk-benefit calculus toward drainage. — "Age >50 with smoking history" is explicitly attributed in the manuscript to the British Thoracic Society guideline — not derived from the review's own RCT synthesis — and its wording there ("age above 50 with a significant smoking history") differs slightly from the figure; no pack-year cut-off is given anywhere. — secondary spontaneous pneumothorax — Pneumothorax occurring in a patient with pre-existing lung disease (e.g. COPD, interstitial lung disease, cystic fibrosis) — carries poorer physiological reserve than primary spontaneous pneumothorax and is managed more cautiously throughout this algorithm. — randomised controlled trial — A study design in which participants are randomly assigned to different interventions to minimise bias when comparing outcomes. — British Thoracic Society — The UK professional body whose pleural disease guideline (2023, and earlier 2010 version) is cited repeatedly in this algorithm for high-risk thresholds and procedural technique details not derived from the review's own randomised evidence.

entries.title: Needle Aspiration versus Tube Thoracostomy
entries.text: Tube thoracostomy — (small-bore 8–14 F preferred) · Admit — Insertion of an indwelling intercostal catheter or chest drain connected to an underwater-seal drainage system, preferring a smaller-calibre drain over a traditional large-bore tube, together with inpatient hospital admission. — Tube thoracostomy provides continuous air evacuation during ongoing air leak and higher immediate re-expansion reliability (risk ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.69–0.89 favouring drainage; number needed to treat ≈ 7), prioritised when physiological reserve is low or high-risk features exist. Small-bore/pigtail catheters achieve comparable success to large-bore chest tubes (79.84% vs 82.87%, RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.93–1.05, no meaningful heterogeneity across 11 studies / 875 patients) with significantly lower complication rates in spontaneous pneumothorax. Indwelling underwater-seal tube thoracostomy mandates hospital admission (100% admission in one pilot trial). — The exact "8–14 F" gauge range appears only in the figure and is never stated anywhere in the manuscript text or tables — it reflects external pleural-guideline convention rather than the review's own synthesis. — spontaneous pneumothorax — Accumulation of air in the pleural space without trauma or iatrogenic instrumentation, occurring either without known lung disease (primary) or with it (secondary). — risk ratio — The ratio of the probability of an outcome in one group to the probability in another; a risk ratio below 1 here favours tube thoracostomy over aspiration for immediate success. — 95% confidence interval — The range within which the true effect size is expected to lie 95% of the time, given the study data; a confidence interval that excludes the null indicates a statistically significant finding.

entries.title: Needle Aspiration versus Tube Thoracostomy
entries.text: Symptomatic? — (breathlessness, chest pain limiting activity) — Decouples intervention from radiographic pneumothorax size in low-risk, haemodynamically stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax, basing the decision to intervene on whether the patient has clinically limiting symptoms rather than being asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic. — Both the 2023 BTS guideline and the 2024 joint ERS/EACTS/ESTS guideline — informed by a conservative-management RCT and an ambulatory-management trial — shifted management away from radiographic size cut-offs toward symptom-driven care, because most minimally symptomatic or uncomplicated primary spontaneous pneumothorax episodes resolve without pleural instrumentation. — The exact parenthetical "(breathlessness, chest pain limiting activity)" appears only in the figure; those words do not appear anywhere in the manuscript body. — spontaneous pneumothorax — Accumulation of air in the pleural space without trauma or iatrogenic instrumentation, occurring either without known lung disease (primary) or with it (secondary). — randomised controlled trial — A study design in which participants are randomly assigned to different interventions to minimise bias when comparing outcomes. — British Thoracic Society — The UK professional body whose pleural disease guideline (2023, and earlier 2010 version) is cited repeatedly in this algorithm for high-risk thresholds and procedural technique details not derived from the review's own randomised evidence. — European Respiratory Society — The European professional body that co-authored (with EACTS and ESTS) the 2024 joint clinical practice guideline on adults with spontaneous pneumothorax cited throughout this algorithm.

entries.title: Needle Aspiration versus Tube Thoracostomy
entries.text: CONSERVATIVE CARE — Observation regardless of size · Supplemental oxygen if indicated · Review at 2–4 days — Watchful waiting — non-interventional outpatient or observational management without pleural aspiration or drainage — irrespective of radiographic pneumothorax size, for asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic low-risk primary spontaneous pneumothorax. — In one RCT of 316 patients with moderate-to-large primary spontaneous pneumothorax, 85% of the conservative arm (137 of 162 patients) needed no interventional procedure at all, with fewer serious adverse events and complete-case 8-week re-expansion of 94.4% vs 98.5% (within the pre-specified non-inferiority margin). A sensitivity analysis imputing outcomes missing after 56 days as failures widened that gap beyond the margin, which is why this evidence carries only Low GRADE certainty. — "Supplemental oxygen if indicated" is never mentioned anywhere in the manuscript prose — note also that significant hypoxia already routes to tube thoracostomy earlier in this algorithm, so this line applies to milder desaturation only. — The "Review at 2–4 days" outpatient interval appears only in the figure (consistent with external BTS guideline practice) and is not stated anywhere in the manuscript text. — spontaneous pneumothorax — Accumulation of air in the pleural space without trauma or iatrogenic instrumentation, occurring either without known lung disease (primary) or with it (secondary). — randomised controlled trial — A study design in which participants are randomly assigned to different interventions to minimise bias when comparing outcomes. — Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation — A structured framework for rating the certainty of evidence for each outcome (High, Moderate, Low, or Very Low) based on risk of bias, imprecision, inconsistency and other factors. — British Thoracic Society — The UK professional body whose pleural disease guideline (2023, and earlier 2010 version) is cited repeatedly in this algorithm for high-risk thresholds and procedural technique details not derived from the review's own randomised evidence.

entries.title: Needle Aspiration versus Tube Thoracostomy
entries.text: NEEDLE (SIMPLE) ASPIRATION — 16–18 G cannula, 2nd ICS mid-clavicular or 5th ICS mid-axillary line · Aspirate to maximum 2.5 L — Manual evacuation of pleural air through a small cannula or catheter that is withdrawn immediately at the end of the procedure, leaving no indwelling chest drain behind. — Across randomised syntheses, tube thoracostomy achieves higher immediate re-expansion (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.69–0.89 across 6 RCTs / 435 participants; Moderate certainty), but immediate success is a surrogate endpoint remediable by escalation without compromising later outcomes — success at one week (93% vs 85%) and at one year (26% vs 27.3% recurrence) do not differ. Aspiration shortens hospital length of stay by a pooled mean difference of −1.70 days (95% CI −2.36 to −1.04 across 5 RCTs / 358 participants), exceeding the pre-specified minimal clinically important difference of roughly 1.25–1.5 days. Aspiration also lowers hospital admission rates (52% vs 100% in one trial), causes less procedural pain, and produces fewer adverse events (Low certainty). — Cannula gauge (16–18 G), the anatomical insertion sites, and the "2.5 L" maximum aspirated volume are not stated anywhere in the manuscript prose or tables — all appear only in the figure, reflecting external BTS/ERS guideline technique. — Figure-vs-text sequencing discrepancy: the manuscript's Abstract, Discussion and Graphical Abstract present "needle aspiration or ambulatory small-bore drainage" as parallel first-line alternatives, whereas this figure places needle aspiration strictly first, reaching ambulatory drainage only after a failed (and possibly repeated) aspiration attempt. — risk ratio — The ratio of the probability of an outcome in one group to the probability in another; a risk ratio below 1 here favours tube thoracostomy over aspiration for immediate success. — 95% confidence interval — The range within which the true effect size is expected to lie 95% of the time, given the study data; a confidence interval that excludes the null indicates a statistically significant finding. — British Thoracic Society — The UK professional body whose pleural disease guideline (2023, and earlier 2010 version) is cited repeatedly in this algorithm for high-risk thresholds and procedural technique details not derived from the review's own randomised evidence. — European Respiratory Society — The European professional body that co-authored (with EACTS and ESTS) the 2024 joint clinical practice guideline on adults with spontaneous pneumothorax cited throughout this algorithm.

entries.title: Needle Aspiration versus Tube Thoracostomy
entries.text: Lung re-expanded and — symptoms resolved at repeat imaging? — Post-aspiration clinical and radiographic reassessment to determine immediate procedural success versus aspiration failure requiring a repeat attempt or escalation to drainage. — Because needle aspiration has a higher immediate failure rate than tube thoracostomy — immediate success ranging from 54.2% to 69% across individual trials — this checkpoint identifies the subset requiring escalation while letting responders avoid admission and an indwelling drain altogether. — The timing of "repeat imaging" isn't specified in the figure, and the manuscript itself notes that constituent trials varied materially in how they defined adequate re-expansion (one trial used 24 hours).

entries.title: Needle Aspiration versus Tube Thoracostomy
entries.text: DISCHARGE — Same-day, with written safety-netting advice · Review at 2–4 weeks — Same-day outpatient discharge without hospital admission following successful aspiration, accompanied by written return precautions and scheduled outpatient follow-up. — Avoiding hospital admission in roughly half of aspirated patients (48% avoided admission in one trial, where 52% required hospitalisation versus 100% with drainage; safe outpatient discharge was also shown in a separate trial) drives the clinically meaningful reduction in bed occupancy, cost and inpatient burden that aspiration offers over drainage. — "With written safety-netting advice" is not mentioned in the manuscript prose; the "Review at 2–4 weeks" follow-up window likewise appears only in the figure, reflecting external BTS guideline recommendation rather than the review's own data. — This box has no visual arrow onward to recurrence-prevention criteria, even though discharged patients carry a roughly 26%–50% recurrence risk across the literature and may qualify for elective VATS consideration. — video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery — A minimally invasive surgical technique using a thoracoscope and small incisions, used here for definitive bullectomy and pleurodesis to prevent recurrence. — British Thoracic Society — The UK professional body whose pleural disease guideline (2023, and earlier 2010 version) is cited repeatedly in this algorithm for high-risk thresholds and procedural technique details not derived from the review's own randomised evidence.

entries.title: Needle Aspiration versus Tube Thoracostomy
entries.text: First aspiration attempt — and residual volume small? — Gates whether a single repeat (second) needle aspiration may be performed, versus escalating straight to ambulatory or standard small-bore drainage. — The manuscript states plainly: "In every trial in which aspiration failed, the remedy was a further aspiration attempt or the placement of a drain, an escalation that did not appear to compromise ultimate outcome." — Neither the cut-off for "residual volume small" nor the criteria for when a clinician should decline a second attempt are defined anywhere in the manuscript — not stated in the manuscript. — After a genuine second attempt has already occurred, "First aspiration attempt" is by definition false, which is how the reassessment loop below resolves downward to ambulatory drainage rather than repeating indefinitely.

entries.title: Needle Aspiration versus Tube Thoracostomy
entries.text: Second aspiration — attempt permissible (maximum of two) — A single permitted repeat needle aspiration when the first attempt failed but the residual pneumothorax volume is judged small, followed by a return to clinical/imaging reassessment (the dashed "Reassess" arrow back to the re-expansion check above). — Same citation as the gating decision above — the manuscript treats a further aspiration attempt as an escalation step that did not appear to compromise the ultimate outcome in any constituent trial. — The explicit numeric cap "(maximum of two)" is not separately discussed in the manuscript prose beyond "a further aspiration attempt" — it reflects external convention rather than a stopping rule derived from the review's own RCT data. — randomised controlled trial — A study design in which participants are randomly assigned to different interventions to minimise bias when comparing outcomes.

entries.title: Needle Aspiration versus Tube Thoracostomy
entries.text: AMBULATORY SMALL-BORE DRAINAGE — 8 F device with one-way valve, where a pneumothorax service with reliable follow-up exists; otherwise tube thoracostomy with admission — Insertion of a small-bore pleural device incorporating a one-way valve, enabling continuous pleural air evacuation on an outpatient/ambulatory basis where structured follow-up infrastructure exists — or conventional inpatient small-bore tube thoracostomy with hospital admission where such a service is unavailable. — Small-bore catheters occupy an intermediate position, delivering the security of continuous drainage during ongoing air leak at a tolerability closer to aspiration. In one open-label RCT of 236 symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax patients across 24 UK hospitals, ambulatory management reduced median hospitalisation (including readmissions) from 4 days to 0 days and reduced further pleural procedures from 35% to 21%. A separate trial showed safe outpatient management using a minichest tube with a Heimlich valve, with equivalent pain, satisfaction and complication rates to needle aspiration.
