Both the 2023 BTS guideline and the 2024 joint ERS/EACTS/ESTS guideline endorse ambulatory management for suitable patients. — The exact "8 F" calibre and "one-way valve" phrasing, and the institutional-infrastructure condition ("where a pneumothorax service with reliable follow-up exists"), appear only in the figure and are not stated anywhere in the manuscript prose or tables. — Carries the same aspiration-vs-ambulatory-drainage sequencing discrepancy flagged above: the manuscript text treats the two as co-equal first-line options, while this figure places ambulatory drainage strictly after a failed aspiration attempt. — spontaneous pneumothorax — Accumulation of air in the pleural space without trauma or iatrogenic instrumentation, occurring either without known lung disease (primary) or with it (secondary). — randomised controlled trial — A study design in which participants are randomly assigned to different interventions to minimise bias when comparing outcomes. — British Thoracic Society — The UK professional body whose pleural disease guideline (2023, and earlier 2010 version) is cited repeatedly in this algorithm for high-risk thresholds and procedural technique details not derived from the review's own randomised evidence. — European Respiratory Society — The European professional body that co-authored (with EACTS and ESTS) the 2024 joint clinical practice guideline on adults with spontaneous pneumothorax cited throughout this algorithm.

entries.title: Needle Aspiration versus Tube Thoracostomy
entries.text: Persistent air leak >48 h — or failure to re-expand? — Evaluation, at 48 hours, of patients managed with a pleural drain for ongoing bubbling/air leak or incomplete lung re-expansion. — Persistent air leak — "conventionally defined as continuing beyond 48 hours" — substantially prolongs hospital admission and requires escalation of pleural or surgical management; the manuscript notes it is disproportionately a problem of secondary spontaneous pneumothorax. — In the figure, only the ambulatory/standard-drainage branch feeds into this checkpoint — no arrow arrives here from the high-risk tube-thoracostomy box or from the immediate-decompression box, even though the manuscript itself notes persistent air leak is disproportionately a secondary-disease problem (i.e., exactly the patients routed to that high-risk branch). — spontaneous pneumothorax — Accumulation of air in the pleural space without trauma or iatrogenic instrumentation, occurring either without known lung disease (primary) or with it (secondary).

entries.title: Needle Aspiration versus Tube Thoracostomy
entries.text: Remove drain after — 24 h without air leak · Confirm on imaging · Discharge — Cessation of pleural drainage, radiographic confirmation of sustained lung expansion, drain removal and discharge once air leak has resolved within 48 hours and remained absent for 24 hours. — Not discussed in the manuscript prose at all — the manuscript addresses overall hospital length of stay and immediate/1-week re-expansion, but never the protocol for timing chest-drain removal or post-removal imaging confirmation. — "24 h without air leak" and "Confirm on imaging" are figure-only details, never stated anywhere in the manuscript text or tables. — Like the discharge box after successful aspiration, this box has no visual arrow onward to recurrence-prevention criteria, even though the same criteria logically apply to these patients too.

entries.title: Needle Aspiration versus Tube Thoracostomy
entries.text: ESCALATE — discuss with thoracic surgery — Thoracic suction · larger-bore drain · chemical or autologous blood pleurodesis · endobronchial valve · VATS bullectomy with pleurodesis — Multidisciplinary escalation involving thoracic surgical consultation and selection among secondary pleural, bronchoscopic or operative interventions when air leak persists beyond 48 hours or the lung fails to re-expand. — The manuscript lists exactly these modalities — thoracic suction, conversion to a larger-bore drain, chemical or autologous blood pleurodesis, endobronchial valves and surgery — while explicitly noting they are "supported by evidence of limited quality" and identified by the 2024 joint European guideline as a principal remaining evidence gap. Suction-versus-water-seal evidence comes from traumatic, not spontaneous, pneumothorax, and the manuscript explicitly cautions against extrapolating. Systematic-review recurrence rates after pleurodesis range from 0.0–3.2% (VATS talc) to 13.0–33.3% (tetracycline via chest drain) to 15.6–18.2% (autologous blood patch). Surgical management in secondary spontaneous pneumothorax carries a mortality of up to 5%. — No suction pressure setting, larger-bore French size, sclerosant dose, or blood-patch volume is stated anywhere in the figure or the manuscript text. — spontaneous pneumothorax — Accumulation of air in the pleural space without trauma or iatrogenic instrumentation, occurring either without known lung disease (primary) or with it (secondary). — video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery — A minimally invasive surgical technique using a thoracoscope and small incisions, used here for definitive bullectomy and pleurodesis to prevent recurrence.

entries.title: Needle Aspiration versus Tube Thoracostomy
entries.text: RECURRENCE PREVENTION — Offer definitive VATS with pleurodesis after a second ipsilateral event, or after a first event where bleb burden, occupation or remoteness from care raise the consequences of recurrence — Elective or semi-elective definitive surgical obliteration/scarification of the pleural space via video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) with bullectomy and pleurodesis, to prevent future ipsilateral pneumothorax episodes. — Recurrence is governed by underlying pleural biology rather than which device evacuated the first episode (26% vs 27.3% at one year in one trial; 26–50% after drainage alone across the wider literature; frequent five-year retreatment after tube thoracostomy alone; paediatric recurrence driven by older age, radiographic bleb burden and smoking rather than device choice). Only pleural-space obliteration reduces recurrence: VATS with bullectomy and pleurodesis is the definitive intervention, achieving recurrence rates below 5% in most series, with established safety and efficacy in adolescents, young adults and children. Dynamic inflammation-based biomarkers have been studied for first-episode surgical risk stratification, and the choice between operating after a first versus second episode depends on individualised assessment of bleb burden, occupational/recreational exposures and patient preference. — Wording differs between the figure ("remoteness from care", "second ipsilateral event", "VATS with pleurodesis") and the manuscript text (which instead lists "recreational exposures" and "patient preference", omitted from the figure, and writes "VATS with bullectomy and pleurodesis"). — The figure shows this box reached only via the escalation path for persistent air leak — but recurrence-prevention criteria logically apply just as much to patients who resolved via conservative care, successful aspiration, drain removal, or high-risk inpatient drainage; the figure draws no arrows from any of those boxes to this one. — video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery — A minimally invasive surgical technique using a thoracoscope and small incisions, used here for definitive bullectomy and pleurodesis to prevent recurrence.

entries.title: Suspected or Witnessed Button Battery Exposure
entries.text: Suspected or Witnessed Button Battery Exposure Recognition and Management Pathway in a Child

entries.title: Suspected or Witnessed Button Battery Exposure
entries.nodeLabel: SUSPECTED OR WITNESSED BUTTON BATTERY EXPOSURE IN A CHILD
entries.text: SUSPECTED OR WITNESSED BUTTON BATTERY EXPOSURE IN A CHILD — Ingestion, nasal insertion or aural insertion – witnessed, suspected, or unexplained drooling, food refusal, vomiting, stridor or haematemesis — Entry criterion for the whole pathway: any child under 18 years (peak median age 18–36 months) with witnessed or suspected button-battery ingestion, nasal insertion, or aural insertion, or presenting with unexplained non-specific or red-flag aerodigestive symptoms. — Up to half of exposures are unwitnessed, and more than half of serious outcomes follow unwitnessed events because of diagnostic delay. Early symptoms overlap with ordinary viral respiratory or gastrointestinal illness, a child who swallowed a 20 mm lithium cell can look deceptively well despite deep mucosal injury already under way, airway symptoms predict tracheo-oesophageal fistula and vocal cord paralysis, and any haematemesis — however small or remote in time — may be a sentinel bleed from an arterio-oesophageal fistula. Society guidance therefore converges on a protocol-driven rather than symptom-driven model of care. — Dysphagia occurs in roughly a third, fever and cough in roughly a quarter, feeding difficulty in 48.1% and respiratory difficulty in 34.6% of pooled ingestion cases — none of this is specific to button-battery exposure, which is precisely why the entry criterion is suspicion-based rather than symptom-based. — odds ratio — A measure of association used throughout this algorithm's evidence base — e.g. oesophageal location carries an OR of 18.66 for any complication versus non-oesophageal locations.

entries.title: Suspected or Witnessed Button Battery Exposure
entries.nodeLabel: IMMEDIATE ACTIONS – ANY SETTING [E, N, P]
entries.text:
IMMEDIATE ACTIONS – ANY SETTING [E, N, P] — • Act on suspicion; do not wait for symptoms or for fasting
• Transfer at once to a centre with paediatric endoscopy and anaesthesia
• Nil by mouth apart from a mitigation agent
• Identify the cell (imprint code, packaging, companion cell) only if this does not delay transfer — Universal first actions in any setting — pre-hospital, primary care or emergency department — on suspicion alone: begin transfer to a facility with paediatric endoscopy and anaesthesia without waiting for symptoms or an anaesthetic fasting interval, keep the child nil by mouth except for an eligible mitigation agent, and check the battery's imprint code only if doing so costs zero delay. — Hydroxide generation at the battery's negative pole raises local tissue pH to 10–13, causing measurable mucosal injury within 15 minutes and full-thickness transmural injury within 2–6 hours experimentally — dwell time is the only variable clinicians can actually control. Even a "spent" or discharged cell retains enough residual voltage to injure tissue. Recent oral intake does not justify postponing extraction, and in rural or resource-limited settings delayed recognition and transfer is the dominant driver of bad outcomes. Imprint codes encode chemistry/voltage and diameter (e.g. CR2032 = 20 mm diameter, 3.2 mm thick; CR/BR = 3.0 V, LR/L = 1.5 V) and can help anticipate severity, but must never be chased at the expense of transfer time. — Because this box sits upstream of the anatomical branch point, the figure applies "transfer at once" and "nil by mouth" to nasal and aural insertions too — yet a series of 176 nasal extractions using a purpose-designed hook needed general anaesthesia in only 6.8% of cases, so the same urgency language covers a substantially lower-acuity group as well. — odds ratio — A measure of association used throughout this algorithm's evidence base — e.g. oesophageal location carries an OR of 18.66 for any complication versus non-oesophageal locations.

entries.title: Suspected or Witnessed Button Battery Exposure
entries.text:
LOW CERTAINTY – MITIGATION [N, P] — Mainly preclinical evidence. Only if age ≥ 12 months, able to swallow and ingestion ≤ 12 h:
• Honey 10 mL every 10 min, max. 6 doses (pre-hospital)
• Sucralfate 1 g/10 mL, 10 mL every 10 min, max. 3 doses (hospital)
Never delays transfer, imaging or removal; omit if oesophageal dwell may exceed 12 h — Oral administration of a viscous, mucosal-coating agent — honey or a sucralfate suspension — as a temporary bridge before endoscopic removal, restricted to children aged 12 months or older who can swallow and whose ingestion occurred within 12 hours. — Porcine and cadaveric studies showed that honey and sucralfate coat the battery, blunt the local pH rise, and reduce burn depth compared with saline. The 12-hour window exists because gross oesophageal perforation rarely manifests early — only 2% of perforations in one series of 290 severe/fatal cases were diagnosed within 24 hours — whereas beyond 12 hours perforation becomes plausible enough that oral agents are withheld. Honey is contraindicated under 12 months because of infant-botulism risk. Mitigation buys time; it is never a substitute for extraction and must never delay transfer, imaging, endoscopy or anaesthesia. — Home-vs-hospital and age-cutoff wording differs slightly between the figure and the guideline sources it draws on — NASPGHAN allows honey or sucralfate without a strict home/hospital split, and ESPGHAN's own caution threshold for honey is phrased as "< 1 year" rather than "≥ 12 months" applied identically to both agents; treat the figure's framing as the operative one for this tool. — All dosing and eligibility numbers in this box are guideline-sourced (NASPGHAN 2020 mitigation update; National Capital Poison Center 2018), resting mainly on preclinical animal and cadaveric data — hence the dashed "LOW CERTAINTY" border. — European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition — One of the three guideline sources this algorithm consolidates (tagged [E] on diagram boxes) — its 2021 position paper on button battery ingestion. — North American Society for Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Nutrition — One of the three guideline sources this algorithm consolidates (tagged [N] on diagram boxes) — its 2015 foreign-body clinical report and 2020 mitigation update. — odds ratio — A measure of association used throughout this algorithm's evidence base — e.g. oesophageal location carries an OR of 18.66 for any complication versus non-oesophageal locations.

entries.title: Suspected or Witnessed Button Battery Exposure
entries.nodeLabel: ANTEROPOSTERIOR AND LATERAL RADIOGRAPHS OF NECK, CHEST AND ABDOMEN [E, N, P]
entries.text: ANTEROPOSTERIOR AND LATERAL RADIOGRAPHS OF NECK, CHEST AND ABDOMEN [E, N, P] — Before any other investigation: number of cells, anatomical level, double-rim (halo) sign, orientation of the narrow negative pole — Immediate two-view plain radiography spanning the entire neck, chest and abdomen, as the mandatory first-line investigation ahead of any other test, regardless of recent oral intake. — Biplane films localise the battery, exclude a second ingested cell, distinguish a button battery from an ordinary coin via the frontal double-rim ("halo") sign and a lateral step-off, and identify the narrower negative pole where hydroxide accumulation and liquefactive necrosis are greatest. Negative-pole orientation predicts which anatomical structures are at risk: anterior proximal-oesophageal orientation threatens the trachea (tracheo-oesophageal fistula), inferior thyroid artery and recurrent laryngeal nerve (vocal cord paralysis); posterior orientation risks spondylodiscitis; mid-oesophageal position carries the highest risk to the aorta. Pre-hospital clinical risk scores and AI radiograph classifiers exist but do not replace plain radiography. — Whether an isolated, witnessed nasal or aural insertion also needs full neck/chest/abdomen radiographs (e.g. to exclude an occult co-ingested cell) is not explicitly addressed in the manuscript — not stated. — odds ratio — A measure of association used throughout this algorithm's evidence base — e.g. oesophageal location carries an OR of 18.66 for any complication versus non-oesophageal locations.

entries.title: Suspected or Witnessed Button Battery Exposure
entries.text: Where is the battery? — The central three-way triage point: subsequent management is governed almost entirely by anatomical location and elapsed time, not by symptom burden. — Oesophageal lodgement carries an odds ratio of 18.66 for any complication and 15.52 for death compared with non-oesophageal locations; roughly three-quarters of oesophageal impactions lodge in the proximal oesophagus. Most cells that traverse the pylorus pass spontaneously (post-pyloric intestinal perforation occurs in only 2.5% of pooled ingestion cases). Nasal and aural insertions cause rapid local tissue destruction — septal perforation in 14% to roughly one-sixth of nasal impactions across two series — and need urgent otolaryngological extraction rather than endoscopy.

entries.title: Suspected or Witnessed Button Battery Exposure
entries.text: OESOPHAGUS — Column header for the oesophageal limb — the highest-complication-risk location, requiring emergency removal.

entries.title: Suspected or Witnessed Button Battery Exposure
entries.text: STOMACH OR BEYOND THE PYLORUS — Column header for cells that have passed the gastro-oesophageal junction — the limb where current guidance diverges most sharply between observation and endoscopy.

entries.title: Suspected or Witnessed Button Battery Exposure
entries.text: NOSE OR EAR — Column header for insertions rather than ingestions — managed as an ENT emergency with no formal gastrointestinal or poison-centre guideline protocol of its own. — odds ratio — A measure of association used throughout this algorithm's evidence base — e.g. oesophageal location carries an OR of 18.66 for any complication versus non-oesophageal locations.

entries.title: Suspected or Witnessed Button Battery Exposure
entries.text: EMERGENCY ENDOSCOPIC REMOVAL [E, N, P] — Immediately – ideally < 2 h from ingestion – under general anaesthesia with a protected airway — Immediate endoscopic extraction under general anaesthesia with endotracheal airway protection, ideally within 2 hours of ingestion, as fast as safe anaesthetic and endoscopic resources allow, without waiting for standard nil-by-mouth fasting intervals. — Transmural histological oesophageal necrosis develops within 2–6 hours experimentally, and complication odds rise sharply with dwell time (greater than 6 hours predicts complications in pooled data; ≥10 hours carries an odds ratio of 3.71, ≥12 hours 5.12). Endoscopy allows direct visualisation for controlled extraction and grading of mucosal burn depth. Senior anaesthetic/surgical backup, large-bore IV access and prepared blood products are advised when the battery sits in the mid-oesophagus or presentation is delayed. — In centres without immediate paediatric endoscopy, extraction of upper oesophageal cells using an optimised Miller size-3 video laryngoscope blade has been described in a single-centre series — not a substitute for endoscopy where it is available. — Real-world impaction-to-removal intervals run far longer than the 2-hour target in practice (a reported median of 10.5 hours in one series), underscoring how much of the complication burden is driven by pre-hospital and transfer delay rather than in-hospital technique. — odds ratio — A measure of association used throughout this algorithm's evidence base — e.g. oesophageal location carries an OR of 18.66 for any complication versus non-oesophageal locations.

entries.title: Suspected or Witnessed Button Battery Exposure
entries.text: ENDOSCOPY [E, N, P] — Any symptom, however minor, or a co-ingested magnet — Mandatory endoscopic evaluation and removal, where accessible, for any child with a battery in the stomach or beyond the pylorus who has any symptom at all — however minor — or who has co-ingested a magnet. — A symptomatic child whose battery already lies beyond the oesophagus may be signalling active gastric/distal mucosal injury, or oesophageal injury sustained in transit before the cell reached the stomach — endoscopic series show clinically significant oesophageal or gastric burns even when the battery itself is now gastric. A co-ingested magnet with a metallic battery creates a high risk of trans-mural magnetic attraction, pressure necrosis, fistula and perforation across adjacent bowel loops. Every compared guideline agrees on this one indication. — The figure stacks this box directly above LOCAL PROTOCOL – ASYMPTOMATIC CHILD with a real connecting arrow between them but no explicit decision diamond — read it as: any symptom or co-ingested magnet routes here; genuinely asymptomatic without a magnet routes to the box below. — If a symptomatic battery (or battery-plus-magnet) has already passed beyond the reach of upper endoscopy, the manuscript mentions surgical, CT or ultrasonographic management for intestinal perforation rather than specifying enteroscopy versus surgery — not resolved in the figure. — odds ratio — A measure of association used throughout this algorithm's evidence base — e.g. oesophageal location carries an OR of 18.66 for any complication versus non-oesophageal locations.

entries.title: Suspected or Witnessed Button Battery Exposure
entries.text:
LOW CERTAINTY – URGENT ENT REMOVAL — Case series and expert opinion; no guideline protocol
• Remove as an emergency
• Inspect for nasal septal perforation and tympanic membrane or ossicular injury
• Septal perforation is the commonest complication of insertion and may appear after discharge: arrange ENT follow-up — Emergency otolaryngological extraction of a nasal or aural button battery, targeted inspection of the nasal septum, tympanic membrane, middle-ear ossicles and facial-nerve function, and scheduled ENT outpatient follow-up after discharge. — Moist nasal and aural cavities complete the same external electrolytic circuit as the oesophagus. Nasal septal perforation — the single commonest complication of insertion — develops within hours to days, occurred in 14% (plus 6% nasal adhesion) in one 159-child series and in roughly one-sixth of a 176-child series with no clean linear relationship to dwell time, and may only become apparent after the child has already been discharged. Aural insertion can destroy the tympanic membrane and ossicles and cause facial-nerve paralysis. — No formal gastrointestinal or poison-centre guideline covers ENT insertion, hence this box carries no [E]/[N]/[P] tag at all — the whole box rests on case series and expert opinion. — In the same 176-case nasal series, general anaesthesia was needed in only 6.8% of extractions using a purpose-designed hook, most patients being boys aged 1–5 years — useful context for how often this "emergency removal" actually escalates to a theatre case. — odds ratio — A measure of association used throughout this algorithm's evidence base — e.g. oesophageal location carries an OR of 18.66 for any complication versus non-oesophageal locations.

entries.title: Suspected or Witnessed Button Battery Exposure
entries.text: LOCAL PROTOCOL – DELAYED DIAGNOSIS [E] — Diagnosis or removal > 12 h after ingestion: CT or CT angiography before removal; remove where cardiothoracic support is available — When battery identification or extraction occurs more than 12 hours after ingestion, obtain contrast-enhanced CT or CT angiography before any endoscopic instrumentation to assess vascular integrity, and perform extraction only where cardiothoracic surgical support is available. — Prolonged oesophageal impaction (≥12 hours, odds ratio 5.12 for complications) is the leading risk factor for lethal vascular injury — an aorto-oesophageal or other arterio-oesophageal fistula. Pre-instrumentation CT shows how close necrosis or oedema lies to the aorta or a major artery, so that extraction does not itself precipitate uncontrolled haemorrhage without cardiothoracic surgery standing by. — Figure-vs-logic ordering issue: the figure draws a sequential arrow from EMERGENCY ENDOSCOPIC REMOVAL into this box, even though this box's own content (CT before removal, cardiothoracic readiness during removal) only makes sense if elapsed time is checked BEFORE endoscopy, not after it. Read this box as a gate to evaluate before removal in any case diagnosed late, not as a step that follows removal. — In an actively bleeding child, this imaging step must not delay operative control. — NASPGHAN and the National Capital Poison Center guideline do not specify this particular > 12 h pre-removal CT rule — it is sourced to ESPGHAN specifically. — European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition — One of the three guideline sources this algorithm consolidates (tagged [E] on diagram boxes) — its 2021 position paper on button battery ingestion. — North American Society for Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Nutrition — One of the three guideline sources this algorithm consolidates (tagged [N] on diagram boxes) — its 2015 foreign-body clinical report and 2020 mitigation update. — odds ratio — A measure of association used throughout this algorithm's evidence base — e.g. oesophageal location carries an OR of 18.66 for any complication versus non-oesophageal locations.

entries.title: Suspected or Witnessed Button Battery Exposure
entries.nodeLabel: LOCAL PROTOCOL – ASYMPTOMATIC CHILD [E, N, P]
entries.text:
LOCAL PROTOCOL – ASYMPTOMATIC CHILD [E, N, P] — Guidance diverges (Table 6):
• Diagnosed ≤ 12 h: observe; repeat radiograph at 7–14 days [E] or if not passed by 10–14 days [P]
• Young child with a large cell: retrieve if retained (≥ 15 mm, < 6 y, ≥ 4 days [P]; age-based, 2–4 days [N])
• Delayed diagnosis (> 12 h): consider endoscopy and CT [E]
• Prior GI surgery or stenosis: lower threshold for endoscopy
• German guidance: endoscopy in all cases — Institution-specific management of an asymptomatic child, without a co-ingested magnet, whose battery has passed into the stomach or beyond the pylorus — choosing between expectant observation with scheduled repeat radiography versus endoscopic retrieval or screening for transit oesophageal injury, according to whichever cited guideline the local team follows. — No comparative study has tested universal endoscopy against expectant observation in this group, so society recommendations genuinely diverge rather than one being simply wrong. The case for observation rests on a high rate of spontaneous passage once past the gastro-oesophageal junction or pylorus, the rarity of severe gastric or post-pyloric injury in unselected cohorts, and the anaesthetic risk and cost of universal endoscopy. The case for retrieval or screening rests on endoscopic series showing real oesophageal or gastric mucosal burns even in cells now sitting in the stomach, the fact that unwitnessed or delayed presentation cannot exclude a prior oesophageal dwell before the cell transited onward, and the added risk from pre-existing intestinal stenosis or prior GI surgery. — An additional NCPC threshold — "consider diagnostic endoscopy if a cell ≥ 20 mm in a child < 5 years may have lodged in the oesophagus > 2 h" — appears in the manuscript's own guideline-comparison table but is omitted from this figure box. — NASPGHAN's "age-based" retrieval thresholds for a large retained gastric cell at 2–4 days are not given as explicit numbers anywhere in the manuscript — not stated; the manuscript itself says the source guideline should be consulted for full criteria. — North American Society for Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Nutrition — One of the three guideline sources this algorithm consolidates (tagged [N] on diagram boxes) — its 2015 foreign-body clinical report and 2020 mitigation update. — National Capital Poison Center — One of the three guideline sources this algorithm consolidates (tagged [P] on diagram boxes) — its button battery ingestion triage and treatment guideline. — odds ratio — A measure of association used throughout this algorithm's evidence base — e.g. oesophageal location carries an OR of 18.66 for any complication versus non-oesophageal locations.

entries.title: Suspected or Witnessed Button Battery Exposure
entries.text:
LOW CERTAINTY – AT REMOVAL [N, P] — If no perforation is seen: irrigate with 0.25% sterile acetic acid, 50–150 mL
Record negative-pole orientation; grade mucosal injury — Immediately after extraction, inspect endoscopically to exclude perforation, irrigate the injured mucosa with 50–150 mL of 0.25% sterile acetic acid if no perforation is seen, record the negative pole's anatomical orientation, and grade the depth of mucosal injury. — In animal models the alkaline tissue milieu persists in devitalised mucosa even after the battery is removed, so liquefactive necrosis keeps progressing; dilute acetic acid neutralises residual alkalinity, reducing injury progression in porcine studies and showing safety and improved mucosal appearance in a small initial clinical series — though no effect on stricture, fistula or mortality has been demonstrated yet. Recording negative-pole orientation and injury grade at this point directly feeds the post-removal imaging and follow-up decisions in the next box. — Placing "record negative-pole orientation; grade mucosal injury" inside this dashed LOW CERTAINTY box visually groups ordinary endoscopic documentation under the preclinical border style — the figure's own caption clarifies that LOW CERTAINTY applies specifically to honey, sucralfate and acetic acid irrigation (and nasal/aural removal), not to documentation itself. — odds ratio — A measure of association used throughout this algorithm's evidence base — e.g. oesophageal location carries an OR of 18.66 for any complication versus non-oesophageal locations.

entries.title: Suspected or Witnessed Button Battery Exposure
entries.nodeLabel: A gastric position does not exclude oesophageal injury sustained in transit
entries.text: A gastric position does not exclude oesophageal injury sustained in transit — A standalone caution, drawn as its own box beneath the asymptomatic-child protocol: finding the battery in the stomach on radiograph does not mean the oesophagus was never injured — the cell may simply have already moved on from where it did its damage. — The same oesophageal-injury-in-transit concern that justifies endoscopic screening for the delayed-diagnosis subgroup above applies, in principle, to any gastric cell — endoscopic series have documented real oesophageal or gastric mucosal burns even when the battery's current resting place is the stomach. — Drawn with a solid border in the source figure despite being a caveat rather than an action step — rendered here without a certainty tag, since the figure's three-tier scheme (core/low/local) is defined for guideline-concordant steps, and this box is better read as a plain cross-cutting note. — odds ratio — A measure of association used throughout this algorithm's evidence base — e.g. oesophageal location carries an OR of 18.66 for any complication versus non-oesophageal locations.

entries.title: Suspected or Witnessed Button Battery Exposure
entries.text: LOCAL PROTOCOL – AFTER REMOVAL [E, P] — Admit if mucosal injury; oesophagram 1–2 days after removal; CT angiography or MRI according to injury grade or suspected vascular injury; diet and discharge decided by the local team — Post-extraction inpatient observation, a contrast oesophagram at 1–2 days, selective cross-sectional imaging (CT angiography or MRI, the latter safe only after the battery itself is out) matched to injury severity or suspected vascular/airway injury, and a multidisciplinary decision on feeding, discharge timing and stricture-surveillance endoscopy. — Gross perforation usually manifests more than 24 hours after lodgement; tracheo-oesophageal fistula and vocal cord paralysis evolve over days; aorto-oesophageal fistula over days to weeks; spondylodiscitis over weeks; oesophageal stricture over weeks to months (43% in one selected tertiary cohort). But the surveillance-imaging evidence itself is expert-derived rather than comparative — surveys show no consensus on which MRI findings should change management, and routine serial MRI increased length of stay and cost without a demonstrable outcome benefit — which is why imaging and discharge decisions are explicitly handed to local multidisciplinary protocol rather than fixed here. — Preserved tracheo-oesophageal fat plane on MRI had 100% negative predictive value for tracheo-oesophageal fistula in one series, while loss of the fat plane had only 50% positive predictive value — useful for reassurance, much less useful for ruling fistula in. — odds ratio — A measure of association used throughout this algorithm's evidence base — e.g. oesophageal location carries an OR of 18.66 for any complication versus non-oesophageal locations.

entries.title: Suspected or Witnessed Button Battery Exposure
entries.nodeLabel: BEFORE DISCHARGE – WRITTEN SAFETY-NETTING FOR THE CAREGIVER [E, P]
entries.text: BEFORE DISCHARGE – WRITTEN SAFETY-NETTING FOR THE CAREGIVER [E, P] — Return IMMEDIATELY for haematemesis or melaena (however small), fever, chest, back or abdominal pain, dysphagia, drooling or respiratory deterioration. Vascular complications may present days to weeks after removal; a small sentinel bleed may precede fatal haemorrhage. — Explicit written discharge instructions for parents/caregivers mandating immediate emergency re-presentation for any red-flag haemorrhagic, infectious, gastrointestinal or airway symptom, given to every child leaving this pathway regardless of which of the three anatomical limbs they came through. — Tissue necrosis and peri-vascular inflammation can keep evolving well after battery extraction. Aorto-oesophageal and other arterio-oesophageal fistulae are the leading cause of death in this condition, can present days to weeks after removal — well beyond the index admission — and frequently announce themselves first with a minor, self-limiting sentinel bleed (haematemesis or melaena) before a catastrophic, fatal haemorrhage. Delayed perforation, mediastinitis, tracheo-oesophageal fistula, vocal cord paralysis, spondylodiscitis, stricture and distal bowel perforation or abscess can likewise all present after discharge. — This box's warning text is written around gastrointestinal/vascular complications; it does not separately mention nasal septal perforation, epistaxis, otorrhoea or facial-nerve weakness, even though the figure draws the NOSE OR EAR limb converging into this very box — the preceding ENT-removal box is where that follow-up gets arranged instead. — The figure lists eight red-flag symptom groups; the manuscript's own narrative summary of this same safety-netting advice lists only six in one sentence (omitting abdominal pain, dysphagia and drooling there, though all three appear elsewhere in the manuscript) — this tool follows the fuller, eight-item figure wording. — odds ratio — A measure of association used throughout this algorithm's evidence base — e.g. oesophageal location carries an OR of 18.66 for any complication versus non-oesophageal locations.

entries.title: Beta-Lactam Infusion Strategy
entries.text: Beta-Lactam Infusion Strategy Continuous versus Extended Infusion in Sepsis and Septic Shock

entries.title: Beta-Lactam Infusion Strategy
entries.nodeLabel: Adult with sepsis or septic shock in the intensive care unit
entries.text: Adult with sepsis or septic shock in the intensive care unit — Intravenous beta-lactam indicated on clinical or microbiological grounds — This identifies the target population for everything that follows: a critically ill adult (18 years or older) in an intensive care or high-dependency unit, meeting Sepsis-3 criteria for sepsis or septic shock, in whom an intravenous broad-spectrum beta-lactam is already indicated on clinical or microbiological grounds. The algorithm assumes a beta-lactam has already been chosen and that source control is being pursued in parallel — it is a delivery-strategy algorithm, not an antibiotic-selection algorithm. — Critical illness distorts beta-lactam pharmacokinetics — expanded volume of distribution, hypoalbuminaemia, augmented renal clearance (ARC), or accumulation in acute kidney injury (AKI) — to a degree that standard intermittent bolus regimens frequently miss pharmacodynamic fT>MIC targets. In the multinational DALI study, 16% of ICU patients failed even the permissive 50% fT>MIC threshold, and failure to reach 100% fT>MIC was associated with worse clinical outcome. Ward-based or non-critically ill populations are deliberately excluded from this algorithm: those cohorts have lower baseline mortality and less pharmacokinetic distortion, and syntheses in that setting have not demonstrated a mortality benefit from prolonged infusion. — This algorithm does not apply to patients receiving renal replacement therapy (RRT) or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) — both were excluded from most of the underlying trials (BLING III explicitly excluded RRT), randomised evidence is absent in those groups, and individualised dosing with therapeutic drug monitoring is preferred instead. — The randomised outcome evidence behind this pathway is almost entirely confined to piperacillin-tazobactam and meropenem. For other beta-lactams, the same sequence rests on pharmacokinetic reasoning alone, not on trial data — see Table 4 in the References for agent-by-agent evidence strength. — Neonates, children, patients with obesity or at the extremes of body weight are under-represented in the underlying trials despite substantially altered volume of distribution in those groups; this is flagged in the source manuscript as persistent uncertainty, not resolved by it. — fraction of the dosing interval during which free drug concentration exceeds the MIC — The single pharmacodynamic parameter that governs killing by a time-dependent antibiotic like a beta-lactam. Unlike a concentration-dependent drug, a higher peak adds little extra bactericidal value — what matters is how much of the dosing interval the free (unbound) drug concentration spends above the pathogen's MIC. Infusion duration, for a fixed total daily dose, is what reshapes the concentration-time curve to raise this fraction. — minimum inhibitory concentration — The lowest concentration of an antibiotic that visibly inhibits growth of a specific bacterial isolate in the laboratory. Prolonged infusion strategies matter most when a pathogen's MIC sits close to the susceptibility breakpoint; when the organism is highly susceptible (a low MIC), intermittent and prolonged dosing tend to converge on the same result. — augmented renal clearance — A state of supranormal kidney filtration seen in a subset of critically ill patients — often younger, with preserved cardiac output — that can clear a renally eliminated drug faster than standard dosing assumes, driving concentrations below target even on a continuous infusion. — acute kidney injury — A sudden decline in kidney function. For beta-lactams dosed on the assumption of normal clearance, AKI works in the opposite direction from augmented renal clearance — it can cause drug to accumulate toward neurotoxic concentrations, particularly with cefepime or high-concentration piperacillin or meropenem. — renal replacement therapy — Dialysis or haemofiltration substituting for kidney function. Patients receiving RRT were excluded from most of the randomised trials behind this pathway (BLING III explicitly excluded them), so this algorithm does not apply to them — individualised dosing with therapeutic drug monitoring is preferred instead. — extracorporeal membrane oxygenation — Mechanical circulatory and/or respiratory support that can sequester lipophilic drugs in the circuit and substantially alter their apparent volume of distribution. Like RRT, ECMO patients are excluded from this algorithm's evidence base, and individualised dosing with TDM is preferred.

entries.title: Beta-Lactam Infusion Strategy
entries.nodeLabel: GIVE A STANDARD LOADING DOSE BY SHORT INFUSION IMMEDIATELY
entries.text:
GIVE A STANDARD LOADING DOSE BY SHORT INFUSION IMMEDIATELY — Prolonged infusion delays the approach to steady state. Without a loading dose the patient spends several hours below target at the moment exposure matters most. The first dose is never delayed and never slowed.
Absence of a loading dose was a recorded protocol deviation in 3.4% of BLING III — Before any continuous or extended maintenance infusion begins, a full standard loading dose is given promptly by short intravenous infusion — never delayed and never slowed to accommodate the maintenance strategy chosen downstream. — Each hour of delay in effective antimicrobial therapy after hypotension onset is associated with increased mortality in septic shock. Starting a continuous infusion without an upfront loading bolus causes a slow approach to steady state, leaving the patient under-exposed for several hours during early sepsis — precisely when volume of distribution is maximally expanded and exposure matters most. This is why the 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines and the 2023 multi-society consensus both treat the initial bolus as mandatory regardless of which maintenance strategy follows. — The figure's own '3.4% of BLING III' line is a narrower statistic than it reads: the manuscript text specifies 3.4% of the continuous arm of the UK national cohort of BLING III (n = 2900, reference 29), not 3.4% of the full 7202-patient BLING III trial (reference 16). Both numbers describe real protocol-deviation data from the same research programme, but they are not interchangeable denominators. — No specific milligram or gram loading dose per agent is stated in the source manuscript — this is a sequencing rule (bolus first, always), not a dosing table. Use local or published agent-specific loading doses.

entries.title: Beta-Lactam Infusion Strategy
entries.text:
Verify in-use physicochemical stability — For the specific agent, diluent, final concentration and ambient ward temperature.
Stability is agent-specific and must not be extrapolated across the class. — Before choosing between 24-hour continuous infusion and a shorter extended infusion, check locally verified physicochemical stability data for the exact agent, diluent (e.g. a citrate-buffered diluent), final infusate concentration, and ambient ward temperature actually in use. — Physicochemical stability in solution is an operational property of a specific formulation, not a property of the beta-lactam class as a whole. An agent that is stable for 24 hours in one diluent at one temperature can degrade appreciably in another combination, at elevated ambient temperature, or at a different concentration — potentially under-dosing the patient or forcing frequent bag changes that add nursing and pharmacy workload. The source manuscript explicitly instructs institutions to adopt published stability schedules rather than improvising this step. — No single numeric temperature or concentration cutoff is given in the source — stability statements in Table 4 are described as indicative and must be verified locally for the specific agent, diluent, concentration and temperature actually used; they are not transferable from one agent to another.

entries.title: Beta-Lactam Infusion Strategy
entries.nodeLabel: Does verified stability support administration of the maintenance dose over a full 24 hours?
entries.text: Does verified stability support administration of the maintenance dose over a full 24 hours? — This branches the maintenance strategy on exactly one question: does the locally verified stability data for this agent, diluent and temperature support running the infusate over a full 24 hours? If yes, continuous infusion is selected; if no or unknown, extended infusion is the default. — Continuous and extended infusion are neither pharmacodynamically nor operationally equivalent. Only continuous infusion sustains steady-state concentrations with no sub-MIC interval and allows a steady-state sample to be drawn at any time — but running an agent continuously for 24 hours without verified 24-hour stability risks meaningful drug degradation inside the infusion bag. Defaulting to extended infusion whenever stability is unproven avoids that risk. — The source manuscript's own Section 4.4.2 flags an internal ambiguity here: meropenem is placed under 'extended infusion' in this algorithm because it is infused over 6-8 hours with frequent bag changes rather than a single 24-hour bag, yet in the pivotal MERCY and BLING III trials meropenem was in fact randomised to the continuous-infusion arm, maintained through periodic bag replacement. A regimen infused over 8 hours and replaced every 8 hours around the clock runs continuously for 24 hours in substance even while this diamond routes it to the 'extended' branch by name. — minimum inhibitory concentration — The lowest concentration of an antibiotic that visibly inhibits growth of a specific bacterial isolate in the laboratory. Prolonged infusion strategies matter most when a pathogen's MIC sits close to the susceptibility breakpoint; when the organism is highly susceptible (a low MIC), intermittent and prolonged dosing tend to converge on the same result.

entries.title: Beta-Lactam Infusion Strategy
entries.text:
CONTINUOUS INFUSION — Deliver the remaining daily dose over 24 hours by infusion pump.
Piperacillin-tazobactam is suitable, particularly in a citrate-buffered diluent.
Allows a steady-state sample to be drawn at any time — The remaining equivalent daily maintenance dose — after the loading bolus above — is delivered continuously over 24 hours by infusion pump, needing only one bag change per 24 hours once 24-hour stability is verified. Piperacillin-tazobactam, particularly in a citrate-buffered diluent, is the agent with the strongest stability and outcome evidence for this route. — Continuous infusion eliminates sub-MIC trough intervals, lowers high peak concentrations that add no bactericidal value for a time-dependent killer, and reliably approaches 100% fT>MIC even as pathogen MIC nears the susceptibility breakpoint. It underpins the majority of the pooled trial evidence, including BLING III, where continuous infusion increased 14-day clinical cure by 5.7 percentage points and lowered the covariate-adjusted odds ratio for 90-day mortality to 0.89 — consistent with the largest pooled meta-analysis behind this pathway, which rated 90-day mortality as high-certainty evidence under GRADE and estimated a number needed to treat (NNT) of roughly 26. Because plasma concentration is constant at steady state, a single therapeutic drug monitoring sample can also be drawn at any time, rather than requiring a precisely timed pre-dose trough. — Augmented renal clearance can push the dose required to maintain target exposure above the licensed maximum even on a continuous regimen — this is a reason to re-check levels, not a reason to avoid continuous infusion. — 'By infusion pump' is this figure's own phrasing; the source manuscript's prose and tables discuss elastomeric devices only in the context of outpatient parenteral therapy, not ICU administration hardware specifically. — A theoretical concern with sustained antibiotic exposure is selection pressure favouring a multidrug-resistant organism (MDRO), but the two largest trials behind this pathway found no significant difference in new MDRO colonisation between continuous and intermittent infusion — reassuring, though surveillance in both was limited to 14 days at most. — fraction of the dosing interval during which free drug concentration exceeds the MIC — The single pharmacodynamic parameter that governs killing by a time-dependent antibiotic like a beta-lactam. Unlike a concentration-dependent drug, a higher peak adds little extra bactericidal value — what matters is how much of the dosing interval the free (unbound) drug concentration spends above the pathogen's MIC. Infusion duration, for a fixed total daily dose, is what reshapes the concentration-time curve to raise this fraction. — minimum inhibitory concentration — The lowest concentration of an antibiotic that visibly inhibits growth of a specific bacterial isolate in the laboratory. Prolonged infusion strategies matter most when a pathogen's MIC sits close to the susceptibility breakpoint; when the organism is highly susceptible (a low MIC), intermittent and prolonged dosing tend to converge on the same result. — Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation — A structured framework for rating how much confidence to place in a body of evidence for a specific outcome, based on domains such as risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. The source manuscript applies GRADE narratively to externally pooled meta-analytic estimates, rather than performing new pooling of its own. — multidrug-resistant organism — A bacterial pathogen resistant to multiple classes of antibiotics. One theoretical concern with prolonged beta-lactam exposure is selection pressure favouring resistant subpopulations; the trial evidence reviewed here found no significant difference in new MDRO colonisation between prolonged and intermittent infusion. — number needed to treat — The number of patients who would need to receive the intervention, compared with the control, for one additional patient to benefit. For 90-day mortality with prolonged beta-lactam infusion, the largest pooled meta-analysis behind this pathway estimated an NNT of roughly 26 — consistent with a real but modest absolute effect.

entries.title: Beta-Lactam Infusion Strategy
entries.text:
EXTENDED INFUSION — Give each dose over 3 to 4 hours.
Meropenem degrades appreciably at in-use temperature: infuse over 6 to 8 hours with more frequent bag changes.
The default choice when 24-hour stability is unproven — When 24-hour stability is not verified or not supported by the agent's own degradation profile, each intermittent maintenance dose is instead infused over 3 to 4 hours — or, specifically for meropenem, over 6 to 8 hours with correspondingly more frequent bag changes, because meropenem degrades appreciably at in-use temperature. — Prolonging each dose to 3-4 hours substantially raises fT>MIC compared with a 30-60 minute bolus, and extended-infusion piperacillin-tazobactam was associated with lower 14-day mortality in more severely ill Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections. This approach also accommodates an agent's limited room-temperature stability and frees the intravenous line between scheduled doses, unlike a continuous regimen. — The source manuscript is internally inconsistent about meropenem's own extended-infusion duration: Section 4.7's summary of the whole pathway says '3 to 4 hours' for both piperacillin-tazobactam and meropenem when stability precludes continuous infusion, while this box, Table 4 and Section 4.3 all specify 6 to 8 hours for meropenem specifically — and Section 4.3's own prose refers to bag changes 'every six hours' in the same paragraph. All three numbers come from the same source; none is presented as superseding the others. — Newer licensed agents sit awkwardly under this box's blanket '3 to 4 hours' instruction: ceftazidime-avibactam's licensed regimen is already a 2-hour infusion (extension to 3-4 hours is still under investigation), and cefiderocol's licensed regimen is already 3 hours — neither is a case of choosing a duration from scratch the way piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem are. — fraction of the dosing interval during which free drug concentration exceeds the MIC — The single pharmacodynamic parameter that governs killing by a time-dependent antibiotic like a beta-lactam. Unlike a concentration-dependent drug, a higher peak adds little extra bactericidal value — what matters is how much of the dosing interval the free (unbound) drug concentration spends above the pathogen's MIC. Infusion duration, for a fixed total daily dose, is what reshapes the concentration-time curve to raise this fraction. — minimum inhibitory concentration — The lowest concentration of an antibiotic that visibly inhibits growth of a specific bacterial isolate in the laboratory. Prolonged infusion strategies matter most when a pathogen's MIC sits close to the susceptibility breakpoint; when the organism is highly susceptible (a low MIC), intermittent and prolonged dosing tend to converge on the same result.

entries.title: Beta-Lactam Infusion Strategy
entries.nodeLabel: Secure the delivery and govern it
entries.text:
Secure the delivery and govern it — Dedicated intravenous lumen · documented Y-site compatibility check
Written standard operating procedure for interruptions, transfers and procedures
Pre-prepared bags where pharmacy capacity allows · audit of interruption rates
36.8% of the continuous arm of BLING III had at least one protocol deviation — Whichever maintenance strategy was chosen, prolonged beta-lactam delivery is treated as an institutional governance process, not just a prescription: a dedicated intravenous lumen, a documented Y-site compatibility check against concurrent infusions, a written standard operating procedure covering interruptions, transfers and bedside procedures, pharmacy-prepared bags where capacity allows, and routine audit of interruption rates. — Even inside a well-resourced randomised trial with detailed protocols — the UK cohort of BLING III — administration errors and protocol deviations occurred in over a third of patients, and interruptions exceeding one hour occurred in roughly a fifth of the continuous-infusion group. Deviations at that frequency cause delivered therapy to drift toward an effectively extended rather than truly continuous pattern, attenuating the clinical benefit toward the null. Building governance into the pathway — not just writing the prescription — is this box's whole purpose. — The figure attributes '36.8% ... protocol deviation' to 'the continuous arm of BLING III', but the manuscript's own Section 3.9 and Table 1 attribute that same 36.8% to overall participants in the smaller UK national cohort of BLING III (n = 2900, reference 29) — not the continuous arm specifically, and not the full 7202-patient trial (reference 16). Table 2 of the same manuscript then reports 36.8% for the continuous column and a separate 35.8% for the intermittent column within that UK cohort. The three figures are all real data from the same research programme but are not simple restatements of one another. — Both the continuous-infusion and extended-infusion branches above flow into this box, including its 'dedicated intravenous lumen' instruction — but the manuscript's own prose repeatedly describes occupying a dedicated lumen throughout therapy as a constraint specific to continuous infusion, stating elsewhere that extended infusion frees the line between doses. Apply the dedicated-lumen requirement according to which strategy was actually chosen, not uniformly to both.

entries.title: Beta-Lactam Infusion Strategy
entries.nodeLabel: Is therapeutic drug monitoring of beta-lactams available?
entries.text: Is therapeutic drug monitoring of beta-lactams available? — This determines the dose-optimisation pathway: if institutional assay capability for beta-lactam therapeutic drug monitoring is available, concentrations are measured and the dose individualised; if not, a published protocolised dosing schedule adjusted for renal function and weight is used instead. — Prolonged infusion improves the likelihood of hitting pharmacodynamic targets but does not guarantee it, because interindividual variability in volume of distribution and renal clearance makes fixed, population-based dosing unreliable at the level of the individual patient. At the same time, in the one included randomised trial of TDM-guided dosing (TARGET), piperacillin-tazobactam dose optimisation improved target attainment without reducing sepsis-related organ dysfunction — showing that pharmacokinetic optimisation on its own is necessary but not sufficient. — therapeutic drug monitoring — Measuring a patient's own drug concentration directly, rather than relying on a population-average dose, and adjusting the regimen to that individual result. For beta-lactams this typically means a free (unbound) concentration sample, because critical illness alters protein binding unpredictably.

entries.title: Beta-Lactam Infusion Strategy
entries.text:
MEASURE AND ADJUST — Sample the unbound steady-state or trough concentration and target 100% fT > MIC, commonly at four times the MIC of the isolate.
Preferred where hypoalbuminaemia is present — A steady-state sample (at any time, for continuous infusion) or a timed pre-dose trough sample (for extended/intermittent regimens) is drawn, measuring unbound (free) beta-lactam concentration directly — particularly important in hypoalbuminaemic patients and for highly protein-bound agents — and the dose is adjusted to keep free concentration above the MIC for the entire dosing interval, commonly targeting four times the isolate's MIC, while avoiding toxic troughs. — Failure to attain 100% fT>MIC was independently associated with worse clinical outcome in the multinational DALI study. Augmented renal clearance frequently causes subtherapeutic levels even on continuous regimens, while acute kidney injury can cause neurotoxic accumulation — notably with cefepime or high-concentration piperacillin or meropenem. Measuring unbound rather than total drug concentration avoids misjudging both exposure and toxicity risk in hypoalbuminaemic critically ill patients. — The '100% fT > MIC, commonly at four times the MIC' target in this box is not actually stated together in the manuscript's own dedicated therapeutic-drug-monitoring section — the 'four times the MIC' figure appears only once elsewhere, as an uncited simulation detail for ceftazidime-avibactam. — A causative pathogen with a known MIC is identified in well under half of patients in the largest trials behind this pathway (as low as 19% in one trial) — the manuscript does not state what MIC surrogate to use when targeting '4× the MIC of the isolate' in a patient with no identified isolate. — Toxicity trough thresholds reported elsewhere in the source for reference, not printed in this box: roughly 50%-risk neurotoxicity troughs of 361.4 mg/L for piperacillin, 64.2 mg/L for meropenem, 125.1 mg/L for flucloxacillin, and above 20 mg/L for cefepime; roughly 50%-risk nephrotoxicity troughs of 452.65 mg/L for piperacillin and 44.45 mg/L for meropenem. — fraction of the dosing interval during which free drug concentration exceeds the MIC — The single pharmacodynamic parameter that governs killing by a time-dependent antibiotic like a beta-lactam. Unlike a concentration-dependent drug, a higher peak adds little extra bactericidal value — what matters is how much of the dosing interval the free (unbound) drug concentration spends above the pathogen's MIC. Infusion duration, for a fixed total daily dose, is what reshapes the concentration-time curve to raise this fraction. — minimum inhibitory concentration — The lowest concentration of an antibiotic that visibly inhibits growth of a specific bacterial isolate in the laboratory. Prolonged infusion strategies matter most when a pathogen's MIC sits close to the susceptibility breakpoint; when the organism is highly susceptible (a low MIC), intermittent and prolonged dosing tend to converge on the same result.

entries.title: Beta-Lactam Infusion Strategy
entries.text:
USE A PROTOCOLISED REGIMEN — Dose by renal function and weight using a published schedule for the specific agent.
Do not improvise.
Guideline-concordant doses still leave many off target — Where beta-lactam therapeutic drug monitoring is unavailable, maintenance doses are prescribed strictly according to a published prolonged-infusion schedule for the specific agent, adjusted for renal function and weight, without ad-hoc institutional or bedside improvisation. — Improvised regimens risk physicochemical degradation or administration error, while renal function — from acute kidney injury to augmented renal clearance — strongly drives beta-lactam clearance and target non-attainment. Even so, multiple prospective pharmacokinetic studies and in-silico evaluations of published dosing guidelines show that standard, guideline-concordant fixed regimens still leave a substantial proportion of critically ill patients outside their target exposure range — this box narrows the uncertainty TDM would otherwise resolve, it does not eliminate it. — The manuscript provides no numerical creatinine-clearance, eGFR, or weight-based dosing brackets anywhere in its text or tables — 'dose by renal function and weight' defers entirely to external published schedules, which must be sourced separately. — Weight-based dosing specifically is not discussed in the manuscript prose at all; the same source instead classifies patients with obesity or at the extremes of body weight as an under-studied population with persistent, unresolved uncertainty, which sits awkwardly alongside this box's instruction to dose by weight using a published schedule. — therapeutic drug monitoring — Measuring a patient's own drug concentration directly, rather than relying on a population-average dose, and adjusting the regimen to that individual result. For beta-lactams this typically means a free (unbound) concentration sample, because critical illness alters protein binding unpredictably.

entries.title: Beta-Lactam Infusion Strategy
entries.text: Reassess at 48 to 72 hours — Review culture and MIC, de-escalate or stop, and reconsider the dose and the infusion strategy — After 48 to 72 hours of therapy under either pathway above, culture and susceptibility (MIC) results are reviewed, beta-lactam therapy is de-escalated or stopped if appropriate, and both the total dose and the choice of infusion strategy are reconsidered in light of what is now known about the pathogen. — Once an isolate and its MIC are known, a highly susceptible, low-MIC organism attains target fT>MIC readily even with intermittent dosing, whereas an isolate with an MIC near the breakpoint is where prolonged infusion matters most — so the earlier choice of strategy is worth revisiting once that information exists, not treated as fixed for the whole course. — This box, and the 48-to-72-hour reassessment window specifically, has no counterpart anywhere in the manuscript's prose, tables, or even in Section 4.7's own text walk-through of this exact figure. It reflects standard external sepsis-stewardship practice (the kind endorsed by general sepsis guidelines) rather than a finding, recommendation or citation from this review's own literature search. — A causative pathogen is identified in well under half of patients in the largest trials underlying this pathway, so 'review culture and MIC' will frequently have nothing agent-specific to review by 48-72 hours — de-escalation decisions in that situation rest on clinical response and local epidemiology rather than a culture result. — fraction of the dosing interval during which free drug concentration exceeds the MIC — The single pharmacodynamic parameter that governs killing by a time-dependent antibiotic like a beta-lactam. Unlike a concentration-dependent drug, a higher peak adds little extra bactericidal value — what matters is how much of the dosing interval the free (unbound) drug concentration spends above the pathogen's MIC. Infusion duration, for a fixed total daily dose, is what reshapes the concentration-time curve to raise this fraction. — minimum inhibitory concentration — The lowest concentration of an antibiotic that visibly inhibits growth of a specific bacterial isolate in the laboratory.
